Indeed, even if we stretch every sinew, we can do nothing against him of ourselves; and therefore it is fitting to join prayer to our effort, that God may deign to break the audacity of that wicked one, to scatter the counsels and endeavours of the world, and to strengthen our weak flesh with his Spirit. And so that our prayers may be more effective, we ought to conceive a sure confidence in God's goodness, which, as it rests on his promises, is also increased by the countless examples that occur everywhere to those who read the Scriptures.

units.la: Cæterum quod discipulis mandat Christus, hoc ipse præstitit: quæ tertia huius loci pars est. Nam à discipulis auulsus quasi ad iactum lapidis, positisq; genibus precatus est, dicens: Pater, si vis, transfer poculum hoc à me: verumtamen non mea voluntas, sed tua fiat. Secessit ab illis aliquanto loci spatio, ne preces eius illorum aut conspectu aut alloquio turbarentur. Vt enim cum amicis vel quibuscunque aliis priuatim & semetis arbitris colloqui cupimus, si quæ causa grauior est, ita cum Deo collocuturis secessu opus est, ut & ardentius & liberius animi sui desideria possint exponere. Porrò non obiter à discipulis suis discessit, sed auulsus est: qua locutione animi dolor natatur, quem ardentissimus amor peperit, quo ille discipulos est complexus. Graue enim ei fuit ab illis auelli, non quòd ipse eorum præsentia aut consilio iuuari posset, sed quòd ipsos sciret suam opem atq; præsentiam sæpe desideraturos esse in periculis & angustijs in quibus erant exercendi. Et quemadmodum pij frequenter cupiunt quidem dissolui, ut cum Christo propius coniungantur (sicut de semetipso Paulus scribit) ægrè tamen suos relinquunt, quos suo consilio & auxilio adhuc opus habere sciunt: ita etiamsi ille magno desiderio mortem appetiuerit, ut humani generis redemptionem perficeret, non libenter tamen (de assumpto humanæ naturæ affectu loquor) à discipulis illis suis, quos fratrum et amicorum intimorū loco diu habuerat, discessit, cum animo voluerit, quid ipsis esset euenturum. Est hoc probè obseruandum, ne nostra infirmitate terreamur, si quid huius in nobis ipsis deprehendimus, uel alios temere damnemus, qui non obscura doloris & animi perturbati indicia ædunt, si quando homines sibi coniunctissimos relinquere coguntur. Nec enim nos lapides aut truncos creauit Deus, hominum autem & Christianorum nomine indigni sunt ἀσοργοι illi, quos nullus humanus affectus mouet, illos certè Paulus (ut non semel monuimus) inter nouissimi seculi pestes numerat, quorum exemplum & mores nemo debeat imitari.
units.tr: Moreover, what Christ commands his disciples, he himself did. This is the third part of this passage. Torn away from the disciples, about a stone's throw off, he knelt and prayed, saying: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done." He withdrew some distance from them, so that his prayer would not be disturbed either by their sight or by their speech. For when we wish to speak privately with friends or anyone else, with no witnesses, and the matter is weighty, we need withdrawal when we are about to speak with God, so that we can lay out the desires of our mind more ardently and more freely. Nor did he leave his disciples in passing, but was torn away. This expression conveys the grief of his mind, which his most ardent love produced, the love with which he embraced them. It was hard for him to be parted from them, not because their presence or counsel could help him, but because he knew they would often long for his help and presence in the dangers and distresses in which they were to be tested. Just as the godly often desire to be dissolved, so as to be more closely joined to Christ (as Paul writes of himself), yet they leave behind with difficulty those whom they know still need their counsel and help, so even though he sought death with great longing, in order to accomplish the redemption of the human race, he did not depart willingly from those disciples of his, whom he had long held in the place of brothers and closest friends, since he had in mind what would befall them. (I speak of the feeling of the human nature he had assumed.) This must be carefully observed, so that we are not frightened by our weakness if we notice anything of this in ourselves, nor rashly condemn others who show clear signs of grief and a troubled mind when they are compelled to leave behind those closest to them. For God did not create us as stones or stumps. Those "without natural affection" [ἄστοργοι], whom no human feeling moves, are unworthy of the name of men and Christians. Paul (as we have noted more than once) counts them among the plagues of the last age, and no one ought to imitate their example or their manners.

units.la: Meminerimus autem Christum in eo quoque nobis exemplum præbuisse, cuius vestigijs nos insistere conueniat: ut nimirum Deo nos uocante uel ad res arduas, uel ad Regni cœlestis possessionem, etiā inuita carne & multùm reluctantibus eius desiderijs, nosipsos auellamus ab illis omnibus, quae nos remorantur. In hoc enim præcipuè consistit nostri ipsius abnegatio, de qua suo loco diximus. Et huc pertinet quod Christus supra dixit: Si quis venit ad me, nec odit patrem suum ac matrem, & uxorem ac liberos, & fratres & sorores, amplius autem etiam animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Exempla huius magnanimitatis multa in Scripturis habentur. Quàm enim durum & graue fuisse putas Abrahamo, cùm ex natali solo & charissimis gentilibus abire iuberetur, incertus ubinam locorū ipsi sedes fixas parauisset Deus? Abiit tamen & simul cor suum auulsit ab ea terra, quam illi minus probari audiebat. Quantò durius autem fuit mandatum illud Dei, quo ancillam Hagaram cum filio Ismaële eijcere iubebatur? At hic quoque animum suum uicit. Quàm graues autem & acerbas putabimus fuisse conuulsiones uiscerū (ut ita dicam) omnium, quando Isaacum, filium illum dilectissimum, quem in extrema senecta ipsi uxor Sara, tot laborum atque curarum socia, peperperat, filium (inquam) promissionis, proprijs manibus sacrificare iussus est? Tamen tunc quoq; à semetipso est auulsus, & quæcunque aduersus mandatum hoc, quo nullum unquam atrocius auditum est, allegari poterant, fidei obedientia uicit. Imitemur ergo patrem credentium, quando de nostris fortunis, dignitate & existimatione, amicis, cognatis aut quibuscunque alijs rebus agitur. Imitemur caput & magistrum nostrum, Iesum Christum, si quando uitam quoq; deponere iubemur. Graue quidem est nobis à corpore hoc & mundi consortio diuelli. At quàm multa sunt, quæ olim inter gentes uiris bonis & prudentibus morte graviora uisa sunt? Lacedæmonij certè, cùm Philippus Macedo intolerabilia onera ciuitati ipsorū imponeret, fortissimè responderunt: Si quid morte grauius imperare persueres, malumus mori. Et multos in morte præsente sese tradidisse legimus, ne patriam dulcissimam opprimi, libertatem eripi, coniuges & liberos uiolari, iura publica euerti, & alia huiusmodi uidere cogerentur, quæ crudelissimi hostes facere consueuerunt. An ergo Christianus mori detrectet, ne à Christo diuellatur, aut salutis æternæ iacturam faciat? Luctemur ergo cum caca carnis affectibus, & hanc quantùmuis inuita auellamus ab huius mundi & uitæ caducæ illecebris, ut nobis cum Christo uiuere liceat.
units.tr: Let us remember, too, that Christ has given us an example in this also, whose footsteps we ought to follow: namely, that when God calls us to difficult tasks or to possession of the heavenly kingdom, we tear ourselves away from everything that holds us back, even though the flesh is unwilling and its desires strongly resist. This is chiefly what self-denial consists in, of which we spoke in its place. To this pertains what Christ said above: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life as well, he cannot be my disciple." Many examples of this greatness of mind are found in Scripture. For how hard and grievous do you think it was for Abraham, when he was ordered to leave his native soil and his dearest kinsfolk, not knowing where God would appoint a settled home for him? Yet he went, and at the same time he tore his heart away from that land which he heard was less pleasing to him. But how much harder was that command of God by which he was ordered to cast out the maidservant Hagar with her son Ishmael? Yet he too overcame his feelings. How grievous and bitter, do we think, were the wrenchings of all his inmost parts (so to speak) when he was ordered to sacrifice with his own hands Isaac, his most beloved son, whom his wife Sarah, companion of so many labours and cares, had borne him in extreme old age, the son (I say) of the promise! Yet even then he tore himself away from himself, and whatever could be alleged against this command, than which none more atrocious was ever heard, the obedience of faith overcame. Let us then imitate the father of believers when the question concerns our fortunes, rank and reputation, friends, kinsfolk, or any other things. Let us imitate our head and master, Jesus Christ, if we are ever commanded to lay down even our life. Indeed it is hard for us to be torn from this body and from fellowship with the world. But how many things were once, among the nations, regarded by good and prudent men as worse than death? The Lacedaemonians, certainly, when Philip of Macedon laid intolerable burdens on their city, answered most bravely: "If you should try to command something worse than death, we prefer to die." And we read that many surrendered themselves to present death rather than be forced to see their most sweet country oppressed, their liberty snatched away, their wives and children violated, public rights overturned, and other things of this kind, which the cruellest enemies are accustomed to do. Shall a Christian then shrink from death, lest he be torn from Christ or suffer the loss of eternal salvation? Let us therefore struggle with the blind affections of the flesh, and tear it away, however unwilling, from the allurements of this world and of fleeting life, so that it may be granted us to live with Christ.

units.la: Porrò à discipulis suis auulsus positis genibus precatus est dicens: Pater, si uis transfer poculum hoc à me: uerumtamen non mea voluntas, sed tua fiat. Breuis oratio, sed in primis seria & uehemens mens. Et confultò nunc breuitati studuit (ut postea in cruce quoq;) qui aliàs totas noctes in precibus perseuerasse legitur, ne nos de Dei bonitate aut precum nostrarum effectu dubitemus, si quando in maiores angustias adducti illas nō possumus diutius continuare. Et Patrem quidem solum inuocat, ut ipsi quoq; ad hunc unum recurramus, de quo iam sæpe diximus. Status autem totius orationis est, ut Pater poculum istud ab eo transferat. Ita uerò omnis generis afflictiones Scripturæ uocant, eò quòd has nobis Deus certa mensura distribuit. Petit ergo Dominus, ut dirum illud & infame crucis supplicium ab ipso Pater auertat. Atqui sciebat, hoc æternum Patris decretum esse, & sic ideo in mundum uenijse & hominem uerum induisse, ut carnem suam daret pro mundi uita. Attamen ut liberetur petit. Vnde colligimus, nobis etiam licere, ut quæ nobis impendent mala, deprecemur. Si enim naturale est propter illa dolere, non possunt impietatis damnari, qui ex illis liberari cupiunt. Sed hic diligenter obseruari debet moderatio, siue correctio quam Christus adhibet, quando mox subijcit: Veruntamen non mea uoluntas, sed tua fiat. Ita autem dicendo hoc petit, quod nos quoq; petere docuit: Fiat uoluntas tua, quemadmodum in cœlo sic etiam in terra. Hæc igitur nobis omnium petitionum regula sit, quæ circa res huius sæculi uersantur & de quibus non constat nobis, quid Deus fieri uelit. Etenim nimis audax & confidens fuerit, qui inter precandum uelit illi præscribere, à cuius nutu omnia nostra dependent. Et hæc causa est, propter quam multorum preces non exaudiuntur, quia non tam precari, quàm quasi pro imperio postulare, uel potius Deo præscribere audent, quid fieri uelint. Cùm enim orationi maximum pondus addat animi uerè fidelis humiliatio, fieri non potest ut exaudiantur, qui tunc quoque confidentius & insolentius agunt, quando ipsos in primis humiliari oportebat. Neq; alicui debet graue uideri, ut se uoluntati Dei totum subijciat: quando hæc non solum iusta, uerumetiam sancta, bona & salutaris est, eoq; tendit, ut omnes homines seruentur, & in Veritatis cognitionem perueniant.
units.tr: Moreover, torn away from his disciples, he knelt and prayed, saying: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done." A brief prayer, but a mind most earnest and fervent. He deliberately aimed at brevity now (as afterwards on the cross also), though at other times he is read to have persevered in prayer through whole nights, so that we may not doubt God's goodness or the effect of our prayers if, when we are brought into greater straits, we cannot continue them for long. He calls upon the Father alone, so that we too may recur to this one alone, of whom we have often spoken already. The purpose of the whole prayer is that the Father would take that cup away from him. Scripture calls afflictions of every kind cups in this way, because God dispenses them to us in a set measure. The Lord therefore asks that the Father turn away from him that dreadful and infamous punishment of the cross. Yet he knew that this was the eternal decree of the Father, and that for this he had come into the world and put on true manhood, that he might give his flesh for the life of the world. Still he asks to be delivered. From this we gather that we too may pray against the evils that threaten us. For if it is natural to grieve over them, those who desire to be freed from them cannot be condemned for impiety. But here the moderation, or correction, which Christ applies must be carefully observed, when he immediately adds: "Nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done." In saying this he asks the very thing he taught us to ask: "Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven." Let this then be the rule for all our petitions that concern the things of this age, and about which we do not know what God wishes to be done. For he would be too bold and presumptuous who, while praying, wished to prescribe to him on whose nod all our affairs depend. And this is the reason why the prayers of many are not heard: they dare not so much to pray as to demand, as if by command, or rather to prescribe to God what they wish done. For while the humility of a truly faithful soul adds the greatest weight to prayer, it cannot be that those are heard who act more confidently and insolently even when above all they ought to be humbled. Nor should it seem hard to anyone to submit himself wholly to the will of God, since that will is not only just but also holy, good and salutary, and tends to this, that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Accidit autem Christo inter precandum, quod multa consideratione dignißimum est. Sic enim scribit Lucas: Et ipse constitutus in angore, intentius orabat. Erat autem sudor eius quasi grumi sanguinis descendentes in terram. Describitur paucis verbis angustia et lucta, ad cuius spectaculum merito totus mundus obstupescat. Vnde enim sudor ille Christi, nisi ex acerbissimo cordis dolore, quæ mortis imminentis meditatio pariebat? Vbi tamen miretur aliquis, quæ tam acuti doloris tam que uehementis angoris causa fuerit in Filio Dei, cùm multi martyres ad dirißima quæq; tormenta alacri mente olim accesserint, & hodie etiam multi corde nihil turbato & vultu sereno infandos cruciatus sustineant? At hic nos meminisse oportet, Christo non cum sola morte luctam fuisse, sed quia omnium nostrum peccata in se receperat, simul illi cum Patris irati iudicio res erat, quo nihil atrocius, nihil intolerabilius excogitari potest. Si enim hominem suorum modò scelerum seria agnitio & pœnarum quas illis meruit consideratio, atq; hinc enascens iræ Dei sensus, eò usq; adigit (nisi gratia Dei Spiritu confirmetur) ut aut sibi ipsi manum inferat, aut inter cordis horribiliter æstuantis fremitus atq; horribiles de Dei ira querelas desperet: quis obsecro verbis exprimat cogitationes, terrores, consternationes & fidei cum desperatione luctantis certamina, quibus illum exerceri oportuit, in quem Deus (ut apud Isaiam scribitur) omnium nostrum transgressiones concurrere fecerat? Eiusdem certè luctæ effectum fuit, quòd postea in cruce clamauit: Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me de reliquisti? Et in præsenti reipsa patitur, dum sudore sanguineo diffluit, quod de extremè laborantibus per Hyperbolem dici consueuit. In isto tamen angore illum superiorem factum fuisse cùm multis aliis indicijs, tum eo euidentissimè apparet, quòd quo grauius tentatus fuit, eò magis orationem intendit: neq; id inutiliter, aut absq; fructu fecit. Nam uisus est ei Angelus, qui corroborauit eum, ut mox animum conciperet inuicta paternæ gratiæ fiducia armatum, ut suo loco uidemimus. Sunt autem in hac parte nobis quædam nunc diligentius consideranda.
units.tr: It also happened to Christ during his prayer, and this is well worth close consideration. Luke writes: "And being in an agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat was as great drops of blood falling down upon the ground." In a few words the anguish and the struggle are described, and the whole world should be astonished at the sight. Where else could that sweat of Christ come from, if not from the most bitter grief of heart, which the thought of impending death produced? Yet someone may wonder what the cause of such sharp pain and such intense anguish was in the Son of God, since many martyrs in former times went eagerly to the most dreadful torments, and today many endure unspeakable sufferings with an untroubled heart and a calm face. But here we must remember that Christ did not struggle with death alone. Because he had taken upon himself the sins of all of us, he also had to face the judgment of the angry Father, and nothing more terrible or more intolerable can be imagined. For if the serious recognition of one's own wicked deeds, and the consideration of the punishments that they have deserved, together with the sense of God's wrath arising from them, drive a man so far (unless he is strengthened by the grace and Spirit of God) that he either lays hands on himself or, amid the terrible seething and roaring of his heart and his dreadful complaints about God's anger, despairs, then who, I ask, could express in words the thoughts, terrors, dismay, and the struggles of faith against despair, with which he had to be exercised, the one on whom God (as is written in Isaiah) caused the iniquities of us all to meet? Certainly it was the effect of that same struggle that afterwards, on the cross, he cried out: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" And even now he suffers in fact, as he pours out bloody sweat, which is the sort of thing usually said of those in extreme distress by way of hyperbole. Yet that he was superior in this anguish appears most clearly from many other signs, and especially from this, that the more severely he was tempted, the more intently he prayed; and he did not do this in vain or without fruit. For an angel appeared to him, who strengthened him, so that he soon took heart, armed with the invincible confidence of his Father's grace, as we shall see in its place. In this part, however, there are some matters that we must now consider more carefully.

units.la: Primò nō solum humanæ naturæ veritas in Christo asseritur, verumetiam illum tam animo quàm corpore veré passum esse demonstratur. Itaq; confutantur hac actione primùm ij, qui carnè verā ab illo assumptā esse negāt: deinde illi quoq;, qui imaginariè modò passū esse cōtendūt, ne quid maiestate eius indignū statuant. Quorū audacia olim (ut D. Hieronymus contra Pelagianos annotat) eò usq; progressa est, ut totum hunc locum expunxerint. Qui dum gloriam Christi inconsultius defendunt, simul & hanc obscurant, & nostræ redemptionis certitudinem in dubium uocant. Quæ enim gloria illa Christi est quam se alij daturū negat? Ea nimirum, quòd semetipsum pro nobis tradidit, & ita noster Dominus, id est vindex & redemptor factus est. Exinaniuit seipsum (inquit Paulus) forma serui sumpta, similis hominibus factus & habitu compertus ut homo: submisit deniq; se factus obedi ens usq; ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: Ideo etiam Deus ipsum exaltauit in summam sublimitatem, ac donauit ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, &c. Vel dum isti proprie intelligenda esse negant, quæ de illis passionibus Euangelistæ tradiderunt, num ipsum quoq; mendacij insimulabunt dicentem: Tristis est anima mea valde usq; ad mortem? Atqui Isaias clamat: Non est inuentus dolus in ore eius. Vere igitur hæc omnia passus est, & ideo uerus quoq; & sufficiens tam animarum quàm corporum nostrorum redemptor est, pontifex deniq; fidelis est, qui cùm nostras infirmitates ipse expertus sit, nobis etiam condolere poterit & compati: ut alibi quoq; annotauimus.
units.tr: First, the reality of human nature in Christ is asserted, and it is shown that he truly suffered both in soul and in body. So by this action, first, are refuted those who deny that he assumed true flesh; then also those who contend that he suffered only in appearance, lest they should think anything unworthy of his majesty. Their audacity once went so far (as Jerome notes against the Pelagians) that they struck out this whole passage. In defending the glory of Christ too rashly, they at the same time obscure it and call into doubt the certainty of our redemption. For what glory of Christ is it that these men deny he would give? Surely that he gave himself up for us, and so became our Lord, that is, our avenger and redeemer. "He emptied himself," says Paul, "taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient even to death, the death of the cross. Therefore God also exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name which is above every name," etc. Or when they deny that what the evangelists have related about those sufferings is to be understood literally, will they not also charge him with lying when he says: "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death"? Yet Isaiah cries out: "There was no deceit in his mouth." Truly, then, he suffered all these things, and therefore he is also a true and sufficient redeemer both of our souls and of our bodies; finally, he is a faithful high priest, who, since he himself has experienced our infirmities, is able also to sympathize with us and to have compassion on us, as we have noted elsewhere.

units.la: Deinde elucet in hoc quasi speculo, quàm magna quamque horribilis sit in Dei conspectu peccatorum atrocitas: & prodest hunc locum opponere blanditijs, quas nobis obijcit Satan, dum scelera fuco multiplici exornat, ne ea tam grauia tamque noxia putemus, quàm reuera sunt. Quin si ille cesset, ipsi nobis delitias facimus, quibus nosipsos induramus, quo minus possimus respipiscere. Sed eho dic tu quis es, num Dei Filium propter te quoque contristatum fuisse, & propter te sudorem sanguineum excreuisse agnoscas? Fateberis opinor, id propter te quoque factum esse: nam si id neges, salute simul omni in uniuersum te spoliaueris. Quid uerò in te fuit, quòd tanto eius angore expiari oportuit? Quid hic aliud adducere poteris præter peccata, quæ tu tantopere extenuare studes? Vides ergo quàm fallaris id leuiculum ducendo, propter quod Christum Iesum tam dira & grauia certamina subire necesse fuit? Itaque arguit hic locus omnium eorum ingratitudinem atque duritiem, quibus peccata sua quantumuis multa & grauia ne gemitum quidem aut lachrymulam unam extorquere possunt: quíque cùm se tanto pretio redemptos esse fateantur, ad scelera non modò redeunt, sed ne unquam quidem ab illis discedunt, neque de turpi illo seruitio relinquendo cogitant. Pios autem hæc consideratio excitare debet, ut ipsi eo ardentius Deum diligant, qui filium suum propter nos tam diris doloribus obijcere dignatus est, utá; ipsi quoque nihil eorum detrectent, quæ Christi nomine ferenda sunt.
units.tr: Next, in this passage, as in a kind of mirror, the great and dreadful enormity of sins in the sight of God shines forth. It is useful to set this passage against the flatteries with which Satan plies us, when he decks out our wickedness with many false colours, so that we do not think it as grievous and as harmful as it really is. Indeed, if he ceases, we ourselves make for ourselves the pleasures by which we harden ourselves, so that we cannot the more easily repent. But come now, tell me, who are you? Do you acknowledge that the Son of God was saddened also on your account, and that on your account he sweated blood? I suppose you will confess that this was done on your account too; for if you deny it, you will strip yourself altogether of all salvation. What then was there in you, that by such anguish of his he had to make atonement? What can you bring forward here besides the sins that you are so eager to belittle? Do you see, then, how wrong you are in counting as a trifle that for which Christ Jesus had to undergo such dreadful and grievous struggles? So this passage condemns the ingratitude and hardness of all those whose sins, however many and grievous, cannot wring from them even a groan or a single tear; who, although they confess that they have been redeemed at so great a price, not only return to their sins but never even depart from them, and do not think of abandoning that shameful slavery. But this consideration ought to stir up the godly, so that they may love God more ardently, who deigned to expose his Son to such dire sufferings for our sake, and so that they too may refuse nothing of those things that must be borne in the name of Christ.

units.la: Est præterea probè obseruandus sudoris atq; agonis isti us fructus, qui consolationem dulcissimam continet. Nam quod sæpe diximus, communis omnibus nobis incumbit moriendi necessitas: & quia mors ex peccato originem ducit, adeoque peccati pœna est, natura ad eius sensum homines exhorruerunt. Videmus deniq; in morituris grauissimos agones, quos sustinent, priusquam anima vinculis suis soluta ex corporis huius ergastulo discedat. Pariunt illi in nobis quoque sudorem illum fri gidissimum, quo in extremis agentes perfundimur. Cessant tunc fere omnium membrorum officia, & plerunque lingua quoque deficit, sensus reliqui hebetantur, & non raro rationis quoque usus nullus est amplius. Sunt hæc dura per se, & astantibus tristissimum spectaculum exhibent, quod utinam tam firmiter animis nostris insideret, quàm illud inter homines frequens est. Plerique certè de illo nunquam cogitant, nisi quando ipsi quoque in istam arenam vocantur, & tunc terroribus diris exagitati tremunt atq; trepidant. Sed tunc meminerimus, Christum Iesum eandem luctam propter nos sustinuisse, & nobis uicisse, ideoque (quod Paulus testatur) neque vitam neque mortem nos separare posse à dilectione Dei, qua hic nos in Christo complexus est: Manet quidem horror ille mortis, quem natura omnes sentimus: & ne omnino extinguatur, nobis utile est ob multas causas, quas alibi recensuimus. Sed breuis est hæc lucta, & finem sortitur beatissimum, quando per hanc ad aeterni Regni possessionem eluctamur, ubi omnis dolor abolebitur, & æternum cum illo gaudebimus, qui eadem pro nobis passus est. Interea quoad licet, precibus uacemus, & quod de Christo hic dicitur, eò intentius oremus, quò magis angimur. Neque preces nostras putemus irritas esse, eò quòd mortem deprecari nemo poterit. Nam ut Christo, etsi poculum hoc ab eo non transferretur, Angelus tamen apparuit, à quo corroboratus est, ut mox intrepido animo hostibus obuiam prodiret: ita quàm uis aut moriendum sit nobis, aut alia pericula subeunda omnino sint, habet tamen suum effectum fidelis oratio, quo & Dei gratiam ampliorem nobis impetrat, & Spiritum consolationis accipit, quo aduersus omnia certamina inuicti reddimur. Neque dubium esse debet, nobis etiam in extremo illo agone constitutis Angelos adesse, qui ut semper castrametantur circa eos qui Dominum timent, ita tunc maximè assistunt, ut animæ luctanti lætum vitæ futuræ gustum suo conspectu exhibeant, & eandem ex corpore migrantem ad sedes illas beatæ immortalitatis colligant, sicut in Lazari parabola vidimus.
units.tr: Moreover, the fruit of that sweat and agony must be carefully observed, for it contains the sweetest consolation. For, as we have often said, the necessity of dying lies upon all of us alike; and because death takes its origin from sin, and is indeed the punishment of sin, nature has shuddered at the sense of it. Finally, we see in the dying the most grievous agonies that they endure before the soul, loosed from its bonds, departs from the prison house of this body. Those agonies produce in us also that most chilling sweat with which we are drenched when we are at the point of death. Then nearly all the functions of the limbs cease, and very often the tongue also fails, the remaining senses are dulled, and not seldom there is no longer any use of reason. These things are hard in themselves, and they present a most sorrowful spectacle to those standing by; and would that they were as firmly fixed in our minds as they are commonly found among men. Certainly most people never think of this until they themselves are also summoned into that arena, and then, harassed by dreadful terrors, they tremble and quake. But then let us remember that Christ Jesus endured the same struggle for our sake and won it for us, and therefore (as Paul bears witness) neither life nor death can separate us from the love of God, by which he has here embraced us in Christ. That horror of death certainly remains, which all of us feel by nature; and it is useful for us, for many reasons that we have listed elsewhere, that it should not be wholly extinguished. But this struggle is brief, and it has a most blessed end, since through it we fight our way to the possession of the eternal kingdom, where all sorrow will be abolished, and we shall rejoice forever with him who suffered the same things for us. Meanwhile, as long as we are able, let us devote ourselves to prayer, and let us pray the more intently, the more we are distressed, as is said here of Christ. Nor should we think our prayers are in vain because no one will be able to avert death. For just as to Christ, although this cup was not taken from him, an angel nevertheless appeared, by whom he was strengthened, so that he soon went forth with fearless spirit to meet his enemies; so, although we must either die or certainly undergo other dangers, faithful prayer still has its effect, by which it obtains for us a greater grace of God and receives the Spirit of consolation, by which we are made invincible against all struggles. Nor ought there to be any doubt that, even when we are placed in that final agony, angels are present to us, who, as they always encamp around those who fear the Lord, so especially do they stand by at that time, so that they may show to the struggling soul, by their presence, a joyful foretaste of future life, and gather the same soul as it departs from the body to those abodes of blessed immortality, as we saw in the parable of Lazarus.

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci pars, qua docetur, quid interea fecerint discipuli. Sic enim scribit Lucas: Et cum surrexisset à precatione, venisset ad discipulos suos, invenit eos dormientes præ tristitia, &c. Est hoc novum argumentum, quo suum erga homines studium Dei Filius declarat: quod in tanto angore constitutus, & mortis terrore undique pressus, suorum tamen non oblivisci tur, sed quid illi faciant, sedulò inspicit. Nam quod Matthæus & Marcus annotaverunt, non semel tantum hoc fecit, sed secundo & tertiò ad eos redijt. Quales verò invenit eos, quos & in ultima Cæna de periculis imminentibus admonuerat, & quibus acerbissimos animæ suæ dolores confessus fuerat, quibus denique dixerat: Precamini, ne intretis in tentationem? Non vigilant, neque precantur, sed dormiunt, & semel atque iterum excitati, in somnum tamen relabuntur. Poterat hæc execrabilis inderi socordia, nisi culpam eorum aliqua ex parte leviore redderet, quod hoc illis ex tristitia & mærore accidit. Solet hoc frequenter fieri, & causas ex rerum natura philosophi proferunt. Quia enim somnus affectio cordis est, quod communis sensus domicilium esse dicunt, fit ut hoc tristitia occupatum reliquos etiam sensus astringat atque bebetiores reddat, deniq; vitalem quoque spiritum admoveat, ut somnum membris omnibus inducat. Estque hoc (ut & reliqua naturæ opera) ingens Dei beneficium, qui ne toti concidamus hac ratione prospicit. Nam quia, ut Solomon air, spiritus constristatus exiccat ossa, corpus totum somni beneficio irrigari nulla Deus, ne vis illa vitalis tota mærore absorbeatur. Interim non extra culpam sunt, qui somno indulgent, quando pericula graviora ad vigiliam nos excitare debebant. Ideo Christus discipulos non excusat, sed potius reprehendit, dicens: Quid dormitis? Quasi dicat. Itaque ex meis admonitionibus conceptus dolor vos obruit, ut somno locum detis, quando tot undique pericula vos circumstant? Iamne dormiendi tempus est, cum me tantis curis & angoribus propter vos discruciari audiatis? Et hunc sensum ea nobis monstrant, quæ illum Petro dixisse Matthæus & Marcus prodiderunt: Simon dormis? Adeò non potuistis una hora vigilare mecum?
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, which teaches what the disciples meanwhile did. Luke writes: "And when he rose up from prayer, and was come to his disciples, he found them sleeping for sorrow," and so on. This is a new argument by which the Son of God declares his care for human beings: though he was placed in such anguish and pressed on every side by the terror of death, he nevertheless does not forget his own, but carefully looks into what they are doing. For, as Matthew and Mark also noted, he did this not once only, but went back to them a second and a third time. Yet what kind of men does he find? These are the men whom, at the final supper, he had warned of the dangers at hand, to whom he had confessed the most bitter sorrows of his soul, and to whom at last he had said: "Pray, lest you enter into temptation." They do not watch, nor do they pray, but sleep; and though roused once and again, they sink back into sleep. This dreadful carelessness could hardly be excused, unless it were in some measure lessened by the fact that their sleep came from sadness and grief. This often happens, and the philosophers give the natural causes. For since sleep is an affection of the heart, which they say is the seat of the common sense, it comes about that when the heart is occupied by sadness, it binds the other senses too and makes them duller, and finally draws the vital spirit to itself, so that sleep is brought over all the limbs. And this, like the other works of nature, is a great benefit of God, who provides in this way that we should not wholly collapse. For, as Solomon says, "a broken spirit dries up the bones," and therefore God has so ordained that the whole body be watered by the benefit of sleep, lest that vital force be entirely swallowed up by grief. Meanwhile, those who indulge in sleep are not free from blame, when more serious dangers ought to rouse them to watchfulness. Therefore Christ does not excuse the disciples, but rather rebukes them, saying: "Why do you sleep?" As if he said: "Has the sorrow conceived from my warnings so overwhelmed you that you give place to sleep, when so many dangers surround you on every side? Is it now the time for sleeping, when you hear that I am tormented with such cares and anguish on your account?" And these words of Matthew and Mark, in which they report that he said to Peter, "Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch with me one hour?", show the same meaning.

units.la: Exprimitur autem hoc exemplo infelix carnis nostræ ingenium, quæ tunc ferè dormit, quando Christus Iesus in membris suis quàm maximè periclitatur. Nam ut de impijs tunc nihil dicamus, qui tunc gaudent quoque & in omne genus lasciviæ effunduntur, pijs quoque id accidit, ut vel non observent ipsorum causam agi, & suam quoque salutem periclitari, dum alij propter Veritatis confessionem affliguntur: vel improvisò stupore perculsi quid agant ignorent, & tandem se nimium socordes atque ignavos præbeant. Estq; hoc malum illud, quod novissimis temporibus vulgo regnaturum esse, alibi Christus præmonuit, & quod hodie nimis vulgare esse videmus. Cavere autem debent pij, ne sibi ipsis blandiantur, quin potius carnem suam suspectam habeant, & adversus eius nitiositatem vigilent, ne paulatim in graviores tentationes demergantur. Discant item nulli mortalium fidere, sed in uno Christo pro nobis excubante spem salutis omnem collocatam habere. Polliciti erant discipuli magnificè Domino, quod in mortem quoque cum ipso abire parati essent. Quid verò præstant? Ne vigilare quidem possunt cum eo, quæ tam graviter videbant affligi. Quid ergo de alijs speres, qui iste neque animi promptitudine neque gloriæ Dei studio conferri possunt? Et ut maxime velint homines omnia præstare quæ debent, non possunt tamen semper quod volunt. Rectè ergo Ieremias maledictum fore pronuntiat, qui homini fidit, & facit carnem brachium suum. Benedictus autem qui Deo fidit, & beata illa gens, cuius Deus est DOMINVS Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: This example reveals the wretched nature of our flesh, which for the most part falls asleep just when Christ Jesus is in the greatest danger in his members. For, to say nothing of the wicked, who at such times rejoice as well and give themselves over to every kind of wantonness, the same thing happens to the godly too: either they do not notice that their own cause is being pleaded, and their own salvation endangered, while others suffer for the confession of the truth; or, struck by sudden stupor, they do not know what to do, and at last show themselves far too slack and idle. And this is that evil which Christ forewarned would prevail commonly in the last times, and which we see today to be all too common. The godly ought to take care not to flatter themselves, but rather to regard their own flesh with suspicion and keep watch against its sluggishness, lest they gradually sink into more serious temptations. Let them also learn to trust no mortal, but to place all their hope of salvation in Christ alone, who keeps watch for us. The disciples had promised the Lord grandly that they were ready to go with him even to death. But what did they accomplish? They could not even keep watch with him, though they saw him so grievously afflicted. What then can you hope from others, who cannot be compared with them in readiness of spirit or in zeal for the glory of God? And however much men may wish to do all that they ought, they cannot always do what they wish. Rightly, therefore, Jeremiah pronounces a curse on him who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm. Blessed, however, is he who trusts in God, and blessed is that nation whose God is the LORD Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CC.
units.tr: HOMILY CC.

units.la: Adhuc autem eo loquente, ecce turba & is qui dicebatur Iudas, unus e duodecim, præibat eis, & appropinquauit Iesu, ut osculareturcum. Iesus autem dixit ei: Iuda, osculo Filium hominis prodis? Videntes autem ij qui circa ipsum erant quod futurum erat, dixerunt ei : Domine percutiemus ne gladio? Et quidam ex ipsis percussit seruum Pontificis maximi, & abstulit auriculam eius dextram. Respondens autem Iesus dixit: Sinite hucusque. Et tacta illius auricula, sanauit eum. Dixit autem Iesus eis qui ad ipsum venerant, nempe Pontificibus Sacerdotum & praefectis templo, & Senioribus: Vt aduersus latronem exiuistis cum gladijs & fustibus? Cum quotidie vobiscum fuerim in templo, non extendistis manus in me. Sed haec est hora illa vestra & potestas tenebrarum.
units.tr: Yet while he was still speaking, behold, a crowd, and the one called Judas, one of the twelve, was going before them and drew near to Jesus to kiss him. But Jesus said to him, Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Seeing those who were around him what was about to happen, they said to him, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? And one of them struck the servant of the chief priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus answered, Let me go this far. And he touched the man's ear and healed him. Then Jesus said to those who had come against him, namely the chief priests, the captains of the temple, and the elders: Have you come out with swords and clubs, as against a robber? When I was with you daily in the temple, you did not stretch out your hands against me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.

units.la: Quemadmodum Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus discipulis suis saepe de morte sua & ijs quae ipsi euentura erant, concionatus est: ita cum iam mortis hora instaret, argumentis pluribus testatur, se non hostium ui & potentia inuitum abripi, sed uolentem mori, ut aeterno Patris decreto obsequatur. Nam etiamsi diris animi doloribus excrucietur, sanguineo sudore totus diffluat, adhuc oret ut Pater hoc tam amarum poculum a se transferre dignetur, seipsum tamen eius uoluntati totum subijcit, & suo exemplo docet, quid nos facere deceat, si discrimen aliquod gravius est subeundum. Facit ad pleniorem huius doctrinae declarationem hic locus, quem modo recitauimus, quo narratur, ut ab hostibus suis ad montem Oliuarum captus & uinctus sit. Vbi ante omnia fine & usum vinculorum spectare oportet, quae ille sustinuit. Est is, quod nos a vinculis peccati & mortis per eius meritum liberari oportuit, ut his soluti in libertate spiritus ipsi seruiamus, patienter autem feramus eius vincula atq; disciplinam, qua interdum carne lasciuientem constringit. Sunt autem loci totius partes tres, de quibus ex ordine dicemus: Prima hostes illius describuntur, qui nimirum hi fuerint, & quibus armis atq; artibus usi sint in illo capiendo: Altera, quid eius discipuli tunc fecerint, docet. Postrema, quid cum hostibus suis ille egerit.
units.tr: Just as our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ often preached to his disciples about his death and about the things that were to befall them, so, when the hour of death was now at hand, he bore witness by many arguments that he was not being dragged away against his will by the force and power of his enemies, but was willing to die, so that he might obey the eternal decree of the Father. For even though he was tormented by dreadful anguish of soul, and his whole body was dripping with bloody sweat, he still prayed that the Father would deign to take this very bitter cup away from him; yet he submitted himself wholly to the Father's will, and by his example he teaches what we ought to do if some more grievous peril must be faced. The passage we have just recited, which tells how he was taken and bound by his enemies on the Mount of Olives, helps to explain this teaching more fully. Here, before all else, one must consider the end and use of the bonds which he endured. It was this: we were to be freed from the chains of sin and death through his merit, so that, released from these, we might serve him in the liberty of the Spirit, and patiently bear his chains and his discipline, by which he sometimes restrains the flesh when it grows wanton. There are three parts to the whole passage, which we shall take up in order. First, his enemies are described: who they were, and with what weapons and arts they went about seizing him. Second, it teaches what his disciples then did. Last, it shows what he himself did with his enemies.

units.la: Quoad hostes eius, statim hi superuenerunt, quando ipse discipulos nequicquam ad uigilandum & praecandum hortatus est: id quod demonstrandi particula indicat, qua hic Lucas utitur, dicens: Adhuc autem eo loquente, ECCE turba & is qui dicebatur Iudas, &c. Nec temere hoc annotatur. Docet enim exemplum hoc, fidas Dei admonitiones nunquam impune contemni aut negligi, sed uerberibus fere excitari eos, qui uerba & rationes nolunt audire. Exempla eius rei alibi adduximus, & multa hodie fiunt, quae id abunde probant: sed ea est nostrorum temporum socordia, ut plerique ne illi quidem sapiant, quo minus apertis iudiciorum Dei exemplis obloquantur. Sunt autem in ijs, quae hoc loco de Christi hostibus dicuntur, tria praecipue consideranda.
units.tr: As for his enemies, they came upon him at once, when he had urged his disciples in vain to watch and pray. This is indicated by the demonstrative particle that Luke uses here, saying: "While he was still speaking, behold, a crowd and the one called Judas," and so on. Nor is this noted without reason. For this example teaches that the faithful warnings of God are never despised or neglected with impunity, but that those who will not hear words and reasons are almost always roused by blows. We have brought forward examples of this elsewhere, and many happen today that abundantly prove it; but such is the sloth of our times that most people do not even have the sense to refrain from speaking against the plain examples of God's judgments. In what is said in this place about Christ's enemies, three things are especially to be considered.

units.la: Primum, qui nam illi fuerint. In praesenti Iudas nominatur, qui ut totius negotij dux alijs praeiuit. Et de hoc hic quoque repetitur, quod unus fuerit ex duodecim discipulorum numero. Huic adfuit turba ex multis alijs collecta, quae partim in ijs quae postea sequuntur, partim ab alijs Euangelistis diserte describitur. Praecipui in ea fuerunt Principes Sacerdotum cum Senioribus, penes quos duos ordines tam Ecclesiasticarum quam politicarum rerum erat potestas. Adduxerunt hi secum suos seruos, quos multos & sui similes alebant, ut ex ijs potest colligi, quae cum Christo postea petulantissime egerunt. Fit praeterea mentio cohortis militum, quam a Pilato praeside haud dubie impetrarunt. Coniuncti fuerunt istis omnibus praefecti templo, quem peculiarem magistratum fuisse, alibi docuimus. Quia enim templum propter loci situm & magnificam structuram inter munitiones censeri poterat, voluerunt ei aliquos praeficere Romani, qui cauerent, ne qua seditio a Iudaeis sub religionis praetextu moueretur. Et quam hoc necesse fuerit, turbae illae docent, quas in Templo frequenter excitatas fuisse Iosephus scribit. Praeterea cum Iudaica religio gentibus omnibus inuisa esset, a multis etiam scurriliter rideretur, ipsis Sacerdotibus praesidio opus erat, ne qui petulantiores sacra turbarent, & ita populo tumultuandi praeberent occasionem. Eo res suas adduxerant suis factionibus & bellis ciuilibus, ut non urbes modo uerum etiam Templum praesidijs militum teneretur, & non nisi inter prophanarum gentium arma sacrificare & cultum suum exercere possent, qui Dei Filium agnoscere nolebant, qui in omnibus istis ceremonijs adumbrabatur. Fuit autem ista mirabilis hominum ex diuerfiffimis uitæ generibus societas. Nec enim eadem omnibus patria fuit aut gentis origo: non eadem doctrinæ & religionis professio: non idē studium, neq; eadem uiuendi ratio. Possunt tamen animos & studia sua coniungere aduersus Christum, quia omnes impij sunt, & omnes Veritatis lucem ex æquo oderunt. Et hic obseruasse prodest, qui nam omnibus sæculis Euangelicæ doctrinæ hostes futuri sint. Sunt inter hos facilè principes ipsi sacrorum antistites, qui religionem sibi ipsis quæstum fecerunt: quod Iudaicos istos fecisse, non uno loco uidimus. Et extant omnium sæculorum exempla, quibus id posset demonstrari, nisi similia quotidie fierent. Nō desunt his seruilis ingenij homines, quos facilè sibi obstringunt, cum opibus abundent, & propter gradus aut dignitatis suæ existimatio nem multos habeant illis prospiciendi occasiones. Habet præterea artes uarias, quibus summos quoque magistratus in societatem consiliorum suorum possunt adducere. Et quod pijs maximè dolet, coniungunt se illis frequenter qui Christum aliquandiu professi sunt, ab eo autem discedunt, uel auari-tia & ambitione excæcati, uel disciplinæ impatientia irritati. Et est quidem inter omnes istos maxima morum atq; studiorum in aliis rebus dissimilitudo: imò cum omnes non nisi sua quærant, quotidianæ inter illos lites de honoribus, dignitatibus, iniurijs uel datis uel acceptis oriuntur. Quia autem pari odio omnes in Christum ardent, possunt ad tempus sua illa dissidia dissimulare, ut ad illum & Verbum eius oppremendū studia sua conferant. Sunt igitur nimium imprudentes, qui sibi pacem altam & perpetuum otium pollicentur, si quando Reges & principes dissidere & bella contra se inuicem moliri audiunt. Facilè enim illis conuenit, si quam ex nobis opprimendæ Veritatis occasione sibi dari uideant. Est autem deploratu dignißima eorum infelicitas, qui cùm Christi nomen & doctrinâ profiteantur, & in præcipuis fidei articulis probè consentiant, lites tamen & rixas nunquam finiendas exitiât de rebus minoris momenti, & propter illas cum publico scandalo & miserabili Ecclesiarū dissipatione inter se digladiantur. Potuerunt olim Pharifæi cum Sadducæis, & utriq; cum Herodianis & Romanis militibus conuenire contra Christum: At hodie multos ita exagitat Erinnys, ut propter factiosa illa Lutheranorum, Zuinglianorum aut Caluinianorum nomina se mutuò lanient, & communibus fidei nostræ hostibus lætum præbeant spectaculum. Vtinam uerò omnes isti perpetuò memores essent Paulinæ illius admonitionis: Quod si alius alium uicißim mordetis & deuo ratis, uidete ne uicißim alius ab alio consumamini. Gal.5.
units.tr: First, who they were. In the present passage Judas is named, who went before the others as leader of the whole affair. And here too it is repeated that he was one of the twelve disciples. With him was a crowd gathered from many others, which is described partly in what follows and partly clearly by the other Evangelists. The chief men among them were the chief priests with the elders, in whose hands was the power over both the ecclesiastical and the civil affairs of the two orders. These men brought with them their servants, whom they kept in large numbers and of their own kind, as can be gathered from what they later did most insolently to Christ. Mention is also made of a cohort of soldiers, which they had doubtless obtained from Pilate the governor. The captains of the temple were joined with all of them; we have shown elsewhere that this was a distinct magistracy. For since the temple, on account of its site and magnificent structure, could be counted among the fortresses, the Romans wished to set certain men over it to guard against any sedition that the Jews might stir up under the pretext of religion. How necessary this was, those riots show which, as Josephus writes, were often roused in the temple. Moreover, since the Jewish religion was hated by all the nations, and was even mocked as ridiculous by many, the priests themselves needed a guard, lest the more unruly should disturb the sacred rites and so give the people an occasion for tumult. Their affairs had come to this, through their factions and civil wars, that not only the cities but also the temple was held by garrisons of soldiers, and that those who refused to acknowledge the Son of God, who was foreshadowed in all those ceremonies, could offer sacrifice and exercise their worship only amid the arms of profane nations. This was a remarkable fellowship of men from the most diverse ways of life. For they did not all share the same country or origin of their nation, nor the same profession of teaching and religion, nor the same pursuits, nor the same manner of living. Yet they could join their minds and efforts against Christ, because they are all ungodly, and all hate the light of truth equally. And it is useful to observe here who will be the enemies of the Evangelical doctrine in every age. Among these the chief are easily the very leaders of the sacred rites, who have made religion a source of gain for themselves; that these Jews did so we have seen in more than one place. And there are examples from every age by which this could be shown, were it not that similar things happen every day. Nor are men of servile disposition lacking, whom they can easily bind to themselves, since they abound in wealth and, on account of the reputation of their rank or dignity, have many occasions of looking after them. Moreover, they have various arts by which they can draw even the highest magistrates into the fellowship of their plans. And what grieves the godly most, those join themselves to these men frequently who for some time have professed Christ, but then depart from him, either blinded by avarice and ambition, or stirred up by impatience of discipline. Among all these there is indeed the greatest difference of morals and pursuits in other matters; indeed, since they all seek only their own, daily quarrels arise among them about honours, dignities, and injuries given or received. But because they all burn with equal hatred against Christ, they can for a time set aside those dissensions, so as to direct their efforts together toward crushing him and his Word. Therefore they are very foolish who promise themselves deep peace and perpetual leisure whenever they hear that kings and princes are at odds and plotting wars against one another. For it readily suits them, if they see any occasion of suppressing the truth from us. Yet most lamentable is the unhappiness of those who, while they profess the name and doctrine of Christ, and agree well in the chief articles of faith, nevertheless stir up quarrels and strife, never to be ended, over matters of lesser moment, and for their sake tear one another apart with public scandal and the wretched dispersal of the Churches. The Pharisees once could join with the Sadducees, and both with the Herodians and the Roman soldiers, against Christ. But today a Fury so harasses many that they mangle one another for the sake of those factious names of Lutherans, Zwinglians, or Calvinists, and offer a joyful spectacle to the common enemies of our faith. Would that all of them were constantly mindful of that admonition of Paul: "But if you bite and devour one another, take heed that you are not consumed one of another." Gal.5.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Christi hostes, in quibus alterum occurrit, non minus diligenter considerandum, Industria nimirum & studium, quo causam istam egerunt. Non potuit ille à suis impetrare, ut uel una hora secum uigilent & precibus incumbant, quod ut factu facile, ita tutissimum quoque & multas ob causas necessarium erat, quæ illos minimè latebant. At isti non uigilant modò sed mirificè student, ne quid negligant eorum, quæ ad ipsorum conatū faciebant. Obseruant enim quam diligentissimè temporis occasionem & loci commoditatem, seq; mutuò audiunt, adeò ut ne Iudam quidē, hominem obscurum & nullius pretij, dedignentur pro suo duce agnoscere, qui aliis omnibus dignitate præstabant. Solet hoc ipsum hodie fieri publicè & priuatim. Quia enim pij pro sui ingenij bonitate nemini nocere, sed potius omnibus prodesse cupiunt, alios quoque ex suo ingenio & moribus æstiman tes, securi uiuunt, & sibi omnia pacifica atque tuta pollicentur. At plurimum spe sua falluntur: quia longè aliud est impiorum ingenium, & alij hostium Veritatis mores. Quia enim & Veritatis lucem & huius sectatores oderunt, quiescere non possunt, sed patrem suum, diabolum, imitantur. Vt enim hic iam inde ab initio homicida fuit, & subinde ut leo rugens oberrat, & quærit quem deuoret: ita ipsi quoque intra animos suos semper æstuant, consilia semper ineunt & omnes occasiones obseruant, ut pijs malum dent, & apud alios accensam Veritatis faciem extinguant. Exempla huius generis passim in historijs tam sacris quàm prophanis occurrunt. Poterat Cainum Abelus ferre, & procul dubio sibi de illo optima quæque pollicebatur: ipsum autem ille sibi intolerabilem putat, neque quiescit donec illum trucidet. Et Iofephum in fratres nihil hostiliter uel cogitauisse scimus: ipsi uero rabie in illum accensi nihil tale opinantem capiunt & exteris uendunt. Debent nos ista admonere ut cautè agamus cum filijs huius sæculi, & serpentina illa utamur sapientia, quam nobis Christus commendat. At non minus in singulis priuatim hæc ignauia sese prodit. Carnis enim hoc ingenium est, ut nihil non facere, ac pati possit, dummodo affectibus suis prauis indulgeat. Est hoc uidere in auaris, ebriosis, scortatoribus, militibus mercenarijs, atque similibus: ita qui
units.tr: But let us return to Christ's enemies, in whom another point appears that deserves no less careful attention: namely the industry and zeal with which they pursued their cause. He could not get his own people to keep watch with him and devote themselves to prayer for even a single hour, though this was easy to do, and was also the safest course and necessary for many reasons, which they well knew. But these men not only keep watch; they labour wonderfully hard to neglect nothing that might advance their enterprise. They observe with the utmost care the opportunity of the time and the convenience of the place, and they consult one another, so much so that they do not disdain to acknowledge as their leader even Judas, an obscure man of no worth, though he was far inferior in rank to all the rest. This same thing is commonly done today, both in public and in private. For since the godly, out of the goodness of their own disposition, wish to harm no one but rather to benefit all, and judge others by their own nature and manners, they live securely and promise themselves that everything will be peaceful and safe. But they are greatly deceived in this hope, for the disposition of the wicked is quite different, and so are the manners of the enemies of the truth. Since they hate both the light of the truth and its followers, they cannot be at rest, but imitate their father, the devil. For as he has been a murderer from the beginning, and roams about from time to time like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, so they too are always seething within their minds, always forming plans and watching every opportunity, so that they may do harm to the godly and extinguish, among others, the kindled face of the truth. Examples of this kind occur everywhere in both sacred and profane histories. Abel could have endured Cain, and no doubt Abel promised himself all good things from him; but Cain thought him intolerable and does not rest until he slaughters him. And we know that Joseph had thought nothing hostile towards his brothers; yet they, inflamed with rage, seize him when he suspects nothing of the kind, and sell him to foreigners. These things ought to warn us to act cautiously with the children of this age, and to use that serpent-like wisdom which Christ commends to us. But this same sluggishness shows itself no less in individuals in private life. For it is the nature of the flesh that it can do and endure anything, provided it indulges its depraved passions. This can be seen in the avaricious, the drunkards, the fornicators, mercenary soldiers, and others of that kind.

units.la: Industria hostium Christi. superstitionibus dediti sunt, ij ieiunijs, cilicijs, uigilijs, circuncurfitando & nihil non faciendo sese fa tigant, neq; impensas ullas facere detrectat, modò animos inani et imaginaria cultus diuini & salu tis suæ persuasione pascant. Quàm primùm uero Euangelij cognitione illuminati aliquid facere iube mur pro asserenda Dei gloria & uera salutis ratione, fere pigerrimi sumus, & undique argumenta corradimus, quibus nostra ignominia excusemus. Demonstratione hic nulla opus est, cū singuli hoc in semetipsis deprehendant, imò deplorent etiam. Ia eum finem autem hanc nostri ingenij uitiosita tem expendere debemus, ut intelligamus uix ullam disciplinam carni sufficere, nosq; perpetuis stimu lis opus habere, quibus hæc plus quàm asinina tarditas nobis excutiatur, quiq; nos ad uerę pietatis stu dium alacriores reddant.
units.tr: The diligence of Christ's enemies. Those given over to superstitions wear themselves out with fasts, hair shirts, vigils, running about in circles, and doing anything at all; nor do they refuse any expense, provided they feed their minds with the empty and imagined persuasion of worshipping God and securing their salvation. But as soon as we are enlightened by knowledge of the gospel and are bidden to do something for the vindication of God's glory and the true way of salvation, we are for the most part very slothful, and on every side we gather arguments with which to excuse our shame. No demonstration is needed here, since each person detects this in himself, and indeed even laments it. Yet to this end we ought to weigh this vice of our disposition, so that we may understand that hardly any discipline is sufficient for the flesh, and that we need constant goads by which this more than asinine sluggishness is shaken off, and which make us more eager for the pursuit of true godliness.

units.la: Tertium in Christi hostibus, ut quibus armis & artibus in illo oppugnando uti sint uidea mus. Antea quidem insidiosas quæstiones sæpius illi proposuerunt, & disputationes mouerunt de Le ge, de repudio, de censu Cæsari soluendo, de resurrectione & alijs quibusdam, quibus illum apud vul gus & præsides, uel in odium uel contemptū adducere conati sunt. Quia uero ea ratione nihil profece runt, quàm quòd ipsorum ignorantia et malitia indies magis magisq; prodebatur, alia uia nunc rem aggrediuntur, et armis agendum esse putant. Ne uero ipsi seditionum authores esse dicantur, afluteè non modò Senatus Hierosolymitani authoritate suum conatum palliant, uerumetiā Præsidem, qui summus tunc in ea gente magistratus erat, in suas partes trahūt, et ab eo milites sibi dari petūt, qua si ipsis cū homine seditioso & publico pacis hoste res sit. Interim proditorijs artibus agūt omnia, qui bus & præsidem recipiunt, & populo ignorante ista faciunt quæ ad hunc maximè pertinebant, Iuda deniq; ministro & duce utuntur, qui et ipse osculo, quod amicitiæ symbolum est antiquissimum, illum prodit. Oportuit autem ista sic fieri, & proditione capi atque occidi Christum, ut suo merito nostram culpam expiaret, qui omnes plus quā proditorio animo apertā feceramus à Regno Dei secessionem. Sunt uerò hæc usitatissima arma, quibus hodie etiam Veritatis doctrina oppugnatur. Postquam enim aduersarij nostri multis exemplis edocti sciunt, nihil aduersus hac profici disputationibus, quæ ex Dei Verbo instituuntur, unicum præsidium sibi in armis repositum esse uident. At quia illud non minus periculosum quàm vulgo exosum est, & principes pleriq; controuersias de religione, si nudè & simpliciter proponantur, facile negligunt, his ante omnia persuadere studeant, de publica pace agi, & ipsorum authoritatem in periculum venire, ideoq; ad restinguendum hoc incendium communibus o mnium ordinū studijs atq; uiribus opus esse. Et ut hoc quoq; facilius persuadeant, multis testantur, quàm ipsis molesta & grauis sit infelix illa discordia, qua Ecclesiæ simul omnes unà cum toto orbe Christiano turbentur, & ad hanc tollendam Concilio generali opus esse aiunt, & ut indicatur, curat, ijs tamen conditionibus, quas nemo pius admittere potest. Concilij executorem summum faciunt aut Imperatorem, aut quemcunq; principem ex suis coniuratis potissimum esse norunt, simul tamen o mnes alios quoq; qui Concilio subscripserunt, ad eius executionem obstringunt. Et ne eo quidē conten ti, simul, controuersias ciuiles passim excitant: quæ maxima ex parte à religione dependēt, & adue ri cultus oppressionem faciunt, si causam suam obtineant. In his autem omnibus non alij magis no cent quàm Iudæ proditores, qui amicitiam simulando appropinquant ut Christum deosculentur, id est, sequestros sese præbent, & mirifico astu sese insinuant, interim uerò hoc unū agunt, ut causa sua cadant pij, & Ecclesiæ hinc inde opprimantur. Quòd si quis exempla quærat, quibus hæc demonstren tur, ueteribus minimè opus est, quando ista passim hodie fiunt, & tam ciuilibus quàm exteris armis regna Christiani orbis quondam florentissima horribiliter distrahuntur: qui Cocilij istius Tridenti ni fructus est, quod ante annos amplius uiginti sub Paulo III. Pontifice inchoatum tandem sub Pio IIII. finitum, hanc toti orbi terrarum Tragœdiam exhibet. Gemunt nunc passim sub hoc onere pij, sed erit citius quàm multi sperent rerum uicissitudo, quando hi quidem Christi denuo surgentis læti simo spectaculo exhilarabuntur, illi uerò suæ audaciæ diras pœnas exoluent.
units.tr: Third, among Christ's enemies, let us see what weapons and arts they used in assailing him. Earlier they often put insidious questions to him and raised disputes about the Law, about divorce, about paying tribute to Caesar, about the resurrection, and about certain other matters, by which they tried to bring him into hatred or contempt among the common people and the governors. But since they gained nothing by this method, except that their ignorance and malice were revealed more and more each day, they now attempt the matter by another way, and think that they must act by force of arms. Lest they themselves be called the authors of sedition, they cleverly cloak their undertaking not only with the authority of the Jerusalem council, but also draw the governor, who was then the chief magistrate in that nation, to their side, and ask him to give them soldiers, as though they had to do with a seditious man and a public enemy of the peace. Meanwhile they do everything by treacherous arts, by which they win over the governor, and they carry out those things which especially concerned him while the people are ignorant of them. Finally they use Judas as their minister and leader, who himself betrays Christ with a kiss, which is the most ancient symbol of friendship. Yet it was necessary that these things be done thus, and that Christ be taken by treachery and put to death, so that by his merit he might atone for our guilt, since all of us had made a departure from the kingdom of God more than treacherous in spirit. Indeed these are the most common weapons with which the teaching of the truth is attacked even today. For when our adversaries, taught by many examples, know that nothing is gained against it by disputations conducted from the Word of God, they see that their only remaining defence lies in arms. But because this method is no less dangerous than it is generally hated, and many princes readily neglect controversies about religion if they are put forward plainly and simply, they strive above all to persuade these princes that public peace is at stake and their own authority is in danger; and therefore that to quench this fire the united efforts and forces of all orders are needed. And to make this easier to persuade, they declare to many that that unhappy discord, by which all the churches together, along with the whole Christian world, are thrown into turmoil, is grievous and burdensome to them; and they say that a general council is needed to remove it, and that it should be convened, yet they arrange it on conditions which no godly person can accept. They make the supreme executor of the council either the emperor or whatever prince they know to be most suited among their conspirators, and at the same time they bind all the others who have subscribed to the council to its execution. And not content even with this, they stir up civil controversies everywhere, which for the most part depend upon religion, and, if they gain their point, they bring about the suppression of the opposing worship. In all these matters none harm more than the traitors like Judas, who draw near under the pretence of friendship in order to kiss Christ, that is, they present themselves as mediators and insinuate themselves with marvellous cunning, while in the meantime they do this one thing: that the godly fall in their cause and the Church is oppressed on every side. But if anyone seeks examples by which these things may be demonstrated, there is no need of older ones, since these things are done everywhere today, and the kingdoms of the Christian world, once most flourishing, are being terribly torn apart by both civil and foreign arms. This is the fruit of that Council of Trent, which, begun more than twenty years ago under Pope Paul III and finally concluded under Pius IV, has put on this tragedy for the whole world. The godly now groan everywhere under this burden, but the turn of events will come sooner than many hope, when these men will be cheered by the joyful spectacle of Christ rising again, while those will pay the dreadful penalties of their audacity.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, qua quid discipuli fecerint. Lucas exponit. Vi dent illi quid futurum sit, & quid moliantur, qui tempore tam importuno cum laternis armati illuc ueniebant. Ideo exclamant: Domine percutiemus ne gladio? Rursus ergo animo coeperunt spiritus illos, quos in Cœna paulò ante iactauerant, & ad pugnam se offerunt: nimirum quod non intel lexissent quod ille tunc de gladijs emendis dixerat. Et admonemur hoc loco obiter, quā periculosum sit, Dei uerba non penitius inspicere, sed eo sensu interpretari, quem ipsi ex nobis concepimus. Hæc certè causa fuit, quòd discipuli temere ad arma ruere voluit, & quòd Petrus nō expectato etiā responso Christi, gladiū stringit, & pugnæ initiū faciendo seipsum & socios omnes in extremū discrimē adducit. Prodest autē in huius exempli consideratione crebrò uersari, ut discamus, quàm parum proficiant, qui in rebus agendis suū potius zelum, quàm Dei uoluntatē sequuntur, quàm nobis per Verbū suum reuelat. Quid enim magis pium uidetur, quàm cum proprij capitis periculo Christi & eius gloria tueri? Aut quæ arma iustiora & sanctiora sunt, quàm quæ pro eius defensione sumuntur, qui seipsum pro nobis tradidit? At in præsenti hoc infelicissimè cedit Petro, qui hoc fecit zelo Christi seruetissimo. Quia enim huic non coniunxit uerā de Regno Christi & eius propagatione scientiam, facit quod ab eius uoluntate alienissimum erat, & inobedientia peccat, dum se totum illi uult impendere. Deinde magni conatus euentu uidet plane ridiculū, dum auriculam solam amputat seruulo Pontificis: & qui triumphos spirabat, à Christo acriter reprehenditur. Deniq; qui tunc totus feruet, & plus quàm gladiatorio animo sese ad mortē & extrema quæuis pericula offert, non multò post cum alijs fugit relicto Christo, cum quo se in carcerē & mortem abire uelle promiserat: nec fugisse contentus, eundem insuper abnegat, ut in sequenti Sermone audiemus. Solet hoc multis accidere hodie, qui pro Christo & religione bella nō necessaria suscipiunt, & magno animo res in primis arduas conantur. Quia enim nulla Dei uocatione nituntur, non modo nihil proficiunt, sed plerunq; sibi ipsis ignominiā conflant, quando animi constantia temerarijs inceptis minus respondet, simulq; multos alios in periculū adducunt, qui se consiliorum eiusmodi socios præbuerunt. Itaq; tanti Apostoli exemplo cautiores facti, zelum nostrum suspectū habeamus, & quæ is nobis suggerit, consilia diligentius examinemus ad nostræ uocationis & diuinæ uoluntatis regulam. Nec enim unquam aut Deo probabitur zelus, aut exitum habebit felicem, qui nos extra nostræ uocationis metas abripit. Quæ de Pontificis famulo & Christi uerbis dicenda essent, quibus Petrum reprehendit, & reliquos discipulos simul omnes continuit, ne eius audaciam sequerentur, ex Marco nostro petant, qui plura uidere cupiunt.
units.tr: Let us now come to the other part of this passage, in which Luke sets out what the disciples did. They see what is going to happen and what those men are plotting, who came there armed with lanterns at such an unseasonable time. So they cry out: "Lord, shall we strike with the sword?" Then again they began to be stirred in spirit, the spirit they had shown a little earlier at the supper, and they offer themselves for battle. Clearly they had not understood what he had said then about buying swords. We are reminded here in passing how dangerous it is not to look more deeply into the words of God, but to interpret them in the sense we have formed for ourselves. This was certainly the reason why the disciples rashly wished to rush to arms, and why Peter, without even waiting for Christ's answer, drew his sword, and by starting the fight brought himself and all his companions into the greatest danger. It is useful, in considering this example, to dwell on it often, so that we may learn how little they gain who in their undertakings follow their own zeal rather than the will of God, which he reveals to us through his Word. For what seems more godly than to defend Christ and his glory at the risk of one's own head? Or what arms are more just and holy than those taken up for the defence of him who gave himself up for us? Yet in this case it turned out most unhappily for Peter, who did it out of most fervent zeal for Christ. Because he had not joined to this the true knowledge of Christ's kingdom and its extension, he did what was most alien to his will, and sinned through disobedience, while he wished to devote himself wholly to him. Then, the outcome of his great effort looks plainly ridiculous, since he cut off only an ear of the high priest's servant. And he who had been breathing triumph was sharply rebuked by Christ. Finally, he who then was all aglow, and offered himself to death and every extreme danger with more than gladiatorial courage, not long after fled with the others, leaving Christ, with whom he had promised to go to prison and death. And not content with fleeing, he even denied him, as we shall hear in the following sermon. Many people today experience this, who undertake wars not necessary for Christ and religion, and attempt with great spirit things that are most arduous. For since they rely on no calling from God, they not only achieve nothing, but for the most part bring shame on themselves, since constancy of spirit does not match rash undertakings, and at the same time they draw many others into danger who have joined them as partners in such plans. Therefore, made more cautious by the example of so great an Apostle, let us hold our zeal under suspicion, and let us examine more carefully the plans it suggests to us by the rule of our calling and the divine will. For zeal will never be approved by God, nor will it have a happy outcome, if it carries us beyond the limits of our calling. What should be said about the high priest's servant and the words of Christ, by which he rebuked Peter and at the same time restrained the rest of the disciples from following his boldness, let those who wish to see more seek from our Mark.

units.la: Nunc tertiam huius loci partem uideamus quæ ea describi diximus, quæ inter hæc omnia Christus fecit. Est in his commemorandis Lucas breuior, quia ab alijs plenius iam expositā esse sciebat. Primum est, quòd qui prius toto animo consternatus præ angore sudabat, nunc nouis uiribus confirmatus, hostibus sponte obuiā processit, & prior illos allocutus, quem quærant quæsiuit. Et ijsdem ita sese cognoscendum præbuit, ut simul diuinæ suæ uirtutis specimē aderet, illos prosternendo. Quod ut nouum est mortis uoluntariæ argumentum, quia nostram inobedientiam expiauit: ita bonitatis & gratiæ singularis opus est, qua eos in sui cognitionem inducere & ab interitu reuocare voluit, qui nefario & impio ausu aduersus ipsum conspirauerant. At quia ijdem hanc eius bonitatem non agnouerunt, inexcusabiles facti sunt.
units.tr: Now let us look at the third part of this passage, namely what Christ did among all these events, as we said we would describe them. In recounting them Luke is briefer, because he knew they had already been explained more fully by the others. First, the one who had been overcome with dread and had sweated in anguish now, strengthened by fresh powers, went out to meet his enemies of his own accord. Speaking first to them, he asked whom they sought. He also made himself known to them in such a way that at the same time he displayed a sign of his divine power by casting them to the ground. This is a new proof of his voluntary death, by which he atoned for our disobedience. It is also a work of his goodness and singular grace, by which he wished to lead to the knowledge of himself, and to recall from destruction, those who had conspired against him with wicked and impious daring. But because they did not recognise this goodness of his, they were made inexcusable.

units.la: Inde ad Iudā conuersus, in oculū eius animo non minus ad omnem impietatē deuoto quàm prodi torio ruentē compellauit, dicens: Iuda, osculo Filiū hominis prodis? Breuis uox, sed quæ adamante frangere posset, nisi ille cor habuisset adamante durius. Nam nomine proprio illum appellat, ne de quouis alio agi putaret. Et apud Matthæu amici uocabulum addit, ut simul pristinā consuetudinē & beneficia accepta eius in mentē reuocet, adeoq; ut dignitatis eū admoneat, qua ipsum ornarat, quan do cū alijs discipulis emissus Euangelium prædicauit, & eius nomine miracula fecit. Addit præterea: Ad quid ades? Quasi diceret: Cogita quæso mi Iuda, qui fueris aliquando, & qui nunc sis, in quem fi nē deniq; huc veneris, quamq; parū quod nunc facis tuæ professioni respondeat? Et quæ hæc est tua infelicitas, quæ perfidia, quod osculo prodis Filiū hominis? Ubi rursum Filij hominis nomine omnia comprehenditur, quæ ille ipsum hoc nomine utentem de seipso dicere audierat, & facere uideratut sensus sit: Eum ne tu prodere audes, quem toties audiuisti ideo in hunc mundum uenisse, & Filium hominis fa ctum esse, ut humani generis redemptor fieret? Eum ne (inquam) prodis, de quo tam tuo quam suo & aliorū omniū nomine Petrus confessionē edidit: Tu es Christus, Filius Dei uiuentis? Et osculo quidē prodis, quo nihil turpius et indignius fieri poterat? &c. Hæc et alia huius generis paucis hisce uerbis infelici proditori Dominus in animū reducit, quibus adhuc suā erga illū beneuolentiā declarat. Quæ consolatione quidē afferre possunt ijs, qui gratiā Dei rectè æstimant: simul tamen cauendū est diligenter, ne nos pari benignitate compellante aspernemur. Nunc quidē uerba hæc Iudas leuicu
units.tr: Then he turned to Judas and addressed him, whose mind was no less devoted to every impiety than his feet were rushing to betrayal, saying: "Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" It is a brief utterance, yet it could break even adamant, unless that man had a heart harder than adamant. For he calls him by his own name, so that he would not think someone else was meant. And in Matthew he adds the word "friend", so that he might at once bring to Judas's mind their former companionship and the benefits he had received, and so remind him of the dignity with which he had been honoured when he was sent out with the other disciples to preach the gospel and did miracles in Christ's name. He adds further: "Why have you come?" As if he said: "Consider, I beg you, my Judas, what you once were and what you are now, and to what end you have finally come here, and how little what you are now doing agrees with your profession. What is this wretchedness of yours, this treachery, that you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" Here again the name "Son of Man" comprehends everything that Judas had heard him say about himself when he used this name, and the sense is: "Would you dare to betray him whom you have so often heard say that he came into this world and became the Son of Man so that he might become the redeemer of the human race? Do you betray him (I say), of whom Peter, in his own name and in the name of all of you, made the confession: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God'?
