And you betray with a kiss, than which nothing could be done more shamefully and unworthily?" etc. With these few words the Lord brings back to the mind of the unhappy traitor these and other things of this kind, by which he still declares his goodwill towards him. These words can indeed bring consolation to those who rightly esteem the grace of God. Yet at the same time we must take care not to despise him when he calls us with the same kindness. Judas at the time thought little of these words.

units.la: Vnu la putauit: sed non multò post grauiora sensit, quàm ferre potuerit, quando et admissi sceleris et contempti verbi Dei conscientia superatus sibi ipsi mortem conscivit, & tam anima quàm corpore perijt, abiectis prius pecunijs, quas propria vita chariores habuerat.
units.tr: But not long afterwards he felt things more grievous than he could bear, when, overcome by the consciousness of the crime he had committed and of the word of God he had despised, he brought death upon himself, and perished both in soul and body, having first cast away the money which he had valued more than his own life.

units.la: Non tamen cum solo Iuda agit Dominus, sed simul ut discipulos alios quoq; periculo praesenti subducat, studet, quos ad graviora certamina adhuc minus instructos esse sciebat. Ideo ut Ioannes scribit hostibus dicit: Si me quaeritis, sinite hos abire. Et tanta huius dicti vis fuit, ut nulli illorum manus iniecerint, & ne Petro quidem molesti fuerint, qui sua importuna temeritate illos provocauerat. Quo loco virtute plane divina cum bonitate & fide plus quam paterna declarauit. Solius enim Dei est animis & voluntatibus hominum imperare, & verbis eos coercere, qui si humana ratione agatur, vix ut aperta contineri possunt. Fidei autem & curae paternae argumentum est, quòd etsi undiq; ab hostibus circùdatus fuerit, & praesente omnia morte intentarint, suorum tamen non fuit immemor, sed de his seruandis cogitauit. Nobis autem huius exempli usus est duplex. Primus, ut ipsi quoq; de aliorum salute seriò cogitemus, eorum autem in primis, qui nobis à Deo crediti sunt; neq; nos iam nihil illis debere amplius putemus, si quando ipsi grauius periclitamur. Nam ad extremum usq; spiritum nos in nostra statione fideles esse oportet, quod Christum praestitisse constat, qui ne in cruce quidem pendens suo officio erga aliquos defuit. Sunt ergo alienissimi ab huius spiritu, qui si quae ipsis imminent pericula, omnes secu perditos vellent, adeoq; alijs meliore fortunam invident, vel etiam à Deo sibi iniuriam fieri cum fremitu queruntur, qui solos periculis obijciat. Alter usus est, ne unquam de Christi erga nos fide dubitemus, aut nos ab hoc putemus derelictos esse. Quomodo enim nos negligeret nunc, qui suorum saluti tam diligenter cauit, quando ut sibi potius consuleret, praesens necessitas monebat? Quin potius memori mente teneamus promissiones eius: Non relinquam uos orphanos, iterum veniam ad uos. Item: Ecce ego uobiscum sum usq; ad consummationem seculi. Quibus adde quae apud Isaiam de suo in Ecclesia amore et studio sub matris parabola cocionatur, unà cum exemplis, quae multa passim occurrunt.
units.tr: Yet the Lord does not deal only with Judas, but at the same time he takes care to withdraw the other disciples also from the present danger, whom he knew to be as yet too little prepared for the harder conflicts. So, as John writes, he says to his enemies: "If you seek me, let these go away." And the force of this saying was so great that none of them laid hands on the disciples, and they did not even trouble Peter, who had provoked them by his rash and unseasonable boldness. In this place he plainly showed a divine power together with a goodness and faithfulness more than fatherly. For it belongs to God alone to rule the minds and wills of men, and to restrain by words those who, if matters were left to human reason, could scarcely be held back. But it is a proof of faithfulness and of a fatherly care that, although he was surrounded on every side by enemies, and although they threatened death on the spot, he was nonetheless not forgetful of his own, but took thought for their safety. We may draw a twofold use from this example. The first is that we too should seriously consider the salvation of others, and especially of those who have been committed to us by God; and we should not think that we owe them nothing more when we ourselves are in greater danger. For we ought to be faithful in our post even to the last breath, as it is plain Christ did, who even hanging on the cross did not fail in his duty towards some. Therefore they are most alien from this spirit who, if any dangers threaten themselves, would wish all others to perish with them, and envy others a better lot, or even complain with indignation that God does them an injury when he exposes only them to dangers. The second use is that we should never doubt Christ's faithfulness towards us, or think that we have been abandoned by him. For how would he neglect us now, who took such careful thought for the safety of his own, when the present necessity urged him rather to look after himself? Rather, let us hold firmly in a mindful heart his promises: "I will not leave you orphans; I will come again to you." Likewise: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." To these add what he preaches through the parable of the mother in Isaiah about his love and care for his Church, together with the many examples that occur everywhere.

units.la: Et quomodo suos negligeret, qui ne hostibus quidem in praesenti defuit? Na Pontificis servulo arriculae restituit, & suo exemplo legem suam exponit atq; confirmat de diligendis inimicis. Inde ad Sacerdotum principes & templo praefectos atq; Seniores conuersus, grauiter admodum cum illis expostulat, dicens: Vt aduersus latronem existis cum gladijs et fustibus? Quasi diceret: Quid haec sibi arma volunt? aut cum quo nam uobis negotium esse putatis? Cum latronum principe ne, qui socijs stipatus non aliter quàm ex insidijs ut maiori opprimi queat? Iduerò illos indignissimè facere, ab antea actis probat: Cum quotidie fuerim uobiscum in templo, nö extendistis manus in me. Qua parte docet, illos male sibi conscios esse & pessimam causam sustinere, qui noctu eum intercipiat, quem interdiu in publico sese offerentem non ausi sint comprehendere. Addit his postremò: Sed haec est hora illa vestra, & potestas tenebrarum. Ita verò dicendo partim ostendit, nihil hic absq; Dei prouidentia fieri, nec illos quicquam effecturos fuisse, nisi iam hora illa adesset, qua ipsum mori oporteat: simul verò illorum iniustam uim atq; tyrannidem arguit, quando potestatem tenebrarum eos dicit: ut qui ipsa temporis circunstantia testentur, se diaboli satellites esse, quem Scriptura principem tenebrarum dicere consueuit. Est autem exemplum hoc admodum memorabile, quo primùm admonemur, quae nam patientiae Christianae leges sint. Quia enim exemplum huius perfectissimum est Christus, ex eo etiam leges eius merito peti debent. Dicitur is ut ouis ad lanienam ductus esse, & idem alibi monet, ne male dicamus ijs qui nos oderunt & persequuntur. Veruntamen idem ille in praesenti suam innocentiam tuetur, et hostium uim iniustam grauiter arguit. Et quod ipse fecit, id olim multos ex Prophetis, & postea Apostolos quoq; fecisse scimus: & ut ita fiat, opus est. Quia enim in nobis Dei gloria periclitatur, quod impiorum uoces in suis contra fidos Dei cultores victorijs abundè testantur, non possumus nostrae causae omnino deesse, nisi simul gloriā Dei prodamus. Rursus exigit hoc charitatis lex, qua hostibus quoq; sumus obstricti, ne ad eorum impietatem coniuendo illos reddamus cotumaciores. Itaq; & in homines & in Deum turpiter peccant, qui hodie suam ignauiam sub patientiae Christianae praetextu excusant. In ijs, quae ad nos solos spectant, quiduis ferre nos decet: at quando nobiscum Dei gloria & Veritatis doctrina in periculum veniunt, tunc quid illi debeamus diligenter nos meminisse decet. At hodie plerique Dei gloriam facile negligunt, in suo autem iure tuendo modo omnem excedunt.
units.tr: And how would he neglect his own, who did not fail even his enemies in the present crisis? For he restored the servant's ear to the high priest's servant, and by his own example he sets forth and confirms his law about loving enemies. Then he turned to the chief priests, the captains of the temple and the elders, and rebuked them very severely, saying: "Have you come out against a robber with swords and clubs?" As if he said: "What do these weapons mean? Or with whom do you think you have business? With the leader of robbers, surrounded by his accomplices, who cannot be overcome except by ambush and by greater force?" By what has been done before he proves that they are acting most unworthily: "Since I was daily with you in the temple, you did not stretch out your hands against me." In this respect he teaches that they were conscious of their own wrong and maintained a very bad cause, since they seized by night him whom they had not dared to arrest by day when he offered himself openly in public. Finally he adds: "But this is your hour, and the power of darkness." In saying this he shows partly that nothing here happens apart from the providence of God, and that they would have achieved nothing unless that hour, in which he had to die, were already at hand; and at the same time he charges them with their unjust violence and tyranny, when he calls them the power of darkness, as though the very circumstances of the time bore witness that they were the devil's henchmen, whom Scripture is accustomed to call the prince of darkness. This example is indeed most worthy of remembrance, by which we are first reminded what the laws of Christian patience are. For since Christ is the most perfect example of this, his laws too ought rightly to be sought from him. He is said to have been led like a sheep to the slaughter, and elsewhere he admonishes us not to speak evil of those who hate and persecute us. Yet the same Christ in the present case defends his innocence and sharply condemns the unjust violence of his enemies. What he himself did, we know that many of the prophets did long ago, and afterwards the apostles too; and it is necessary that it be so. For since the glory of God is endangered in us, which the boasts of the wicked in their victories over the faithful worshippers of God amply testify, we cannot altogether fail our cause without at the same time betraying the glory of God. Again, the law of charity requires this, by which we are bound even to our enemies, lest by overlooking their impiety we make them more stubborn. Therefore those men sin shamefully both against other men and against God who today excuse their cowardice under the pretext of Christian patience. In those matters which concern us alone we ought to bear whatever comes; but when the glory of God and the doctrine of truth are brought into danger along with us, then we ought carefully to remember what we owe to them. Yet today most people readily neglect the glory of God, and in defending their own right they go beyond all bounds.

units.la: Debent praeterea hoc Christi dictum probe expendere uiri principes, & quicunq; magistratus gerunt. runt. Nam à Deo quidè est omnis potestas, ut Paulus ait: qui verò hanc obtinent, tunc demum Dei ministri sunt, si eius iudicia exequantur, eius cultū promovēt, ius dicāt cuiq; innocentibus adsint, impios autē & iniustos aliorū oppressores dignis poenis coerceant. Quòd si ista non negligant modò, verum etiā his contraria faciant, dum Dei cultū verū extinguunt, Veritatis doctrinā persequuntur, viduas & pupillos opprimunt, innoxios laedunt, impijs verò aduersus hos patrocinium suum deferunt, denique sanguine fundunt innocentes: tunc tenebrarum potestas & diaboli ministri sunt, cum quo debita suæ impietati stipendia accipient. Sunt hæc nō ipsis modò observanda, verumetiā omnibus alijs, ne talibus obtemperet in ijs, quæ ipsi contra Dei Verbū & veræ pietatis leges mandant. Patienter quidem ferri debent dura quæq; & iniusta principum imperia, ijsq; obedire nos convenit, quoad de solis fortunis, corporibus & vita nostra agitur. At si ulterius progressi ea iubeant, quæ neq; salvo Dei honore, neq; cum conscientiæ integritate fieri possunt, tunc Apostolorum regula locum habeat: Oportet Deo potius obedire quàm hominibus. Est hæc confirmata plurimorum Martyrum exemplis, & proinde abrogari non potest, nisi illos simul omnes pro seditiosis damnare velimus. Sed quia de hac re alibi sæpe diximus, nunc sufficiat tenuisse, nos Iesu Christi vinculis assertos esse in libertate filiorum Dei, & proinde nostri esse officij, ut nos totos illi consecremus, ei denique viuamus atq; moriamur: cui soli debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Princes and all who hold magistracy should also weigh well this saying of Christ. For indeed all power is from God, as Paul says; but those who hold it are then truly ministers of God if they carry out his judgments, promote his worship, administer justice and stand by the innocent, and restrain the wicked and the unjust oppressors of others with fitting punishments. But if they not only neglect these duties but even act contrary to them, extinguishing the true worship of God, persecuting the doctrine of truth, oppressing widows and orphans, harming the innocent, extending their protection to the impious against these, and finally shedding innocent blood, then they are ministers of the power of darkness and of the devil, and from him they receive the wages owed to their impiety. These things must be observed not only by the magistrates themselves but by all others too, so that they do not obey such men in those things which they command against the Word of God and the laws of true piety. Harsh and unjust commands of princes ought indeed to be borne patiently, and we ought to obey them so far as only our fortunes, bodies and life are at stake. But if they go further and command things which can be done neither with the honour of God preserved nor with integrity of conscience, then the rule of the Apostles must apply: We ought to obey God rather than men. This is confirmed by the examples of very many martyrs, and therefore it cannot be abrogated, unless we wish to condemn all of them together as seditious. But since we have often spoken of this matter elsewhere, let it now suffice to have held that we, bound by the chains of Jesus Christ, are asserted in the liberty of the sons of God, and therefore it is our duty to consecrate ourselves wholly to him, and to live and die for him, to whom alone belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCI.

units.la: Comprehensum autē eum duxerunt, & introduxerunt in domū Pontificis Maximi: Petrus verò sequebatur procul. Cumq; accēdissent ignē in medio aulæ, atq; vnà consedissent, sedit & Petrus inter eos. Cùm verò eum vidisset ancilla quædam sedentem ad ignem, intentis in eum oculis dixit: Et iste cum eo erat. Ipse autem abnegauit eum, dicens: Mulier non noui eum. Et paulò post alius videns eum, dixit: Et tu ex ipsis es. Petrus verò ait: Homo, non sum. Et interposita quasi hora vna alius quìdam affirmabat, dicens: Verè & iste cum illo erat: etenim Galilæus est. Ait autem Petrus, Homo, nescio quid dicas. Et illico adhuc ipso loquente, gallus cecinit. Tum conuersus Dominus intuitus est Petrum, et recordatus est Petrus sermonis Domini, quomodo dixisset ei: Priusquam gallus cecinerit, ter me abnegabis. Et egressus foras Petrus, fleuit amare.
units.tr: But they took him and led him away, and brought him into the house of the high priest. Peter followed afar off. When they had kindled a fire in the midst of the hall and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. A certain maid saw him sitting by the fire, looked intently at him, and said, "This man was also with him." But he denied it, saying, "Woman, I do not know him." A little later another saw him and said, "You also are one of them." But Peter said, "Man, I am not." About an hour later another man insisted, saying, "Certainly this fellow also was with him, for he is a Galilean." But Peter said, "Man, I do not know what you are saying." And immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed. Then the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him, "Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times." And Peter went out and wept bitterly.

units.la: SIcuti Deus suos cultores ex gratuita misericordia eligit, & eosdem vocat, ut publica uerae fidei et pietatis exempla in illis toti mundo proponat: ita in ijsdem nostrae etiam carnis infirmitatem spectandam præbet, dum illorum lapsus & vitia non vulgaria in Scripturis commemorat. Et huc in primis debet referri quod de Petro Apostolo narratur. Hic enim inter discipulos, si eius dicta & facta considerentur, Christi amantissimus & in eius gloria asserenda feruentissimus fuit. Eum etiam cum Ioanne & Iacobo Dominus inter intimos habuit, sicuti in resuscitatae Iairi filiæ & clarificationis in monte Thabor facta historijs est uidere: ut iam non repetamus quòd acerbissimæ illius luctæ spectatorem esse voluit, in qua (ut nuper audiuimus) sanguineum sudorem profudit. At nunc hic idem Christum à Sacerdotibus captum primò turpi fuga deserit in hostium manibus, deinde turpius multò eundem abnegat. Est hæc historia admodum memorabilis, & ideò eam Spiritus Sanctus ab omnibus Euangelistis describi voluit. Etenim facit primò ad nostram institutionem, ut nosipsos agnoscere discamus (quam olim nonnulli præcipuam sapientiæ partem esse dixerunt) & nostra infirmitate agnita minus simus confidentes. Deinde perspicuè docet, quàm fallantur quicunque in aliquo hominum fiduciam collocant, quando constat sanctissimos quosque non aliter quàm gratia Dei esse seruatos. Et potest unum hoc exemplum nobis sufficere aduersus eos, qui Petrum Ecclesiæ fundamentū esse contendunt, & in eo quærere docent, quæ in uno Christo habentur. Præterea uerae & salutaris poenitentiæ exemplum hic proponitur, cuius cognitio quàm necessaria sit, omnes norūt, qui in seipsos paulò altius descendunt. Veruntamen breviores erimus in istorum tractatione, quià de his in Marco & Ioanne nostro prolixius est dictum.
units.tr: Just as God chooses his worshippers out of free mercy and calls them, so that in them he may set before the whole world public examples of true faith and piety, so also in the same men he shows the weakness of our own flesh, since Scripture records their lapses and faults, which are no ordinary ones. Chief among these is what is told of the Apostle Peter. For among the disciples, if his words and deeds are considered, he was most devoted to Christ and most fervent in asserting his glory. The Lord also counted him among his intimate companions, as we can see from the histories of the raising of Jairus's daughter and of the transfiguration on Mount Tabor. I need not mention that he wished Peter to be a witness of his most bitter struggle, in which, as we lately heard, he sweated drops of blood. Yet now this same Peter, after Christ has been seized by the priests, first deserts him in shameful flight into the hands of his enemies, and then, far more shamefully, denies him. This story is very memorable, and that is why the Holy Spirit wished it to be described by all the Evangelists. For it serves first for our instruction, so that we learn to know ourselves (which some of old called the chief part of wisdom), and, having recognized our weakness, become less confident. Second, it clearly teaches how deceived all those are who place their trust in any man, since it is plain that the most holy are preserved only by the grace of God. This one example can be enough for us against those who contend that Peter is the foundation of the Church and teach that what is found in Christ alone should be sought in him. Moreover, here is set before us an example of true and saving repentance, the necessity of which everyone knows who descends somewhat deeper into himself. Nevertheless, we shall be brief in treating these matters, because they have been discussed at greater length in Mark and John.

units.la: Orditur autem huius historiae narrationē Euangelista à loci circunstantia his verbis: Comprehensum Iesum duxerunt, & introduxerunt in domū Pontificis Maximi: Petrus verò sequebatur procul. Ioannes diligentius exponit, quomodo & cuius opera in hanc domum peruenerit. Et mirum uideri poterat, Christum in Pontificis domum captiuum abripi, & eius abnegandi occasionem illic inueniri potuisse, ubi uera fidei confessione omnia resonare debebant. Sed quales tunc temporis Sacerdotes Iudaeorum fuerint, non uno loco demonstrauimus: & uoluit isto exemplo nos Spiritus sanctus admonere, ubi maxima fidei & saluti nostrae pericula struantur. Inter eos nimirum, qui ut religionem sibi quaestum faciat, à simplici Veritatis doctrina discedunt, & eam humanis traditionibus corrumpunt. Neminem ergo uel locorum uetus authoritas, uel magnificus antistitum splendor & tituli ambitiosi decipiant, quò minus tunc quoq; salutē suam (ut Paulus monuit) cum timore & tremore custodiant atq; perficiant pij, ubi nihil periculi esse uidetur. Vt autē ex Petri historia plus ad nos fructus redundet, tria eius capita praecipua excutienda erunt. Inter quae primum est ipsum peccatum, quod commisit. Alterum huius occasio & causa. Postremum illius conuersio siue poenitentia.
units.tr: The Evangelist begins the narration of this history with the circumstances of the place, in these words: "They took Jesus and led him into the house of the high priest, but Peter followed afar off." John describes more carefully how and by whose agency Peter came into this house. And it might seem strange that Christ should be dragged away captive into the house of the high priest, and that the occasion of denying him should be found there, where everything ought to resound with the true confession of faith. But we have shown in more than one place what the priests of the Jews were like at that time, and the Holy Spirit wished by this example to warn us where the greatest dangers to our faith and salvation are laid. Namely, among those who make religion a source of gain, who depart from the simple doctrine of truth and corrupt it with human traditions. Therefore let no one be deceived either by the ancient authority of a place or by the splendour and ambitious titles of the bishops, so that the godly, as Paul warned, may still work out their salvation with fear and trembling, even where no danger seems to exist. Now, so that more fruit may flow to us from Peter's history, three of its chief points must be examined. The first among them is the sin itself which he committed. The second is its occasion and cause. The last is his conversion or repentance.

units.la: Quoad peccatū, scio aliquos praepostero Petri studio illud extenuare, uel potiùs id facere, ut suā leuitate excusent, qua ipsi quotidie Christū abnegant. Sed neq; nostra defensione opus habet ille, qui iam pridē cum Deo in gratia redijt, neq; nos quicquā proficiemus aduersus Spiritus sancti ipsum accusantis testimonia. Extat enim Christi generalis de hoc peccato sententia, quā aduersus oēs pronunciat, qui ipsum aut Euangelium suum coram homi[?]bus negauerint. Idē Petrū de illo praemonuerat, & omne hoc Satanae opus fore dixerat, qui ipsos[?] oēs uentilare ac dissipare expetiuerit. Sed et conuersionis Petri illic mentione fecit, quae solauox illū à Christo recessisse docet. Quid, quòd ille ipse peccati sui magnitudinem agnouit, et huius cōscientia perculsus amare fleuit? Ita certè suis lachrymis (quod et D. Augustinus annotauit) suos defensores arguit. Quare nos omissa hac inutili examinatione peccati istius, potius uideamus quid ille fecerit, ut facilius nobis possimus cauere, ne quid simile etiā nobis accidat. Primò cum ancilla quaedā eū uidisset, & intentis oculis in eū, dixisset: Et iste cū eo erat: ita nimirum illum quoq; Christi discipulū esse innuens: respondit ille: Mulier, nō noui eum. Ioannes ancillā ostiariā fuisse scribit. Matthaeus verò Petrū palam coram omnibus dixisse tradit: Mulier, nescio quid dicas. Fuit haec ignaua & turpis dissimulatio, qua fingit se non intelligere, de quo nam uerba fiant. Pudet ergo illū iam Christi, quem non puduerat ipsius, cum piscator esset uilis & obscurus. Interim verò non pudet eum mendacij, quo se illū nouisse negat, de quo communi omnium discipulorum nomine dixerat, Tu es Christus, Filius Dei uiuentis. Item: Verba uitae aeternae habes, & nos credimus & cognouimus, quòd tu es Christus, Filius Dei uiuentis. Est ergo haec inexcusabilis timiditas, qua id palam negat, quod prius in publico fuerat confessus. Nec dubitauerim hoc nō alio consilio ab ipso factū fuisse, quàm ut ista dissimulatione sibi caueret, ne quod grauius incurreret periculū, et contra Christū aliquid facere cogeretur, maiori reprehensione dignū. Sed multùm animo suo falsus est. Nam foras egressum (ut Marcus annotauit) eadē ancilla rursus conspicata, denuo eum astantibus prodit, & causa est, ut ab ijs quoq; compellaretur, & quidam ipsum ex sectatoribus captiui istius Iesu esse diceret. Iam ergo secundò negat, idq; cum iure iurando: sicuti apud Matthaeu est uidere. Itaq; cum abnegatione, alterū quoq; peccatum concurrit, quòd temerarium iusiurandum adhibet, contra Christi praeceptum, qui ne iuremus mandat. Nec multò post alius quidam ei fortius instat, qui argumentis quoq; cum conuincere studet, quòd & in horto eum cum Christo uiderit, & sermonis dialectus ipsum Galilaeum esse demonstret. Ibi ne iuramento quidem contentus, execrationibus quoq; & diris utitur, ut ista suspicione sese liberet. Sunt haec dura & horrenda admodum, si cum eo Petri zelo atq; feruore conferantur, quo illū prius flagrauisse uidimus. Et sufficit exemplum hoc ad argumentum nostrae carnis infirmitatem, et quàm non temere à Paulo dictum sit: Qui stat, uideat ne cadat.
units.tr: As to the sin, I know that some, with misplaced zeal for Peter, minimize it, or rather do so in order to excuse their own levity, by which they deny Christ every day. But he who long ago returned to God in grace has no need of our defence, nor shall we gain anything against the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who accuses him. For there is Christ's general sentence on this sin, which he pronounces against all who deny him or his Gospel before men. He had forewarned Peter about this very thing, and had said that all this would be the work of Satan, who sought to sift them all like wheat. But he also made mention there of Peter's conversion, which alone shows that he had withdrawn from Christ. What of the fact that he recognized the greatness of his sin, and, struck by the awareness of it, wept bitterly? Surely by his tears (as St. Augustine also observed) he convicts those who defend him. Wherefore, setting aside this unprofitable examination of the sin, let us rather see what he did, so that we may more easily guard against anything similar happening to us. First, when a certain maid had seen him and, looking intently at him, had said, "This man was also with him," thereby hinting that he too was a disciple of Christ, he replied, "Woman, I do not know him." John writes that the maid was a doorkeeper. Matthew, however, relates that Peter said openly before everyone, "Woman, I do not know what you are saying." This was an idle and shameful pretence, by which he feigned not to understand of whom the words were spoken. He was therefore ashamed of Christ, whom he had not been ashamed of when he was a humble and obscure fisherman. Meanwhile, however, he was not ashamed of the lie by which he denies that he knows him, of whom he had spoken in the name of all the disciples: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Likewise: "You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God." This is therefore an inexcusable cowardice, by which he denies openly what he had earlier confessed in public. Nor do I doubt that he did this with no other purpose than to protect himself by this dissimulation, lest he incur some graver danger and be compelled to do something against Christ, which would deserve a greater reproach. But he was greatly mistaken in his mind. For when he had gone out (as Mark noted), the same maid saw him again and betrayed him once more to the bystanders, with the result that they too addressed him, and one of them said that he was one of the followers of that captive Jesus. So now, for the second time, he denies him, and this with an oath, as may be seen in Matthew. Thus, along with the denial, a second sin is added, namely that he uses a rash oath, against Christ's command, who forbids us to swear. Not long after, another man presses him more strongly, seeking to convict him by arguments too, since he had seen him with Christ in the garden and his dialect shows that he is a Galilean. Here, not content with an oath, he also uses curses and imprecations, so that he may free himself from this suspicion. These things are very harsh and dreadful, if they are compared with that zeal and fervour of Peter's which we have seen blazing in him before. And this example is enough for the argument of our fleshly weakness, and of how rightly Paul said: "Let him who stands take heed lest he fall."

units.la: In primis autē obseruari hic debet, quod Christus praedixerat: Priusquā gallus cecinerit, tu me ter abnegabis. Exeo enim colligitur, illius abnegatione tūc quoq; fieri, quādo fide in illū obiter modò dissimulamus. Scio equidē multis hoc durius uideri, quādo haec hodie prima sapientia esse uidetur, si quis oēs de religione & fide quaestiones declinare, aut his motis aliarū rerum mentione inijcere possit. Et hi sunt, quos pleriq; à sapientia & modestia commendant. Sed ut ij, qui in primo scalae gradu labuntur, ferè per alios quoq; ruunt: ita qui semel in fidei ac religionis causa claudicare aut labi incipiunt, cipiunt, & à libera illa confitendi ingenuitate discedunt, ij quoq; in peius subinde proficiunt, ut mox diuersis uerbis Christum abnegent, adhæc alienis sacris communicando tantumnon iusiurandū dent ijs, qui ad superstitiones illos solicitant: quò fit, ut tandem dirus imprecationibus seipsos devoueant, & toti à Christo disiellantur, in quo uno benedictio & salus habetur. Sequitur tandem, quod ijdē in sensum reprobum traditi uitam uiuunt ab omni professione Christiana alienam, qua omne id quod ex hac reliquum esse uidebatur, totum quoq; abijciunt atq; conculcant. Discant ergo hoc Petri exemplo admoniti primum abnegationis Christi gradum cauere, qui ulterius progredi nolunt.
units.tr: In the first place it must be noted here what Christ had foretold: "Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times." From this it is gathered that denial of him also takes place whenever we dissemble our faith in him, even only in passing. I know that many think this harsher than it should be, since today it seems the first wisdom if someone can sidestep all questions of religion and faith, or, when they are raised, turn the talk to other matters. And these are the people whom most commend for wisdom and moderation. But just as those who slip on the first step of a ladder usually fall the rest of the way, so those who once begin to limp or slip in the cause of faith and religion, and depart from that free frankness of confession, go further downhill after that, so that soon they deny Christ in different words. Moreover, by sharing in alien rites they practically swear an oath to those who solicit them to superstitions. The result is that at last they devote themselves to dreadful curses and are wholly cut off from Christ, in whom alone blessing and salvation are found. Finally it follows that they, given over to a reprobate mind, live a life alien to every Christian profession, and throw away and trample underfoot whatever remained of that profession. Let those, then, who are unwilling to go further, learn from Peter's example to beware first of the initial step of denying Christ.

units.la: Quod ut facilius fiat, proderit uidere, qua occasione & quibus causis Petrus ut Christum abnegaret, adductus fuerit, quod alterū huius historiæ caput est. Scribit Lucas, eum procul aut à longinquo secutū fuisse, cum Christus duceretur. Ergo ex fuga redijt, in quam discipuli omnes dispersi fuerant, ut apud Matthæum legitur, & quod fore omnino ille prædixerat. Neq; ei satis fuit aliquo usq; illum sequi, in domū quoq; Pontificis cupit ingredi, nec desistit ab instituto donec intromittatur. Et hoc magni amoris argumentū, quo eum præ aliis flagrauisse scimus, & quem periculi uix dum præteriti recordatio extinguere non potuit. Confidentiæ autem est, quod admonitionum Christi immemor in eam domum ingreditur, in qua uerę fidei & eius confessioni locum nullum esse non poterat ignorare. Neq; excusat eum alterius discipuli exemplum, qui & ipse eò ingressus est. Nam ut huic propter notitiam & familiaritatem minus periculi erat: ita Petrum cautiorem esse oportuit, cùm quod ipsi hac nocte adhuc euenturum esset, Christus aperte prædixisset. Et quamuis alter ille ingressus sit, credibile est, eum prudentius rem gessisse, ut ex occulto omnia spectaret, non autè se prophano illi & impio furum siue seruorum sacerdotalium manipulo immiscéret. Certè nihil huius de illo Euangelistæ tradunt. At Petrus quàm primùm intromissus est, se improbis illis coniungit, & propter frigus quòd paulò acrius erat, ad eundem ignem cum illis confidet. Deinde oblitus ingenuitatis fidei & præceptorum Christi, quibus liberam sui confessionē requirit, quam nullus siue metus siue pudor impediat, ad artes ipse conuertitur. Et primò quidem (ut audiuimus) ignorantiam prætexit, ut ij qui quod illis minus gratum est audiunt. Adhæc cum se iam labascere sentiret, ne quidè subito pedem retrahit, sed sensim se in ueštibulum subducit, ut uel illic lateat, uel rursus inde per occasionem se foras propripiat. Tria ergo Petro tam pudendi lapsus causa fuerunt: Confidentia nimirum ex inconsiderato Christi zelo enata, Consortium cum hostibus Christi, & Prudentia carnis.
units.tr: To make this easier, it will help to see by what occasion and for what causes Peter was led to deny Christ, which is the second point of this history. Luke writes that he followed afar off, when Christ was led away. So he returned from the flight into which all the disciples had scattered, as Matthew relates, and as Christ had foretold would certainly happen. Nor was it enough for him to follow Christ up to a point; he also wished to enter the high priest's house, and he did not give up his purpose until he was admitted. This is a great proof of love, by which we know he burned more fiercely than the others, and which the memory of a danger scarcely past could not quench. But it was presumption that led him, forgetful of Christ's warnings, into that house, where he could not fail to know there was no place for true faith and its confession. Nor does the example of the other disciple, who also went in there, excuse him. For as that disciple was in less danger because of his acquaintance and familiarity, so Peter ought to have been the more cautious, since Christ had plainly foretold what was to happen to him that very night. And although the other did go in, it is credible that he acted more prudently, watching everything from a hidden place, and did not mingle himself with that profane and impious band of thieves or priestly servants. Certainly the Evangelists hand down nothing of this about him. But Peter, as soon as he was admitted, joins himself to those wicked men, and because of the cold, which was rather sharp, he sits down with them by the same fire. Then, forgetting the frankness of faith and the precepts of Christ, which demand a free confession that neither fear nor shame should hinder, he himself turns to crafty devices. And first, indeed, as we heard, he feigns ignorance, as people do when they hear what is unwelcome to them. Besides, when he now felt himself already faltering, he did not draw back his foot at once, but gradually withdrew into the vestibule, so that he might either hide there or slip out again from there when an opportunity offered. There were therefore three causes of Peter's so shameful a fall: confidence arising from ill-considered zeal for Christ; fellowship with the enemies of Christ; and the prudence of the flesh.

units.la: Et hæc sunt, qui hodie etiā multos eò adducunt, ut Christi aut fidei uerę abnegatores fiant. Sunt enim nonnulli, qui Euangelij doctrinā nō solum audiūt, uerumetiā amāt, & se pro eius defensione nihil nō facturos esse sibi persuadent. At quia minus attendunt, quāta sit nostra infirmitas, & quàm lubrica atq; periculosa in uasis hisce cestaceis (ut Pauli uerbis utar) fidei atq; salutis possessio, frequenter sese periculis nō necessarijs obijciunt. Cùm enim domi possent quieté uiuere, & sua forte contenti Christo in libertate spiritus atq; corporis seruire, in ea loca se conferunt, ubi neq; prædicatio uerbi, nec exercitia uerę religionis admittuntur, et illic se nō modò fidei integritate seruaturos, sed simul multos alios ad huius cognitionē adducturos esse, deniq; toti Ecclesiæ se utiles fore sibi persuadet. Et hoc ferè ab illis fit, qui uel principū Papisticorū, siue Episcoporū atq; Abbatū seruitijs se mancipant. Metuunt tales, ne culina ipsis frigeat, & horū famulitio se coiungūt, ut ad eundē cū illis focū calescat, opes augeat, dignitatibus accumulentur, & ita generis sui splendore atq; nobilitate facilius tueri & ad posteros quoq; propagare possint. Nihil aut minus in animo habent, quā defectione à fide & Christi siue Veritatis abnegatione. Quid uero illis accidit? Idē planè quod Petro. Ut enim hic ad prunas pontificias ex feruentissimo Christi discipulo & oppugnatore languidissimus factus est: ita illi indies, frigescunt, & culinarū taliū nidore oppleti feruore paulatim omne deponūt. Quò fit, ut quando inge nua et costanti confessione maximè opus erat, ipsi ad ignauas, artes & humanæ prudentiæ cōsilia conuertantur, quæ proxima quæq; pericula declinare & subterfugere docet. Itaq; quando impios aduersus Christi meritū sermones audiunt, quibus tota salutis ratio proscinditur, & fideles illius ministri turpissimè lacerātur, illi surdis auribus illos prætereunt, seq; aliquid huius audiuisse dissimulat. Sin ue rō suā super his sententia rogentur, plus quàm pueriliter balbutiūt, & omne de ijs iudiciū declinant, idq; ad eos pertinere aiunt, quorū ea sit professio, ut causam religionis dijudicare & propugnare debeant. Et quàmuis multis indicijs quotidie deprehendat quàm parū tutū sit ipsis inter tales uiuere, et quàm plena insidiarū sint omnia: adhuc tamen moras nectūt, & ne quā fortunarū iactura faciant.
units.tr: And these are the things which even today lead many to become deniers of Christ or of true faith. For there are some who not only hear the doctrine of the Gospel but even love it, and persuade themselves that they would do anything in its defence. But because they pay less attention to how great our weakness is, and how slippery and perilous is the possession of faith and salvation in these earthen vessels (to use Paul's words), they often expose themselves to unnecessary dangers. For when they could live quietly at home, content perhaps with their own means, and serve Christ in freedom of spirit and body, they betake themselves to places where neither the preaching of the Word nor the exercises of true religion are admitted. There they persuade themselves that they will not only keep the integrity of their faith but at the same time lead many others to know it, and that they will finally be useful to the whole Church. This is mostly done by those who put themselves at the service of Papist princes, or of bishops and abbots. Such people fear that their kitchen may grow cold, so they join these men's households, so that they may warm themselves at the same hearth, increase their wealth, be heaped with dignities, and thus more easily protect the splendour and nobility of their family and pass it on to posterity. Yet they have nothing less in mind than defection from the faith and abnegation of Christ or of the Truth. And what happens to them? Exactly what happened to Peter. For just as he, from being the most fervent disciple and opponent of Christ, became most languid at the Papist fire, so they grow colder day by day, and, overcome by the fumes of such kitchens, gradually lay aside all their fervour. The result is that when frank and steadfast confession is most needed, they turn to cowardly devices and the counsels of human prudence, which teach them to avoid and slip away from every nearby danger. So when they hear impious words against the merit of Christ, by which the whole basis of salvation is torn apart, and his faithful ministers are most shamefully mangled, they pass by with deaf ears and pretend they have heard nothing of it. But if they are asked their opinion on these matters, they stammer more than childishly and evade all judgement, saying that this belongs to those whose profession it is to judge and defend the cause of religion. And although every day they perceive by many signs how little safe it is for them to live among such people, and how full of snares everything is, still they delay, and they do not want to suffer any loss of fortune.

units.la: Occasio, quæ Petrum fecit abnegatorem.
units.tr: The occasion which made Peter a denier.

units.la: Quid hodie ab negatores fa ciat. aut eos offendant, quorum amicitiam atq; fautore sibi utilem experti sunt, paulatim discessione mo- liuntur, & nescio quâ temporis occasionem commodiorem subinde expectant. Ita verò seipsos magis atq; magis implicant, ut vel fide abiurare & seipsos execrari cogantur, aut vitâ cum fortunis omni- bus amittere. Exempla quibus hoc probari poterat, multa in historijs omnibus occurrunt. Sed heu prob dolor, quotidie, quæ me vera dicere testantur. Discite ergo ô fratres Christiani suspectâ habere spiritus aut animi vestri confidentiam, neq; vos vel lucri vel cuiuscunque commoditatis spe periculis nō necessarijs obijcite. Quin potius Mosem imitamini, qui populi Dei afflictissimâ conditionem opi- bus & voluptatibus Ægypti anteposuit. Danielem item & socios, qui etsi aulâ Babylonicam relin- quere non possent, leguminibus tamē vesci maluerunt, ne aulicis cupedijs legem patriam violarent. Melior est dies unus in domo Domini, quàm mille in tentorijs impiorum. Potior item eorum condi- tio, qui ad Ecclesiæ limen sedent, quàm qui in Antichristi Synagoga primos subsellioru gradus oc- cupant. Si qui verò inter illos versamini, citò ex Babylone illa vos proripite, & memores estote u- xoris Lothi, ne dum moras vestro iudicio quæstuosas nectitis, vobisipsis sempiternâ ignominiam ac- cersatis. Nullus humanæ prudentiæ locus, ubi Dei gloria et animarum salus in periculum veniunt. In his enim unum Deum audire oportet, cuius verbo obtemperare suprema sapientia est.
units.tr: What deniers do today: when they have offended those whose friendship and favour they found useful to themselves, they gradually plan a break, and meanwhile keep waiting for some more convenient opportunity. Thus they entangle themselves more and more, until they are compelled either to abjure the faith and curse themselves, or to lose their lives along with all their fortunes. Examples proving this are found in abundance in all histories. But alas, to our grief, daily ones attest that what I say is true. Learn, therefore, O Christian brothers, to regard as suspect the confidence of your spirit or mind, and do not expose yourselves to unnecessary dangers in hope of gain or of any advantage. Rather imitate Moses, who preferred the afflicted condition of God's people to the riches and pleasures of Egypt. Likewise Daniel and his companions, who, although they could not leave the Babylonian court, preferred to eat pulses rather than violate the law of their fathers with courtly delicacies. "One day in the house of the Lord is better than a thousand in the tents of the wicked." Likewise better is the condition of those who sit at the threshold of the Church than of those who occupy the first rows of seats in the synagogue of Antichrist. But if any of you are living among them, tear yourselves quickly out of that Babylon, and remember Lot's wife, lest, while you make delays that seem profitable to your judgement, you bring upon yourselves everlasting shame. There is no place for human prudence where the glory of God and the salvation of souls are in danger. For in these matters one must hear the one God, and to obey his word is the highest wisdom.

units.la: Caeterum accedamus ad tertiu huius loci caput, quo Petri pœnitentia describitur, qua ad Deū re- uersus damnationis æternæ supplicium effugit, quod abnegando meruerat. Narrat hanc Lucas eo or- dine, ut primo quæ illa præcesserunt, eiusq; vel occasio vel causa fuerunt, exponat: deinde verò quid fecerit docet, eiusq; pœnitentiam à signis siue effectis describit. Ad primum hæc verba pertinent: Et illico adhuc ipso loquente gallus cecinit: Tum conuersus Dominus intuitus est Petrum. Conti- nentur his antecedentia: quæ nos pœnitentiæ huius occasionem primam & causam efficientem possu- mus dicere. Occasio fuit, quòd canit gallus, & ita fit illud, cuius Dominus in ultima Cœna memine- rat. Fuitq; hoc signum eo efficacius, quòd in ipso temporis puncto aut momento accidit. Nam illico (inquit Lucas) adhuc ipso loquente gallus cecinit. Adumbrantur autè per galli cantum omnes ex- ternæ admonitiones, quibus carnem nostram dormitantem excitari necesse est, ut excusso slupore, quo fere detinetur, de peccatis suis, de Dei ira, & de eadem placanda cogitet. Nam nisi id fiat, ferè securi in luto hoc iacemus, & tunc quoq; optimè de nobis agi arbitramur, quando salus nostra in ex- tremo discrimine est constituta. Hic autem variis medijs ac rationibus Deus utitur. Ordinarium & iam inde à rerum origine usitatissimum est Verbum eius, quod olim patribus propria voce re- uelauit, ut in Adami, Caini & aliorum historijs cernitur: postea autem per homines ad hoc legitimè vocatos publicè prædicari voluit, & cuius usus etiam hisce novissimis temporibus frequens est. Ad hoc pertinent admonitiones priuatæ, quæ per amicos aut homines aliqua authoritate præditos, siue nobis aliqua ratione coiunctos fiunt. Conuitia item et obtrectationes inimicorum, qui etiamsi prauo odij affectu rapiantur, sæpe tamen nos excitant ad seriam nostræ salutis curam, quando ea nobis ob- iiciunt & exprobrant, quæ amici hactenus dissimulauerunt. Galli quoq; cantus censeri debent im- prouisi casus, morbi subiti, aut quæcunq; aliquid mali molientibus accidunt. Refer deniq; huc prodi- gia, omina, ostenta, & nunquâ visos impune Cometas: fulmina quoq;, & quæcunq; alia sunt eius ge- neris, quibus erga gentes quoq; usus est olim Deus, & quæ irae eius & alicuius futuri mali præsagia esse, adeò tritum fuit apud omnes, ut nobilis ille Poeta vili & obscuro pastori hæc verba tribuat: Sæpe malum hoc nobis, si mens non læua fuisset, De cœlo tactas memini prædicere quercus.
units.tr: But let us come to the third part of this passage, in which Peter's repentance is described. By it, having turned back to God, he escaped the punishment of eternal damnation that his denial had deserved. Luke narrates this in an order: first he sets out what came before and what was the occasion or cause of it, then he teaches what Peter did, and describes his repentance by its signs or effects. The words that belong to the first part are these: "And immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed. Then the Lord turned and looked at Peter." What precedes these words we may call the first occasion and the efficient cause of this repentance. The occasion was the crowing of the cock, and so the thing the Lord had mentioned at the last supper came to pass. This sign was all the more effective because it happened at that very point or moment of time. For Luke says, "immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed." By the crowing of the cock are represented all the outward warnings by which our drowsy flesh must be roused, so that, shaking off the stupor that generally holds us, we may think about our sins, about the wrath of God, and about how it might be appeased. For unless this happens, we lie in this mud almost carelessly secure, and we think that all is well with us even when our salvation is in the greatest danger. God uses various means and methods here. The most common and customary means, from the very beginning of things, is his Word, which he once revealed to the fathers by his own voice, as can be seen in the histories of Adam, Cain and others; afterwards he willed it to be preached publicly through men lawfully called to this, and its use is frequent even in these latest times. To this belong the private admonitions that come through friends, or through men endowed with some authority, or those joined to us by some tie. Likewise the reproaches and censures of enemies, who, though they are carried away by a wicked hatred, often still stir us to a serious care for our salvation, when they throw in our faces and upbraid us with things that friends have hitherto passed over in silence. The crowing of the cock must also be counted as unforeseen misfortunes, sudden illnesses, or whatever happens to those who are plotting some evil. Finally, refer here prodigies, omens, portents, and comets that have never been seen without consequence; and lightnings too, and whatever else is of that kind, by which God in the past dealt with the nations also, and which are signs of his anger and of some future evil. It has been so commonplace among all people that the famous poet attributes these words to a humble and obscure shepherd: "Often, had my mind not been heedless, I remember the oaks struck from heaven foretelling this evil to us."

units.la: Et quoadista, nunquâ suo officio deest Deus, quod Amos testatur, quando illū negat aliquid facere, quin prius seruis suis Prophetis id reuelet, ut alij per hos admoneantur. Quia aut tanta est hominū uaecordia, ut illa nō semper obseruent, aut saltem nō cogitent, in què finè aut usum fiant, alterū acce- dat oportet: ut nimirū nos sua gratia respiciat Christus et animi aures nobis vellicet, quod hic Petro fecit: & nunquâ non nobis quoq; facit, quando conscientiæ stimulis nos pungit, ut cogitemus hæc iræ diuinæ indicia esse, & ideò nos de peccatis, quibus hanc meruimus, deq; nostra cū Deo reconciliatio- ne cogitare debere. Simul autè ad hoc nobis seruit istorū cōsideratio, ne in pœnitentia nostra meritū statuamus, quando de illa ne cogitamus quidē, nisi animos nostros Deus excitet, & meliores cogita- tiones suggerat. Quæ causa est, quòd Christum nobis non modò remissionis peccatorum, nerumeti- am pœnitentiæ authorem Apostoli docent, & idem hanc quoq; in suo nomine prædicare iubet.
units.tr: And in this matter God never fails in his duty, as Amos bears witness, when he says that he does nothing without first revealing it to his servants the prophets, so that others may be warned through them. But because human folly is so great that people do not always heed these things, or at least do not consider to what end or purpose they happen, a second thing must be added: namely, that Christ should look upon us with his grace and pluck at the ears of our minds, as he did here with Peter. And he never fails to do this for us too, when he pricks us with the goads of conscience, so that we may think these are tokens of the divine wrath, and therefore that we ought to think about the sins by which we have deserved it, and about our reconciliation with God. At the same time, the consideration of these things serves us so that we do not set up merit in our repentance, since we would not even think about it unless God stirred up our minds and suggested better thoughts. This is why the apostles teach that Christ is the author not only of the forgiveness of sins but also of repentance, and he himself commands that it be preached in his name too.

units.la: Porrò quando Deus suo erga nos officio fungitur, nos Petrum imitari conuenit, de quo Lucas sic scribit: Et recordatus est Petrus sermonis Domini, quomodo dixisset ei: Priusquam gallus cecinerit, ter me abnegabis: Et egressus foras Petrus flevit amarè. Tria fecisse dicitur: Primo recordatus est uerborum Domini: Non quidem eorum modo, quae in ultima Cœna illi dixerat, verumetiam aliorum quibus idem huius sceleris magnitudinem exposuerat, dicens: Si quem puduerit meæt uerborum meorum coram natione hac prava & adultera, eius pudebit & Filium hominis, quando veniet in gloria Patris sui, cum Angelis suis sanctis. Elucet autem in eo indoles filiorum Dei, qui etiamsi ex carnis infirmitate sæpe labantur, manet tamen in eis semen Dei, quo fit ut leuissima quæq; occasio illius uerbum eius in mentem reuocet, & mox in uiam redeant. Nec enim frigidam fuisse hanc recordationem, ex eo apparet, quod mox foras exiuit Petrus, quod alterum suæ poenitentiæ membrum est. Multum illum peccati odiū, quod tantum animo suo concepit, ut iam omnia detestetur, quæ illius el minima ex parte illius causa fuerunt. Sequitur tertio loco fletus amarus & tristes lachrimæ, quas pristinæ cum Christo familiaritatis & præsentis huius ingratitudinis & turpissimæ abnegationis considerationi illi extorsit. Habes igitur in Petri exemplo ueræ poenitentiæ typum, ad quam (ut alibi monuimus) requiruntur peccati agnitio, contritio siue dolor, & uitæ emendatio. At ne in ipso (quod aiunt) limine offendamus, uerborum Dei nos meminisse oportet, ut ex illis de peccatis nostris iudicemus. Nam nisi id fiat, facilè nobis ipsis blandiemur, & leuia putabimus ea esse, quæ Deo quam maximè exosa sunt. Qui verò de peccatis rectè iudicant, ij procul dubio dolorem animo grauissimum concipient, quia illorum memoriam nō possunt excutere, quæ simul iræ Dei sensum parit, quo germanis eius filijs nihil intolerabilius potest accidere. Parit hic publicam peccati confessionem & pias lachrymas, quibus Dei gratiam & misericordiam imploramus. Non autem in his consistit poenitentia vera, sed peccatum detestatur, occasiones illius omnes declinat, & his relictis ad Deum reuertitur, in cuius gratiam certam salutis fiduciam collocat. Ideo illam vulgo conuersionem ad Deum esse definiunt. Delineamus hæc breuiter, quia causam hac alibi fusius tractauimus. Nunc quæ nostri officij sunt tenere sufficiat. Apparent passim irati Dei argumenta, & nos poenas quanta cunq; meruisse non potest negare, quisquis effrenem, quæ passim regnat, peccandi licentiam & immanem Dei contemptum obseruauerit. Flagitat hic poenitentiam à nobis, & ad se conuersis gratiam suam sponte offert. Neq; desunt tristia eorum exempla, qui in contumacia sua misere pereunt. Excitent nos ista, ut relicto in felici illo diaboli & peccati seruitio, totis animis ad Deum conuertamur, & uitam uiuamus nouam in Christo Iesu, qui nobis iustitia, satisfactio & redemptio à Patre factus est. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, when God performs his office toward us, it is fitting that we imitate Peter, of whom Luke writes thus: "And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him: Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. And going out, Peter wept bitterly." He is said to have done three things. First, he remembered the words of the Lord: not only those he had spoken to him at the last supper, but also the others in which he had set out to them the greatness of this crime, saying: "If anyone is ashamed of me and of my words before this adulterous and perverse generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with his holy angels." Now in this appears the character of the sons of God, who, even if they often stumble through the weakness of the flesh, still have the seed of God remaining in them; so it happens that the slightest occasion brings his word back to mind, and they soon return to the way. For that this remembrance was not cold appears from the fact that Peter soon went out, which is the second part of his repentance. He conceived such a hatred of sin in his mind that he now detests everything that was even in the smallest part the cause of it. Thirdly follows bitter weeping and sad tears, which the consideration of his former familiarity with Christ, of this present ingratitude, and of his most shameful denial wrung from him. You have, then, in Peter's example, the pattern of true repentance, for which (as we have noted elsewhere) the recognition of sin, contrition or sorrow, and the amendment of life are required. But so that we do not stumble at the very threshold, as they say, we must remember the words of God, so that we may judge our sins by them. For unless we do this, we will easily flatter ourselves and think those things trivial which are most hateful to God. Those, however, who judge rightly about sins will undoubtedly conceive a very grave sorrow in their minds, because they cannot shake off the memory of them; this at the same time brings forth a sense of God's wrath, and nothing can be more intolerable to his true children. This produces the public confession of sin and pious tears, by which we implore God's grace and mercy. But true repentance does not consist in these things alone; it detests sin, avoids all its occasions, and, leaving these behind, turns back to God, in whose grace it places a sure confidence of salvation. Therefore they commonly define it as conversion to God. We have sketched these things briefly, because we have treated this cause more fully elsewhere; for now it is enough to hold to what belongs to our task. Signs of God's anger appear everywhere, and no one who observes the unbridled license for sinning that reigns everywhere, and the monstrous contempt of God, can deny that we have deserved punishments, however great. He demands repentance from us, and to those who turn to him he freely offers his grace. Nor are there lacking sad examples of those who perish miserably in their obstinacy. Let these things stir us, so that, having left behind the unhappy slavery of the devil and sin, we may turn to God with our whole souls and live a new life in Christ Jesus, who has been made by the Father our righteousness, satisfaction and redemption. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCII.
units.tr: HOMILY 202.

units.la: At ij qui vnà tenebant Iesum, ei illudebant, cædentes eum. Et cum eum obuoluissent, verberabant faciem eius, & interrogabant eum, dicentes: Vaticinare, quis sit qui te percusit? Et alia multa conuitiantes dicebant in eum. Et ut ortus est dies, conuenit ordo seniorum populi, & principes Sacerdotum & Scribæ: & adduxerunt eum in suum consessum, dicentes: Nū tu es ille Christus? dic nobis. Dixit autē eis: Si vobis dixero, nequaquā credetis: Quod si etiam interrogauero, nequaquā respondebitis mihi, neque dimittetis. Ab hoc tempore erit Filius hominis sedens ad dextram potentiæ Dei. Dixerunt autē omnes: Tu ergo es Filius Dei? Ipse verò dixit eis: Vos dicitis me esse. At illi dixerunt: Quid amplius egemus testimonio? Ipsi enim audiuimus ex ore ipsius.
units.tr: And the men who held Jesus mocked him and beat him. And when they had blindfolded him, they struck his face and asked him, saying, "Prophesy: who is it that struck you?" And they said many other insulting things against him. And as day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered, both the chief priests and the scribes, and they led him into their council, saying, "If you are the Christ, tell us." But he said to them, "If I tell you, you will not believe; and if I ask you, you will not answer me or let me go. From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God." And they all said, "Are you then the Son of God?" He said to them, "You say that I am." And they said, "What further need do we have of testimony? For we ourselves have heard it from his own mouth."

units.la: Dui Euangelistæ multis & prolixè describunt passionis dominicæ historiam, partim quidem ut certior nobis esse possit, quæ in huius merito fundata est, salutis nostræ fiducia, quando æternū Dei Filiū οἷα ea sustinuisse cōstat, quæ nos merebamur: partim uerò, ne aduersis, quæ nobis accidunt, offendamur. Est hoc obseruatu ualde necessarium. Nam etsi pleriq; fateantur salutē nostram omnem ex solius Christi merito pendere, ijdem tamē de huius doctrina fere dubitare incipiunt, quando hanc à
units.tr: The two Evangelists describe the history of the Lord's Passion at length and in detail, partly so that we may have more certain confidence in our salvation, which rests on his merit, since it is clear that the eternal Son of God endured those things which we had deserved; and partly so that we may not be offended by the adversities that befall us. This is very necessary to observe. For although most people acknowledge that all our salvation depends on the merit of Christ alone, yet these same people almost begin to doubt this doctrine when they see it attacked and condemned by the most powerful and learned men, and often even crushed by force and arms.

units.la: Marcus homil. 123. & 124. potentissimis doctissimis oppugnari & damnari, frequenter etiā ui et armis opprimi uident. Tunc ergo meminerimus, Christum pro nobis ita passum esse, ut exemplū quoq; nobis reliquerit, quo admoneamur, quæ Euangelij & seruorum ipsius conditio semper in terris futura sit. Etenim si tanta fuit aduersus illum mundi rabies, quando ipsemet prædicauit, in cuius sermone diuina quædam authoritas elucebat, & qui doctrinam suam miraculis non minus salutaribus quàm stupendis confirmabat, quid de nobis hodie sperabimus, qui præter Euangelij lucem nihil afferimus, quàm eo maiori odio dignam mundus hic esse iudicat, quò plenior & clarior illa fulget? Facit autem ad hoc scandalum tolendum in primis loci huius consideratio diligens, quo narratur, quàm ignominiosé ille tractatus, & quàm indigne ab ipsis ædificantibus damnatus atque reiectus sit, quod fore olim Dauid prædixerat. Prius enim narrauit Lucas, illum ex monte Oliuarum ad Caiapham, qui anni illius Pontifex erat, ductum fuisse, narrationem uero nonnihil interrupit interiecta Petri historia, quam nuper audiuimus. Nunc ergo redit eò unde digressus fuerat.
units.tr: Mark, homily 123 and 124. Therefore let us remember that Christ suffered for us in such a way that he also left us an example, by which we are admonished what the condition of the gospel and of his servants will always be on earth. For if there was such a rage of the world against him, when he himself preached, whose speech shone with a certain divine authority, and who confirmed his teaching by miracles no less saving than astonishing, what shall we hope for today, we who bring nothing beyond the light of the gospel, which the world judges to be worthy of all the greater hatred the fuller and clearer that light shines? Moreover, to remove this scandal, a careful consideration of this passage is especially helpful, in which it is told how ignominiously that Stone was handled, and how unworthily it was condemned and rejected by the builders, as David had foretold long before. For Luke first related that he had been led from the Mount of Olives to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year; but in the narrative he interrupted it somewhat by inserting the story of Peter which we heard recently. Now, therefore, he returns to where he had left off.

units.la: Et primò quidem de iis, qui Iesum uinctum adduxerunt, disserit, quos ex Sacerdotum seruis & militum cohorte collectos fuisse nuper dictum est. Hi (inquit) ei illudebant cædentes eum: Et cùm eum obuoluissent, uerberabant faciem eius, & interrogabant eum, dicentes: Vaticinare, quis sit qui te percussit? Et alia multa conuitiantes dicebant in eum. Quo loco aliqui ordinem ab Euangelistis inuersum esse suspicantur, cùm quod Lucas ante Cœcilij confessum factum fuisse scribit, Matthæus postea factū narret, quando iá blasphemiæ damnatus erat. At ego (quod sæpe iá monui) nō libenter diuinos scriptores in alicuius negligentiæ aut oscitantiæ suspicionem adduco, cùm illos Spiritu duce & suggestore scripsisse, cōstet, & Lucas initio operis sui, se omnia ex ordine scripturū esse profiteatur. Quare eorū potius sententiæ subscribo, qui improbos istos petulantia hac scurrili bus Christo illusisse putant. Quia enim noctu demum ad illum capiendum profecti erant, credibile est, non omnes Seniores atq; Sacerdotes apud Caiapham præsentes adfuisse, cùm primùm adduceretur. Annam certè abfuisse, Ioannes diserte annotauit. Ergo dū illi conuenirent, crediderim ego impios istos nebulones istud designauisse: quod postea quasi optimo iure iterauerunt, cùm Concilij authoritate damnatus esset. Facit hoc ad amplificandam rei indignitatem, nec temere factū putabimus, quòd eandem ignominiam bis Christus sustinuit. Quia enim propter nos ista omnia facta sunt, extremis iniurijs atq; contumeliis eum nō semel affici oportuit, ut nos sempiternæ damnationis ignominia liberaret. Nobis enim propter peccatū abscondita erat facies Dei, & quia per inobedientiam cum illo quodammodo luserant primi parentes, omnibus creaturis ludibrium facti fuimus. Itaq; Christus suam faciem obnubi (quod facinorosis fieri solebat) passus est: & conspui atq; ignominiosé cædi uoluit, ut nobis liberum in conspectum Patris sui aditum faceret. Est hoc præclarum diuinæ erga nos bonitatis argumentum, quo nos excitari conuenit, ut non solùm diligamus eum, qui tam dira pro nobis sufferre dignatus est, uerumetiam, ut de peccatis recte iudicemus, et abominemur horribilem istam noxam, quæ non aliter expiari potuit. Debet præterea nos ad patientiam armare, huius indignitatis, quam Christus sustinuit, consideratio. Natura quidem sic comparatum est, ut nulla iniuria nobis indignior & intolerabilior uideatur, quàm quæ cum nostri contemptu coniuncta est: multi etiā parum generosi animi indicium esse putant, si quis se ignominia impunè affici patiatur. Ita uerò fit, ut dum honorem suum inconsultius tuentur, multa indignissimè contra charitatis legem faciant, seq; ipsos maiori contumelia afficiant. Christi igitur exemplo discamus patienter ferre impiorum scurrarū ludibria: quando non tam ignominiosum est iniurias perpeti quā alijs inferre. Quod si mundus hoc ignaui animi argumentum esse iudicat, nos è contra cogitemus, eò laudem fortitudinis maiorem nos mereri, quod id constanter ferimus, quod multis alijs intolerabile uidetur. Hæc autem nobis cura sit, ne ipsi nostram authoritatē indignis nostra professione dictis & factis profituamur, & ita digni simus quibus omnes illudat.
units.tr: And first of all he speaks of those who brought Jesus bound, whom it was said just now were gathered from the servants of the priests and the company of soldiers. "These," he says, "mocked him and beat him. And when they had blindfolded him, they struck his face and asked him, saying, 'Prophesy: who is it that struck you?' And they said many other insulting things against him." At this point some suspect that the order in the Evangelists has been reversed, since Luke writes that what was done before the council of Caiaphas, and Matthew later narrates it as done when he had already been condemned for blasphemy. But I, as I have often already warned, am not willing to bring the divine writers under suspicion of carelessness or oversight, since it is established that they wrote under the guidance and inspiration of the Spirit, and Luke at the beginning of his work professes that he will write everything in order. Therefore I rather agree with those who think that these wicked men mocked Christ with this buffoonish insolence. For since they had set out to seize him only at night, it is credible that not all the elders and priests were present at Caiaphas' house when he was first brought in. John plainly noted that Annas was certainly absent. So while they were gathering, I believe these impious rascals marked out this mockery, which they afterwards repeated, as if with the best right, when he had been condemned by the authority of the council. This serves to heighten the indignity of the matter, and we shall not think it was done by chance that Christ endured the same disgrace twice. For since all these things were done on our account, it was necessary that he be subjected not once to the extreme injuries and insults, so that he might free us from the shame of eternal damnation. For on account of sin the face of God was hidden from us, and because our first parents, through disobedience, had in a sense trifled with him, we were made a mockery to all creatures. Therefore Christ suffered his face to be veiled (as was customary for criminals), and he willed to be spat upon and shamefully struck, so that he might open for us a free approach into the sight of his Father. This is a splendid proof of the divine goodness toward us, by which we ought to be stirred, not only to love him who deigned to suffer such dreadful things for us, but also to judge rightly concerning sins and to abhor that horrible evil which could not be atoned for in any other way. Moreover, the consideration of this indignity which Christ endured ought to arm us for patience. By nature it is so ordered that no injury seems more unworthy and intolerable to us than one joined with contempt of us; many even think it a sign of a small and ungenerous spirit if someone allows himself to be treated with impunity in disgrace. But so it happens that while they guard their honor too rashly, they do many things most unworthily against the law of charity, and bring greater insult upon themselves. Let us therefore learn from Christ's example to bear patiently the mockeries of impious buffoons, since it is not so shameful to suffer injuries as to inflict them. And if the world judges this a sign of a cowardly spirit, let us on the contrary consider that we deserve greater praise for courage in that we bear constantly what seems intolerable to many others. Yet let this be our care: that we do not by unworthy words and deeds in our profession bring our own authority into question, and so become worthy to be mocked by all.

units.la: Cæterum etiamsi hæc ex æterno Patris decreto Christus passus sit, non tamen id impunè tulerunt illusores isti, qui & improba odij sui rabie saciare, & suis heris gratificari studuerunt. Nā quæ Christo fecerunt, ipsi postea passi sunt. Abstulit enim ab illis gratiam suam Deus, & à facie sua procul repulit. Idem etiam Romanorum armis subacti extrema quaq; sustinuerunt. Nam præter innumerabilem cæsorum multitudinem, supra nonaginta septem millia Iudæorum (ut Iosephus tradidit) in hostium potestatem uenerunt, quorum aliqui ad metalla relegati, alij in seruitutem uenditi, plurimi autem
units.tr: Moreover, although Christ suffered these things by the eternal decree of the Father, those mockers did not go unpunished, who sought both to satisfy the wicked rage of their hatred and to gratify their masters. For what they did to Christ, they themselves afterwards suffered. For God withdrew his grace from them and cast them far from his face. The same people, subdued by the arms of the Romans, endured the utmost calamities. For besides the countless multitude of the slain, more than ninety-seven thousand Jews (as Josephus relates) came into the power of the enemy, of whom some were sent to the mines, others were sold into slavery, and very many

units.la: Serui Sacerdotum Christo illudunt.
units.tr: The servants of the priests mock Christ.

units.la: Pœna, quibus Filij sui illusores ultus est Deus. autem in spectaculis bestiarum atq; gladiatorū crudeliter occisi sunt. Nec adhuc cessat Dei ipsorum impietatem persequentis iudicium. Nam hodie etiam in omnes orbis terrarū angulos disperji omnium ludibria sustinent, conuitijs diris proscinduntur, & vulgi quoq; prouerbijs infames sunt. Atqui hoc illud est, quod olim Deus per Mosem ipsis minatus erat, dicens: Fiet ut caput super te commune ant omnia regna terræ: erisq; ut à te stupeant, te exemplo utantur, de lingua acuant omnes populi, ad quos te Dominus duxerit. Itē: Ponā vos in stupore, in sibilum & in uastitates perpetuas. At hic nos meminisse decet, Deū commune exemplū edidisse, quo omnium locorū atq; temporum homines discant, quid Filij sui contemptores & Euangelij hostes maneat. Nam cū naturalibus ramis non peperit, multo minus eos inultos dimittet, qui ex oleastro decerpti & in stirpem siue truncum sanctissimorum patrum insiti, illius beneficium non agnoscunt, & eius prædicationem sanniis atq; ludibrijs prosequuntur. Et utinā non viderem° hodie dura & horrenda diuinæ vindictæ exempla. Vnde enim fieri putamus, quòd Christianum nomen Turcis illudendum propinatur, & ipsis quoq; Iudæis sæpe ludibrio sunt, qui illud profitentur? Ex eo nimirum, quòd quam nobis in Filio suo Deus gratiam offert, pleriq; proscinduntur atq; conculcant. Riserunt quidem infelices illi propheticam Christi dignitatem, quam aliquoties à populo prædicari audierant, at non potuerunt suis illusionibus fidem derogare illius uaticinio, quo urbis excidium & totius gentis miserabilem dispersionem ipse minatus fuerat. Ita semper rata erunt minæ Dei, quibus contumaces Christi contemptores æterno exitio addicit, etiamsi plerique illas negent, & ex earum derisione scurrili voluptatem capiant.
units.tr: The punishment by which God avenged the mockers of his Son. were cruelly put to death in the spectacles of wild beasts and gladiators. Nor does the judgment of God pursuing their impiety yet cease. For today too they are scattered into every corner of the earth, they undergo the mockery of all, they are torn apart by dreadful insults, and they are infamous even by the proverbs of the common people. And yet this is what God long ago threatened them through Moses, saying: "It will come about that you will become a horror and a byword among all the kingdoms of the earth; and they will be astonished at you, use you as an example, and all the peoples to whom the Lord leads you will sharpen their tongues against you." Likewise: "I will make you an astonishment, a hissing and perpetual desolations." But here we ought to remember that God has set forth a common example, from which men of all places and times may learn what awaits the despisers of his Son and the enemies of the gospel. For since he did not spare the natural branches, he will much less leave unpunished those who, though cut from the wild olive and grafted in place of the most holy fathers, do not acknowledge his kindness and pursue his preaching with sneers and mockery. And would that I did not see today the hard and dreadful examples of divine vengeance. For whence do we think it comes that the Christian name is held up to mockery by the Turks, and is often a laughingstock even to the Jews themselves who profess it? Surely from this: that many people tear apart and trample underfoot the grace which God offers to us in his Son. Those unhappy men indeed laughed at the prophetic dignity of Christ, which they had often heard proclaimed by the people; yet they could not, by their mockery, take away the credit of his prophecy, in which he had foretold the destruction of the city and the wretched dispersion of the whole nation. Thus the threats of God will always stand firm, by which he dooms the obstinate despisers of Christ to eternal ruin, even though many deny them and take buffoonish pleasure in mocking them.

units.la: Sed relictis seruis atq; militibus ad heros eorum transeamus cum Euangelista, qui quid ipsi fecerint, narrat. Et ut ortus est dies, conuenit ordo Seniorum populi, & principes Sacerdotum & Scribæ, & adduxerunt eum in suum consessum, &c. Quo loco ante omnia obseruari debet, qui nam aduersus Dominum conuenerint. Nominatur primò ἡ πρεσβυτέριον τῶν λαῶν. Ita vero dicebatur ordo Seniorum, qui summus in ea gente magistratus quondam fuerat, & nunc quoq; aliquam pristinæ dignitatis speciem præ se ferebat. His accedunt principes Sacerdotum, penes quos summa erat in sacris authoritas. Scribæ item, de quibus alibi diximus. Fuit ergo hic non vulgaris cætus, sed Concilium fuit, & de hoc nos admonere voluit Spiritus sanctus, ut Christum publica tam politicorum quàm ecclesiasticorum procerum authoritate damnatum esse sciremus, quemadmodum antea quoq; de eo occidendo illos in Concilio consultauisse, Ioannes scribit. Vbi rursus quidem docemur, qui nā acerrimi grauissimiq; veritatis Euangelicæ hostes sint: Principes nimirum, qui absq; Deo regnare volunt; & Sacerdotes, qui religionem sibi quæstum faciunt, aut sub doctrinæ titulo non aliud quàm gloriā priuatam uænantur: simul autem admonemur, non debere alicui mirum videri, si etiam hodie Concilia aduersus Euangeli doctrinam cogantur, & illorum authoritate eius sectatores damnentur. Quod enim Christo accidit, id ille nobis quoq; euenturum prædixit: Tradent(inquit) uos in Concilia, & in Synagogis suis flagellabunt uos. Olim quidem magna fuit Conciliorum utilitas, quando illa Christianî Imperatores cogebant, & sua præsentia atq; authoritate Episcoporum contentiosorum atq; ambitiosorum certamina moderabantur atq; dirimebant (quod quàm necesse fuerit fieri in Niceno illo historici non dissimulant) sed postquam Episcopi potentia auctì sunt, & sibi omne in Ecclesia ius vendicarunt, Conciliorum quoq; usus pernitiosus potius quàm salutaris esse cœpit: quia horum authoritate errores confirmati, & bellorū semina iacta sunt: adeò ut in proverbium abierit hoc dictum: Omne Concilium parit bellum. Quod quàm uere dicatur, hoc nostrum sæculum magno cum totius Christianî orbis malo experitur. Docet autem Christianos homines, ut à solo Dei uerbo pendeant, cuius veritas rata & æterna erit, etiamsi mille Conciliorum decretis damnetur.
units.tr: But let us leave the servants and soldiers and follow the Evangelist to their masters, and tell what the masters themselves did. "And as soon as it was day, the council of the elders of the people assembled, both the chief priests and the scribes, and they led him into their council," etc. Here we must first note who it was that gathered against the Lord. He is named first as the council of elders of the people [τὸ πρεσβυτέριον τοῦ λαοῦ]. This was the name for the order of elders, which had once been the highest magistracy in that nation and still kept some show of its former dignity. To them are added the chief priests, in whose hands the supreme authority in sacred matters lay, and likewise the scribes, of whom we have spoken elsewhere. So this was no ordinary gathering but a formal council, and the Holy Spirit wished to remind us of this, so that we might know that Christ was condemned by the public authority of both the civil and the ecclesiastical leaders, just as John also writes that they had earlier consulted together in council about putting him to death. Here we are taught again who are the fiercest and most determined enemies of the Gospel truth: princes who want to reign without God, and priests who make religion a source of gain or, under the title of doctrine, hunt only after private glory. At the same time we are warned that no one should think it strange if even today councils are convened against the doctrine of the Gospel and its followers are condemned by their authority. For what happened to Christ, he foretold would happen to us too: "They will deliver you up to councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues" (Matt. 10). In former times councils were of great use, when Christian emperors convened them and by their presence and authority restrained and settled the contentions of quarrelsome and ambitious bishops (as historians do not conceal, how necessary this was at Nicaea).
