But after the bishops grew in power and claimed for themselves every right in the Church, the use of councils also began to be harmful rather than helpful, because errors were confirmed by their authority and the seeds of wars were sown, so much so that the saying became proverbial: "Every council breeds war." How truly this is said our own age experiences to the great harm of the whole Christian world. Yet it teaches Christians to depend on the Word of God alone, whose truth is firm and eternal even if it is condemned by a thousand decrees of councils.

units.la: Præstat autem videre, quo ordine & quibus artibus isti hanc causam egerint, ut facilius intelligamus dolos, quibus hodie nobis multi insidiantur. Et quia Lucas hic brevior est, paucis repetemus, ex aliis Euangelistis, quæ ad hunc locum pertinent. Ioannes Christum à Caiaphâ de doctrina & discipulis interrogatum fuisse scribit: nimirum ut eum non solùm falsæ doctrinæ veruemetiam scismatis & turbati ordinis ecclesiastici accusare possent. Scimus enim nemini licere docendi munus in Ecclesia subire, qui nō legitimè uocatus fuerit; & horribile exemplum olim in Cora & eius coniuratos ædidit Deus, qui eam dignitatem sibi uendicare ausi fuerunt, in quā Aaron cum filijs suis erat euectus. Quid, quod Vzias Rex lepra percussus est, quòd contra Dei institutum ipse vellet incensum offerre?
units.tr: It is worth seeing, however, in what order and by what devices these men conducted this case, so that we may more easily understand the snares by which many now lay traps for us. And since Luke is briefer here, we shall briefly recall from the other Evangelists what pertains to this place. John writes that Christ was questioned by Caiaphas about his doctrine and his disciples, plainly so that they could accuse him not only of false doctrine but also of schism and of disturbing the ecclesiastical order. For we know that no one is permitted to take up the office of teaching in the Church unless he has been lawfully called; and God set forth a dreadful example long ago in Korah and his fellow conspirators, who dared to claim for themselves the dignity to which Aaron and his sons had been raised. And what of King Uzziah, who was struck with leprosy because he wanted to offer incense contrary to God's ordinance?

units.la: Concilium cōgitur aduersus Christum. Quia uero Christus non ignorabat apud istos iudices, nullu iustæ defensioni locum esse, paucis respondet, & ad ipsam Ecclesiam quodamodo prouocat, petens, ut qui ipsum audierint, de sua doctrina testentur. Simul quoq; fe ex impostorum numero eximit, quando fe in publico & in locis doctrinæ destinatis docuisse ait. Fuit responsum hoc simplex, moderatum & æquum. Quid autem eo proficit? Vapulat à Pontificis feruo, ut qui inciuilius & contumeliosius Summo Sacerdoti responderit. Neque in tanto consessu aliquis auditur, qui iniquissimam hanc impiffimi nebulonis proteruiam uel uerbulo uno corripuerit. Imo adeo non pudet illos uim fecisse homini innocenti in loco Iustitiæ & ueritatis sacro, ut falsis quoq; illu testibus oppugnare conentur, quos prius in eufum studiose conquisitos produ cunt. Sed turbat illorum linguas Deus, ut quemadmodu olim in Babylonis extructione fe mutuo in telligere non potuerunt, qui aduersus illius decretu coniurauerant: ita hic quoq; etsi una eademq; omnibus mens fit, & impijs illis præsulibus gratificari cupiant, non possunt tamen inter fe conuenire, quin de re una eademq; diuersa loquantur. Quo loco consolationis plenum est, quod uidemus impios neq; linguas neq; manus in sua potestate habere; ueritate item calumnijs & mendacijs oppugnari quidem & premi, expugnari autem & opprimi non posse. Vidit hoc astutus ille Pontifex, & ideo ex ipsius Christi ore aliquid uanari instituit, ex quo ipsius damnandi occasionem habeat. Quæstionem ergo mouet, in qua totius causæ huius cardo uersabatur: Nunc uidelicet fit Christus ille, id est, promissus & diu expectatus populi Seruator, quem sub uncti nomine Prophetæ descripserunt, eo quod hunc Deus Ecclesiæ suæ Regem & Pontificem constituit? Ideo autem de hoc quærit, quia ex Prophetarum oraculis abunde constabat, illum non uulgarem hominem, sed Deum fore uerum & æternum. Notum est enim illud Ifaiæ: Deus ipse ueniet, & seruabit nos. Item: Generationem eius quis enarrabit? Et Micheas, cum ex Bethlehemo proditurum dicat, quoad incarnationem, addit tamen: Exitus eius ab initio, à diebus æternitatis. Ieremias autem de eodem pronuntiat: Et hoc nomen eius, quo uocabunt eum: IEHO VA iustitia nostra. Taceo innumera alia, quæ huius generis sunt, & quæ tunc uulgo notissima erant. Si ergo fe Christum fiue unctum illum dicat, iam blasphemum dicet Caiaphas, ut qui fe Deum esse dixerit. Fuit itaq; quæstio hæc admodum insidiosa, in ea tamen mouenda singulari etiam astutia ueterator ille utitur. Nam adiurat illu, fiue per facrofanctu Dei nomen obtestatur, ut diserte quod uerum est dicat: & ut ex gestu quoq; aliquod pondus accedat, assurgit, & in medium progressus clamat: Adiuro te per Deum uiuentem, ut dicas nobis, fi tu es Christus ille, Filius Dei? Eftq; obtestatio ista tam captiosa, ut elabi non possit quicquid faciat. Nam fi neget, excipient illi: Cur ergo doces? cur discipulos colligis? cur cultus diuini reformationem moliris? Adhæc mendacij conuinci potuerit, cum multa dixerit & fecerit, quæ de nullo alio quam de Meffia intelligi possunt. Si affirmet, habent quod quærunt, & dissimulatis argumentis omnibus, quibus fe & Dei Filium & Meffiam esse probauerat, in hoc uno insistent, quod non fine aperta blasphemia sese Deum esse dixerit. Restabat ergo unum, ut omnino sileret. Sed neq; hoc proderat. Dicent enim hominem esse contumacem, temerarium & impudentem, qui in Ecclesia quiduis statuendi sibi ius fumat, nolit autem rationem suorum factorum cuiquam reddere. Adhæc prophanum & impium nominis diuini contemptorem esse clamabunt, qui per hoc factas obtestationes negligat atq; contemnat. Est ergo hoc euidens calliditatis & astutiæ argumentum, qua ueritatis hostes instructos esse, & aduersus quam nos ferpentina prudentia uti oportere, alibi monuit. Et est huius exempli cognitio nobis quoq; perquam necessaria, quibus cum Antichristo res est, cui oculos hominis Daniel tribuit.
units.tr: A council is assembled against Christ. But since Christ knew that before such judges there was no place for a just defence, he answers briefly and in a way calls the Church itself to witness, asking that those who heard him should testify to his doctrine. At the same time he removes himself from the number of impostors when he says that he taught openly and in places set apart for teaching. His answer was plain, measured and fair. But what did it gain him? He is struck by the high priest's servant, as one who had answered the high priest too uncivilly and insolently. And in so great an assembly no one is heard to rebuke with a single word this most unjust insolence of a most wicked scoundrel. Indeed they are so far from being ashamed to do violence to an innocent man in a place sacred to justice and truth that they even try to overwhelm him with false witnesses, whom they had previously sought out carefully and brought forward for this purpose. But God confuses their tongues, just as once at the building of Babel those who had conspired against his decree could not understand one another. So here too, although all have one and the same mind and desire to please those impious prelates, they cannot agree with one another without speaking diversely about one and the same matter. In this there is great comfort: we see that the wicked have control neither of their tongues nor of their hands; and that the truth, though it may be attacked and pressed by slanders and lies, cannot be overcome or crushed. That crafty pontiff saw this, and so he set about trapping something from the very mouth of Christ, from which he might have an occasion to condemn him. He therefore raises the question on which the whole cardinal point of this case turned: "Are you now, then, that Christ, that is, the promised and long-awaited Saviour of the people, whom the prophets described under the name of 'the Anointed', because God appointed him King and High Priest of his Church?" He asked this because it was abundantly clear from the oracles of the prophets that he would be not an ordinary man but true and eternal God. For that saying of Isaiah is well known: "God himself will come and save us" (Isa. 35). Likewise: "Who will declare his generation?" (Isa. 53). And Micah, though he says he will come forth from Bethlehem as regards his incarnation, adds nonetheless: "His goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting" (Mic. 5). Jeremiah also proclaims concerning the same one: "And this is his name by which they will call him: the LORD our righteousness" (Jer. 23). I pass over countless other passages of this kind, which were then most widely known among the people. So if he said that he was Christ or that Anointed One, Caiaphas would at once call it blasphemy, since he would be claiming to be God. This question was therefore very insidious; yet in raising it the old schemer uses a singular cunning. For he adjures him, that is, calls upon him by the sacred name of God, so that he will plainly say what is true; and so that some weight may be added by his gesture too, he rises, comes forward into the midst and cries out: "I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God" (Matt. 26). And this adjuration was so cunningly framed that whatever he did, he could not escape. For if he denied it, they would reply: "Why then do you teach? Why do you gather disciples? Why do you undertake to reform the worship of God?" Moreover he could be convicted of lying, since he had said and done many things that can be understood of no one but the Messiah. If he affirmed it, they would have what they were seeking, and setting aside all the arguments by which he had proved that he was both the Son of God and the Messiah, they would insist on this one point alone, that he had called himself God, which is plain blasphemy. There remained, then, one course: to be altogether silent. But even this would not help him. For they would say that he was a stubborn, rash and shameless man, who claimed for himself the right to decree anything in the Church, yet was unwilling to give anyone an account of his actions. Besides, they would cry out that he was a profane and impious despiser of the divine name, since he neglected and scorned the oaths laid upon him. This, then, is clear evidence of the cunning and craftiness with which the enemies of the truth are equipped, and against which we ought to use serpentine wisdom, as he has taught elsewhere. And the knowledge of this example is also most necessary for us, since we have to do with Antichrist, to whom Daniel ascribes the eyes of a man.

units.la: Est uero pro alijs, quæ hic proponuntur, obferuatu dignissimis, Concilij Antichristiani typus. Ita enim iure appellamus istorum consessu, qui aduersus Christu iampridem coniurauerant, & nunc ad illu tollendu conuenerant. Præsident hic rebus agendis, qui potius iudicio sisti debuissent, & cogi ut suae doctrinae multis modis corruptissimae & prophanati cultus ratione redderent: ut ia multa alia eorum facinora omittamus. Damnauerut hi illu antea, cu resuscitati Lazari miraculo irritati statuerut eum occidi debere, ut Ioan. ca. 11. prodidit. Interim nunc iustitiam & ueritatis studiu simulant, quasi causam cognoscere & ipsi plena respondendi potestatem facere uelint. Præfidiu uero omne habent in armis, quibus ia usi sunt in illo capiendo, & in aperta ui, qua ipsis conuenientibus impius ille Pontificis seruus adhibuit. Sed & testimonijs falsis res agitur, quibus horribilis & plus qua prophanus diuini nominis abusus accedit, cuius religione sua impietate palliant, & innocentem proditorie circumueniunt atq;
units.tr: The passage that follows, besides the other matters set out here, is well worth noting: it is a picture of an Antichristian council. We rightly call this the gathering of those men who had long ago conspired against Christ and had now met to bring about his death. Here the men who ought rather to have been brought to trial preside over the proceedings, and they are forcing him to give an account of his teaching, which is corrupted in many ways, and of their profaned worship, to say nothing of their many other crimes. These men had already condemned him once, when, angered by the raising of Lazarus, they resolved that he must be killed, as John 11 reports. Now they pretend to care for justice and for the truth, as if they wished to examine the case and give him full power to answer. But they rely entirely on arms, the same ones they used to seize him, and on open force, which that impious servant of the High Priest brought along with the men who had gathered. The case is also being pursued with false testimony, and a dreadful and more than profane abuse of the name of God is added to it. Under the pretence of religion they cover their impiety, and they treacherously entrap and oppress the innocent man.

units.la: Ifa. 35. & 53. Mich. 5. Ierem. 23. atq; opprimunt. Talia iam seculis aliquot fuisse Pontificū Cocilia, alibi demonstrauimus, & nostro etiam tempore sumus experti. Neminem ergo illorum authoritas moueat, ut aut seipsum aut suae fidei creditas Ecclesias illis subijciat. Nam qui id faciunt, ij (quod proverbio dicitur) ouē lupo committunt, atq; veritatis doctrinam cum ecclesijs produnt.
units.tr: Isa. 35. & 53. Mich. 5. Jer. 23. We have shown elsewhere that councils of the Popes of this kind have been held for some centuries, and in our own time we too have had experience of them. Let no one, therefore, be moved by their authority so as to subject either himself or the Churches entrusted to his faith to them. For those who do so, as the proverb says, commit the sheep to the wolf, and they betray the doctrine of truth together with the Churches.

units.la: Quid autem Christus, ubi se undiq; premi, & insidiosa illa adiuratione iam circumuentum uidit? Primū liberè & ingenuè illorū iniustitia arguit. Si (inquit) uobis dixero, nequaquam credetis: Quod si etiam uos interrogauero, non respondebitis mihi, neq; dimittetis. Sensus uerborū est hic: Qui in religione causa sibi iudicium sumūt, ij audita & cognita rei veritate credere debent, & Deo gloriā dare: adhæc si ipsi rogetur, ut errore ostendat, aut suā sententiā rationib. siue testimonijs idoneis cōfirment, ipsorū fuerit respondere, ut ab errore reducantur qui uel propria ignoratia & simplicitate, uel aliorū improbitate seducti à uero deuiarūt. At nihil horū de uobis ego mihi polliceri possum. Nā toties absmo edocti, toties argumetis & miraculis cōuicti, nūquā uoluistis credere. Quid ergo nūc uos facturos sperē, quādo uos plena cōtra me uictoria in manib. habere arbitramini? Sed neq; mihi ad quæstiones propositas respondebitis: ut qui iāpridē eā uobis authoritate usurpauistis, ut pro authenticis ac diuinis oraculis haberi debeant, quæcunq; à uobis pronunciatur. Estis ergo iudices iniquissimi & veritatis cōtumacissimi hostes. Hæc & alia quæ in hac sententia dici poterat, paucis hisce uerbis Christus cōprahēdit. At ne veritatis cōfessione turpi ignauia aut metu detrectare putetur, secūdo loco quod res erat edicit. Ab hoc tēpore erit Filius hominis sedēs ad dextrā potentiæ Dei. Apud Matthæum illos ipsos eorū quæ nunc dicit, oculatos testes fore ait: Dico uobis, ab hoc tempore uidebitis Filiū hominis sedentē à dextra potestatis Dei, & uenientem in nubibus cæli. Alludit ad ea quæ apud ueteres Prophetas de Messia haberi, ipsi non ignorabat. Dauid enim huic à Deo dictū esse canit: Sede ad dextrā meā, donec posuero inimicos tuos scabellū pedū tuorū. Et Daniel quendā ut Filiū hominis se in nubibus uenientem uidisse scribit, cui traditus sit dominatus & honor & regnū, ut omnes populi, nationes & linguæ colant eū, &c. Habent ergo uerba Christi cū veritatis confessione coniunctā pœnæ comminationem, qua docet fore, ut aui nunc iudices sedeant & iniquis sententijs ipsum opprimant, ad suum tribunal comparere cogantur, ut digna suis factis præmia recipiant. Et hoc ipsum uelle illi facilè intelligunt. Nam ex eo inferunt & urgent quæstionem ante propositā. Tu ergo es Filius Dei? Non ergo tam stupidi fuerunt, ut quæ Scripturæ olim de Messia tradiderunt, prorsus ignorarent: sed auaritia & ambitione fascinati in luce meridiana cæcutire voluerunt. Itaque ne quis illis reliquus esset, alicuius defensionis prætextus, respondet illis: Vos dicitis me esse. Quasi dicat: Propriæ conscientiæ & Prophetarum testimonijs conuicti, uos me illum esse fatemini, cum non possitis dissimulare de me dicta esse quæ modò ex illis adduxi. Quod ergo uos dicitis, & uere quidem dicitis ego disseri aut negare non possum neq; debeo. Docet autem nos suo exemplo Dominus, quid fieri debeat, si nos in deploratos & incurabiles veritatis hostes incidisse uideamus. Argui & accusari debet eorum iniquitas, & ijdem pœnarū quoq; denuntiatione terreri debent, ne se metui arbitrentur. Nihil enim tam feroces & arrogantes facit, quàm si se pijs formidini aut terrori esse uideant. Quāmuis autem correptionibus quoque & minis exasperentur, nunquam tamen effugere possunt, quin in animis ipsorum aculei aliqui hæreant, quibus conuincantur. At ne bilem releuare et priuatæ uindictæ studio agitari uideamur, simul addi debet libera & ingenua ueritatis confessio, eaq; ex Scripturis desumpta, & quoad eius fieri potest, Scripturis confirmata: de qua sæpe iam diximus.
units.tr: But what did Christ do when he saw himself hemmed in on every side and already trapped by that treacherous oath? First, he freely and openly charged them with their injustice. "If I tell you," he says, "you will by no means believe; and if I also question you, you will not answer me or let me go." The sense of these words is this: those who take judgement upon themselves in matters of religion ought, once the truth of the matter has been heard and known, to believe and give glory to God. Moreover, if they are asked to show an error, or to confirm their opinion by sound reasons or testimonies, it is for them to answer, so that those who have strayed from the truth, misled either by their own ignorance and simplicity or by the wickedness of others, may be brought back from error. But I can promise myself nothing of this from you. For though you have been taught so often, and convicted so often by arguments and miracles, you have never been willing to believe. What then can I hope you will do now, when you think you hold a complete victory over me in your hands? Nor will you answer my questions, since you have long ago claimed for yourselves such authority that whatever you pronounce ought to be regarded as authentic and divine oracles. You are therefore most unjust judges and the most obstinate enemies of the truth. Christ sums up these and the other things that could be said on this point in these few words. But so that it should not be thought that he shrank from confessing the truth out of shameful cowardice or fear, in the second place he declares how the matter really stands: "From now on the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of the power of God." In Matthew he says that they themselves will be eyewitnesses of what he is now saying: "I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming on the clouds of heaven." He alludes to what was known to him from the ancient prophets concerning the Messiah. For David sings that it was said to him by God: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." And Daniel writes that he saw one like a Son of Man coming on the clouds, to whom dominion and honour and kingdom were given, so that all peoples, nations and tongues should serve him, and so on. Thus the words of Christ join to the confession of the truth a warning of punishment, teaching that the time will come when these men, now judges, will sit and oppress him with unjust sentences, and will themselves be compelled to appear before his tribunal, to receive rewards worthy of their deeds. And they readily understand that this is what he means. For from it they draw the question put before and press it: "Are you then the Son of God?" They were not so stupid, then, as to be utterly ignorant of what the Scriptures had handed down concerning the Messiah; but, bewitched by greed and ambition, they chose to be blind in broad daylight. Therefore, so that they should have no pretext of defence left to them, he answers them: "You say that I am." As if he were saying: "Convicted by your own conscience and by the testimonies of the Prophets, you confess that I am he, since you cannot deny that what I have just cited from them has been said about me. What you say, then, and you say truly, I cannot and ought not to deny." The Lord, by his own example, teaches us what should be done if we see that we have fallen among enemies of the truth who are hopeless and incurable. Their wickedness ought to be rebuked and accused, and they ought to be frightened by the declaration of punishments too, lest they think that they are feared. For nothing makes them so fierce and arrogant as seeing that they inspire fear or terror in the godly. Yet although they are provoked by rebukes and threats, they can never escape without some sting remaining in their minds, by which they are convicted. But so that we should not seem to be relieving our bile or driven by a desire for private vengeance, a free and open confession of the truth must at the same time be added, drawn from the Scriptures and, as far as possible, confirmed by the Scriptures, about which we have often spoken already.

units.la: Audiamus nunc, quis tam libræ confessionis effectus apud istos homines fuerit. Lucas paucis ex tremum Concilij actū indicat, quando illos simul omnes respondisse scribit: Quid amplius egemus testimonio? Ipsi enim audiuimus ex ore ipsius. Plenius autē omnia Matth. & Mar. narrat ad hunc modū: Tūc Pōtifex dirupit uestimēta sua dicens: Blasphemauit, quid amplius egemus testibus? Ecce audistis blasphemiā eius. Quid uobis uidetur? Ipsi uero respondentes, dixerunt, obnoxius est morti. In his apparet, quid quæstione & obtestatione illa captiosa quæsuerit. Vestes aut scindit Pōtifex, quo rituacerbum et intolerabile cordis dolorem, ex blasphemijs auditis aut alia re tristi conceptū, Iudæi, si gnificare solebant. Ita ergo impietatis Christū damnat, ut ipse animū gloriæ Dei studio ardentem simulet: quod hypocritis propriū esse scimus. At ijs de sola veritatis doctrina & ingenua Christi cōfessio blasphema & intolerabilis esse putatur: eò quòd hæc ipsorum existimationi & quæstui derogat. Vtinam uero qui hodie Christiani dici uolunt, non ita frigerent, ut manifesta in Dei maiestatem conuitia surdis auribus prætereant. Quàm multos enim audimus, qui immani audacia Dei uerbum negant, Scripturæ sacræ fidem scurriliter eleuant, Christi uulnera, mortem et meritū diris execrationibus conspuunt? Quotus uero quisq; ad illa exhorresćit? quis uestes scindit? quis iusta animi indignationem aut pium dolorem aliquo indicio prodit? Quid uero de Pontificibus dicam, qui & diuinos honores sibi uendicant, & ipsius Christi meritum negant, imò quæ huius sunt sacrilega audacia in se transferunt, quando se Ecclesiæ caput & illius vicarios esse gloriantur, qui plenā peccata remittendi, animas in cœlum euehendi aut ad inferos deturbandi potestatem habeant? In illorum certè Decretis & Decretalibus leguntur, quæ non tam impiam & blasphemam quàm stupendam istorum homisium arrogantiam arguunt. Quale est illud Distinćt.19. Sic omnes sanctiones apostolicæ sedis accipiendæ sunt, tanquam ipsius diuina uoce Petri firmatæ. Itē in Glossa de Translat.episcopi. Titul.7. Quanto: Papa dicitur habere cœleste arbitrium, & ideo potest sententiā quæ nulla est, aliquam facere: Quia in his quæ vult est pro ratione voluntas. Necest qui dicat ei, Cur ita facis? Ipse enim potest supra ius dispensare, & deiniustitia facere iustitiam, corrigendo iura & mutando: Nam plenitudinem obtinet potestatis. Addē his, quod Papam tunc quoq; a quoquam reprehendi debere negant, si animas secum cateruatim ad inferos rapiat. Et hi ipsi sunt, quorum omnium nomine Bonifacius Octauus Canonem de Maioritate & Obedientia ædidit, cuius hæc est conclusio: Porrò subesse Romano Pontifici omnem humanam creaturam, declaramus, dicimus, definimus & pronuntiamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis. Quis hic non agnoscat illud Danielis de cornu illo Antichristiano dicentis: Fuerunt in ipso oculi hominis, & os loquens grandia? Et rursum: Tum speciabā præcipuē propter uocem grandium sermonum, quos cornu loquebatur. Quàm uero pauci sunt hodie reuelatæ lucis Euangelicæ tempore, quos ista moueant & offendant? Iora Israelis princeps, parum aliâs latus, olim uestes scidit, cum Syriæ Rex ab ipso per literos peteret, ut Naamanum à lepra purgaret. Impium enim & blasphemum esse putabat ab homine postulare, quod in solius Dei potestate est. At hodie atroces illas et Sodomæo incendio dignas blasphemias, sub quarum pondere terra fatiscit, potentissimi Reges & principes cum multo suorum sanguine defendunt.
units.tr: Let us now hear what effect such a free confession had on those men. Luke briefly indicates the final act of the council, where he writes that they all replied together: "What further need do we have of testimony? For we ourselves have heard it from his own mouth." But Matthew and Mark relate everything more fully, in this way: "Then the High Priest tore his garments, saying: 'He has blasphemed. What further need do we have of witnesses? Behold, you have now heard his blasphemy. What do you think?' But they answered and said, 'He is liable to death.'" In these words it is clear what that captious question and oath were aimed at. The High Priest tears his clothes, a sign which the Jews were accustomed to use to signify bitter and unbearable grief of heart conceived from blasphemies heard or from some other sad matter. So he condemns Christ for impiety, while himself pretending to be burning with zeal for the glory of God, which we know is characteristic of hypocrites. But with them the bare doctrine of the truth and the free confession of Christ are thought to be blasphemous and intolerable, because these detract from their reputation and their gain. Would that those who now wish to be called Christians were not so cold that they pass by with deaf ears the open insults against the majesty of God! For how many do we hear who with monstrous audacity deny the Word of God, scornfully belittle the faith of Sacred Scripture, and spit out with dreadful curses the wounds, death and merit of Christ? But how few of anyone at all shudder at these things? Who tears his garments? Who reveals by any sign his righteous indignation or godly grief? And what shall I say of the Popes, who claim divine honours for themselves, deny the very merit of Christ, and, what is more, transfer to themselves in sacrilegious audacity what belongs to him, when they boast that they are the head of the Church and its vicars, having the full power of forgiving sins, of carrying souls up to heaven, or of thrusting them down to hell? Indeed, in their Decrees and Decretals there are passages which prove not so much the impious and blasphemous as the stupendous arrogance of these men. Such is that in Distinction 19: "All the decrees of the apostolic see are to be received as if confirmed by the divine voice of Peter himself." Likewise in the Gloss on De translatione episcopi, title 7, "Quanto": the Pope is said to have a heavenly judgement, and therefore he can make a sentence which is nothing into something; for in those things which he wills, his will stands for reason. Nor is there anyone who may say to him, "Why do you do so?" For he can dispense above the law, and by injustice make justice, correcting and changing laws, since he holds the fullness of power. Add to these that they deny that the Pope may be rebuked by anyone even if he drags souls with him in droves down to hell. And these are the very men in whose name Boniface VIII published the canon Of the Majority and Obedience, whose conclusion is this: "Moreover, we declare, say, define and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff." Who here does not recognise that saying of Daniel about that Antichristian horn, which said: "There were in it the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things"? And again: "I was looking especially at the voice of the great words which the horn was speaking." But how few are there in these days, in the time of the revealed light of the Gospel, whom such things move and offend? Joram, king of Israel, who had little interest in these matters, once tore his garments when the King of Syria asked him by letter to cleanse Naaman of leprosy; for he thought it impious and blasphemous to demand of a man what lies in the power of God alone. But today the most powerful kings and princes defend, at the cost of much of their subjects' blood, those atrocious blasphemies worthy of the fire of Sodom, beneath whose weight the earth groans.

units.la: Sed ut reuertamur unde digressi sumus, Pontifex primus de Christi responso pronuntiat: Blasphemauit: quid amplius egemus testibus? Ecce nunc audistis blasphemiam eius. Quid uobis uidetur? Egregius sanè iudex, qui priusquam aliorum sententias roget, quid illi dicere debeant, præscribit. Sed hunc illi morem fuisse, ex ea actione apparet, quam Ioan.Cap. ii. describit: ubi pro imperio eos omnes corripit & obiurgat, qui non ex eius arbitrio loquebantur. In præsenti tamen nen multa correptione aut ui opus fuit. Nam eadem omnium animis sententia insidebat, & ideo Caiaphæ subscribunt & mortis supplicio dignum esse pronunciant. Ergo cùm de multis prius accusauissent Christum, & falsis quoq; testimonijs eum conuincere conati essent, nunc tamen propter solam ueritatis conféssionem damnatur. Solet hoc ipsum hodie quoq; fieri. Accusantur quidem pij, quòd multa iniustè, multa seditiose, multa impiè faciant atq; dicant. Colliguntur undiq; testimonia, quibus crimina ista probentur. Post multa autem, unica damnationis ipsorum causa est, libera fidei in Iesum Christum confessio. At neminem hoc offendere debet: quin potius eorum quæ illi acciderunt consideratione, nos ad certamina ista præparemus: & agnoscamus hoc singulare Dei consilium, qui nos, quo ad crucem, Filio suo conformes facit, ut cum eodem in cælis uiuamus & regnemus. Ipsi debetur benediction, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But to return to where we digressed: the High Priest first pronounces on Christ's answer: "He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard his blasphemy. What do you think?" A splendid judge indeed, who, before asking the opinions of others, dictates what they ought to say! That this was his custom appears from the action which John describes in chapter 2, where he rebukes and scolds by authority all those who did not speak according to his will. In the present case, however, there was no need for much rebuke or force, for the same judgment was fixed in the minds of all, and so they subscribe to Caiaphas and declare him worthy of the punishment of death. Therefore, although they had earlier accused Christ of many things and had tried to convict him even by false testimony, now he is condemned for the sole reason of his open confession of the truth. The same thing is commonly done today. The godly are indeed accused that they act and speak unjustly, seditiously and impiously in many ways. Testimonies are gathered from every side to prove these crimes. But after all the many charges, the only cause of their condemnation is their free confession of faith in Jesus Christ. Yet no one should be troubled by this; rather, by considering what happened to them, let us prepare ourselves for such conflicts, and let us acknowledge this singular counsel of God, who makes us conformed to his Son in the cross, so that we may live and reign with him in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CCIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCIII.

units.la: TVm surgens vniuersa multitudo eorum, duxit eum ad Pilatum. Cœperunt autē eum accusare, dicentes: Comperimus istum peruerte-regentem, & vetare tributa dare Cæsari, dicentem se Christum Regem esse. Pilatus autem interrogauit eum, dicens: Tu ne es Rex Iudæorum? Ipse verò respondens ei dixit: Tu dicis. Ait verò Pilatus ad principes Sacerdotum & turbam: Nullam inuenio noxam in hoc homine. At illi inualescebant, dicentes. Concitat populum, docens per vniuersam Iudæā, exorsus à Galilæa hucusq.
units.tr: Then the whole multitude of them rose up and led him to Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying: "We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ, a King." And Pilate asked him, saying: "Art thou the King of the Jews?" And he answered him and said: "Thou sayest it." Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowd: "I find no fault in this man." But they were the more fierce, saying: "He stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Judaea, beginning from Galilee even to this place."

units.la: IOannes Apostolus & Euangelista non minus vere quam graviter de æterno Dei Filio in carne manifestato pronuntiat: In sua venit, at sui illum non receperunt. Potes{?} hoc multis probari, si totam eius historiam ex ordine consideres: omnium tamen evidentissimum est, quod in passionis eius narratione proponitur argumentum. Fuit enim Iudæorum gens electum illud Dei peculium, quod is sibi consecrarat, & ex illis Christus, quoad carnem natus est. Idem vero Pater in omnes gentes ius dedit, & has illius hæreditatem sive patrimonium esse noluit, ut David in Psalm. 2. testatur. Quis vero ex Iudæis aut gentibus venientem agnovit? quis debita obedientia & fide illi excepit? Inter Iudæos certè (si paucas illas reliquias excipias, quas ex communi gentis excidio salvas fore, olim Prophetæ prædixerant) omnes hominum ordines adversus illum conspiraverunt. Principes impiæ coniurationis fuerunt, qui minimè debebant, Sacerdotes nimirum & Scribæ, quorum erat de illo testari, & populum ei adducere. Coniungunt se iis Seniores, qui in Repub. eminebant. Utrosque sequitur mobile vulgus, in quo alij magistratibus, alij Sacerdotibus adulari iampridem assueuerant. In vulgo etiam fuerunt servi, qui toti ab herorum nutu pendebant. Et hi quidem simul omnes collecti illum gentibus prophanis tradunt, ut ab his in crucem suffixus diro & infami supplicio vitam finiat. Inter gentes autem similiter, omnis loci & ordinis homines manus atque linguas suas adversus illum acuerunt. Illudit ei Herodes rex, damnat Romani Imperij ac Cæsareæ Maiestatis nomine Pilatus Iudææ Præses, in crucem agunt milites: & postea cum illius doctrina in toto orbe prædicarent Apostoli, ubique locorum philosophos, opifices & quosvis obvios contra eum insurexisse constat. Non autem absque peculiari providentiæ Dei decreto hæc facta esse putabimus. Oportuit enim ita fieri, ut traditi & occisi Christi reatus ad omnis ordinis & loci homines extenderetur, ne aliquis ordo se à tanto scelere immunem posset dicere, & proinde omnes ad huius meritum sibi confugiendum esse sentirent. Adhæc seruit istud nobis contra scandalum, ad quod multi offenduntur, quando hodie quoque fidem in Christum eiusque doctrinam universali quodammodo totius mundi & omnium ordinum consensu damnari vident. Sed accedamus ad præsentis loci tractationem, cuius summa modo capita percurremus, cum de omnibus in Marci & Ioannis expositione copiosius sit dictum.
units.tr: John the Apostle and Evangelist declares, no less truly than gravely, that the eternal Son of God was manifested in the flesh: "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." This can be proved by many things, if you consider his whole history in order; yet the clearest of all is the argument set forth in the account of his passion. For the nation of the Jews was that chosen peculiar people of God, which he had consecrated to himself, and from them Christ was born according to the flesh. Yet the same Father gave the right over all nations, and was unwilling that these should be the inheritance or patrimony of the Jews alone, as David testifies in Psalm 2. But who among the Jews or the Gentiles acknowledged him when he came? Who received him with due obedience and faith? Certainly among the Jews (if you except those few remnants which the Prophets had long ago foretold would be saved from the common destruction of the nation) all the orders of men conspired against him. The leaders of the impious conspiracy were those who least ought to have been, namely the priests and scribes, whose duty it was to bear witness concerning him and to bring the people to him. The elders, who were prominent in the commonwealth, joined them. The fickle crowd followed both, in which some had long been accustomed to flatter the magistrates, others the priests. Among the common people there were also slaves, who depended entirely on the nod of their masters. And these all together handed him over to the profane Gentiles, so that, fixed to the cross, he might end his life by a cruel and infamous punishment. Among the Gentiles, likewise, men of every place and rank sharpened their hands and tongues against him. Herod the king mocked him; Pilate, governor of Judaea, condemned him in the name of the Roman Empire and of Caesar's majesty; soldiers carried him to the cross. And afterwards, when the Apostles preached his teaching throughout the world, it is well known that everywhere philosophers, craftsmen and whoever else they met rose up against him. Nor shall we think that these things were done without the special decree of God's providence. For it was fitting that the guilt of the betrayed and slain Christ should extend to men of every rank and place, lest any order could say it was free from so great a crime, and so that all should feel they must take refuge in his merit. Moreover, this serves us against the scandal at which many are offended, when today too they see faith in Christ and his doctrine condemned, as it were, by the almost universal consent of the whole world and of all orders. But let us come to the treatment of the present passage, whose sum we will only run through by its heads, since everything has been said more fully in the exposition of Mark and John.

units.la: Primo, ut ad Romanum Præsidem ductus sit Christus narratur. Tum surgens universa multitudo eorum duxit eum ad Pilatum. Videntur quidem de solis Sacerdotibus, Senioribus & Scribis hoc dici: at paulo post hos à turba distinguit: unde colligimus, populum capti Christi fama excitatum ad Caiaphæ domum confluxisse, & illos hoc comitante illum Pilato occidendum tradidisse. Quod ita fieri oportere ille prædixerat his verbis: Ecce ascendimus Hierosolymam; & Filius hominis tradetur principibus Sacerdotum ac Scribis, & condemnabunt eum morte, TRADENTQVE EVM GENTIBVS ad hoc ut illudant ac flagellent, & crucifigant. Fuit autem hoc facinus multò indignissimum. Nam illos Christum propter doctrinam & religionem accusavisse constat: imò causæ totius hic status fuit: An Iesus iste sit Christus, id est, Vnctus Dei & promissus humani generis redemptor. Itaque dum hunc Pilato tradunt, simul causam istam, ex qua omnis illorum religio dependebat, hominis ethnici & prophani iudicio subijciunt, & ut Christus è medio tollatur, cum eo iam possunt convenire, qui multa in gentem ipsorum iniustè, multa hostiliter & crudeliter gesserat: sicuti in historijs est videre. Sic olim Iacobi Israelis filij Iosephu fratre Madianitis vendiderunt, & horum opera ad eum tollendum usi sunt, quem non alia de causa oderant, quàm quod eum nequitiæ & libidini ipsorum obstare viderent. Et prodesse huius nunquam oblivisci, quando eandem seruorum suorum sortem fore ille prædixit: nimirum, ut parentes adversus filios insurgant, & cuiusque hostes acerrimi sint domestici eius. Neque hoc cuiquam mirum videri debet. Sunt enim omnium acerbissima odia, quæ religionis causa suscipiuntur. Nam ut hæc, si vera fuerit, homines Deo, & vicissim illos inter se mutuo obstringit, ut in unum quasi corpus coalescant: ita si qui falsam secuti fuerint, non possunt non totis animis excandescere adversus illos, quos abs se secessionem facere vident, & quorum ore atque exemplo superstitiones ipsorum arguuntur. Similiter qui à Veritate deficiunt, etiam huius sectatores oderunt, & omnes perditos vellent, ne quos haberent suæ leuitatis accusatores: adeò ut in proverbium abierit, Omnes apostatæ esse persecutores sui ordinis. Exempla huius mali multa hodie adduntur: nec est quòd Iudæorum iniquos & crudeles in Christi animos miremur, quando hodie multi sunt, quos non pudet ad Turcarum tribunalia cultoribus Christi propter solam doctrinam & religionem lites
units.tr: First, it is related that Christ was led before the Roman governor. "Then the whole multitude of them rose up and led him to Pilate." These words seem to refer only to the priests, elders and scribes; but a little later he distinguishes them from the crowd. From this we gather that the people, roused by the report of Christ's arrest, flocked to the house of Caiaphas, and that these, with the crowd accompanying them, handed him over to Pilate to be put to death. That this must so come to pass he had foretold in these words: "Behold, we go up to Jerusalem; and the Son of man shall be delivered unto the chief priests and scribes, and they shall condemn him to death, AND SHALL DELIVER HIM TO THE GENTILES to mock, scourge and crucify him." This deed, however, was most unworthy. For it is well known that they accused Christ on account of his teaching and religion; indeed, the whole issue of this trial was this: whether this Jesus is the Christ, that is, the Anointed of God and the promised redeemer of the human race. So, while they handed him over to Pilate, at the same time they submitted that cause, on which their entire religion depended, to the judgement of a heathen and profane man; and in order that Christ might be removed from the midst, they could now agree with one who had done many unjust and many hostile and cruel things against their nation, as may be seen in the histories. So of old the sons of Jacob Israel sold Joseph, their brother, to the Midianites, and used their help to remove him whom they hated for no other reason than that they saw him standing in the way of their wickedness and lust. And it is worth remembering that he foretold that his servants would meet the same fate: namely, that parents would rise up against their children, and a man's bitterest enemies would be those of his own household. Nor should anyone think this strange. For the most bitter hatreds of all are those undertaken for the sake of religion. For just as true religion binds men to God, and likewise binds them mutually to one another, so that they grow together into one body, so those who have followed a false religion cannot help but burn with all their soul against those whom they see withdrawing from them, and whose speech and example expose their superstitions. Likewise those who fall away from the Truth also hate its followers, and would wish all of them destroyed, lest they have accusers of their own inconstancy; so much so that it has passed into a proverb: all apostates are persecutors of their own order. Many examples of this evil are cited today; nor is there cause for us to wonder at the wicked and cruel minds of the Jews against Christ, since today there are many who are not ashamed to bring lawsuits against the worshippers of Christ, for the sake of doctrine and religion alone, before the tribunals of the Turks, to say nothing of those who summon a barbarian enemy from afar, and who stir up strife between brothers, kinsmen, relatives, and finally spouses, through which the purer knowledge of God is crushed together with all the godly.

units.la: Christus Rom. praesidi tradi-tur.
units.tr: Christ is handed over to the Roman governor.

units.la: Matth.10. moueret: ut nunc eos taceam, qui hostem barbarū è longinquo accersunt, qui inter fratres germanos, cognatos, affines, coniuges denique dissidia ferunt, per quae purior Dei cognitio cū pijs omnibus opprimatur. Sunt haec multis dura & acerba admodum: sed tunc nobis exemplum Christi in mente veniat, & Prophetae consilium sequamur, qui eadem sui seculi hominibus propter effrenem morum licentiam denuntians, simul admonet, quid tunc pij facere debeant. Ne credatis (inquit) amico, ne spere tis in duce: ab ea quae dormit in sinu tuo, custodi ostia oris tui: Quia filius contumelia afficit patrem, filia surgit contra matrem suam, nurus contra socrum suam, inimici cuiusque sunt domestici eius: EGO AVTEM AD DOMINVM SPECTABO, expectabo Deum salutis meae: exaudiet me Deus meus. Loquitur haec Micheas in communi omnium credentium persona, qui & ipsi in tanta hominum perfidia Dei praesidio tuti erunt. Qui vero Iudaeorum crudelitatem atque perfidam imitantur, easdem aliquando poenas Deo & communi patriae exoluent, quas illi senserunt.
units.tr: Matth. 10. These things are very hard and bitter for many; but let the example of Christ come to mind, and let us follow the counsel of the Prophet, who, announcing the same things to the men of his age on account of their unbridled licence of morals, at the same time warns what the godly ought then to do. "Trust not a friend," he says, "put not your confidence in a leader; keep the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom. For the son dishonours the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are those of his own household. BUT AS FOR ME, I WILL LOOK UNTO THE LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me." Micah speaks these words in the common person of all believers, who also in such great faithlessness of men will be safe under the protection of God. But those who imitate the cruelty and faithlessness of the Jews will sooner or later pay to God and to their common country the same penalties which they suffered.

units.la: Priusquam autem ab hoc loco discedamus, vulgi quoque inconstantiam atque ingratitudinem observasse proderit. Secuti sunt paulo ante Christum magnis turmis, adeo ut concursus ille, qui ad ipsum fiebat, Sacerdotibus ac Senioribus formidabilis esset. In templo ite auditi sunt, qui de ipso, testarentur, & Messiā (siquidem quis alius venire debeat) signa maiora facere posse negarent. Denique in eius ad urbē aduentu omnes attoniti magnū quid animo concipiebant: neque repertus est, qui eius conatui se se opponeret, cum templi et cultus externi repurgatione magno cū periculo coniuncta aggrederetur. Tanta fuit apud omnes divinae potentiae in miraculis eius sese exeretis authoritas. Nunc aut, quādo hostiū insidijs interceptū, et publica Concilij authoritate damnatū esse uident, subitò omnis illa spes in fumū abijt, nec modò de illo honorificè sentire desinunt, sed principum suorum partes sequuntur, his se adsunt, ut tam horū quam totius populi nomine & consensu Pilato tradatur. Quid, quod paulò post Sacerdotū uerbis eò se adduci patiuntur, ut illum ad crucis supplicium deposcant furiosis atque seditiosis clamoribus? Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quàm nihil tribui debeat vulgo ignobili, & quàm parum rebus suis consulant, qui ab huius multorū capitum bestiae fauore pendent, quo nihil incertius, nihil instabilius aut mutabilius esse, omnium gentium historiae testantur. Vt enim mare partim æstu naturali fluit ac refluit, partim uentis hinc inde agitatur: ita populus innata inconstantia nunc in has nunc in illas partes transit, & si noua aliqua fortuna mutatio accedat, subitò totus à pristina mente aut institu̇o alienatur. Fit ergo, ut qui rempub. suis curis & laboribus uehementer iuuarunt, tandem non solum ingratos, uerumetiam acerrimos hostes experiantur eos, pro quibus ipsi saepe periclitati sunt, & proprium sanguinem deposuerunt. Pertinent huc quae olim Athenienses in Phocionem, Aristidem, Themistoclem, Romani in Scipiones, Ciceronem & similes designarunt. In primis tamen hoc in religionis & fidei causa fieri solet, quam maior hominum pars utilitate & quaestu metitur. Feruent ergo pleriq;, quando Dei Verbum praedicatur, in quo multa de libertate filiorum Dei, de peccatorū remissione et gratia Dei dici audiūt. Quia enim ista carnis sensu accipiunt, ex illis sibi immunitatem ab oneribus publicis, opes, dignitates & quiduis audendi licentiā pollicentur. Quàm primum uero haec spes eos fallit, animos mutant, se turpiter deceptos esse querunter, hostes deniq; fiunt omnium nocentissimi, qui & ui aperta & proditorijs artibus omnem de Christo doctrinam extinguere satagunt. Et hi omnes ad illorum numerum pertinent, quos ille in sementis parabola προσκαιρος siue temporarios uocat, eò quòd uel praecocium fructuum similes nō diu durant, uel quòd pro temporum ratione suam de fide & religione sententiā mutant. Fiūt hodie multa huius generis, quae neminem debent offendere. Quid enim aliud faciat mundus hic, qui in sola inconstantia sua constans est? Quid homines aliud faciant, quos natura mendaces esse Spiritus Sanctus per Dauidē testatur? Soletur autē nos, quòd Domini Verbum in aeternum manet, & quòd coronam iustitiae suis praeparauit Deus, quam certò consequentur, qui in finem usq; perseueraverint.
units.tr: Before we depart from this place, it will be useful to note also the inconstancy and ingratitude of the crowd. A little before, they had followed Christ in great throngs, so that the concourse which gathered about him was a source of dread to the priests and elders. In the temple, some were heard who bore witness concerning him and denied that the Messiah (since, indeed, who else ought to come?) could do greater signs. Finally, at his arrival in the city, all were astonished and conceived great hopes in their minds; nor was anyone found who opposed his attempt when he undertook the cleansing of the temple and of external worship, a thing joined with great danger. So great was the authority, among all, of the divine power displayed in his miracles. But now, when they see him caught by the snares of enemies and condemned by the public authority of the Council, suddenly all that hope has vanished into smoke; they not only cease to think honourably of him, but follow their leaders' side, attend upon them, so that in the name and by the consent of both these and the whole people he may be handed over to Pilate. What of the fact that a little later they allow themselves to be led by the words of the priests to such a point that they demand his crucifixion with furious and seditious shouts? This is a memorable example, by which we are taught how little should be ascribed to the ignoble crowd, and how little they consult their own interests who depend on the favour of that many-headed beast, than which nothing is more uncertain, nothing more unstable or changeable, as the histories of all nations bear witness. For just as the sea partly flows and ebbs by its natural tide, and partly is driven hither and thither by the winds, so the people, through innate inconstancy, passes now to these, now to those parties; and if some new turn of fortune comes, suddenly the whole multitude is alienated from its former mind or institution. So it happens that those who have greatly helped the commonwealth by their cares and labours at last experience not only ungrateful but the most bitter enemies in those for whom they have often been in danger and have shed their own blood. To this belong the things which the Athenians once did against Phocion, Aristides and Themistocles, and the Romans against the Scipios, Cicero and the like. Yet this is especially wont to happen in the cause of religion and faith, which the greater part of men measure by profit and gain. Therefore many grow ardent when the Word of God is preached, in which they hear much about the freedom of the sons of God, the forgiveness of sins and the grace of God. For since they understand these things in a carnal sense, they promise themselves from them exemption from public burdens, wealth, honours, and licence to dare whatever they like. But as soon as this hope disappoints them, they change their minds, complain that they have been shamefully deceived, and finally become the most harmful of all enemies of Christ, striving by open force and by treacherous arts to extinguish all doctrine concerning him. And all these belong to the number of those whom he, in the parable of the sower, calls πρόσκαιρος, that is, temporary; because, like early fruits, they either do not last long, or they change their opinion about faith and religion according to the times. Many things of this kind happen today, which ought to offend no one. For what else does this world do, which is constant only in its own inconstancy? What else do men do, whom the Holy Spirit through David testifies to be liars by nature? Yet this comforts us, that the Word of the Lord abides for ever, and that God has prepared a crown of righteousness for his own, which those surely obtain who persevere to the end.

units.la: Sed tempus est uidere, quales in hac causa non minus turpi & inhonesta quàm impia Sacerdotes sese gesserint: ubi eos cū hypocrisi et iniustitia impudentissimam arrogantiā coniunxisse uidebis. His enim artibus et armis opus erat, cùm se pessima causā agere nō possent ignorare. Occurrit inter haec primū, quod Ioānes annotauit, illos noluisse in Prætorium ingredi, ne loci prophani contactu pollue rentur, & indigni fierent qui epulum paschale manducarent. Fuit haec hypocrisis cum stupida ignorantia coniuncta. Prætorium enim, quod iustitiae domicilium erat, pro prophano ducunt, quasi uerò omnia
units.tr: But it is time to see how the priests conducted themselves in this cause, in a way that was no less base and dishonourable than impious. Here you will see them joining hypocrisy and injustice with the most shameless arrogance. They needed these arts and weapons, since they could not fail to know that they were pleading a very bad cause. Among these things, first comes what John noted: that they refused to enter the praetorium, lest they be polluted by contact with a profane place and so become unfit to eat the Passover meal. This hypocrisy was joined with stupid ignorance. For they regarded the praetorium, which was the home of justice, as profane, as though all holiness were tied to the Temple and the synagogues.

units.la: omnis sanctitas Templo & Synagogis esset alligata. Quo errore nostri etiam Papista religionem & sanctitatem templis per suos Suffraganeos consecratis astringunt, curias vero & iudicum tribunalia prophana loca esse dicunt: neq; eo contenti, magistratus quoq; et iudices ignominioso seculari-um nomine notant, quasi inter prophanos huius seculi filios, non autem inter filios Dei, qui omnes a Spiritu Christi, quem acceperunt, Spirituales dicuntur, censeri debeant. Quanto rectius Romani, qui ne Reipub. gubernatione a sacris & religione alienam facerent, Iouem Capitolinum coluerunt, cui in praecipuo urbis loco, ubi res ad Rempub. pertinentes tractabantur, templum constituerunt. Mirum ergo est iflos ta stupidos fuisse, qui ex Scripturis didicisse debebant, Deum ipsum iudicium consessibus medium interesse. Peperit ignorantia ista superstitione & simulatum sanctitatis studium, ut a loco illo abhorreret: quod quam praeposterè & ridicule fecerint, ex eo apparet, quod innocentem ea ipsa hora damnauerunt, & nunc eunde prophano homini tradunt. Quid, quod de epulo paschali soliciti, eu pro dunt impie, qui eo adumbrabatur, & qui vere Agnus ille Dei est, qui tollit peccatum mundi? Quid hoc aliud fuit, quam culicem colare, camelum autem deglutire? Ita vero fit, ut proprio indicio sese prodat hypocrisis. Solet hoc ipsum multis hodie euenire, qui religione et sanctitate in externis constistere sibi persuaserunt. Exempla quae alibi commemorauimus, & quae passim occurrunt, repetere non est opus.
units.tr: By this same error our own Papists also bind religion and holiness to temples consecrated through their suffragans, but they call law courts and the tribunals of judges profane places. Not content with this, they also brand magistrates and judges with the disgraceful name of "secular", as though they ought to be counted among the profane sons of this age and not among the sons of God, who are all called spiritual through the Spirit of Christ which they have received. How much more correctly did the Romans act, who, lest they make the government of the commonwealth alien from sacred things and religion, worshipped Jupiter of the Capitol and set up his temple in the most prominent place of the city, where affairs concerning the commonwealth were transacted. It is strange, then, that those men were so stupid, when they ought to have learned from the Scriptures that God himself is present in the midst of judicial assemblies. That ignorance produced superstition and a pretended zeal for holiness, so that they shrank from that place. How preposterously and ridiculously they acted appears from this: at that very hour they condemned the innocent man, and now they hand him over to the profane man. What of the fact that, anxious about the Passover meal, they impiously betray him who was foreshadowed by it, and who truly is that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world? What was this other than straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel? Thus hypocrisy betrays itself by its own sign. This happens to many today who have persuaded themselves that religion and holiness consist in externals. There is no need to repeat the examples which we have mentioned elsewhere and which occur everywhere.

units.la: Vt autem idem Ioannes scribit, ipsis in Praetorium ingredi non volentibus, Pilatus foras ad ipsos egreditur (quod non contemnendum est modestiae & aequitatis civilis exemplum) & quaerit quid nam designarit Iesus, quem ideo ad se duci non potuit ignorare, ut occideretur. Ipsi vero cum sibi male conscii esset, hoc agunt, ne quam accusationem instituere cogantur: ideo superbe ac insolenter minimis suam authoritatem urgent, dicentes: Si hic non esset nocens, non tradidissemus eum tibi. Quasi vero nihil unquam designassent, cuius causa ipsorum actiones atq; studia suspecta esse deberent: cum omnibus nota essent, quae circa doctrinae depravationem, sacrorum nundinationem & totius cultus prophanationem quotidie ab ipsis fiebant. Sed hoc illud argumentum est, quo hodie multi Pontificum & Monachorum sanguinaria aduersus homines vere Christianos consilia excusant. Nisi (inquiunt) Iupiter & impie isti errarent, nisi haeretici essent, Deo exosi & religionis pestes, nunquam certe a patribus illis sanctissimis damnarentur. Egregia sane ratio. Quasi vero nihil unquam illi aduersus iustitiam & pietatis leges perpetrauerint. Iflis haec dicantur, qui Simoniacas illorum hominum artes, prodigiosas libidines, venefcia & alia atrocissima flagitia ignorant. Illis haec ratio ingeratur, qui illorum artibus proditoris iam per saecula aliquot principes circumuentos, & orbem terrarum bellis civilibus atq; exteris turbatum esse nescunt. Imo bonos, sanctos & Veritatis studiosos esse oportet eos, quos isti non possunt ferre, quorum nequitia toti mundo notissima est. Veruntamen merito deploramus nostrorum temporum caecitatem, quando potentissimi reges hoc tam ludicro argumento sese decipi patiuntur, ut vel bella non necessaria in nihil hostile meritos suscipiant, vel in proprium populum praeter omne fas ferro & igne horribiliter grassentur. Pudeat illos a Pilato iustitia & aequitate superari: qui etsi inter Sacerdotes authoritate multa graues et Christum, hominem quoad munedi iudicium nullius pretij, iniquissima esset comparatio, noluit tamen hunc in illorum gratiam causa incognita damnare, sed cum indignatione impiam hanc insolentiam reicit, dicens: Accipite eum vos, & secundum legem vestram iudicate eum, &c. Cogitate quaeso o principes, pretiosam esse in oculis Domini morte sanctorum eius, & principum esse, ut populi sui sanguine pretiosum ducant. Psalm 6. & 72.
units.tr: But, as the same John writes, when they would not enter the praetorium, Pilate went out to them (an example of modesty and civil fairness that is not to be despised) and asked what Jesus had done, for he could not be ignorant that he had been brought before him in order to be put to death. But they, being conscious of their guilt, did this, that they might not be forced to bring any accusation. So they pressed their authority arrogantly and insolently on the smallest matters, saying: "If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you." As though they had never done anything which ought to make their actions and pursuits suspect, when all knew what they were doing every day: the corruption of doctrine, the selling of sacred things, and the profanation of all worship. But this is that argument by which many Pontiffs and monks today excuse their bloody counsels against men who are truly Christian. "Unless" (they say) "Jupiter and those impious men were in error, unless they were heretics, hateful to God and pests of religion, they would certainly never have been condemned by those most holy fathers." An excellent argument indeed! As though those men had never committed anything against the laws of justice and piety. Let these things be said to those who do not know the simoniacal arts of those men, their monstrous lusts, their poisonings and other most atrocious crimes. Let this argument be thrown at those who do not know that for some centuries now princes have been surrounded by their treachery, and the whole world has been thrown into turmoil by civil and foreign wars. Indeed, those whom they cannot bear, and whose wickedness is best known to the whole world, must be good, holy, and zealous for the truth! Yet we rightly lament the blindness of our times, when the most powerful kings allow themselves to be deceived by so ridiculous an argument, so that they either undertake unnecessary wars against men who have deserved nothing hostile, or else rage horribly with sword and fire against their own people, beyond all right. Let them be ashamed to be outdone by Pilate in justice and fairness. Although the priests were weighty in authority, and Christ was a man of no worth in the world's judgement (the comparison would be most unjust), Pilate nevertheless did not wish to condemn him without a hearing merely to please them. He rejected this impious insolence with indignation, saying: "Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law, etc." Consider, I beg you, O princes, that the death of his saints is precious in the eyes of the Lord, and that it is fitting for princes to hold as precious the blood of their people. Psalm 6. & 72.

units.la: Porrò cum Sacerdotes Pilatus tam graviter increpuissent, illi accusatione eiusmodi instituunt: Coperimus istum peruertere gentem, et vetare tributa dare Caesari, dicentes se Christum Regem esse. Paucis verbis tria crimina grauissima comprehendunt. Primum, quod gentem peruertat. Id vero ad doctrinam referri debet, quae ab illo populum rudem & simpliciter seduci queruntur. Quam vero indigne hoc faciant, ex eo apparet, quod ipsi seductores erant pessimi. Nam quae Dominus docebat, ea ex Mose & Prophetis poterant demonstrari: & vere licuit illi dicere: Doctrina mea non est mea, sed eius qui misit me. At illi cum Lege humanas traditiones miscuerat, quibus verus illius sensus & usus omnino depravatus & extinctus erat. Agnum ergo accusant lupi, et huic crime intentat, quo ipsi maxime tenebatur. Alterum adremp. pertinet, & seditione spirat, quando illum prohibere aiunt, ne Caesari tributa dentur: Vbi impudentia illorum magis aut iniustitia atq; calumnia admirere nescio. Recens enim adhuc erat disputationis cum illo de hac re instituta memoria, in qua adhibitis in societate Sadducaeis & Herodianis quæstione hanc propofuerūt: Num liceat censum dare Cæsari? Quid autē ille? Cùm denarìū sibi exhiberi iussisset, et de eius inscriptione ipsos interrogauisset, proprio oris testimonio coactis dixit: Date quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei, Deo. Et hæc quidē non in angulo obscuro, sed in urbe Hierosolyma, sed in tēplo, imò in frequenti multorū auditorū corona ille dixerat. Audēt tamē hanc illi mouere calumniā, neq; uerentur, ne quis ex populo istud audiēs, rei indignitate offensus illos mendacij arguat. Tanta est hypocrisis audacia. Et simul novo rursus argumento populi istius ingratitu-do atq; leuitas arguitur, quando in tanta multitudine ne unus quidem reperitur, qui tam impudenti mendacio contradicat. Ne tamē absq; omni ratione istud dicere uideātur, tertio crimine alterū istud probare student, quòd nimirū se Christū illū populi Dei Regem esse gloriētur. Quia enim reges tribu-ta nō alijs sed sibi dari voluerunt, credibile uideri poterat, Iesum, si regnum sibi in ulla gente uendicaret, nō permissurū posthac, ut tributa amplius Cæsari darentur. Fuit autē hoc quoq; cū turpi ignorantia & calumnia coniunctū. Quæ enim de regno Christi spirituali in Prophetis dicūtur, illi de terreno ex-ponunt, ut sæpe iam diximus; & cùm nō possunt ignorare, nihil huius unquā illū dixisse, imò fugisse etiam, quando populus ipsorū falsis traditionibus seductus eum voluit Regē creare, impudenter ta-men hoc quoq; prioribus audēt adijcere. Et hæc quidē præcipua sunt, de quibus Veritatis ministri in hoc mundo accusantur. Seductores eos esse dicunt superstitionū magistri, cùm illi unū Christum præ-dicent, qui est Veritas, Via & Lux. Vt uerò principes quoq;, qui religionis causam fere non magni faciunt, aduersus illos prouocentur, alia crimina coniungunt, quæ ad remp. spectant. Dicuntur er-gorebus nouis studere, populū contra magistratū concitare, leges et receptos mores euertere, pacē pu-blicam turbare, deniq; cum patriæ communis hostibus colludere, & nihil tam absurdū & iniquum est, quod nō liceat fingere ijs, qui semel contra Veritatē coniurauerunt. Factū est hoc olim Prophetarū temporibus, & Apostolos ijsdem criminibus grauatos fuisse, non uno loco ostendimus. De neteri Ec-clesia, quid dicere attinet? quando omnes historiæ testātur, Christianos hoc potissimùm nomine ad diros exquisitissimorū tormentorum cruciatus abreptos fuisse, quòd noua de religione doctrina uete-res cultus abolerent, ipsi cœtus nocturnos haberent infandos & scelerātos, quòd item deorum iram prouocarent, quòd propter illos cessarent oracula, & orbis terrarū infinitis plagis multaretur. Et hodie uulgò ista audiuntur, nec aliud tam tritum est, quàm quòd sacrorum & Diuorum cœlitum hostes & reipub. turbatores dicimur, qui toti in hoc sumus, ut Deo uni omnis cultus exhibeatur, ut Christus supra omnes emineat, & huc ceu capiti suo omnes uniantur, & in illo uicamuiuant pi-am, pacificam & Christiana professione dignam. Sed non offendat aliquem ista calumniarum li-centia. Nouit enim innocentiam nostram Dominus, & idem memoriam suorum tuetur.
units.tr: Moreover, when Pilate had so sharply rebuked the priests, they brought against him an accusation of this kind: "We have found this man perverting our nation and forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ the King." In a few words they include three most grave crimes. The first is that he perverts the nation. This must refer to doctrine, by which they complain that the simple people are led astray. How unworthily they do this appears from the fact that they themselves were the worst seducers. For what the Lord taught could be demonstrated from Moses and the Prophets, and he could rightly say: "My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me." But they had mixed human traditions with the Law, by which its true sense and use had been wholly corrupted and extinguished. So wolves accuse the lamb, and bring against him the very crime by which they themselves were most held. The second charge pertains to the state and breathes sedition, when they say he forbids tribute to be given to Caesar. Here I do not know whether to wonder more at their impudence, their injustice, or their calumny. For the memory of the discussion held with him on this very matter was still fresh. In it, with Sadducees and Herodians joined in alliance, they put the question: "Is it lawful to give the census to Caesar?" And what did he do? When he had ordered a denarius to be shown to him, and asked them about its inscription, he said, compelled by their own testimony: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And he had said this not in some obscure corner, but in the city of Jerusalem, indeed in the Temple, and in fact before a large crowd of listeners. Yet they dare to bring this slander against him, and do not fear that someone from the people, hearing it and offended at the indignity of the matter, would convict them of lying. Such is the audacity of hypocrisy. At the same time, the ingratitude and fickleness of that people is again exposed by this new argument, since in so great a multitude not even one is found who contradicts so shameless a lie. Yet, lest they seem to say this without any reason, they try to prove the third charge, namely that he boasted of being the King of God's people. For since kings wished tribute to be given not to others but to themselves, it could seem credible that Jesus, if he claimed a kingdom among any people, would no longer allow tribute to be given to Caesar. This too was joined with base ignorance and calumny. For what is said in the Prophets about the spiritual kingdom of Christ they expound of an earthly one, as we have often said already. Although they cannot be ignorant that he never said anything of the kind, indeed that he even fled when the people, seduced by their false traditions, wished to make him king, they shamelessly dare to add this too to the former charges. These are indeed the chief things for which the ministers of the Truth in this world are accused. They say they are seducers and masters of superstitions, whereas they preach the one Christ, who is Truth, Way and Light. Moreover, to stir up princes also, who hardly care much for the cause of religion, against them, they join other charges which concern the commonwealth. They are said therefore to pursue new things, to stir up the people against the magistrate, to overturn laws and accepted customs, to disturb the public peace, and finally to collude with the common enemies of the fatherland. Nothing is so absurd or unjust that it may not be invented against those who have once conspired against the Truth. This happened in the times of the Prophets, and that the Apostles were burdened with the same charges we have shown in more than one place. Of the ancient Church, what need is there to speak, since all histories testify that Christians were dragged to dreadful and most exquisite torments chiefly on this name: because by a new doctrine of religion they abolished the old worship, held nightly assemblies that were unspeakable and wicked, and likewise because they provoked the anger of the gods, because on their account the oracles ceased, and the whole world was punished with infinite plagues. Even today these things are commonly heard, and nothing is so worn as the saying that we are enemies of the sacred rites and the heavenly divinities and disturbers of the commonwealth, when we are wholly intent on this: that the one God be given all worship, that Christ stand above all, and that all be united to him as to their head, and in him live a life that is pious, peaceful, and worthy of the Christian profession. But let not such licence of calumny offend anyone. The Lord knows our innocence, and he guards the memory of his own.

units.la: Redeamus nunc ad Pilatum, qui de doctrina non multum solicitus, quod inter reliqua præci-puum erat, examine diligentiori dignum putat: & merito quidem, quando in Iudæam ideo missus e-rat cum imperio, ut motus nullos oriri pateretur, & pacem publicā custodiret, deniq; prohiberet, ne qui in seditiosa Iudæorum gente regnum affectantes cum Parthis conspirarent, qui Imperij Roma-ni hostes erant grauissimi, & non ita pridem Crassum & legiones Romanas cum uistricibus illis a-quilis horribili clade oppresserant. Itaq; Iesum ex populi tumultuantis turba in Prætorium intro-duētum interrogat: Tu ne es Rex Iudæorum? Sciebat enim illos regem quendam in ore habere, qui populum in libertatem vindicaturus esset. Et quia ex officio in hanc causam inquirit, nequaquam illum Christus responso dedignatur, sed ingenue et diligenter se Regem esse profitetur, simulq; totam regni sui rationem describit: quæ omnia Ioannes prolixè narrat, Lucas autem uno uerbo rem om-nem expedit. Et est obseruatu dignißimum Christi exemplum, quem non puduit cum prophano iu-dice de regno suo colloqui, & ad eius quæstiones amicè respondere, quoad ille officium faciebat, nec àsolita & æqua iuris dicendi forma discedebat. At hodie Anabaptistæ in hoc omnem pietatis & syncerę religionis zelum cosistere arbitrantur, si magistratus clament tenebrarum potestatem esse, si & iudices & Ecclesiarū ministros non solùm responso dedignentur, sed insuper scurrilibus di-ctis fungant, & conuiciis quoq; diris obruant. Mirum hominum genus, qui cùm absq; omni legitima ue-cationis testimonio ubiq; locorum Respub. & Ecclesias turbent, nemini tamen eorum rationem red-dere uolunt, quæ dicunt & faciunt. Sed sufficit illis conuincendis uel sola ista proteruia & contu-macia, quæ satis docet, quàm procul absint à Spiritu Christi, quo maximè gloriantur.
units.tr: Let us now return to Pilate, who, not very concerned about the doctrine, nonetheless judged the examination of it, the chief of the other matters, worthy of closer scrutiny. And rightly so, since he had been sent into Judea with authority to see that no disturbances arose, to keep the peace, and above all to prevent those in the seditious nation of the Jews who aspired to kingship from conspiring with the Parthians, the most dangerous enemies of the Roman Empire, who not long before had overwhelmed Crassus and the Roman legions, with their victorious eagles, in a dreadful slaughter. So he questions Jesus, who had been brought into the Praetorium from the tumultuous crowd: "Are you the King of the Jews?" For he knew that they had a certain king constantly on their lips, one who was going to liberate the people. And since he inquires into the case by virtue of his office, Christ by no means refuses to answer him, but frankly and carefully professes that he is King, and at the same time describes the whole nature of his kingdom. John narrates all of this at length, while Luke disposes of the whole matter in a single word. And Christ's example is most worthy of notice: he was not ashamed to speak of his kingdom with a profane judge, and he answered his questions kindly, insofar as the judge was performing his duty, and did not depart from the usual and fair form of judicial procedure. But today the Anabaptists think that all zeal for piety and sincere religion consists in this: if they shout that the magistrates are the power of darkness, and if they not only refuse an answer to judges and ministers of the Churches, but also pour out buffoonish words and overwhelm them with dreadful insults. A strange kind of men: although, without any lawful testimony of their calling, they disturb the commonwealth and the Churches everywhere, they are unwilling to give an account to anyone of what they say and do. But to convict them, their own sheer insolence and obstinacy is enough, which teaches well enough how far they are from the Spirit of Christ, in whom they most glory.

units.la: Caterum Cæterùm audito Christo, facilè intelligit Pilatus illum iniquè & per calumniā accusari, ideoq; fo ras egressus, diserte eum innocentè esse pronuntiat. Nulla (inquit) inuenio noxa in hoc homine. Est hoc magnum innocentiæ Christi testimoniū, cuius hic nobis usus esse debet, ut quando ipse nulla pro pria culpa mortis supplicium meruit, illum proter nos hoc omne sustinuisse, firmiter credamus, ut suo merito nostra noxa expiaret. Quod ut nō intelligunt Sacerdotes & Seniores, quos auaritiæ & ambitionis affectus totos excæcauerat: ita neq; calumniæ eos pudet: & quàmuis se in mendacio deprehe fos esse sentiant, tamen primū accusationis caput denuo urgent, crimenq; amplificant, dum doctrina eius populū concitari dicunt, simulq; quam longè lateq; iam sparsa sit, ostendunt, ne Pilatus rem hāc nullius momenti esse existimet, quæ absq; periculo posset negligi. Clamant ergo: Concitat populū, docens per uniuersam Iudæam, exorsus à Galilæa hucusq;. Vbi uerè quidè dicunt, ipsum tam Galilæam quàm Iudæa doctrina sua perlustrauisse: falsissimū uerò est, q; populū ab ipso cocitari aiunt, & in hoc mox ipse Herodes eos mendaci arguet, ut in sequenti Sermone audiemus. Et solet hoc euenire hosti bus Veritatis, ut quò magis insaniunt, quoq; impudentius calumnias congerunt, eò magis propriam infamiā prodant, pluresq; inueniāt mendaciorū suorū reprehensores. Nunc uerò ista nos admonere debent, ut maiori studio nostrā innocentiam tueamur, quando nos scimus tam iniquos & impuden tes habere nostrarū actionū atq; consiliorum iudices. Interim non moueant nos illorū calumniæ, quò minùs fortes simus in Christo Iesu, qui & olim istorum impudentiam arguet, & in suis quoq; de mun do eius q; principe triumphabit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, having heard Christ, Pilate easily understands that he is being accused unjustly and through calumny; therefore, going out, he plainly pronounces him innocent. "I find," he says, "no fault in this man." This is a great testimony to Christ's innocence, and we ought to use it here: since he himself deserved the punishment of death through no fault of his own, we should firmly believe that he endured all this on our account, so that by his merit he might expiate our guilt. The chief priests and elders, whom the desire for greed and ambition had wholly blinded, do not understand this, and so they are not ashamed of their calumny. Although they perceive that they have been caught in a lie, they nevertheless press again the first point of the accusation and magnify the charge, saying that by his teaching the people are being stirred up, and showing how far and wide it has already spread, lest Pilate think the matter to be of no importance, something that could be neglected without danger. So they cry out: "He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place." Here they indeed speak truly that he has traversed both Galilee and Judea with his teaching; but it is utterly false that they say he stirred up the people, and in this Herod himself will soon prove them liars, as we shall hear in the following sermon. And it is the habit of the enemies of the truth that the more they rave, and the more shamelessly they heap up calumnies, the more they betray their own infamy and find more critics of their lies. Now these things ought to warn us to guard our innocence with greater zeal, since we know that we have such unjust and shameless judges of our actions and counsels. Meanwhile let their calumnies not move us to be less brave in Christ Jesus, who will one day also condemn their impudence and triumph over them and over the prince of this world who is theirs. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXXIIII.

units.la: Pilatus verò audita Galilæa, interrogauit nū Galilæus esset. Et cum cognouisset eum ad Herodis potestatē pertinere, remisit eū ad Herodē, qui & ipse Hierosolymis erat per eos dies.
