Herodes autē viso Iesu gaudisus est valde: cupiebat enim à multo tempore eū videre, eò quòd audiret multa de eo: et sperabat se signū aliquod visurū ab eo fieri. Interrogauit autem eum multis sermonibus: sed ipse nihil ei respondit. Stabant autē principes sacerdotum & Scribæ magna contentione eū accusantes. Herodes autē cum militibus suis, cùm eum pro nihilo habuisset, & illusisset ei, amictum vestē splendida remisit ad Pilatum. Et facti sunt amici inter sese Pilatus & Herodes eo ipso die: nam antea inimici erant inter se.
units.tr: When Pilate heard that he was a Galilean, he asked whether he was of Galilee. And when he learned that Jesus belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem at that time. When Herod saw Jesus he was very glad, for he had long wished to see him, because he had heard many things about him, and he hoped to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at length, but Jesus made him no answer. The chief priests and scribes stood by, accusing him vehemently. Then Herod, with his soldiers, treated him with contempt and mocked him, and clothed him in a gorgeous robe and sent him back to Pilate. And Pilate and Herod became friends with each other that same day, for before this they had been enemies.

units.la: EVangelista ex Spiritus sancti instinctu et suggestione nō summatim modò aut simpliciter narrant, Dei Filium pro nobis passum & mortuū esse, sed per singulas partes diligenter exponunt quid cum illo sit gestum. Causa eius diligentiæ est, ut magis confirmetur quæ nobis in eius merito reposita est nostræ salutis fiducia, & ut in eius exemplo spectemus, quæ semper credentium fors futura sit, & quid nos facere conueniat, si quando eadem nobis accidunt. Est autem memorabilis admodum actio illa, quam Sacerdotes & Seniores populi Iudaici contra illum apud Pilati tribunal instituerunt. Accusatus fuit, quòd populum seducat, quòd seditiosam rerum nouationem siue mutationem moliatur, & quod ipse sibi in Iudæa regnum uendicet. Sunt hæc uulgaria crimina, quæ hodie etiam intentantur iis, qui Christum prædicant, aut hunc unum Seruatorem suum agnoscunt. Et eo argumento deprehenditur infelix mundi huius peruersitas, qui dum seductores esse clamat eos, qui iuxta salutis fideliter monstrat, interim eos sibi duces deligit, qui per mille ambages ducunt ad interitum: seditionis item accusat eos, qui magistratuum authoritatem sedulò tuentur, eos autem in pretio habet, qui & immunitatem sibi quærunt, & Regum quoq; capitibus insolentissimè insultant: deniq; regni affectatores esse dicit eos, qui omnes uni Christo subiici uolunt (quæ unica & certa hominis salus est) illorum autem blanditiis se circuduci finit, qui hoc unum agunt, ut suum regnum stabiliant. Vt olim Christus minimè dimissus est, etiamsi eius innocentia ipsis quoq; iudicibus notissima esset: ita hodie nulla excusatio admittitur, sed eos quoque pro sceleratissimis mori oportet, qui nullius criminis possunt convinci. Id uerò in eo, quem nunc recitauimus, loco euidentissimè patebit, quo noua actio describitur, quæ coram Herode contra illum instituta fuit.
units.tr: The Evangelists, prompted and guided by the Holy Spirit, do not merely tell in summary or in plain terms that the Son of God suffered and died for us, but they set out carefully each part of what was done to him. The reason for this care is that the confidence of our salvation, laid up in his merit, may be strengthened, and that in his example we may see what the lot of believers will always be, and what we ought to do if the same things happen to us. That proceeding which the priests and elders of the Jewish people brought against him before Pilate's judgment seat is truly memorable. He was accused of seducing the people, of plotting a seditious upheaval or change of affairs, and of claiming for himself the kingdom of Judea. These are common charges, which are still brought today against those who preach Christ, or who acknowledge him alone as their Saviour. By this argument the unhappy perversity of this world is revealed: while it cries that those are seducers who faithfully point out the way of salvation, it chooses for itself as leaders those who lead men by a thousand detours to destruction; likewise it accuses of sedition those who zealously defend the authority of magistrates, yet it holds in high esteem those who seek immunity for themselves and insult even the heads of kings most insolently; finally it says that those are aspirants to kingdoms who want all men to be subject to Christ alone, which is the one and sure salvation of man, while it allows itself to be led astray by the flatteries of those whose only aim is to establish their own kingdom. As Christ was not released long ago, even though his innocence was well known even to his judges, so today no excuse is admitted, but those too must die as the worst criminals who cannot be convicted of any crime. This will be most plainly evident in the passage we have just recited, where a new proceeding is described, which was brought against him before Herod.

units.la: Causam et occasionē ei præbuit Pilatus, qui quàmuis eius innocentiā satis compertā haberet, et de illa publicum tulisset testimonium, uidens tamen illum absq; inuidia magna dimitti non posse, carnem in consilium adhibet, hoc unum quærens, ut causam hanc totam abs se reiiciat, & ita simul sese inuidia & odio liberet. Nam audita Galilææ mentione, num inde oriundus sit quæritr; & hoc cognito, illum ad Herodem Galilææ regem transmittit. Nec dubium est, quin hoc consilium ipsi uehementer placuerit, quod & tutissimum & honestissimum uidebatur: sed si rem paulò diligentius excutiamus, non uno modo ipsum peccauisse patebit. Primò iniquus & iniustus est, quòd quem innocentem esse sciebat, non liberat ex calumniatorum manibus, sed nouo periculo obijcit. Deinde plus quàm seruilis, imò scelerata ignauia est, quod hominis innocentis sanguine Sacerdotum et Seniorum gratiam redimere studet, quorum nequitiā non poterat ignorare. Adde his, quòd neque Romano Imperatori fidelis est, dum eū, qui Hierosolymæ captus & suæ potestati traditus erat, Herodi subijcit. Quid enim hoc aliud erat, quàm suo iure cedere, et Imperatoriam Maiestatem inferiorum magistratuum subsellijs subijcere? Terreri saltē debuerat L. Flaminij exemplo, quē Porcius Cato Censor è numero Senatorū mouerat, quòd in prouincia quenda iure & legitimè dānatū securi percussisset eo tempore & eo in loco, quæ ad supplicij huius executionē meretricula eius delegerat, quæ spectaculo nunquam abs se uisoculos obiectare cupiebat. Quantò autē grauior Pilati culpa fuit, qui innocentē & quem paulò ante propriæ uocis testimonio absoluerat, discrimini uitæ obijcit, ut hominibus pessimis rem gratā faciat, quos alioqui oderat, et quorū nulla extabat in rempub. Romana merita? Sed nō erat amplius ea tempora, quando Censoria maiestas potentissimorū quoq; licentia coercebat: quare hoc Pilati factū merito inter argumenta ea recenseri potest, quæ reipub. statū tunc modis omnibus corruptissimū fuisse probat. At ex historijs constat, ab eo tempore res Romanorū in peius prolapsas fuisse, adeo ut nō multos post annos sublata in Nerone Cæsarū stirpe Imperiū prædæ esse coeperit, quando illud milites pro sua libidine modo in hos modò in illos transferebat: sub quib. feliciter militauerant.
units.tr: Pilate gave both the cause and the occasion for it. Although he had satisfactory knowledge of Jesus' innocence, and had given public testimony to it, yet, seeing that he could not release him without great ill will, he called flesh into counsel, seeking only this, that he might cast the whole case from himself and so free himself at once from odium and hatred. For when he heard the mention of Galilee, he asked whether Jesus was from there, and having learned this, he sent him to Herod, the king of Galilee. There is no doubt that this plan greatly pleased him, since it seemed both very safe and very honourable. But if we examine the matter a little more carefully, it will appear that he sinned in more ways than one. First, he is unjust and unrighteous, because he does not free from the hands of his accusers the man whom he knew to be innocent, but exposes him to a new danger. Next, it is more than servile, indeed it is wicked cowardice, that he strives to purchase the favour of the priests and elders with the blood of an innocent man, whose wickedness he could not have failed to know. Add to this that he is not faithful even to the Roman Emperor, when he hands over to Herod one who had been taken at Jerusalem and delivered into his own power. For what else was this than to surrender his own right and to subject the majesty of the Emperor to the tribunals of inferior magistrates? At least he should have been alarmed by the example of Lucius Flamininus, whom Porcius Cato the Censor removed from the number of the senators, because in a certain province he had struck with the axe a man who had been justly and lawfully condemned, at a time and place chosen by his mistress, a courtesan who wanted, as a spectacle, to have the execution set before her eyes. But how much graver was the fault of Pilate, who exposed to the peril of life a man whom he had himself acquitted a little before by his own voice, in order to do a favour to the worst men, whom he otherwise hated, and who had deserved nothing from the Roman commonwealth? But those times were no longer such that the majesty of the censors restrained even the greatest men's licence. Therefore this act of Pilate may rightly be counted among those proofs which show that the state of the commonwealth was then utterly corrupt in every way. Yet from the histories it is clear that from that time the affairs of the Romans went downhill, so that not many years later, after the line of the Caesars was destroyed in Nero, the empire began to be a prey, when the soldiers transferred it now to this man, now to that, at their own pleasure; under such rulers they had served happily.

units.la: Exprimitur autē in hoc exemplo ingeniū principū, qui nulla ueri Dei cognitione & studio religionis illuminati sunt. Habent hi præclarā sæpe iuris & legum cognitionē, interdū quoq; iustitiā politicam amant, & hanc omnino salua uellent, quia sine illa neq; rempub. neq; pacē inter cœes diu continere posse intelligunt. At ijdē pro nemine periclitari uolunt, & quàm primùm causam aliquā cum manifesto periculo, aut saltē cum inuidia & odio coniunctam uident, toti in hoc sunt, ut eius cognitione abs se reijciant, & ita fit, ut aliorū libidini subijciatur, & omni præsidio destituti perēat, qui defendi debebāt. Fiunt ista hodie passim publicè & priuatim. Hæc enim causa est, quòd alij religions defensionē non suscipiunt, & hanc inter suos intercidere, aut iniquissimis conditionibus circumscribi patiuntur: alij fœdera & pacta uiolant, dum socios in periculo deserunt, ne aliquos sibi hostes faciant: primatim uero uiduæ & pupilli deseruntur, pauperes causis etiam æquissimis cadunt, populus usurarijs ac fœneratoribus prædæ est, qui suis monopolijs et artibus infandis oēs grauat atq; diripiunt. Quæ omnes surdis auribus praeterennt, qui in repub. primas tenent, modò eos nō offendant ex quibus aut lucrū aliquod sperari, aut periculū enasci poterit. Peccauit in eo Saul quoq;, qui cùm sub initiū regni sui Iabitas fideliter defendisset cōtra Ammonitarū iniquā tyrannidē, et à Deo insigni donatus esset ui gloria, per quā in regno suo cōfirmatus fuit, postea ignauior factus sua ambitione ōia perfundedit. Ignauiæ istius argumentū fuit, q; magnus eorū numerus, qui ære alieno grauati et animo amaro erant, ad Dauidem, quem ide ille eiecerat, profugerunt. Vnde enim illa animi amaritudine exortam fuisse putabimus? Ex eo nimirū, quòd potentioribus & opulentioribus omnia liceret, & per hos multi ad egestatē redigerentur, multi alijs iniurijs afficerentur, qui ius suū obtinere non poterant, & tribunalia omnia sibi præclusa esse uidebant. Quid enim multis alijs acciderit, ex Dauidis historia conijcere possumus, qui in Psalmis de eo passim cōqueritur, quòd nemo inueniretur, qui causam suam uellet uel auderet cognoscere. Sed utinā ignaui illi meminisset, nihil profici eiusmodi artibus, et frustra hominū potentia & fauore eos niti, qui Deum sibi inimicum habent. Atqui constat amicitiā mundi huius, quæ impietate & iniustitia paratur, inimicitiam esse cum Deo. Quid uerò tutum aut salvum esse potest ijs, quorum hostis Deus est, omnipotens ille Dominus exercituum, cui facillimum est scelerratas impiorum conspirationes euertere, consilia eorum omnia turbare, & potentissimos quosque ex suis sedibus detrahere? Extant in historijs passim tristissima exempla, quæ docent infelicissimum
units.tr: Yet in this example is expressed the character of princes who are not enlightened by any true knowledge of God or by zeal for religion. Such men often have a fine knowledge of right and of laws, and sometimes they also love political justice, and would wish it wholly preserved, since they understand that without it neither the commonwealth nor peace among citizens can long be maintained. But these same men do not wish to risk themselves for anyone, and as soon as they see some cause joined with manifest danger, or at least with ill will and hatred, they devote themselves wholly to casting its hearing from themselves; and so it comes about that it is subjected to the lust of others, and those who ought to have been defended perish, stripped of all protection. Such things happen today everywhere, both publicly and privately. For this is the reason why some do not take up the defence of religion, and allow it to perish among their own people, or to be hemmed in by most unjust terms; others break covenants and pacts, deserting their allies in danger, lest they make enemies for themselves. Widows and orphans in particular are abandoned, the poor fall even in most just causes, and the people are made prey to usurers and moneylenders, who burden and plunder everyone by their monopolies and unspeakable tricks. All these things are passed over with deaf ears by those who hold the first places in the commonwealth, provided they do not offend those from whom some gain may be hoped for or some danger may arise. Saul also sinned in this way: although at the beginning of his reign he had faithfully defended the men of Jabesh against the unjust tyranny of the Ammonites, and had been endowed by God with a remarkable glory, by which he was confirmed in his kingdom, he afterwards became more slothful and, through his ambition, ruined everything. A sign of this sloth was that a great number of men who were burdened with debt and bitter in mind fled to David, whom that same Saul had driven out. For whence should we think that bitterness of mind arose? Surely from this, that everything was permitted to the more powerful and the wealthier, and through them many were reduced to poverty, many were injured in other ways, who could not obtain their right, and all courts seemed closed to them. What befell many others we may conjecture from the history of David, who in the Psalms complains everywhere about him, that no one could be found who would wish or dare to hear his cause. But would that that sluggish man had remembered that nothing is gained by such arts, and that it is in vain for those to rely on human power and favour who have God as their enemy. And yet it is established that friendship with this world, which is gained by impiety and injustice, is enmity with God. What then can be safe or secure for those whose enemy is God, that almighty Lord of hosts, to whom it is most easy to overthrow the wicked plots of the ungodly, to confound all their counsels, and to drag down the most powerful from their seats? Sad examples are found throughout the histories which teach that the most unhappy is the end of those who, having cast aside care for justice, allow the innocent to be oppressed.

units.la: 1. Sam. 22. infelicissimum esse eorum exitum, qui deposita cura iustitiæ innocentes opprimi patiuntur. Si enim scelus est, fi homo priuatus esurienti, nudo, extorri aut morbis male affecto non ferat opem, quanto grauiorem illorum culpam fore putabimus, qui cum à Deo ordinati publicæ iustitiæ ministri sint, eos negligût, quos iniquis modis affligi nouerunt? Et solet fere fieri, ut qui propter ueritatem & iustitiæ causam periclitari nolunt, tandem aut volentes propter res turpes & inquas sibi malum accersant, aut etiam inuiti cum improbis illis grauissima pericula subire cogantur, quorum iniustitiam ipsi sua ignauia nouerunt & confirmarunt.
units.tr: 1. Sam. 22. Their end is most wretched who, having abandoned the care of justice, allow the innocent to be oppressed. For if it is a crime for a private person not to bring help to the hungry, the naked, the exile, or the sick, how much graver will we judge the guilt of those who, appointed by God as ministers of public justice, neglect those whom they know are afflicted by unjust means? And it usually happens that those who are unwilling to be endangered for the sake of truth and the cause of justice either, willingly, bring evil upon themselves through shameful and wicked dealings, or else, even against their will, are compelled to undergo the gravest dangers with those wicked men whose injustice they themselves have recognised and confirmed by their own cowardice.

units.la: Porrò uideamus quid apud Herodem gestum fit: ubi cum multa & uaria inciderint, consultissimum fuerit, personas singulas, de quibus hic agitur, inspicere. Primus autem ipse Herodes occurrit, quem cognomine Antipa dictum fuisse historici testantur. Fuit hic Herodis illius Magni filius, qui Iudæis libertatem abstulit, Romanorum authoritate & fauore illorum Rex factus, & qui infantes Bethlehemiticos inauditæ & plus quam paricidalis crudelitatis exemplo trucidari iussit, ut inter hos Chriftu quoq; tolleret, quem regem Iudæorum fore timebat. Noster uero iste Antipas patre nihilo melior, sed (ut prouerbio dicitur) mali corui malum ouum fuit, homo nimirum impurus, coniugalis fidei contemptor, adulter, incestus, uoluptatibus & uanitati deditus, & cui lusus iocufq; erat uiolato hospitij iure, quod gentes quoq; facrofanctu iudicarunt esse, uxorem fratris rapere, & Ioanne tanti flagitij iustissimum correptorem sententia mortis inter pocula pronuntiata occidere, ut suo loco uidimus. Accedebat his uitijs prophana quædam leuitas, ut quamuis religionis ut doctrinæ cura nulla tenere-tur, Christum tamen longo iam tempore uidere cuperet, eo quod ab illo opera miraculosa fieri audiret. Itaq; hoc illi perquàm iucundum & optatum accidit, quod hunc ipsi Pilatus transmisit. Ià enim occasione sibi oblatam putauit, per quam nouis quibusdam & nunquam antea uisis signis aut miraculis oculos pasceret. Unde colligimus, eum de Christo nihil maius aut honorificentius sensisse, quàm de cirulatore aliquo, qui magicis præstigijs oculis vulgi & curiosorum hominum illudunt. Verè ergo nunc Dominus ex Charybdi in Scyllam incidit, à Pilato nimirum, inexplebili auaritiæ uoragine, ad hominem impurum, impudentem & turpissimum libidinis mancipium transmissus. Facit hoc ad augendam ignominiam, qua propter nos ille suffinuit, ut nos à sempiternæ damnationis ignominia liberaret. At sinoftra tempora spectes, non unus Herodes inuenietur, & idem passim illis accidit, qui Christu hodie prædicant. Herodis certè ingenium atque mores referunt non pauci principes atq; magistratus, qui cùm à religione prorsus alieni sint, Christum tamen per Euangelium suum loquentem atq; agentem uidere & audire cupiunt. Audiunt enim ex aliorum relatione, qui ipsorum fere similes sunt, mirabilem rerum mutationem per illius doctrinam fieri, monachos & sacrificulos ex nidis suis eijci, traditionum iugo homines liberari, peccatorum remissionem omnibus gratuitam promitti, in honorum ecclesiasticorum possessione sub dispensationis melioris prætextu succedere principes & multos alios, qui alio qui uix possent cômodè uiuere. Hæc & alia huius generis istos excitant, ut ipsi quoq; Euangelij præcones, qui alijs celebriores sunt, audire cupiant: & si quando in tales inciderint, multa quærunt ex illis, quæ omnia ad eum finem tendunt, de quo modò diximus: de rebus autem cognitu utilibus & necessarijs ne gry quidé loquuntur. Nec multùm dissimiles bis sunt homines plebei, qui & ipsi in Christo aut diuitias quærunt, aut peccandi licentiam siue immunitatem. Sunt enim in papatu grauamina omnis generis, quibus & corpora & conscientiæ premuntur, & illis ipsi semel liberari uellent: qualia sunt ieiunia, confessio auricularis, feriarum multitudo, exequiarum impensæ, annua sacra pro defunctis, idulgentiarum usurarij contractus & infinita alia huius generis. De his ergo multùm & solicitè quarunt: at quæ ad puriorem Dei cultum, ad ueræ fidei cognitionem, ad carnis mortificationem, ad morum disciplinam & uitam Christianam faciunt, ea omnia facilè negligunt. Imò interea scurrilcs disputationes mouent, quibus & Dei præcepta euertere, & omnibus eis promissis atq; minis fidem derogare studient. Et hi sunt, quibus cum Christi ministris perpetuò res est.
units.tr: Let us look further at what happened under Herod. Since many and varied things occurred here, it will be most useful to consider the individual persons with whom we are concerned. Herod himself comes first, whom the historians testify was called by the surname Antipas. He was the son of that Herod the Great who took away the liberty of the Jews, who was made king by the authority and favour of the Romans, and who ordered the infants of Bethlehem to be slaughtered in a display of unheard-of cruelty, more than parricidal, so that among them he might also remove Christ, whom he feared would be king of the Jews. Yet this Antipas of ours was no better than his father; but, as the proverb says, the bad raven had a bad egg. He was indeed an impure man, a despiser of the faith of marriage, an adulterer, an incestuous man, given over to pleasures and vanity, and for whom it was a game and a joke to violate the right of hospitality, which even the heathen judged to be sacred, to seize his brother's wife, and to kill John, the most just rebuker of so great a crime, by a sentence of death pronounced over his cups, as we saw in its place. To these vices was added a certain profane frivolity, so that although he had no care for religion or doctrine, he nevertheless desired for a long time to see Christ, because he heard that miraculous works were done by him. And so it came to him as most pleasant and welcome when Pilate sent him this man. For he thought that an occasion had been offered him by which he might feast his eyes on some novel signs or miracles never seen before. From this we gather that he thought of Christ no more highly or honourably than of some charlatan who deceives the eyes of the crowd and of curious men with magic tricks. Truly, then, the Lord now fell from Charybdis into Scylla: sent from Pilate, that is, from the bottomless whirlpool of avarice, to a man impure, shameless, and a most vile slave of lust. This served to increase the disgrace which he bore for us, so that he might free us from the disgrace of everlasting damnation. But if you look at our own times, you will find not one Herod only, and the same things happen everywhere to those who preach Christ today. Certainly not a few princes and magistrates, who are utterly estranged from religion, bear the character and manners of Herod; and yet they desire to see and hear Christ speaking and acting through his Gospel. For they hear from the reports of others, who are much like themselves, that a wonderful change of affairs is taking place through his teaching: that monks and little priests are being driven from their nests, that men are being freed from the yoke of traditions, that forgiveness of sins is being promised freely to all, and that princes and many others are succeeding, under the pretext of a better stewardship, to the possession of ecclesiastical offices and benefices, by which they might scarcely be able to live comfortably elsewhere. These and other things of this kind stir them up, so that they too wish to hear those heralds of the Gospel who are more famous than others; and if ever they fall in with such men, they ask them many questions, all of which tend toward that end of which we have just spoken, while of matters useful and necessary to know they do not say a single word. Not very unlike these are the common people, who likewise seek in Christ either riches or a licence or immunity for sinning. For in the papacy there are burdens of every kind, by which both bodies and consciences are weighed down, and from which they would wish once for all to be freed: such as fasts, auricular confession, the multitude of holy days, the expense of funerals, annual masses for the dead, the usurious contracts of indulgences, and countless others of this sort. Therefore they inquire much and anxiously about these matters; but those things which pertain to the purer worship of God, to the knowledge of the true faith, to the mortification of the flesh, to the discipline of morals and the Christian life, these they easily neglect. Indeed, in the meantime they raise frivolous disputes, by which they strive both to overturn God's precepts and to undermine faith in all his promises and threats. And these are the people with whom the ministers of Christ are always at odds.

units.la: Quid ergo faciet? Dominu imitentur, qui exemplo suo ipsis præiuit. Nihil respondit ille ad curiosas & inutiles Herodis quæstiones: nimirum, quòd animum eius prophanum probè cognitum haberet. Nam ut apud Ioanne scribitur, non opus habuit, ut aliquis de quoquà ipsi testaretur, eo quòd ipsemet sciebat quidin homine esset. Qui ergo nos alibi monuit, ne sanctum canibus proijciamus, aut regni cœlestis margaritas porcis calcandas substernamus, noluit nunc cum illo multis agere, quem quouis porco immundiorem, & quouis cane rabiosiorem esse nouerat. units.tr: What, then, shall they do? Let them imitate the Lord, who went before them in this by his own example. He made no answer to Herod's curious and useless questions, plainly because he knew well that Herod's heart was profane. For, as is written in John, he had no need that anyone should bear witness to him about anyone, because he himself knew what was in man. Therefore he who elsewhere warned us not to cast what is holy to the dogs, nor to throw the pearls of the kingdom of heaven before swine to be trampled, was unwilling now to have dealings with a man whom he knew to be more unclean than any swine and more rabid than any dog. units.la: Herodes quis & qualis. uitijs suis infames nunquam ille fastidiuit, et hodie etiam tales alta uoce & magnificis promissionib. ad se uocat. Conscientias ite peccatorum pondere pressas & æstuantes amicè fouet, & ne uel modicum mi cantes fidei scintillæ omnino extinguantur, diligenter cauet. Idem tamen à nobis animos humiles, contritos & pia reuerentia uerbu suum amplectentes requirit, sicuti per Isaiam his uerbis testatur: Ad quem respiciam? Ad pauperem & contritum spiritu, & qui ad uerbum meum contremiscit. E contra uero illusores impios atq; prophanos non probat, qui eius nomini & uerbo scurriliter insultant, aut eo ad suam libidinem abutuntur. Imò Spiritus sanctus eos demù beatos fore pronuntiat, qui in consessu illusorum non sedent. Quia ergo ex horum numero erat Herodes, neq; de eodem aliqua pœnitentiæ spes erat, illi ne alloquio quidem aut responso dignatur. Et suo exemplo ministros uerbi omnes admonet, ne cum eiusmodi hominibus non necessaria colloquia aut disputationes temerarias instituant, ex quibus non aliud quàm contemptus & ignominia sperari potest. Hi enim reuera stulti illi & deplorati Nabales sunt, quos Solomon scribit disciplinam & castigationem omnem respuere, & de quibus ipse prudenter nos admonet: Ne respondeas stulto secundum eius stultitiam, ne & tu illi similis fias. Et præstat omnino tacere, etiamsi silentio nostro eos uel ferociores fieri, uel etiam eo ad nostri contemptum abuti sciamus, quàm illis nouam aduersus Dei uerbum proteruiendi occasionem præbere: Nisi eiusmodi responsum occurrat, quo uel ipsis inuitis eorum conscientias altius penetrare, uel eorum dicacitatem ipsis digno scomate retundere possimus. Prioris generis est, quod nuper Christus Caiaphæ respondit: Ab hoc tempore uidebitis Filium hominis sedentem à dextra virtutis Dei, & uenientem in nubibus cæli. Ad alterum genus referri potest, quod Augustinus quondam cuidam petulantius quaerenti, Quid Deus fecerit priusquam fecisset cælum & terram? respondisse scribit: Alta quærentibus gehennam parabat. Simul autem huius, quod in præsenti Christus fecit, nos meminisse oportet, quando nobis cum improbis hominibus res est, apud quos nullus iustæ defensioni locus datur, & quos omnia nostra uel cum risu prophano eludere, uel amarulentis calumniis in alienum sensum detorquere uidemus. Feramus tunc patienter nostram hanc sortem, quæ nobis cum Dei Filio communis est. Promisit is nobis aduocatum omnium fidelissimum, Spiritum uidelicet ueritatis, qui ut corda & linguas suorum gubernat, ita eorundem memoriam asserit atq; custodit.
units.tr: Who and what sort of man Herod was. Though he was infamous for his vices, the Lord never scorned them, and even today he calls such people to himself with a loud voice and with magnificent promises. He lovingly cherishes consciences pressed down and burning under the weight of sins, and he takes diligent care that not even the slightest spark of faith be wholly extinguished. Yet at the same time he requires from us humble, contrite souls that embrace his word with holy reverence, as he testifies through Isaiah in these words: "To whom shall I look? To the poor and contrite in spirit, and to him who trembles at my word." On the other hand, he does not approve of impious and profane mockers, who insult his name and word with buffoonery, or abuse him for their own lust. Indeed, the Holy Spirit pronounces those blessed who do not sit in the seat of scorners. Therefore, since Herod was of their number, and there was no hope of repentance in him, the Lord does not even deign to speak with him or answer him. And by his example he admonishes all ministers of the word not to enter into unnecessary conversations or rash disputations with such men, from which nothing can be expected but contempt and disgrace. For these are truly the foolish and hardened Nabals, whom Solomon writes despise all instruction and correction, and about whom he himself warns us prudently: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also become like him." And it is altogether better to keep silent, even though we know that by our silence they become more fierce, or even abuse it to our contempt, than to give them a new occasion for insolence against the word of God, unless there occurs such an answer by which we can penetrate their consciences more deeply, even against their will, or repel their scoffing with a fitting rebuke. Of the former kind is what Christ lately answered to Caiaphas: "From now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, and coming on the clouds of heaven." To the second kind may be referred what Augustine writes that he once answered a certain man who asked somewhat impudently, "What did God do before he made heaven and earth?": "He was preparing hell for those who pry into lofty things." At the same time we ought to remember what Christ did in the present case, whenever we have to do with wicked men, among whom there is no room for a just defence, and whom we see mocking all our words either with profane laughter or twisting them into a false sense with bitter calumnies. Let us then bear this lot of ours patiently, which we share in common with the Son of God. He promised us a most faithful advocate of all, namely the Spirit of truth, who, as he governs the hearts and tongues of his people, so also preserves and guards their memory.

units.la: Priusquam tamen ab hoc loco discedamus, illud quoq; expendi debet, quod de aduersarijs Christi Lucas annotauit. Stabant autem (inquit) principes Sacerdotum & Scribæ magna contentione eum accusantes. Eo enim facto incurabile contumacia cum summa impudentia coniunctâ amplius produnt. Nã etiamsi apud tribunal Pilati causa sua cecidissent, & insuper in mendacio deprehensi essent, actum tamen agunt, & adhuc ut turbarum & seditionum authorem accusant eum, de quo ne ipse quidem Herodes quicquam querebatur. Ita nihil pudet eos, qui aduersus Christi doctrinam conjurauerunt: quia enim ipsi Deo bellum mouere audent, nihil non sibi licere arbitrantur. At ijdem simul se dignam contumeliam inde reportant, sicuti in horum exemplo est uidere. Scimus eos ambitionis plus quàm seruilia mancipia fuisse, & hanc potissimum ob causam cum Christo inimicitiam suscepisse, quòd honori suo & existimationi per eius doctrinam plurimùm derogari uiderent. At quàm turpiter suam existimationem ijdem hic prostituunt, quando à Pilati Præsidis tribunali reiecti, nunc maiori cum contentione causam hanc apud Herodem agunt, qui quàm nihil eos faceret sæpe multis argumentis demonstrauerat, & nunc eo ipso magis probat, quando ipsos cum Christo eò remittit un de uenerant? Doluit hoc procul dubio hominibus ambitiosissimis, quòd se ne audiri quidem uiderent à Rege illo, qui simul causam hanc totam ludibrio habebat. Fiunt multa huius generis hodie, quando personati illi præsules magno cum conatu ueritatis Euangelicæ doctores apud eos principes accusant, qui aut causam hanc cognitione indignam iudicant, aut illorum ambitionem atq; auaritiam iampridem cognitam habent. Est quidem reprehensione dignus contemptus ille prophanus uerbi Dei & totius religionis: idem tamen nobis consolationem non pœnitendam affert, quando uidemus hostes ueritatis ne apud eos quidem omnia obtinere posse, qui & ipsi hanc contemnunt & oderunt.
units.tr: Before we leave this passage, we should also consider what Luke noted about Christ's adversaries: "The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him." By this act they reveal an incurable obstinacy joined with the utmost shamelessness. Even though their case had collapsed before Pilate's tribunal and they had been caught in a lie, they still carry on the business and accuse him of being the author of disturbances and sedition, when not even Herod himself complained of anything in him. So nothing shames those who have conspired against Christ's teaching. Because they dare to make war on God himself, they think nothing is forbidden to them. Yet at the same time they bring back a fitting insult, as the example of these men shows. We know they were more ambitious than servile slaves, and that they took up enmity with Christ chiefly for this reason: they saw their honour and reputation greatly diminished by his teaching. How shamefully these same men now prostitute their reputation! Rejected by the tribunal of Pilate the governor, they now pursue the case with greater vehemence before Herod, who had often shown by many arguments that he thought nothing of their charges, and who now proves it all the more by sending Christ back to the very place from which they had come. Without doubt this grieved these most ambitious men, that they saw themselves not even heard by that king, who at the same time treated the whole case as a joke. Many things of this kind happen today, when those personated prelates, with great effort, accuse before princes the teachers of the Gospel of truth, princes who either judge the case unworthy of investigation or already know well the ambition and avarice of those men. That profane contempt for the word of God and for all religion certainly deserves rebuke. Yet it brings us a consolation not to be regretted when we see that the enemies of the truth cannot obtain everything, even among those who themselves despise and hate it.

units.la: Facit ad huius confirmationem exitus istius actionis, quem Lucas his uerbis describit: Herodes autem cum militibus suis, cùm eum pro nihilo habuisset, & illusisset ei, amictum uestę splendida remisit ad Pilatum. Et facti sunt amici inter sese Pilatus & Herodes eo ipso die: nam antea inimici erant inter se. Duo dicuntur: Primum, quòd Herodes unà cum uiris militaribus & corporis sui custodibus, qui praesto aderant, Christo illuserint. Quo loco non exprimuntur quidem uerba & contumelia siue scurrilia dicta quibus sunt usi, sed in illis non dubium est eos petulantissimos fuisse. Tanta enim fuit illorum levitas, ut verba illis non sufficere uisa sint, nisi uestitu quoque ludicro illum magis contemptui facerent. Itaque uestes splendidae siue albae amictu Pilato remisit. Scimus autem apud Romanos, quorum mores Herodes non potuit ignorare, in usu fuisse, ut qui magistratum aut munus aliquod publicum ambiebant, candidis togis uestiti ad comitia descenderent: eo nimirum colore, qui simplicitatem & ab omni mixtione alienus est, animi integritate testantes & syncerum erga rempub. amorem. Ad eum ergo more prophanum homo alluisse uidetur, ut Christum morionis loco haberet, & cum risu abs se relegaret, ut stultum atque fanaticum regni affectatorem. Quanquam ista ignominia ad totam Iudaeorum gentem redundarit, quibus ipse Messiae sui simul exprobrauit hoc facto, quem illos nunquam non in ore habere sciebat. Quasi diceret: Facescite procul hinc stulti & ridiculi homines, qui cum Rege quendam gentis uestrae uindicem gloriosum & ueteris regni instauratorem subinde expectetis, hunc tamen non agnoscitis. Ego igitur ut & hunc digno honore prosequar, & uobis gratificer, hisce regni insignibus eum dono, hac illum trabea indutum dimitto, & uos sic ornatum ad Praesidem reducite, ut tam Regis quam regni uestri maiestas omnibus innotescat. Et hoc loco adumbratur nouum, quae fere Christi fortis inter eos quoque, qui se Dei populum esse profitentur. Maior inter hos semper eorum numerus est, qui omnia ea suauiter rident, quae de eius regno et toto humanae salutis negotio dicuntur. Et utinam non hodie passim extarent exempla eorum, qui cum Euangelij praedicationem cum cruce perpetuo coniunctam esse uideant, simili scurrilitate nobis quoque spem regni coelestis exprobrant.
units.tr: The outcome of this affair, which Luke describes in these words, helps to confirm this: "Herod with his soldiers, when he had treated him with contempt and mocked him, sent him back to Pilate clothed in a gorgeous robe. And Pilate and Herod became friends with each other that very day, for before they had been enemies." Two things are stated. (1) Herod, together with his military men and the bodyguards who were at hand, mocked Christ. The words and the insulting or buffoonish remarks they used are not given, but there is no doubt they were very wanton. Their frivolity was so great that words seemed not enough to them, unless they made him more contemptible by a ridiculous garment. So Herod sent back to Pilate Christ wearing a splendid, that is, white, robe. We know that among the Romans, whose customs Herod could not have been ignorant, it was the practice for those who sought a magistracy or some public office to go down to the assemblies dressed in white togas, in that colour which is simple and free from any mixture, attesting the integrity of their mind and their pure love of the commonwealth. So in that profane fashion Herod seems to have made sport of him, to treat Christ as a fool, and to send him away with laughter, as a mad and fanatical aspirant to the kingdom. Yet this disgrace also fell back upon the whole Jewish nation, since by this deed Herod at the same time mocked their Messiah, whom he knew they always had on their lips. It was as if he were saying: "Away with you, foolish and ridiculous men, who keep waiting for some glorious avenger of your nation and restorer of the ancient kingdom, and yet do not recognise him when he comes. I, therefore, both to honour him as he deserves and to oblige you, give him these royal insignia and send him away clothed in this robe. Take him back thus adorned to the governor, so that the majesty of both your king and your kingdom may be known to all." In this place there is also foreshadowed what is almost always Christ's lot among those too who profess themselves to be God's people. The greater number among them always laughs pleasantly at everything that is said about his kingdom and the whole business of human salvation. And would that there were not today, everywhere, examples of those who, seeing that the preaching of the Gospel is always joined with the cross, mock us with the same buffoonery for the hope of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Alterum est, quod qui prius inimici fuerant, Pilatus & Herodes, nouam amicitiam ineunt. Quia enim Iudaea prius Herodi Magno cesserat, post eius uero mortem prouincia facta & per Praesides administrata fuit, non facile conuenire potuit Herodis posteris cum Praesidibus, cum hi insatiabili auaritia accensi omnia ad se raperent, illi uero regni paterni fines in angustum redigi indignius ferrent. Hac autem occasione factum est, ut depositis odiis aut simultatibus nouo amicitiae foedere coirent, qui antehac dissidebant. Ut enim Herodi gratissimum fuit, quod hominis Galilei causam ad ipsum remiserat, eo quod id ad suae iuris dictionis confirmationem facere uidebatur: ita Pilatus gaudet, quod tantum haberet iam innocentiae Christi testem, de qua ipse paulo ante pronuntiauerat. At dum sibi mutuo gratificantur, uterque Christum negligit, & huius pretioso sanguine scelerata isto-rum amicitia sanciturque siue redimitur.
units.tr: (2) The other point is that Pilate and Herod, who had previously been enemies, enter into a new friendship. For Judaea had formerly yielded to Herod the Great, but after his death it became a province, administered by governors. It could not easily happen that Herod's heirs would agree with the governors, since the latter, burning with insatiable greed, snatched everything to themselves, while the former took it more hardly that the boundaries of their father's kingdom were reduced to a narrow compass. On this occasion, then, those who had quarrelled before laid aside their hatreds and rivalries and came together in a new bond of friendship. For just as it was most welcome to Herod that Pilate had sent back to him the case of the Galilean, since this seemed to confirm his own jurisdiction, so Pilate rejoiced that he now had, as a witness to Christ's innocence, the very man about whom he himself had declared it a little before. But while they gratify one another, both neglect Christ, and by his precious blood the wicked friendship of these men is sealed, or rather bought.

units.la: Est autem exemplum hoc multa consideratione dignissimum. Nam quasi in tabula depictos nobis exhibet mores principum, quos nulla religionis & gloriae Dei cura tangit. Ardent isti auaritia & ambitione, & ut sui imperij aut potestatis suae consortes ferre non possunt: ita cum uicinis quoque lites habent perpetuas de finibus, de iurisdictione, de insignibus, & frequenter propter ceruum aut aprum in loco controuerso captum & occisum ad arma deuenire solent. At idem contra Christi fere inter se conspirant, & sepositis odiis sua ad illum opprimendum consilia conferunt. Et quamuis in terdum cultorum Christi innocentia probe perspectam habeant, neque hostium Christi improbitatem ignorent, tamen pro ueritate tuenda cum nemine uolunt contendere. Exempla tot scelerata ignauiae passim cernuntur hodie. Quam multos enim est uidere, qui ab alijs intra suae ditionis fines feram alia quia capi nunquam paterentur, qui tamen Pontificios legatos & Inquisitores monachos in suorum subditorum fortunas & corpora saeuire patiuntur? Nihil nunc de illis dicam, qui cum Euangelij studium profiteantur, in Pontificum gratia uerbi ministros, si qui feruentiores sunt, eiiciunt, alijs uero dicendi leges praescribunt. Et hi quidem omnes sibi ipsis applaudunt, quod ista moderatione consiliorum (ita enim hanc suam proditoriam uacordiam uocant) amicos sibi faciant multos, & pace publica seruent. Sed non omnis amicitia Deo probatur, & infelix illa pax est, quae innocentium hominum sanguine & ueritatis oppressione redimitur. Qua uero infeliciter cedant eiusmodi consilia, istorum exemplis docemur. Amicitia coeunt inter se cum Christi ludibrio Pilatus ac Herodes, nec multo post ille eundem in Sacerdotum gratiam cruce dignum iudicat, & ita illi diu optata uictoria potiuntur. Quis ergo non pacem firmam speret & tuta omnia in tam plausibili animorum & consiliorum consensione? Sed longe aliud Deo visum est, qui de omnibus istis poenas sumpsit grauissimas. Pilatus enim post multa inter Iudaeos auare & cruderiter gesta, a Tyberio Caesare Viennam Galliae relegatus sibi ipsi manum in-
units.tr: This example is indeed most worthy of close consideration. For it sets before us, as if painted on a tablet, the character of princes whom no care for religion or for the glory of God touches. These men burn with greed and ambition, and as they cannot bear partners in their rule or power, so they also have perpetual quarrels with their neighbours over boundaries, over jurisdiction, over insignia, and often, over a stag or a boar taken and killed in a disputed place, they are accustomed to come to arms. But against Christ they almost always conspire together, and, setting aside their hatreds, they combine their plans to crush him. And although they sometimes clearly perceive the innocence of Christ's worshippers and are not ignorant of the wickedness of Christ's enemies, yet they do not want to contend with anyone in defence of the truth. Many such wicked examples of cowardice are everywhere to be seen today. How many men are there who will not allow wild beasts from other lands to be taken within the bounds of their territory, yet who allow papal legates and monkish inquisitors to rage against the goods and bodies of their subjects? I say nothing now of those who, while professing zeal for the Gospel, expel from their territories the ministers of the Word, if they are rather fervent, to please the Pontiffs, and prescribe rules of speech for the others. All of these applaud themselves, because by this moderation of counsels (for so they call their treacherous spinelessness) they make many friends for themselves and keep public peace. But not every friendship is approved by God, and that is an unhappy peace which is bought with the blood of innocent men and the oppression of the truth. The examples of these men teach us how unhappily such counsels turn out. Pilate and Herod come together in friendship at the mockery of Christ, and not long after, to win the favour of the chief priests, Pilate judges him worthy of the cross, and so they obtain the victory they had long desired. Who then would not hope for a firm peace and for all things to be safe in such a plausible agreement of minds and counsels? But God judged otherwise, and he exacted the most severe punishments from all of them. For Pilate, after many acts of greed and cruelty among the Jews, was banished by the Emperor Tiberius to Vienne in Gaul, where he laid violent hands on himself...

units.la: Herodes & Pilatus amici fiunt.
units.tr: Herod and Pilate become friends.

units.la: Mores principum. tulit. Herodes quoq; regno exutus & cum sua Herodiade exilio multatus est, ut alibi ostendimus: Sacerdotes uero cum urbe & templo excisi sunt, neq; potuit ab eo tempore unquam instaurari sacerdotium illud, pro quo tantopere pugnauerunt. Expectent ergo simile Dei iudicium, qui hodie contra ueritatem conspirant, & cum piorum sanguine ludunt. Viuit enim & regnat Iesus Christus, & qui per ludibrium ab Herode ueste candida indutus fuit, breui ueniet in gloria Patris sui ad iudicandum uiuos & mortuos, ut & suos ex impiorum manibus asserat, & hos digno ipsis exitio male perdat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Manners of princes. He laid violent hands on himself. Herod too was stripped of his kingdom and, together with his Herodias, punished with exile, as we have shown elsewhere. The priests, however, were cut off along with the city and the temple, and that priesthood, for which they had fought so hard, could never be restored from that time on. Let those who today conspire against the truth and make sport of the blood of the godly therefore expect a similar judgment of God. For Jesus Christ lives and reigns, and he who was mocked by Herod and clothed in a white robe will soon come in the glory of his Father to judge the living and the dead, so that he may rescue his own from the hands of the wicked and destroy these with the fitting ruin they deserve. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCV.
units.tr: HOMILIA CCV.

units.la: Pilatus vero convocatis principibus Sacerdotum, & magistratibus, ac populo, dixit eis: Obtulistis mihi hunc hominem, vt qui auertat populum: & ecce ego in vestri conspectu quaestione habita, nullam noxam inueni in homine isto, ex iis de quibus accusatis eum. Sed neque Herodes quidem: nam remisi vos ad illum: & ecce nihil dignum morte factum est ab eo: Castigatum ergo eum dimittam. Necesse autem habebat dimittere eis in festo vnum quempiam. Exclamauit autem simul vniuersa turba dicens: Tolle hunc, dimitte vero nobis Barrabam, qui erat propter seditionem quandam & caedem factam in vrbe, coniectus in carcerem. Rursus ergo Pilatus allocutus est eos, volens dimittere Iesum. Ipsi vero reclamabant, dicentes: Crucifige, Crucifige eum. Ille autem tertio dixit eis: Quid enim iste mali fecit? nullam noxam capitalem inueni in eo: Castigatum ergo eum dimittam. At illi instabant vocibus magnis, petentes vt crucifigeretur: & inualescebant voces eorum ac principum Sacerdotum. Tum Pilatus iudicauit vt fieret quod ipsi petebant: dimisit autem eis illum, qui propter seditionem & caedem coniectus fuerat in carcerem, quem petierant: Iesum vero tradidit eorum cupiditati.
units.tr: Then Pilate called together the chief priests, the magistrates and the people, and said to them: "You have brought this man before me as one who turns the people away. And behold, I have examined him in your presence and found no guilt in this man in respect of those things of which you accuse him. Nor indeed has Herod, for I sent you back to him, and behold, nothing worthy of death has been done by him. I will therefore chastise him and let him go." Now he was bound to release one man to them at the feast. But the whole crowd cried out together, saying: "Away with this man, and release Barabbas to us," who had been thrown into prison for a certain sedition and murder committed in the city. Pilate spoke to them again, wishing to release Jesus. But they shouted back, saying: "Crucify him, crucify him!" And he said to them a third time: "Why, what evil has this man done? I have found no capital guilt in him. I will therefore chastise him and let him go." But they pressed on with loud voices, asking that he be crucified, and their voices and those of the chief priests grew stronger. Then Pilate gave judgment that what they asked should be done. He released to them the man who had been thrown into prison for sedition and murder, whom they had asked for, but he handed Jesus over to their will.

units.la: In tota passionis dominicae historia perquam memorabilis est actio, quae apud Pilati praesidis tribunal magna cum contentione instituta & habita fuit. In ea enim evidenter cernitur, quo ingenio sint hostes veritatis, quibus armis & artibus idem pugnent, & quae sub his sit piorum conditio. Superat tamen haec omnia Iesu Christi innocentia, quae illic testimonijs luculentissimis asseritur, & quidem ab ipso Pilato, qui illum postea multum reluctante conscientia damnauit. Fuit enim in illo aliquod iustitiae ciuilis studium, & ideo licet Concilij authoritate iam damnatum esse audiret, noluit tamen in eius mortem consentire, nisi prius ipse quoque causam totam cognosceret. Et quia iudicio quoque ualuit, mox deprehendit, Iudaeos ex inuidia & odio hoc omne agere, & proinde sua sententia illum absoluit. Idem tamen in eo peccat, quod pro eo quem sciebat iustum atq; innocentem esse, non periculum aliquod subire, imo ne inuidia quidem sibi gravare vult. Quae causa est, quod ad humanae sapientiae rationes siue artes conuertitur, quibus seipsum magis & magis subinde intricat, & suam quidem iniustitiam magis prodit, Christi vero innocentiam illustriorem reddit. Et huc facit in primis huius loci narratio, qua ut Christus post multam & longam altercationem tandem ad crucis supplicium damnatus sit, exponitur. Discant autem isto exemplo omnes qui magistratum gerunt, sibi non solum sapientia & rerum cognitione atque usu opus esse, verumetiam fortitudine, qua improborum audaciam retundant, & eorum superbiae obstent, qui suae authoritatis splendore oculos illorum perstringere conantur. Prae alijs tamen consideratione dignissima est Christi innocentia, quam multis euidentibus & saepe repetitis testimonijs asseri oportuit, ut certo constaret, illum propter nos mortem indignam subijsse, ut pro nostris peccatis satisfaceret, & nos a sententia aeternae damnationis, quam merueramus, absolveret. Quae omnia ut rectius intelligantur, singulas partes ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: In the whole history of the Lord's passion, the proceeding that was held and conducted with great contention before the tribunal of Pilate the governor is particularly memorable. For in it one can clearly see with what cunning the enemies of truth act, with what weapons and arts they fight, and what the condition of the godly is under them. Yet the innocence of Jesus Christ surpasses all these things, and it is asserted there by the most striking testimonies, and indeed by Pilate himself, who afterwards condemned him, though his conscience struggled greatly. For there was in him some zeal for civil justice, and therefore, although he heard that Jesus had already been condemned by the authority of the council, he was unwilling to consent to his death until he himself had first examined the whole case. And because he was also strong in judgment, he soon perceived that the Jews were doing all this out of envy and hatred, and so he acquitted him by his own sentence. Yet he sins in this respect: for the man whom he knew to be just and innocent, he is unwilling to undergo any danger for him, or even to incur the ill will of others. This is why he turns to the devices of human wisdom and arts, by which he entangles himself more and more, and so indeed betrays his own injustice all the more while making the innocence of Christ shine more brightly. This passage, which describes how Christ, after a long and bitter dispute, was at last condemned to the punishment of the cross, serves this purpose above all. Let all who hold magistracy learn from this example that they need not only wisdom, knowledge of affairs and experience, but also fortitude, by which they may break the boldness of the wicked and resist the pride of those who try to dazzle people's eyes with the glitter of their authority. Yet above all else, the innocence of Christ is worthy of consideration, for it had to be asserted by many clear and often repeated testimonies, so that it might be certain that he underwent an unworthy death for our sake, to make satisfaction for our sins and to absolve us from the sentence of eternal damnation which we had deserved. So that all these things may be understood more correctly, we shall examine the individual parts in order.

units.la: Pilatus qui causam hanc inuidiæ ac odij plenam ad Herodem deriuare voluit, vbi se sspe sua frustratum uidet, nouum commentum orditur. Quod ea diligentia Lucas describit, ut illum hoc scirio fecisse non possimus dubitare: nullo tamen cum fructu, neq; cum laude aliqua facit, quia animi for titudine destitutus non vult pro causa bona periclitari. Conuocat enim omnes, qui eam agebant: prin cipes nimirum Sacerdotum, magistratus siue seniores, populum denique uniuersum: sperans nimirū in tanta multitudine aliquos fore, qui aut miraculorum & acceptorum beneficiorum memores, aut ipsi us authoritate perculsi ab actione ista desisterent. Ideo orationem habet breuem quidem, sed quæ re fertissima est argumentis quibus moueri poterant, nisi cum iustitia & æquitate sensum quoq; commu nem & pudorem omnem depositissent. Nam primò ab eorum accusatione exorsus præcipuum huius caput repetit, ne quid in illa minus attentè obseruasse, aut nunc subdole dissimulare uideretur: Obtu listis mihi hunc hominem, ut qui auertat populum: nimirum à cultu inter vos recepto, & ab obedien tia, quam Cæsari debent. Et hic ue stræ accusationis, hic actionis aduersus istum institutæ status est. His mox infert: Et ecce, ego inuestri conspectu quæstione habita, nullam noxam inueni in homine isto ex ijs, de quibus accusatis eum. Demonstrandi particula emphaticè utitur, ut proprio testimo nio illos convincat. Ecce (inquit) ego non neglexi causam hanc, neq; negligenter aut oscitanter illam egi: sed vobis uidentibus atque audientibus quæstionem instituti diligentem. Quid vero in illo deprae hendi vobis ipsis testibus supplicio dignum? Cerce ex omnibus ijs, de quibus eum accusatis, ne unum quidem inueniri potuit. Fuit hoc dictum admodum graue, & procul dubio intolerabile vijsum fuit am bitiosis illis suæ dignitatis ostentatoribus, cum suam existimationem illo letaliter vulnerari sentirent. Non tamen eo contentus, testem innocentiæ alium adhuc sistit, authoritate grauem, & ad quem pro pter Christi patriam causæ huius cognitio in primis pertinebat: Herodē uidelicet, Regem Galilææ, in qua ille plerunq; docuerat. Sed ne Herodes quidem, aliquid noxæ in illo reperit. Et ne quis obijce ret: Atqui aliqua inter vos collusio forsitan fuit, neq; quid ille cum eo fecerit, scire possumus, addit: Nam remisi uos ad illū. Quasi diceret: Nolui quicquā uobis inscijs agere, nolui meo præiudicio ue stræ causam grauare: sed eam integrā unà uobisc͞u ad illum retuli, ubi eam denuo agere licuit. Et ec ce, ne Herodes quidē de aliquo motu aut tumultu per illū excitato queritur. Quid multis? Ecce, nihil dignum morte factū est ab eo. Hæc ad illos Pilati oratio fuit, qua nihil iustius, nihil grauius & liberi us in hac causa dici poterat. Imo ex ea discere possunt iudices qua ingenuitate & æquitate in cau fis cognoscendis uti, & quam liberè innocentiæ testimonium aduersus quosuis ferre debeant. Et si sic ille perrexisset, iam priori culpæ remedium inuenerat, & suæ simul existimationi consuluisset. At quia infelix inuidiam omnem declinare studet, orationi tam graui & egregiæ conclusionem infert, qua nihil absurdius, nihil iniustius, stultius, impudentius posset fingi. Et quæ nā illa est? Castigatum ergo eum dimittam. Deum immortalem, tantāmne uecordiam, tantam impudentiam in animum eius incidere potuisse, ut homo politicus, ciuis Romanus, multo rerum usu celebris, adhac Præses ei us regionis, quam in officio contineri plurimum reipub. intererat, imò Imperatoris Romani vicari us, in loco iustitiæ sacro, in iudicio deniq; ad hunc modum argumentetur: Nulla est in homine isto noxa; Ergo castigatum aut uirgis cæsum dimittam? Ergone in eum locum res Romanæ peruene runt Pilate, ut qui innocentes sunt castigentur? Quæ unquam gens tam barbara fuit, in qua huic similis sententia audita sit? Et quid in Christo castigatione & uerberibus aut flagris dignum est, si neq; tu, neq; Herodes noxam aliquam in eo potuisti deprehendere? Sed ita solet accidere, ut qui ho minum fauorem & huius sæculi gloriam Deo & huius gloriæ præferunt, sibijpsis ignominiam ex tremam accersant. Et non desunt exempla hodie multorum, qui dum pios ferro & igne persequun tur, interim non obscura innocentiæ eorum testimonia perhibet. Quid enim aliud faciunt, qui cū nul la pœna dignos esse iudicent, tamen ex patriis sedibus in exilium eiciunt, publica infamia notant, & infinitis alijs rationibus multant, ut apud iuratos illorum hostes bonam gratiam ineant?
units.tr: Pilate, who wished to refer this case, full of envy and hatred, to Herod, when he saw himself often frustrated there, begins a new contrivance. Luke describes this with such care that we cannot doubt he did it in that way; yet he does so to no profit and to no credit, for, lacking courage of mind, he is unwilling to run any risk for a good cause. For he summons all who were pursuing it: namely the chief priests, the magistrates or elders, and finally the whole people, hoping that among so great a multitude there would be some who, either mindful of the miracles and benefits they had received, or struck by his authority, would desist from that action. He therefore gives a speech that is brief, but very rich in arguments by which they could have been moved, had they not put aside justice and fairness, and common sense and all shame. For, beginning with their accusation, he first repeats the main point of it, so that he might not seem to have observed anything in it carelessly, or now to be dissembling craftily: "You have brought this man to me as one who turns the people away," namely from the worship received among you and from the obedience they owe to Caesar. Here is the sum of your accusation, here the state of the case brought against him. Next he adds: "And behold, I have examined him in your presence, and found no guilt in this man in respect of those things of which you accuse him." He uses the emphatic particle of demonstration, so as to convince them by their own testimony. "Behold," he says, "I have not neglected this case, nor have I handled it carelessly or half-heartedly, but I have conducted a diligent inquiry before your eyes and ears. What then have you yourselves, as witnesses, found in him that deserves punishment? Indeed, of all the things of which you accuse him, not even one could be found." This was a very weighty statement, and no doubt it seemed intolerable to those ambitious displayers of their own dignity, when they felt their reputation mortally wounded by it. Yet not content with this, he brings forward yet another witness of innocence, one of great authority, and one to whom the inquiry into this cause especially belonged, since Christ's homeland was Galilee, where he had mostly taught: namely Herod, king of Galilee. But not even Herod found any guilt in him. And lest anyone object, "Yet perhaps there was some collusion between you and him, and we cannot know what he did with him," he adds: "For I sent you back to him." As if he said: "I did not wish to act in anything without your knowledge, nor did I wish to burden your case by my own prejudgment; but I referred it to him intact, together with you, where it was permitted to bring it again before him." "And behold, not even Herod complains of any disturbance or tumult stirred up by him." What more is there to say? "Behold, nothing worthy of death has been done by him." This was Pilate's speech to them, and nothing more just, nothing more weighty and more free, could have been said in this case. Indeed, judges can learn from it with what candour and fairness they ought to proceed in examining causes, and how freely they ought to bear witness to innocence against anyone at all. And if he had continued in this way, he would already have found a remedy for his earlier fault, and would at the same time have looked to his own reputation. But because the unhappy man is eager to avoid all envy, he brings to so weighty and excellent a speech a conclusion than which nothing more absurd, more unjust, more foolish or more shameless could be invented. And what is that? "I will therefore chastise him and let him go." Good God, could such madness and such impudence have entered his mind, that a man of affairs, a Roman citizen renowned for long experience in governing, moreover the governor of that region, which it greatly concerned the commonwealth to keep in order, indeed the vicar of the Roman emperor, sitting in a sacred place of justice and in a judgment, should reason in this manner: "There is no guilt in this man; therefore I will let him go after he has been chastised, or beaten with rods"? Has Roman affairs come to such a state, Pilate, that the innocent are chastised? What people was ever so barbarous that a sentence like this has been heard among them? And what in Christ deserves chastisement, blows or scourging, if neither you nor Herod could find any guilt in him? But it usually happens that those who prefer the favour of men and the glory of this world to God and his glory bring shame upon themselves in the end. Nor are there lacking today examples of many who, while they persecute the godly with sword and fire, meanwhile give no obscure testimony to their innocence. For what else do those do who, while judging them worthy of no punishment, nonetheless drive them from their native homes into exile, brand them with public infamy, and punish them by countless other means, in order to win good favour with their sworn enemies?

units.la: Sed tertiū Pilati cōmentū uideamus, quo se ex causa ista extricare, & simul Christum absq; inuidia liberare conatus est. Conectit id cum priori Lucas, sed ab eo aperte satis apud alios Euangelistas distinguitur. Occasionem huius arripit ex more ueteri siue recepto, qui erat ut die Paschatis ali-" quis facinorosorum, qui morte multari meruerant, in populi gratiam dimitteretur. Sunt qui hoc fa ctum putent propter lætā liberationis ex Ægypto memoriā, quæ tunc agebatur. Quod si uerum est, καχοξηλεία fuit cum superstitione coniuncta, quæ excusari nō poterat. Nam Dei bonitatem imitari voluerunt, cuius exemplum ille memorabile in ista liberatione ediderat: rationem autem huius imitationis ab eius voluntate alienissimam secuti sunt. Is enim fontes non dimittere, sed punire iusserat, & nisi id facerent, idem excidiū illis minatus fuerat, quo Chananæi eiecti fuerunt, quod terram istam scelerum impunitate polluissent. Et notum est illud Solomonis: Qui sceleratum absoluit, & qui insontem damnat, utrumque Deo abominabilis est. Quoad vero bonitatis & beneficentiæ officia, longè alia Deus præscripserat: Nimirum, ut nexus iniquorum debitorum soluerent, ut fasciculos iugi humeris obæratorum auferrent, ut iugum iniustū confringeret, esurientibus panem distribuerent, afflictos & extorres hospitio amico exciperent, nudos vestirent, neq; oculos abscònderent à carne sua. At egregij isti religionis veræ sectatores omissis iis, quæ ad ipsos privatim spectabant, ex alieno liberales erant, & cum nemini quicquam remitterent ex suis debitis, tunc se pietatis officio probè defunctos putabant, si nebulonem aliquem morte dignum liberauissent. Et credibile est, Romanos hac consuetudinem ipsis inviolatam reliquisse, ut populum facilius in officio continerent, qui ferè privilegijs & immunitatibus eiusmodi non minus ridiculis quàm inhonestis delectatur. Certè quicquid huius sit, constat, consuetudinem hanc iniquissimam & hoc populo indignam fuisse, in qua veræ religionis atq; iustitiæ domicilium Deus esse voluerat. Ideo in præsenti etiam eius fructus fuit tristissimus. Nā Pilatus hinc arrepta occasione, Christū cum Barraba seditioso & homicida cōfert, comparatione omnium iniquissima, & non tam iniquos aut impudentes fore sibi persuadet, ut hunc potius quàm illum sibi donari postulent. At idem interea se bis iniquū & impudentè præbet. Qui enim de Christi innocentia iam secundò publicum testimonium dederat, nunc eundem cum Barrabā socians, hominibus flagitiosis & capitalem pœnam meritis accenset. Adhæc uitam hominis innocentis furiosi populi iudicio permittit, qui in eius exitium iampridē conspirauerat cum Sacerdotibus, quos ille sciebat omnia per invidiam agere. Fuit ergo hoc consilium priori detestabilius, quia notoria contumelia Christum affecit, cuius famam atq; vitam debebat tueri. Euentum quoq; infeliciorem habuit, quia in eas angustias illum adduxit, unde pedem referre non licuit postea, cum rem omnem populi arbitrio iam subiecisset. Etenim illi simul omnes à Sacerdotibus & Senioribus persuasi (quod Matthæus annotauit) exclamauerunt: Tolle hunc, dimitte verò nobis Barrabam.
units.tr: But let us look at Pilate's third device, by which he tried to extricate himself from this affair and at the same time to free Christ without arousing envy. Luke connects it with the previous one, but it is clearly distinguished from it in the other Evangelists. He takes his occasion from the old or established custom that on the day of the Passover one of the criminals who deserved death should be released to please the people. Some think this was done in memory of the joyful deliverance from Egypt, which was then being celebrated. If that is true, the misguided zeal [καχοξηλεία] was joined with superstition, and it could not be excused. For they wished to imitate God's goodness, whose memorable example he had shown in that deliverance, but they followed a principle of imitation most alien to his will. For he had ordered that the guilty not be released but punished, and unless they did so he had threatened the same destruction with which the Canaanites were driven out, because they had polluted that land by letting crimes go unpunished. And the saying of Solomon is well known: "He who acquits the guilty and he who condemns the innocent are both an abomination to the LORD" (Prov. 17.). As for the duties of kindness and beneficence, God had prescribed quite different things: namely, that they should loosen the bonds of wicked debts, take away the burdens from the shoulders of the oppressed, break the unjust yoke, give bread to the hungry, receive the afflicted and the exiles into friendly hospitality, clothe the naked, and not hide their eyes from their own flesh (Isa. 58.). But these outstanding followers of true religion, passing over those things which concerned them privately, were generous with what belonged to others. Though they remitted nothing of their own debts to anyone, they thought they had discharged the duty of piety well enough if they set free some scoundrel who deserved death. And it is likely that the Romans left this custom to them unbroken, so that they could more easily keep the people in obedience; for such a people delights almost as much in privileges and immunities of this kind, as ridiculous as they are dishonourable. Whatever the reason, it is certain that this custom was most unjust and unworthy of this people, when God had wished the home of true religion and justice to be among them. Therefore its fruit in the present case was also most sorrowful. For Pilate, seizing the occasion, compares Christ with Barabbas, a seditious murderer, in a comparison most unjust of all, and he persuades himself that they would not be so wicked or shameless as to ask for this man rather than that one. Yet at the same time he shows himself doubly unjust and shameless. For he who had already twice given public testimony to Christ's innocence now links him with Barabbas and numbers him among shameful men who deserve capital punishment. Moreover, he hands the life of an innocent man over to the judgement of a raging people, who had long been conspiring with the priests for his destruction, and whom Pilate knew to act always out of envy. This counsel was therefore more detestable than the earlier one, because it dealt Christ an open insult, when he ought to have defended his reputation and life. It also had a more unhappy outcome, because it brought him into such straits that he could not afterwards draw back, since he had already put the whole matter at the people's discretion. For all of them, persuaded at once by the chief priests and elders (as Matthew noted), cried out: "Away with this man, but release Barabbas to us."

units.la: Est hoc insigne exemplū, quo docemur quàm periculosum sit causas hominū innocentium vulgi iudicio permittere. Si enim unius hominis contumacioris sensū corrigere difficillimū est, quid de vulgo speres bestia multorum capitū, in quo sensus mille & diuersissimi tumultuatur, neq; unquam nisi in eo quod pessimū est, cōuenire possunt? Accedit iudicij inopia, quæ nō solum ingratos facit et iniquos ac ceptorū beneficiorū æstimatores, nerumetiā insanos & furentes, adeò ut plerique ex eo sibijpsis gloriā & triumphos immortales polliceantur, si viros magnos & de repub. optimè meritos opprimat. Exēpla huius uitij in amplissimis ciuitatibus, Roma & Athenis, infinita extat. Scipio certè maior, qui rēpub. bellis Punicis tantumnō extinctā et exangue seruarat, et Carthaginis dominā fecerat, populi Rom. iniurijs fatigatus & tandē uictus urbe excessit, & exul uoluntarius in obscura villa Linternis mortuus sepulchro inscribi iussit: Ingrata patria, ne ossa quidē mea habes. Eiusdem fratrem, quē Asiaticū dixerunt, idem populus peculatus reū egit, et in carcerē duci iussit. At Nasica Scipio post multa in repub. merita, ut populi iniqua de suis uirtutibus iudicia declinaret, sub legationis titulo Pergamum discessit, & illic quod reliquum fuit uitæ transegit. Apud Atheniensses autem, populi furentis & ingrati tumultibus Themistocles in exilium actus, ad Xerxem, quē communis patriæ hostem debellauerat, confugit: Miltiades, qui Persis in Marathone ingenti prælio uictis Græciam omnem metu atque terrore liberauit, à populo in carcerem coniectus illic expirauit, corpus autem tam diu sepultura caruit, donec filius Cimon se ijsdem uinculis constringendum tradidit. Phocion autem ab ijsdem non solum in eculeo impositus est, sed post obitum finibus Atticis eiectus glebulam terræ Atticæ nullam inuenit, quæ ossibus eius iniiceretur. Superat tamen exempla hæc omnia, quod in præsenti Iudæorū gens in Christum, æternæ salutis authorē, desiignauit. Libuit tamen uetera quoque commemorare, quò minus quod illi accidit admiremur, utque non offendamur, si ipsi quoq; plerosq; uidemus pessimā gratiā iis referre, qui pro ipsorū salute dies noctesq; excubant. At hic simul pœnas in mentem reuocare debemus diras & horribiles, quibus ipsorum ingratitudinem Deus ultus us ultus est, ut alibi diximus. Non dormitat enim hic, & eo etiam uindice atq; ultore punientur, qui illos imitati fuerint.
units.tr: This is a notable example, by which we are taught how dangerous it is to leave the causes of innocent men to the judgement of the crowd. For if it is most difficult to correct the opinion of one stubborn man, what can you hope for from the crowd, the beast of many heads, in which a thousand very different opinions are stirred up, and which can never agree except in what is worst? Add to this the lack of judgement, which makes people not only ungrateful, unjust and poor judges of the benefits they have received, but also mad and raging, so that many of them promise themselves immortal glory and triumphs if they crush great men who have deserved well of the commonwealth. Examples of this vice are endless in the most famous cities, Rome and Athens. Surely Scipio the Elder, who had saved the commonwealth, all but extinct and drained of blood in the Punic wars, and had made Carthage its subject, was worn down by the injustices of the Roman people, and at last, defeated, left the city. As a voluntary exile he died in an obscure villa at Liternum, and ordered this inscription placed on his tomb: "Ungrateful country, you do not even have my bones." The same people prosecuted his brother, whom they called Asiaticus, for embezzlement, and ordered him to be led to prison. But Scipio Nasica, after many services to the commonwealth, in order to escape the unjust judgements of the people about his virtues, withdrew to Pergamum under the title of an embassy, and there spent the rest of his life. Among the Athenians, however, Themistocles, driven into exile by the tumults of a raging and ungrateful people, fled to Xerxes, whose enemy of the common fatherland he had defeated. Miltiades, who freed all Greece from fear and terror by defeating the Persians in the great battle at Marathon, was thrown into prison by the people and died there; his body was for a long time without burial, until his son Cimon handed himself over to be bound with the same chains. Phocion was not only put on the rack by the same people, but after his death, being cast out of Attica, he found no clod of Attic earth into which his bones could be thrown. Yet the people of the Jews, in the present case, has surpassed all these examples in its designs against Christ, the author of eternal salvation. Nevertheless, I have been pleased to recall the older examples too, so that we may wonder less at what happened to him, and so that we are not offended if we see that many also repay with the worst thanks those who keep watch day and night for their salvation. But here we must at the same time call to mind the dreadful and horrible punishments with which God avenged their ingratitude, as we have said elsewhere. For he does not sleep, and those who have imitated them will also be punished by him as avenger and punisher.

units.la: Interim feruit tota hac actio nostrae redemptionis atq; salutis mysterio. Peccarat Adam super bia, quando ut Dei similis fieret, ex uetita arbore comedit. Et ideo superbia peccati principium esse dicitur. Ergo Christum, qui fecundus Adamus uocatur, extremè humiliari oportebat, ut su-perbiam illam expiaret, adeoque nobis omnibus subueniret, quibus hæc præcipua omnium scelerum causa est, quod Deo subesse nolumus, & eius præceptis obedire. At quæ humiliatio ignominiosior excogitari poterat, quàm quòd Pilatus quidem illum Barrabæ, homini seditioso & latroni confert, eundem uero populus ex Sacerdotum & Seniorum consilio illi postponit? Dolet generosis ingenijs quàm maximè si suum honorem & existimationem labefactari sentiant; & qui omnes alias iniurias patienter ferre norunt, hic fere impatientia superantur. Voluit tamen hanc contumeliam sustinere Dei Filius, ut nos ab æternæ damnationis ignominia liberaret, & gloriæ suæ cœlestis socios atq; cohæredes faceret. Id uero ita à nobis considerari debet, ne nobis graue sit, si quando ipsi quoque contemnimur & contumeliarum aut iniuriarum omni genere obruimur propter illum, qui prior pro nobis tam indigna passus est. Soletur autem, quòd ut ille per hanc ignominiam in Patris gloria euectus est: ita nobis quoque uiam parauit; qua per huius sæculi ludibria ad Regni sui gloriosi possessionem peruenia-mus. At simul eius exemplo humilitatem nobis commendari cogitemus. Pudeat ergo Christianos homines superbiæ, qua multi suæ professionis immemores aduersus Deum simul & homines sese extollunt, dum quosuis prase contemnunt; & ipsi etiam Deo Leges Regni sui nouas prescribere audent. Faciunt hoc minus impudenter, qui peccatorum remissionem & salutem æternam suorum operum meritis deberi contendunt, & illa coram Deo plus quàm Pharisaica arrogantia ostentant. Ergóne Christus ideo cum iniquis reputatus est, ut tu propriam iustitiam iactares? Ergo Barraba latrone inferior haberi debuit, ut tu eũ sui meriti gloria spolies, & tuis operibus id tribuas, quod ille sui sanguinis pretio acquisiuit? Sunt hæc absurda admodum, & quia in Filij Dei ignominiam tendunt magis, quàm quod in præsenti Pilatus & Iudæi fecerunt, à Christianis hominibus procul abesse debent.
units.tr: Meanwhile the whole of this action is full of the mystery of our redemption and salvation. Adam sinned through pride, when he ate from the forbidden tree in order to become like God; and so pride is said to be the beginning of sin. Therefore Christ, who is called the second Adam, had to be humbled to the utmost, so that he might atone for that pride and so help all of us, for whom this is the chief cause of all sins: that we are unwilling to submit to God and to obey his commands. But what more shameful humiliation could be devised than that Pilate should set Christ against Barabbas, a seditious man and a robber, and that the people, on the counsel of the chief priests and elders, should put him after Barabbas?
