Noble minds grieve most of all when they feel their honour and reputation being shaken; and those who know how to bear all other injuries patiently are here almost overcome by impatience. Yet the Son of God wished to endure this insult, so that he might free us from the shame of eternal damnation and make us heavenly companions and co-heirs of his glory. This must indeed be so considered by us, that it will not be hard for us if at any time we too are despised and overwhelmed with insults or injuries of every kind for his sake, who first suffered such unworthy things for us. And we are consoled by the fact that, just as he was raised through this shame into the glory of the Father, so he has also prepared for us a way by which, through the mockeries of this age, we may come to the possession of his glorious kingdom. But at the same time let us consider that humility is commended to us by his example. Let Christians therefore be ashamed of pride, by which many, forgetful of their profession, exalt themselves against God and men alike, while they despise whomever they please, and even dare to prescribe new laws of his kingdom to God himself. Those who maintain that forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation are owed to the merits of their own works do this less shamelessly, and display such arrogance before God as is more than Pharisaical. Was Christ then counted among the wicked so that you might boast of your own righteousness? Was Barabbas the robber to be held inferior, so that you might strip him of the glory of his merit and attribute to your works what he acquired by the price of his blood? These things are utterly absurd, and since they tend more toward the shame of the Son of God than what Pilate and the Jews did in the present case, they ought to be far from Christian men.

units.la: Porrò ad Pilatum redeamus, qui quod de castigatione aut flagellatione prius proposuerat, reperit, & quidem magna cum gratuitate, ut animi inter diuersos affectuum motus fluctuantis luctam nō obscure deprehendas. Et hanc quoq; partem Lucas diligentissime describit. Rursus ergo Pilatus (inquit) alloquutus est eos, uolens dimittere Iesum. Quasi diceret: Etiamsi se hac etiam spe frustratum cerneret, seq; proprio consilio captu iam teneri sentiret, nondum tamen ab incœpto desiit: sed adhuc conatus est Iesum ex illorum manibus eripere. Matthæus equidem eum nouam de illo quæstionem diserte mouisse scribit, si forte rei indignitas illos abstulerer. Dixit enim: Quid igitur faciam Iesu, qui dicitur Christus? Quod perinde est, ac si dixisset: Age habeatis uobis Barrabam, quoniam ita lubet, & latronem atq; seditiosum nebulonem homini iusto atq; innocenti præfertis: Scire tamen uelim ex uobis, quid de Iesu hoc faciendum putetis, qui præter id quòd nihil mali fecit, Christi quoq; id est, Regis & liberatoris nomen uulgò obtinuuit? Quid uero illi? Iam totum animi uirus non minus impudenter quàm impiè & crudeliter expuunt, clamantes: Crucifige, crucifige eum: At ipse tertiò iam obijcit illis. Quid uero ipse mali fecit? Nullam noxam capitalem inueni in eo. Quæ uerba rursus animum iustitiæ studio ardentem præ se ferunt: sed quia religione uera aut Dei timore nõ confirmatur, ad eundem lapidem iterum offendit. Cùm enim deberet inferre: Ergo dimittam illum, uobis autem edico & impero, ne manus iniustas illi iniiciatis, neq; innocenti uim faciatis: indignum illud & iniquissimum dictum repetit: Castigatum ergo eum dimittam. Et quia se uerbis minus proficere uidebat, mox eum in Prætorium reducit, & militibus flagellandũ tradit. Hi uero nõ contenti flagrus illum cæcidisse, insuper licentia militari utuntur, & eidem contumeliosissimè illudunt. Quia enim eum regni affectati accusari audierant, ut Regi contemptissimo petulanter insultant: Et coronam quidem ex spinis contexta capiti eius imponunt, sceptro arundineo dexteram eius ornant, & pallio purpureo amiciunt. Inde gestibus et uerbis ad contumeliam compositis illum salutant dicentes: Aue Rex Iudæorum. Conspuunt præterea faciem eius, & caput arundine atque bacillis percutiunt. Quæ omnia ab illis non tam in illius quàm totius gentis Iudaicæ ignominiam facta sunt. Quia enim (ut aliâs quoq; monnimus) in omnium ore erat Meßias & promissus ille populi redemptor, simul spem illorum omnem ludibrio habent & ridẽt. Tanti autem sceleris reatu ipsi sese polluerunt, ut incon-sulto odio Iesu abrepti ueteres promissiones & Prophetarum oracula, spem deniq; patrũ suorum sce-leratissimorum Goijm(ut ipsi loquuntur)ludibrijs subiecerint. Seipsos ergo maiori quàm illum con-tumelia affecerũt: quod fere omnibus accidit, qui aduersus Christum coniurantes in cœlum expuũt, ut prouerbio dicitur. Cæterùm Pilatus illum denuo ad se recipit, & flagris conscissum sanguineque multo & sputis fœdatum, spinis item coronatũ & militari pallio indutum in populi conspectum pro-duxit sperans fore, ut miserabili illo aspectu mouerentur, & animis satiati in eius liberationem seu dimissionem consentirent. At ferarum instar illo uiso in maiorem rabiem accensi, clamant: Crucifi-ge, crucifige eum. Et Pilato cum indignatione dicente: Accipite eum uos, & crucifigite, ego enim nõ inuenio in eo crimen: Illi suam legẽ urgere incipiunt, & aiunt: Nos habemus Legem, & secundùm Legem nostram debet mori: quia Filium Dei sefecit. Et cùm hinc nouus scrupulus Præsidis animo iniectus esset, & is nouam cum illo actionẽ institueret, tandẽ maiori tum importunitate illi instant, clamantes: Si hunc absoluëris, non es amicus Cæsaris: quicunq; se Regi facit, cõtradicit Cæsari. Et hæc quidẽ omnia Lucas paucis hisce uerbis complexus est. At alij instabant uocibus magnis, peten-tes ut crucifigeretur: & inualescebant uoces eorum, ac principum Sacerdotum. Et latet sub ista con-tentione aliud adhuc, & quidẽ luculentissimũ innocentiæ Christi testimonium. Videmus enim eius accusatores nullum aduersus eum crimen protulisse, quod uel in speciem probabile fuerit. Quid ergo restat, quàm ut illum non tam calumniis quàm clamatoribus seditiosis & aperta ui oppressum esse di-camus? Et hæ illæ rationes, hæc argumenta sunt, quibus etiam hodie Pontificũ serui contra germa-nos Christi cultores pugnant. Cùm enim hos accusent, quòd res nouas moliantur & seditiones con-citent, ipsi in ciuilibus armis & populi furentis moribus atq; minis omne præsidiũ collocatũ habent: & quia se rationibus destitutos esse uident, ad Catilinarium illud consilium sese conuertunt, ut salu-berrimum illud Euangelicæ lucis incendium ruina ciuitatum simul atq; regnorum extinguant. Sed utinam illi meminissent, quàm grauiter Deus Iudæorum principes ultus sit. Qui enim seditiosorum hominum improbis clamoribus ad Christum opprimendum abusi sunt, non multò post cõtinuis sedi-tionibus totam terrã turbari senserũt, quæ causa fuit, ut Romani tandem missis eò legionibus suis bellũ genti inferrent, quo miserabiliter excißa est: & qui ex ea hodie superstites sunt, ij in omnes ter-ras dispersi omnium iniurijs atq; contumelijs obruuntur. Sentient idem aliquando omnes illi, quibus hodie uolupe est cum Christianorum sanguine & capitibus ludere.
units.tr: But let us return to Pilate, who, having first proposed to punish or scourge Jesus, now finds a way out, though with great ease, so that you can clearly see the struggle of his mind as it wavers among different emotions. Luke describes this part very carefully as well. So Pilate (he says) again addressed them, wishing to release Jesus. It is as if he were saying: even though he saw himself frustrated in this hope too, and felt that he was already caught in his own plan, he still did not give up what he had begun, but tried once more to snatch Jesus out of their hands. Matthew indeed writes that he clearly raised a new question about him, in case the very unworthiness of the matter might turn them away. For he said: "What then shall I do with Jesus, who is called Christ?" This comes to the same as saying: "Very well, have Barabbas, since that is your pleasure, and prefer a robber and a seditious rogue to a righteous and innocent man. Yet I should like to know from you what you think ought to be done with this Jesus, who, besides having done no wrong, has commonly won the name of Christ, that is, of King and Deliverer." And what did they do? Now they spit out all the venom of their minds, no less shamelessly than impiously and cruelly, shouting: "Crucify, crucify him!" But Pilate, now for the third time, objects to them: "What evil has he in fact done? I have found no capital offence in him." These words again show a mind burning with zeal for justice, but because it is not supported by true religion or the fear of God, it strikes against the same stone again. For when he ought to have said, "Then I will release him, but I order and command you not to lay unjust hands on him or to do violence to the innocent," he repeats that shameful and most unjust proposal: "Then I will release him after having him scourged." And since he saw that he was making little headway with words, he soon led him back into the Praetorium and handed him over to the soldiers to be scourged. They, not content with having lashed him, further took advantage of military licence and mocked him most insolently. Because they had heard that he was accused of aspiring to kingship, they wantonly insulted him as a most contemptible king: they set on his head a crown woven of thorns, put a reed in his right hand as a sceptre, and clothed him in a purple cloak. Then, with gestures and words designed for insult, they greeted him, saying: "Hail, King of the Jews!" Moreover they spat in his face and struck his head with reeds and sticks. All these things were done by them not so much to his disgrace as to the disgrace of the whole Jewish nation. For since (as we have noted elsewhere too) the Messiah, that promised redeemer of the people, was on everyone's lips, they made a mockery and a laughing-stock of all their hope. And they polluted themselves with such guilt of crime that, carried away by an unconsidered hatred of Jesus, they subjected the ancient promises and the oracles of the Prophets, and finally the hope of their most wicked fathers, to the mockery of the Goijm (as they themselves call the Gentiles). Thus they inflicted on themselves a greater insult than on him, which happens to almost all who conspire against Christ and spit at heaven, as the proverb says. Meanwhile Pilate took him back again and, having brought him out before the eyes of the people, torn with scourges, befouled with much blood and spittle, likewise crowned with thorns and clothed in a soldier's cloak, hoped that they would be moved by that pitiful sight and, their appetite for blood satisfied, would agree to his release or dismissal. But at the sight of him they flared into greater fury like wild beasts, and shouted: "Crucify, crucify him!" And when Pilate said with indignation, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no crime in him," they began to press their own law and said: "We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God." And when this new scruple had been planted in the governor's mind, and he began a fresh inquiry with him, at last they pressed him with still greater insistence, shouting: "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend; whoever makes himself a king speaks against Caesar." Luke has embraced all of this in these few words. But others kept urging with loud voices, asking that he be crucified, and their voices grew stronger, and those of the chief priests as well. And under this contention there lies hidden yet another thing, a most manifest testimony to the innocence of Christ. For we see that his accusers brought forward no charge against him that could even seem plausible. What remains, then, but to say that he was overcome not so much by calumnies as by seditious shouters and open force? These are the very reasons and arguments by which even today the servants of the Papists fight against the true worshippers of Christ. For when they accuse these men of plotting novelties and stirring up sedition, they themselves place all their protection in civil arms and in the habits and threats of a raging people; and since they see themselves lacking reasons, they turn to that Catilinarian plan, so as to extinguish that most salutary fire of the Gospel light along with the ruin of cities and kingdoms. But would that they remembered how grievously God has avenged the rulers of the Jews. For those who misused the wicked clamours of seditious men to oppress Christ soon afterwards felt the whole land thrown into turmoil by continual seditions, which was the cause that the Romans at last sent their legions there and waged war on that nation, by which it was miserably destroyed; and those of them who survive today are scattered through all lands and overwhelmed with the injuries and insults of all. All those too who today delight to play with the blood and heads of Christians will one day feel the same.

units.la: Sequitur actionis totius non tam molestæ quàm iniquissimæ finis. Pilatus enim uictus illorum clamoribus, iudicauit ut fieret quod ipsi petebãt. Matthæus eum prius manibus cum publica prote-statione ablutis sententiam pronunciauisse scribit. Extorsit illam quoq; mens sibi male cõscia: adeò tamen nõ profuit ea, ut potius seipsum accusarit. Dum enim innoxij sanguinis meminit, sese eius rea-tu simul obstringit. Ad sceleris uerò amplificationẽ facit, quod de Barraba repetit Lucas: Dimisit autem eis illum, qui propter seditionem et cædem coniectus fuerat in carcerem, quẽ petierant: Iesum uerò tradidit eorum cupiditati. Quæ ita dicuntur, ut quàmuis Pilatus minimè extra culpam sit, ma-ior tamẽ in Iudæis hæreat, quod & ipse Christus testatus fuit, illi dicens: Qui me tradidit tibi, maius peccatum habet. Quod ipsum noster Euangelista innuit, dum istud omne in Iudæorum gratiam fa-ctum fuisse ait: Dimisit (inquit) eis illum, &c. Itẽ: QVEM PETIERANT. Et rursus: Iesum uerò tradidit eorum cupiditati. Est autem tota hæc actio speculum clarissimum, in quo principum huius sæculi ingeniũ atq; mores spectare licet. Habent hi plerunq; aliquam iuris & æqui cognitionẽ, sed sua potius quærunt, quàm ut suum cuiq; ius reddant. Ideo in suo iure tuendo acerrimi sunt, dum hoc suis cupiditatibus seruire uident. At si quid pro causa ueritatis, pro religione, pro Christi seruis atq; cultoribus fieri debet, quod cum inuidia & odio coniunctum est, tunc qui inter illos optimi sunt, ad artes & iniquissimas compositiones conuertuntur, ne quem offendant. Frequenter item, quos tue-ri debent, in aliorum gratiam indignius tractari sinunt. Est enim hoc humanæ prudentiæ axioma: Leuius malum patienter ferri debere, ut quod grauius est effugiamus. Vnde illi concludunt, satius esse, ut ijs subscribant, qui pios fortunis aut exilio multãre uolunt, quàm ut ijdem omnino occidan-tur. Sed quàm infelix sit consiliorum eiusmodi euentus, multa exempla docent, & quod hic accidit, omnium
units.tr: There follows the end of the whole proceeding, which is not so much troublesome as most unjust. For Pilate, overcome by their outcries, decided that what they asked should be done. Matthew writes that he first pronounced sentence after washing his hands with a public declaration. A guilty conscience also extorted this from him, yet it did him no good, but rather accused himself further. For while he remembers the innocent blood, he at the same time binds himself to its guilt. Luke adds to the enormity of the crime when he repeats about Barabbas: "He released to them the man who had been thrown into prison for sedition and murder, whom they had asked for; but Jesus he handed over to their desire." These things are said in such a way that, although Pilate is by no means free from blame, the greater guilt nonetheless clings to the Jews, as Christ himself testified when he said to him: "He who handed me over to you has the greater sin." Our Evangelist hints at this very thing when he says that all of this was done for the favour of the Jews: "He released to them" (he says) "etc." Likewise: "WHOM THEY HAD ASKED FOR." And again: "But Jesus he handed over to their desire." Now this whole action is a most clear mirror, in which one may observe the character and morals of the rulers of this age. They usually have some knowledge of law and equity, but they seek their own advantage rather than rendering to each his right. Therefore they are most fierce in defending their own right, when they see that this serves their desires. But if something must be done for the cause of truth, for religion, for the servants and worshippers of Christ, something that is bound up with envy and hatred, then even the best among them turn to tricks and most unjust compromises, lest they offend anyone. Often, too, they allow those whom they ought to protect to be treated more shamefully for the favour of others. For this is an axiom of human prudence: that one ought to endure a lesser evil patiently in order to escape a greater. Hence they conclude that it is better to put their names to the decrees of those who wish to punish the godly with loss of property or exile, than that these same people should be altogether destroyed. But how unhappy the outcome of counsels of this kind is, many examples teach, and what happened here is an example for all.

units.la: Christus innocens seditiosis clamatoribus opprimitur.
units.tr: Christ, innocent, is oppressed by seditious clamourers.

units.la: Pilatus Christum damnat. omnium loco esse posset. Quia enim insatiabilis est hostium Christi rabies, coguntur subinde longius progredi, qui illis semel inaulgere coeperunt. Nihil ergo consultius fuerit, quàm ingenuè & fortiter agere, euentum uero rei Deo permittere, qui tunc quoq; uiam inueniet seruandi suos, quando nobis nulla alia esse uidetur, quàm quæ cum iniquitate aliqua coniuncta est. Quòd si uero idem ille suorum corpora & uitam tueri nolit, & illis omnino moriendum est, tunc sufficiat iudicibus æquoribus, si ipsi manus ab illorum sanguine puras seruent, neq; ijs consentiant, qui aliquid iniustum tentant. Hoc nomine Iosephum Arimathæum postea Lucas commendabit, nec temere à Spiritu sancto dictum est: Beatus ille vir, qui non ambulauit in consilio impiorum.
units.tr: Pilate condemns Christ. ... could be the case for all. For the rage of Christ's enemies is insatiable, and those who have once begun to yield to them are subsequently compelled to go further and further. Nothing therefore will be more prudent than to act openly and bravely, and to leave the outcome of the matter to God, who will then also find a way of preserving his people, when no other way seems open to us except one joined with some wrong. But if he himself is unwilling to protect the bodies and lives of his people, and they must in any case die, then it will be enough for the judges, if they keep their hands pure from their blood and do not consent to those who attempt anything unjust. For this reason Luke will afterwards commend Joseph of Arimathea, and it was not said rashly by the Holy Spirit: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked.

units.la: Præcipuum autem huius loci caput est Iesu Christi innocentia, quam tot argumentis & testimonijs asseri atque probari oportuit, quot nullius hominis unquam probatam aut defensam fuisse legimus. Nam in triplici foro (ut sic loquar) ille causam dixit, & in nullo alicuius criminis convictus est. Primò enim in Concilium adductus est, ubi falsis quoque testibus locus fuit, & fortasssis ijsdem præmia proposita fuerunt. Verumtamen adeò nihil morte dignum in illo inveniri potuit, ut tandem non alio prætextu, quàm quòd se Dei Filium esse dixisset, & proinde propter veritatis confessionem damnatus sit, quia impius Pontifex adiuratione aut obtestatione insidiosa ex ipso elicuerat. Deinde Pilato traditum de multis quidem eum accusarunt, sed in mendacijs deprehensi, Præsidè coegerunt, innocentiæ eius terè, quaterè, testimonium reddere. Præterea Herodes quoque quod in illo desideraret non habuit, & risu potius dignos Sacerdotes quàm illum supplicio iudicauit. Adde his, quod cum publica protestatione Pilatus damnationis sententiam protulit dicens: Innoxius ego sum à sanguine huius iusti, uos uideritis. Neque omitti debet uxoris Pilati testimonium, quæ insomniorum terroribus totam noctem uexata marito renuntiauit: Nihil tibi rei sit cum iusto illo. Quid, quòd illo iam mortuo, Centurio exclamauit: Verè hic homo iustus erat: alij uerò pectora percutientes inde discesserunt? Quantam ergo esse oportuit eius innocentiam, quæ ab hominibus summa authoritate prædictis & magnam doctrinæ & pietatis existimationem sustinentibus, apud prophanorum hominum tribunalia, oppugnata quidem, fortissimè uerò defensa est? Huius ergo usum nos diligenter obseruare conuenit, qui omnino duplex est. Primus, ut certò nobis persuasum sit, nostra peccata in Christo damnata & eiusdem merito expiata esse, idq; ad illorum expiationem potuisse sufficere, cum ipse ab omni culpa liber fuerit. Alter, ne offendamur, si quando nos quoq; immerentes iniquis iudicijs impij damnant. Hæc enim gloria nostra est, quòd nos Christi socios facit infelix mundus, dum nos propter iustitiam odit atq; persequitur. Et notum est illud Petri: Ne quis uestrum affligatur ut homicida, aut fur, aut maleficus, aut alienarum rerum inspector: sed si ut Christianus, ne pudefiat: imò glorificet Deum hac in parte. Socrates olim cùm illo iam cicutâ ori admouente, uxor clamaret: Ah innocens moritur, respondebat: An ergo me nocentem mori uolebas? Tantum in illo potuit philosophiæ humanæ studium, ut indignam putaret eam querimoniam, quæ ipsum præcipua suæ mortis gloria spoliare uidebatur. Quanto maior ergo fortitudo eos decet, qui in Christi schola instituti, se cum illo in cœlis regnaturos esse norunt, si propter ueritatem & fidem cum ipso passi fuerint? Nec est, quòd de nostri nominis fama soliciti simus, sed hanc quoq; unà cum anima nostra in Dei manus deponamus, qui illam seruare, & hostium quoque testimonio si uolet, tueri poterit. Quòd si id non fiat in hoc sæculo, in cœlis tamen nomina nostra adscripta sunt in libro uitæ, qui est Iesus Christus, redemptor noster, & pastor ille bonus, ex cuius manibus nos nemo potest rapere. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The chief point of this passage, however, is the innocence of Jesus Christ, which had to be asserted and proved by as many arguments and testimonies as we read were ever brought to prove or defend the innocence of any man. For he pleaded his case, so to speak, in three courts, and was convicted of no crime in any of them. First he was brought before the Council, where there was also room for false witnesses, and perhaps rewards were offered to the same men. Yet nothing deserving of death could be found in him, so that at last he was condemned on no other pretext than that he had said he was the Son of God, and therefore for confessing the truth, since the wicked high priest had drawn this out of him by an insidious oath or adjuration. Then, handed over to Pilate, they accused him of many things, but being caught in lies they forced the governor to bear witness three and four times to his innocence. Moreover Herod too found nothing in him that he wanted, and judged the priests more worthy of laughter than of punishment for him. Add to these that Pilate, with a public protestation, pronounced the sentence of condemnation, saying: I am innocent of the blood of this just man; see to it yourselves. Nor should the testimony of Pilate's wife be passed over, who, tormented through the night by terrors of dreams, sent word to her husband: Have nothing to do with that just man. What of the fact that, when he was already dead, the centurion cried out: Truly this man was just; while others, beating their breasts, departed from there? How great, then, must his innocence have been, which, though assailed before the tribunals of profane men by people endowed with the highest authority and enjoying a great reputation for learning and piety, was nevertheless most courageously defended! We ought therefore to observe carefully the use of this, which is twofold. The first is that we may be firmly persuaded that our sins were condemned in Christ and expiated by his merit, and that this was enough for their expiation, since he himself was free from all guilt. The second is that we should not be offended if at any time the wicked condemn us by unjust judgments although we deserve nothing. For this is our glory, that the unhappy world makes us companions of Christ, while it hates and persecutes us on account of righteousness. And that saying of Peter is well known: Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or a meddler in other men's affairs; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this respect. Socrates once, when his wife was crying out, "Ah, the innocent man dies," as he was already bringing the hemlock to his lips, answered: "Did you then want me to die guilty?" So much could the study of human philosophy do in him that he thought that complaint unworthy, which seemed to rob him of the chief glory of his death. How much greater courage, then, should befit those who have been trained in the school of Christ and know that they will reign with him in heaven, if they suffer with him for the truth and the faith! Nor should we be anxious about the reputation of our name, but commit it together with our soul into the hands of God, who can preserve it and, if he wills, defend it even by the testimony of enemies. But if this does not happen in this age, our names are nevertheless written in heaven in the book of life, which is Jesus Christ, our redeemer and that good shepherd, from whose hands no one can snatch us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCVI.
units.tr: Homily 206.

units.la: Cùm igitur abduceret eum, prehenso Simone quodam Cyrenæo qui veniebat è rure, imposuerunt ei crucem ferendam post Iesum. Sequebatur autem eum magna multitudo populi & mulierum, quæ & plangebāt & lamentabantur eum. Conuersus autem ad eas Iesus dixit: Filiæ Hierusalem, ne flete super me, verū super vobismetipsis flete, & super liberis vestris: Nam ecce venient dies quibus dicent: Beatæ steriles, & uteri qui non genuerunt, & ubera quæ non lactauerunt. Tum incipient pient dicere montibus : Cadite super nos, & collibus, Operite nos. Nam si in virente ligno ista faciunt, in arido quid fiet?
units.tr: So when they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry after Jesus. A great crowd of people followed him, and of women, who both beat their breasts and lamented him. But Jesus, turning to them, said: Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For behold, the days will come when they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never gave suck. Then they will begin to say to the mountains: Fall on us; and to the hills: Cover us. For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?

units.la: Quamuis Deus Filium suum nobis Seruatorem dederit, & in eodem omnes suae bonitatis thesauros aperiat, hunc ipsum tamen infelix mundus fastidit, & inter alia Dei beneficia hoc in primis turpissima ingratitudine conculcare solet. Nam ut olim Iudaei in sua uenientem non receperunt, quin potius iniquissimè damnatum gentibus tradiderunt, ut in crucem suspensus dira & infami morte tolleretur: ita eiusdem ingratitudinis exempla hodie etiam passim uidere licet. Multi enim ne apud Pontifices & horum propugnatores malam gratiam ineant, illum per Euangelij praedicationem ad se uenientem excludunt. Alij iam admissum rursus eijciunt, ne quod periculum subire cogantur. Alij uoluptates & peccandi licentiam illi anteponunt, & ne disciplina arctiori coerceantur, illo potius carere malunt. Taceo nunc eos, qui ut primum persecutio aliqua exoritur, non modo tur piter deficiunt, uerumetiam aperti hostes fiunt. Offenduntur ista multos, qui dum ea uident, ipsi quoque dubitare & fluctuare incipiunt. Sed proderit tunc uetera illa in mente reuocare, & ad Christi exemplum respicere, quem neque uulgi leuitas, neque Sacerdotum truculentia, neque Pilati perfidia & ignauia, neque militum improbitas aut petulantia mouit, quò minus constans esset in eo, quod ipsi Pater mandauerat. Cuius exemplum si imitemur, ipsi quoque uictores erimus, deque mundo ac eius principe sub crucis uexillo triumphabimus. Sequitur nunc, ut Praesidis quoque sententia damnatum duxerint, ut in crucem suffigerent. Quo loco multa concurrunt, quae ad illustrandum nostrae redemptionis negotium faciunt, & fidem nostram confirmant, nostrique nos officij admonent.
units.tr: Although God has given his Son to us as Saviour, and in him opens all the treasures of his goodness, the wretched world nonetheless despises this very gift, and among God's benefits it is accustomed to trample this one underfoot above all, with the most shameful ingratitude. For just as the Jews of old did not receive him when he came to his own, but instead handed him over, most unjustly condemned, to the Gentiles, so that he might be lifted up on the cross and taken away by a dreadful and infamous death, so examples of the same ingratitude can be seen everywhere today. For many, lest they incur ill will with the Pontiffs and their champions, shut him out when he comes to them through the preaching of the Gospel. Others, having once admitted him, cast him out again, lest they be forced to undergo some danger. Others prefer pleasures and licence to sin to him, and would rather be without him than be restrained by stricter discipline. I say nothing now of those who, as soon as some persecution arises, not only fall away shamefully but even become open enemies. Many are offended by these things, and while they see them, they themselves begin to doubt and waver. But it will be profitable then to call those old examples to mind and to look to the example of Christ, whom neither the fickleness of the crowd, nor the savagery of the priests, nor the treachery and cowardice of Pilate, nor the wickedness and insolence of the soldiers moved, so that he was less steadfast in what the Father had commanded him. If we imitate his example, we too shall be victors, and we shall triumph over the world and its prince under the banner of the cross. Now follows the point that they took him, condemned also by the sentence of the governor, so that they might fix him to the cross. Many things come together in this place which serve to illustrate the business of our redemption, confirm our faith, and remind us of our duty.

units.la: Occurrit inter haec primum, quod pallio illo purpureo eum spoliarunt, quo per ludibrium induerant, & suis uestibus uestitum duxerunt. Et primò quidem ipse crucem suam gestauit extra portam usque, postea autem cum vigilijs nocturnis atque laboribus improbis fatigatus tanto oneri non suffi ceret, Simonem quendam Cyrenaeum, qui rure ueniebat, coegerunt, ut illam post eum portaret. Est hoc non contemnendum licentiae militaris exemplum, ex quo apparet, quàm multa isti homines indignè, quàm multa iniustè & iniquè fecerint, & quae sub his fuerit populi Iudaici conditio. Quod enim iniuriae genus fuisse putas, à quo illi abstinuerint, qui hominem immerentem et temere sibi obuium aufsunt ad opus istud priuata temeritate abripere, quod cum manifesta infamia erat coniunctum? At istam miseriam & infelix hoc seruitutis iugum Iudaei sua inobedientia et intestinis dissidijs bellisque ciuilibus sibi accersiuerant, quado Aristobulo et Hircano ducibus in partes scissi extera auxilia utrinque attraxerunt. Ita enim factum est, ut qui mutuam inter se pacem colere & suae gentis hominibus obedire noluerunt, nunc prophanorum militum praesidia passim per urbes dispositá habeant, & horum tyrannide pressi multa hominibus ingenuis indignissima & ipsa morte duriora ferre coacti sunt. Sunt huius generis exempla in aliarum quoque gentium historijs. Graeci certè olim, cùm inter se de imperio contenderent, Persis occasionem dederunt, ut cum ingentibus copijs in illam ingressi totâ ferro & igne uastarent. Romani item bellis ciuilibus non solum libertatem ueterem perdiderunt, sed postea Imperium totum militibus prodiderunt, quorum petulantia multi peregrini & qui aliquando gregarij milites fuerant, ad summum totius orbis fastigium magna cū Romae illius gentium domitricis ignominia euecti sunt. Nihil nunc dico de ijs, quae nostro tempore uidimus, quia eorum memoria tam recens est, ut absque dolore repeti non possint. Vtinam uerò inde exempla & praecepta sibi sumerent alij, qui ciuilibus armis et motibus atq; dissidijs intestinis delectantur. Sed omissa istorum odiosa commemoratione, quae proprie ad hunc locum pertinent, uideamus.
units.tr: Among these things, first of all, it occurs to us that they stripped him of that purple cloak with which they had dressed him in mockery, and led him away in his own clothes. At first he himself carried his cross outside the gate, but afterwards, worn out by the night watches and the harsh labours and unable to bear so great a burden, they compelled a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, to carry it after him. This is an example of military licence not to be scorned, from which it appears how many things these men did unworthily, how many things unjustly and wrongfully, and what the condition of the Jewish people was under them. For what kind of injury do you suppose they would have refrained from, those who seized a man who had done no wrong and happened to meet them by chance, and dragged him off by private rashness to that task, which was attended by open disgrace? But the Jews had brought this misery and this wretched yoke of slavery upon themselves by their disobedience, their internal dissensions and civil wars, when, divided into factions under the leaders Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, they drew foreign auxiliaries to their side on both sides. So it came about that those who would not keep peace among themselves nor obey the men of their own nation now have garrisons of profane soldiers stationed everywhere through the cities, and, oppressed by their tyranny, they have been compelled to endure many things most unworthy of free men and harder than death itself. There are examples of this kind in the histories of other nations as well. The Greeks certainly, when they contended among themselves for power, gave the Persians an opportunity to enter their land with huge forces and to lay it waste entirely with sword and fire. Likewise the Romans, by their civil wars, not only lost their ancient liberty but afterwards handed over the whole empire to the soldiers, by whose insolence many foreigners, and some who had once been common soldiers, were raised to the summit of the whole world, to the great shame of Rome, the conqueror of the nations. I say nothing now of those things which we have seen in our own time, because their memory is so recent that they cannot be recalled without grief. Would that others, who delight in civil arms, movements and internal dissensions, would take examples and precepts from them! But, setting aside the hateful recounting of those things, which pertain particularly to this place, let us look at what follows.

units.la: Praecipuum in his est nostrae redemptionis atq; salutis mysterium, quod hic Christus egit. Crucis supplicium maledictionis diuinae infamiae notatum fuisse, alibi annotauimus. Moses enim scripsit: Maledictio Dei est, qui pendet in ligno. At crucem in se recipit Christus, & eandem propriis humeris extra urbem effert: ut eo facto ostendat, se eum esse, qui peccata mundi in se receperit, & eadem procul abstulerit, ut neque illa nobis porrò Deus imputet, neque maledictione illa premat amplius quam per illa nobis accersiueramus. Et hoc olim Legalibus quoq; sacris adumbratum fuisse, Apostolus obseruit, quando ad Hebraeos scribit: Quorum animalium sanguis infertur pro peccato in Sacrarium per Pontificem, horum corpora exuruntur extra castra. Et mox huius moris rationem affert: Quapropter pter & Iesus, ut sanctificaret per proprium sanguinem populum, extra portam passus est. Hinc ergo consolationem petamus in tentationibus, quando peccatorum conscientia nos Satan territat, quasi illa nobis adhuc inhaereant, & eorum poenas à nobis Deus exigat. Tunc (inquam) cogitemus, non te meram factum esse, quòd Dei Filius crucem in suos humeros sublatam extra urbem portavit. Eius enim merito peccata nostra expiata sunt, & proinde nulla damnatio eos porrò manet, qui illi per fidem sunt insiti, ut Paulus ad Rom.8.cap.testatur.
units.tr: Chief among these things is the mystery of our redemption and salvation, which Christ accomplished here. We have noted elsewhere that the punishment of the cross was marked by the curse of God and by infamy. For Moses wrote: "Cursed of God is he who hangs on a tree." But Christ takes up the cross on himself and carries it on his own shoulders outside the city, so that by this deed he may show that he is the one who has taken upon himself the sins of the world and has carried them far away, so that God may no longer impute them to us, nor press upon us with that curse more than we had brought upon ourselves. The Apostle also observed that this had been foreshadowed even by the legal sacrifices, when he writes to the Hebrews: "The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp." And soon after he gives the reason for this custom: "Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate." Let us therefore seek consolation here in temptations, when the consciousness of our sins terrifies us, as Satan does, as if those sins still clung to us and God demanded their punishment from us. Then (I say) let us reflect that it was not in vain that the Son of God, having lifted the cross on his shoulders, carried it outside the city. For by his merit our sins have been expiated, and therefore no condemnation remains for those who are grafted into him by faith, as Paul testifies in Romans 8.

units.la: Deinde fidelium aut credentium conditio in terris hisce & eorundem officium in Simone Cyrenaeo adumbratur. Venit is rure, & mox à militibus interceptus crucem Christi ferre cogitur. Solent fideles relictis agris suis, id est, procul abiectis huius mundi studijs ad coelestem illam Hierosolymam contendere, ubi ipsis patria est atque haereditas. Quàm primùm vero hoc iter suscipiunt, mox in diaboli satellites incidunt, qui ut eos in sancto hoc instituto remorentur, crucí subiiciunt, & novos illis quotidie labores exhibent. Nam ut alias monuimus, non potest lucem ferre mundus hic, quia opera eius mala arguntur. Idcirco quia pij tam verbo quàm vitae exemplo faciunt, adversus hos illa insurgit, & ita nunquam non impletur illud Pauli: Quotquot volunt pie vivere in Iesu Christo, persecutionem patientur. At hic nos consolari debet, quòd Christi crucem ferimus. Nam licet nobis nihil praeter mericum accidat, si Dei iudicium spectes (omnes enim in peccato concepti & geniti sumus, & quotidie in multis labimur) attamen Christi crux esse censetur, quicquid aut propter nomen eius sustinemus, aut fide in illam confirmati patienter ferimus. At si cum illo patiamur, cum eodem regnabimus, si eum illo moriamur, cum eodem viviemus. Et illius promissio est: Ubi ego sum, illic volo sit & minister meus. Est autem hic diligenter nobis cavendus scopulus ad quem multi ita impingunt, & non solùm nullum ex suis afflictionibus atq; laboribus fructum reportent, verumetiam in illis vitae ac salutis aeternae iacturam faciant. Accidit hoc illis, qui in afflictionibus, quas sustinent, meritum statuunt, & se per illas divinae iustitiae satis facere arbitrantur. Sed qui ita sentiunt, non Christi crucem ferunt, sed huius gloriam in se transferunt, & Pauli verbis convincuntur, qui afflictiones huius saeculi non pares esse dicit ei gloriae, quae olim revelabitur, quaeque nobis in coelo reposita est. Imò confutat horum confidentiam nostrer hic Simon, quem crucis suae socium Christus hab bere dignatus est. Nam fert quidem illam iste patienter, sed ubi ad locum supplicij ventum fuit, ubi terrae totius iniquitas (ut Propheta olim praedixerat) uno die auferri atque expiari debebat, non Cyrenaeus ille (ut impurus Mahumet fabulatur) sed solus Christus in crucem actus est, solus item pro nobis mortuus est, & solus suo sanguine pro totius mundi peccatis perlitavit: Simon autem ille non suo, sed eiusdem Christi merito servatus est, cui nos quoq; omnem salutis gloriam transcribere debemus. Omnium enim Christianorum eadem cum Paulo sententia atque vox est: Absit ut gloriar, praeterquam in cruce Iesu Christi. Galat.6.
units.tr: Next, the condition of the faithful, or believers, on this earth and their duty are foreshadowed in Simon of Cyrene. He comes in from the country, and is at once seized by the soldiers and compelled to carry the cross of Christ. The faithful, having left their fields, that is, having cast far away the pursuits of this world, are wont to press on towards that heavenly Jerusalem, where their homeland and inheritance are. But as soon as they undertake this journey, they fall in with the devil's henchmen, who, to hold them back in this holy undertaking, subject them to the cross and impose new labours on them every day. For, as we have said elsewhere, this world cannot bear the light, because its works are exposed as evil. Therefore, because the godly act both by word and by the example of their life, it rises up against them, and so that saying of Paul is never not fulfilled: "All who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." Yet this ought to console us, that we bear the cross of Christ. For although nothing but what we deserve befalls us, if you look at God's judgment (for we are all conceived and born in sin, and every day we stumble in many things), nevertheless whatever we endure on account of his name, or patiently bear, being confirmed in faith in him, is counted as the cross of Christ. And if we suffer with him, we shall reign with him; if we die with him, we shall live with him. His promise is: "Where I am, there my minister also will be." But here we must carefully beware of a rock on which many strike, and so not only gain no fruit from their afflictions and labours, but even suffer the loss of life and eternal salvation in them. This happens to those who set up merit in the afflictions they undergo, and think that by them they make sufficient satisfaction to divine justice. But those who think so do not bear the cross of Christ; they transfer its glory to themselves, and they are refuted by the words of Paul, who says that the afflictions of this age are not worthy to be compared with the glory that will one day be revealed, and that is laid up for us in heaven. Indeed, this Simon here refutes their confidence, whom Christ thought worthy to be the companion of his cross. For he indeed bears it patiently, but when they came to the place of punishment, where the iniquity of the whole earth (as the Prophet had foretold long before) was to be taken away and expiated in one day, it was not that Cyrenian (as the impure Mahomet fables) but Christ alone who was led to the cross; Christ alone likewise died for us, and Christ alone with his blood made atonement for the sins of the whole world. Simon, however, was saved not by his own merit but by the merit of that same Christ, to whom we too must ascribe all the glory of salvation. For the sentiment and voice of all Christians is the same as that of Paul: "God forbid that I should glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Galatians 6.

units.la: Porrò comitatum quoq; Christi, quem tunc habuit Lucas describit, in quem actio memorabilis incidit cum mulierculis, quae eius mortem deflebant. Sequebatur autem eum (inquit) magna multitudo populi & mulierum, quae & plangebant & lamentabantur eum. Antea quoque cum doctrina & miraculis celebris per Iudaeam & Galilaeam iter faciebat, ingentes populi undique confluentis turbas post se traxit. At non minor neque obscurior fuit comitatus iste, qui eum ad mortis supplicium euntem secutus est. Nam praeter innumerabilem populi multitudinem, qui propter festum ex locis diversis atq; longinquis convenerat, adfuerunt milites cum Centurione, Sacerdotes, Seniores, Scribae, & quicunque alij aliqua authoritate praestabant. Et voluit hoc ita fieri Deus, ut plures essent mortis Filij sui testes, & eiusdem nuntium citius per orbem totum spargeretur. Nec obstat, quòd multi supplicium illud oculis lividis spectarunt, & eo impiè delectati sunt. Nam hi quoque ex eo stimulos conscientiae conceperunt, qui alijs quidem ad poenitentiam adiumento (ut Actorum secundo capite scribitur) alijs verò iustae damnationis testimonium fuerunt. Et debent exemplum hoc Christi sibi ob oculos ponere pij Martyres, quàdo ipsi pro facinorosis ad rogos, ad gladios, ad furcas & aliatores meta rapiuntur. Fit tunc quoq; concursus ingens, & de illis triumphare videtur scelerati Antichristi satellites. Sed tunc meminerint se (quod Paulus monuit) spectaculu fieri non hominibus solis, sed insuper Deo & Angelis. Videt enim illos certantes fidelis ille Agonothetes, qui laborantibus & fatigatis novas subinde vires inspirat, ut in finem usq; perseverare possint. Circumstant eosdem Am-
units.tr: Luke also describes the company that Christ had at that time, in which a memorable incident occurred involving some women who were mourning his death. "A great multitude of the people and of women followed him," he says, "who both beat their breasts and lamented him." Earlier too, when he travelled through Judea and Galilee, famous for his teaching and miracles, he drew after him great crowds flocking from every side. But this company which followed him as he went to the punishment of death was no less numerous and no less conspicuous. For besides the countless multitude of people who had gathered from various and distant places because of the feast, there were present soldiers with the centurion, priests, elders, scribes, and whoever else held some authority. God willed it so, that there should be more witnesses of his Son's death and that the news of it should be spread more quickly through the whole world. Nor is it an objection that many watched that punishment with malicious eyes and were impiously delighted by it. For these too received from it the goads of conscience, which were for some an aid to repentance (as is written in the second chapter of Acts), and for others a testimony of their just condemnation. Holy martyrs ought to keep this example of Christ before their eyes when they themselves are dragged, as if they were criminals, to the stakes, the swords, the gallows, the mines and other punishments. Then too a great crowd gathers, and the wicked satellites of Antichrist seem to triumph over them. But then let them remember that (as Paul warned) they are made a spectacle not only to men but also to God and the angels. For that faithful president of the games sees them contending, and he continually breathes fresh strength into those who labour and grow weary, so that they can persevere to the end.

units.la: 1.Cor.4. gelorum turmæ, qui & ipsi suæ præsentia illos confortant (sicuti de Christo ad Oliueti monte sudan-te dictum est) & eorum dissolutionem beatam expectant, vt animas illas felices ad beatæ immortali tatis sedes deportent. Inter homines verò alij quidem crudeli spectaculo oculos impios pascunt, qui-bus hæc voluptas nimium magno constabit: alij suæ curiositati indulgent, de quibus spes adhuc bona est, vt ea occasione ad veritatis cognitionem perueniant, quod multis olim & nostro quoq; sæculo ac-cidisse constat: alios verò pius affectus trahit, qui vt precibus suis illos certantes iuuant, ita pijs quoq; lachrymis iniustitiæ eorum arguunt & accusant, qui sanctos Dei cultores iniquè damnare audent. Nunquam enim ita regnat & furit impietas, quin suos inueniat reprehensores: & nunquam ita de-relinquuntur pij, quin inter medios carnifices inueniant, qui ipsis pie condoleant, et aliquam illis af-ferant consolationem. Et potest hoc reuera Dei theatrum dici, in quo ipse præsidet, & in quo victo-ria potiuntur, quos cæcus hic & infelix mundus succubuisse ac totos periisse putat.
units.tr: 1.Cor.4. Companies of angels surround these same contenders, and they too strengthen them by their presence (as was said of Christ sweating on the Mount of Olives), and await their blessed dissolution, so that they may carry those happy souls to the seats of immortal blessedness. Among men, some feed their impious eyes on the cruel spectacle, and this pleasure will cost them very dearly. Others indulge their curiosity, and there is still good hope for them, that on that occasion they may come to the knowledge of the truth, as is known to have happened to many in former times and in our own age too. Others a pious feeling draws, and as they help the contenders with their prayers, so with holy tears they also rebuke and accuse the injustice of those who dare to condemn the holy worshippers of God unjustly. For impiety never reigns and rages so much that it does not find its own critics, and the godly are never so abandoned that among the very executioners they do not find some who sympathise with them piously and offer them some consolation. This can truly be called God's theatre, in which he presides and in which those win the victory whom this blind and unhappy world thinks have succumbed and perished utterly.

units.la: Et huc in primis referri debet, quod de mulieribus istis dicitur, quòd indignam hanc Christi mor-tem planxerint atq; lamentatæ sint. Nam etiamsi tanta rei, quæ tunc agebatur, mysterium non intel-lexerint (ut mox audiemus) pius tamen ille affectus fuit, quo illius sors indigna ipsis doluit. Ita ue-rò nostri nos officij admonent, quod ex charitatis lege miseris & afflictis debemus. Iubet hæc, ut il-lis opem feramus pro uirili, sicuti in Samaritani parabola didicimus. Quia autem id non semper pos-sumus, proximus gradus est, ut animi nostri benevolentiam pio dolore testemur, ut uel ex eo illi con-solationem aliquam capiant. Facit huc corporis humani & membrorum similitudo, quam Apostolus in priori ad Corinth. prolixè tractat. Et idem eius nos admonet, quando in epistola ad Hebr. horta-tur, ut unius memores simus, & perinde illorum curis atq; molestijs afficiamur, ac si ipsi esse-mus in illorum corpore. Etenim aliter fieri non potest inter homines Christianos, qui Christi corpus sunt & omnes eodem spiritu animantur atq; reguntur. Est hodie nobis amplissima de his cogitandi oc-casio atq; materia. Nam ut de priuatis calamitatibus nihil dicamus, quibus multi passim exer-centur, quibus cum egestate, cum fame, cum morbis diuturnis, cum conscientiæ terroribus res est: quis non uidet, quæ & quanta pericula Ecclesijs passim immineant, quam multæ dissipentur, quam mul-tæ sub carnificum manibus in medio luporum gemant & suspirent, quam multæ pastoribus destituta trepident? Oberrat passim misera fidelium turba, quos tyrannis plus quam Phalarica patrios fines relinquere & in spontaneum exilium abire cogit. Multi post se relictis coniugibus & charis liberis, dolore acerbo consumuntur. Multi interea patriæ suæ ruinam & horribilem oppressionem eminus cum gemitu spectant, alij uerò eadem se quoq; obrui sentiunt, & ipsi calamitatum istarum pars sunt aliqua. Debebat ista nobis quoq; pias lachrymas mouere, ad preces excitare et beneficentiæ studiū. Sed quàm multi, proh dolor, Scythica & barbara immanitate tantas piorum calamitates contem-nunt, et siccis oculis absque omni gemitu tempestates illas spectant, quæ (nisi eas Dominus auertat) Ecclesias omnes, adeoque totum terrarum orbem obruent? Potuit unius Christi indigna mors mu-lierculas illas, quæ nihil in illo maius homine agnoscebant, ad piam commiserationem mouere, quam lachrymis et plantu publicè testatæ sunt. Quàm ergo turpis illa barbaries, quàm execrabilis crude-litas est, quæ hodie obstat, quò minus tot Ecclesiarum ruinas miserabiles deploremus? Certè qui ista nihil ad se pertinere putant, ij se à Christi corpore alienos esse produnt.
units.tr: This is chiefly to be referred to what is said of those women, that they wept and lamented this unworthy death of Christ. For even though they did not understand the mystery of so great an event that was then taking place (as we shall hear presently), that pious feeling was nonetheless there, by which they grieved at his unworthy fate. Our own duty, moreover, admonishes us in this way, as the law of charity requires us to do towards the wretched and afflicted. It bids us help them as far as we are able, as we learned from the parable of the Good Samaritan. But since we cannot always do this, the next step is to show the goodwill of our minds by pious grief, so that they may at least take some consolation from it. The likeness of the human body and its members is relevant here, which the Apostle treats at length in his first letter to the Corinthians. He also admonishes us of the same thing when, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, he exhorts us to remember those in bonds and to be afflicted with their cares and troubles as if we ourselves were in their body. For among Christian men, who are the body of Christ and are all animated and ruled by one Spirit, it cannot happen otherwise. Today we have a very ample occasion and matter for thinking about these things. For, to say nothing of private calamities, with which many are everywhere afflicted, with poverty, hunger, lasting diseases, and terrors of conscience: who does not see what great dangers hang over the Churches everywhere, how many are being scattered, how many groan and sigh under the hands of executioners in the midst of wolves, how many tremble, deprived of their ministers? The wretched crowd of the faithful wanders everywhere, whom the tyrant, more than with the Phalarica, forces to leave their native lands and go into voluntary exile. Many, having left behind their wives and dear children, are consumed with bitter grief. Many meanwhile watch from afar, with groans, the ruin and dreadful oppression of their country, while others feel themselves being crushed in the same way and are themselves some part of those calamities. These things ought to move us too to pious tears, to prayers, and to a zeal for beneficence. But how many, alas, with Scythian and barbarous savagery, despise such great calamities of the godly, and watch with dry eyes and without any groaning those storms which, unless the Lord turns them away, will overwhelm all the Churches and indeed the whole globe? The unworthy death of Christ alone could move those little women, who recognised nothing greater than that man in him, to pious compassion, which they bore witness to publicly with tears and lamentation. How base, then, is that barbarity, how execrable that cruelty, which today prevents us from lamenting the miserable ruins of so many Churches? Certainly those who think these things do not concern them show that they are alien to the body of Christ.

units.la: Sed illum audiamus mulieribus istis loquentem: Filiæ Hierusalem, ne flete super me, uerum super uobisipsis flete, & super liberis uestris. Nam ecce, uenient dies quibus dicent: Beatæ ste-riles, & uteri qui non genuerunt: & ubera quæ non lactauerunt. Tum incipient dicere montibus, Cadite super nos: & collibus, Operite nos. Nam si in uirente ligno ista faciunt, in arido quid fiet? Corrigit illarum affectum atque fletum Dominus, non quòd pius iste affectus ipsi displiceat, sed quòd eas de rebus maioris momenti admoneri oportebat, quas adhuc ignorabant. Sciebant qui-dem illum immerentem ad dirum crucis supplicium rapi: id uerò propter nostra peccata fieri nescie-bant. Deinde afficiebantur tristi illo spectaculo, quod innocentem cum latronibus duci uiderent, non autè cogitabant, quàm horribiles & graues pœnas hæc gentis Iudaicæ ingratitudo et iniustitia mererentur. De utroq; ergo eas admoneri oportuit, ut affectus iste ipsas ad ueram pœnitentiam ad-duceret, utq; de propria salute diligentius cogitarent. Dicit ergo: Filiæ Hierusalem, ne flete super me, sed super uobisipsis flete, & super liberis uestris. Quasi diceret: Vobis quidem mea fors digna vi-detur, quam plantu & lachrymis prosequamini. At multo iustior & grauior lugendi causa nos pre-met, si met, si quid toti uestri genti breui euenturum sit, & quantum hic mysterium agatur, probè expende ritus. Et mox calamitates uenturas comparationibus amplificat. Nā ecce (inquit) uenient dies qui bus dicent: Beati steriles, & uteri qui non genuerunt: & ubera quæ non lactauerunt, &c. Alludit ad Legis promissiones, inter quas nō postrema habetur de facunda sobolis multiplicatione, quæ apud pios tanto in pretio fuit, ut sterilitas probri loco haberetur, sicuti Rahelis, Annæ, Elizabetæ & similium exempla testantur. Vult ergo dicere, tantas fore calamitates, ut felices putentur, quæ nunquā pepererunt. Conuenit cum his uerbis, quod apud Hoseam habetur. Cum enim Israelitis bella grauissima minatus esset Propheta, in quibus filios eorum exterminari & crudeliter occidi oporteat, tantarum cladium consideratione ad commiserationem motus ad preces conuertitur, quibus aliquam pœnarū mitigationem postulans dicit: Da eis Domine. Quid dabis? Da eis uterum abortiente & ubera aret ia. Quasi diceret: Satis sit quæso, si ipsi male pereant, hanc modò calamitatē ab ipsis remoue, ne filios generent & educent ad mactationem, quorum horribiles cædes miseriam istā augeant. Cum his ergo Prophetæ uerbis conuenit, quod in præsenti Dominus minatur. Et mox ex eodem Hosea aliud profert, quo calamitates istas, quæ uenturæ sint, amplificat, dicens: Tum incipient dicere montibus, Cadite super nos, & collibus, Operite nos. Magna sit oportet miseria, ingens ite & horribile periculum, quod quis mortis beneficio auertere aut subterfugere cupiat, & quidē mortis non vulgaris. At talia ipsis euentura ait, ut vellent sibi terram dehiscere, seq̃ montibus obrui optarent, ne illa cogerentur intueri. Vtq̃ minus dubitent, rationem adducit: Nā si in virente ligno hoc faciunt, in arido quid fiet? Virens lignum phrasi Hebraica dicit arborem quæ adhuc uiriditate uiget, & ad fructus seren dos idonea est, & per eam seipsum intelligit. Aridis verò lignis Iudæos confert, qui hucusq̃ non solū steriles fuerant, sed eò delapsi iam erant, ut fructus ex illis omnino nullus porrò sperari posset: quod Ioannes quoq̃ iam pridem illis exprobrauerat, cùm securim iam ad arboris radicem positam esse diceret. Sensus ergo est: Cùm ex æterno Patris consilio me, qui arbor sum uerè fœcunda & fructifera, imò qui Filius ille dilectus sum, tam dira & infami morte tolli oporteat, ut peccata hominum expientur, quid de illis fiet, qui trunci aridi, & uerissimi illi Nabales sunt, quos nullus pietatis sensus mouet, & quorū fructus iampridē desperatus est? Et hæc quidē non inania uerba fuisse, rei euentus declarauit. Quàm diris enim quamq̃ grauibus pœnis Deus Iudaici populi & quidē in primis Hierosolymitanæ urbis crudelitatem & ingratitudinē ultus sit, alibi ostendimus. Et quis non tunc beatas fuisse dixerit eas, quæ nunquam pepererunt, quando dira fames matres adegit, ut infantes ex se natos proprijs manibus occiderent, & sibijpsis in cibos parārēt? Quantò item illis satius & optabilius fuisset à terra uiuas absorberi, aut montium incidentium pondere sepeliri?
units.tr: But let us hear him speaking to those women: "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. For behold, the days will come when they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not give suck. Then they will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us. For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?" The Lord corrects their feeling and their weeping, not because that pious feeling displeases him, but because they had to be admonished about matters of greater weight, which they did not yet know. They indeed knew that he was being dragged, innocent, to the dreadful punishment of the cross; but they did not know that this was done on account of our sins. Then they were moved by that sad spectacle, seeing the innocent led away with robbers, but they did not consider how dreadful and grievous punishments the ingratitude and injustice of the Jewish nation deserved. So they had to be admonished about both, so that this feeling might lead them to true repentance and make them think more carefully about their own salvation. He therefore says: "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children." As if he said: "My fate may seem worthy to you of lamentation and tears. But a much more just and grave cause for mourning presses upon you, if you weigh carefully what will soon befall your whole nation, and how great a mystery is being enacted here." And soon he amplifies the coming calamities by comparisons: "For behold," he says, "the days will come when they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not give suck, etc." He alludes to the promises of the Law, among which is not the least the promise of a fruitful multiplication of offspring, which was held in such esteem among the godly that barrenness was regarded as a disgrace, as the examples of Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth and the like attest. He means, therefore, that the calamities will be so great that those who never bore children will be thought fortunate. This agrees with the words found in Hosea. When the prophet had threatened the Israelites with most grievous wars, in which their sons must be exterminated and cruelly slain, he was moved to compassion by consideration of such great slaughter and turned to prayer, asking for some mitigation of the punishments and saying: "Give them, O Lord. What wilt thou give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts." As if he said: "Let it be enough, I beg, that they perish themselves; only remove from them this calamity, that they should not bear sons and bring them up for slaughter, whose dreadful murders would increase this misery." So what the Lord threatens in the present passage agrees with these words of the prophet. Soon after, from the same Hosea he brings forward another passage by which he amplifies the calamities that are to come, saying: "Then they will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us." The misery must be great, the danger immense and dreadful, which someone would wish to avert or escape by the boon of death, and indeed not a common death. But he says that such things will befall them, that they would wish the earth to open for them and would desire to be buried under the mountains, so as not to be forced to look upon them. And so that they may have no doubt, he gives the reason: "For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?" The Hebrew idiom "green wood" means a tree that still flourishes with vigour and is fit to bear fruit, and by it he means himself. But he compares the Jews to dry wood, who had hitherto not only been barren, but had now fallen to such a point that no fruit could any longer be hoped for from them at all; John had long before reproached them with this, when he said that the axe was already laid to the root of the tree. The sense, then, is this: since by the eternal counsel of the Father I, who am truly a fruitful and fertile tree, indeed the beloved Son, must be taken away by so dire and infamous a death, in order that the sins of men may be expiated, what will become of those who are dry trunks and the very Nabals, whom no sense of piety moves, and whose fruit has long been despaired of? And that these were not empty words the outcome of the event made clear. For with what dire and grievous punishments God has avenged the cruelty and ingratitude of the Jewish people, and especially of the city of Jerusalem, we have shown elsewhere. And who would not say that those women who never bore children were then blessed, when dire famine drove mothers to kill with their own hands the infants born of them and to prepare them as food for themselves? How much more agreeable and desirable it would have been for them to be swallowed alive by the earth, or buried under the weight of falling mountains!

units.la: Debet autem hinc generalis doctrina peti, Deum non inultā sinere crudelitatem hostium suorum, qui Christum in membris suis persequuntur. Ad tota enim Ecclesiam credentiū pertinet, quod Abra hamo dictum fuit. Benedicā eis, qui tibi benedicunt, maledicentibus autē tibi ego maledicam. Et per Prophetam idem Ecclesiæ dicit: Qui uos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Exempla quoq̃ omnibus sæculis edita sunt, quibus totum orbem terrarum Deus admoneri voluit, quanti faciat suorum sanguinem, qui propter nominis sui confessionem occiduntur. Neminem ergo indigna piorum sors offendat, quamin terris hisce sustinent. Habent enim uindicem fortissimum, Deum, qui etsi iudiciū suum aliquando differat, die tamen & horâ iam constituit, qua hostes suos puniet, illos autē ex horum manibus ereptos seruabit: & momentanea nostræ oppressionis leuitas (ut Paulus ait) excellentissimū gloriæ æternæ pondus nobis conficit. Discant etiam priuatim omnes, ne quam uim aut iniuriam faciant Christi cultoribus quocunq̃ prætextu, ne tanti uindicis iram aduersus se prouocent.
units.tr: From this passage a general doctrine may be drawn: God does not allow the cruelty of his enemies toward those who persecute Christ in his members to go unpunished. What was said to Abraham pertains to the whole Church of believers: "I will bless those who bless you, but I will curse those who curse you" (Gen. 12). Through the prophet God says the same to the Church: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye" (Zech. 2). Examples have also been set forth in every age, by which God wanted the whole world to be reminded how highly he values the blood of those who are killed for confessing his name. Let no one, then, be offended by the unworthy lot that the godly endure in this world. They have a most mighty avenger, God, who, although he sometimes defers his judgment, has already appointed the day and the hour when he will punish his enemies and will preserve those who have been snatched from their hands. And the momentary lightness of our affliction (as Paul says) produces for us an exceeding and eternal weight of glory (2 Cor. 4). Let everyone also learn privately not to inflict violence or injury on the worshippers of Christ under any pretext, lest they provoke against themselves the wrath of so great an avenger.

units.la: Admonet præterea locus iste, quomodo mortē Christi deflere debeamus, in quo nimium ridiculos (ne quid grauius dicā) sese prebent Monachi, qui quasi omnis doctrinæ & prædicationis huius fructus in lachrymis inanibus consistat, sermones suos in eum finē dirigunt, ut ad fletum prouocent mulierculas, & ut gemitus atq̃ suspiria crebra in templis exaudiantur? Quod ut facilius impetrent, nō contenti ijs, quæ Euangelistæ nobis tradiderunt, multa affingunt de Maria virginis cōpassionibus, quæ ut salsissima, ita indignissima sunt, quæ illi tribuantur. Quid, quòd ijdē historiā hanc totā in ludum Scenicū conuerterunt? At nihil huius docuerunt Apostoli, nihil etiā simile à nobis ille requirit. Neq̃ ut propter ipsum ploremus iubet, qui iā in cælis triumphat & regnat: sed propter nos, qui ipsi tam acerbæ mortis authores fuimus. In teipsum ergo descendito, & quid tu merea{ris} cogita, qui re- uera aridum, ficulneum & inutile lignum es. Tibi igitur hoc illius dictum accommoda, ut idem diaboli suggestionibus & peccati blanditiis opponas, quibus caro facile decipitur. Similiter si qui te multò meliores affliguntur, illud ipsum in animum revoca, & illos tibi in exemplum affligi credito, duriores autem gravioresque pœnas tibi paratas esse, nisi ex animo resipiscas. Denique in Iesu Christi mortem ita intenti simus, ut eius consideratione ad pœnitentiæ veræ studium excitemur, & in fide confirmemur, qua sola ille apprehenditur, ut nobis salutifer fiat. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This passage also teaches us how we ought to lament the death of Christ. In this matter the monks make themselves appear absurdly ridiculous (to say nothing harsher). As if the whole fruit of this doctrine and preaching lay in empty tears, they direct their sermons to this end: to provoke silly women to weeping, and to have groans and frequent sighs heard in the churches. To obtain this more easily, not content with what the Evangelists have handed down to us, they add many things about the compassions of the Virgin Mary, which, as they are most insipid, so are they most unworthy to be attributed to her. What of the fact that these same men have turned this whole history into a theatrical play? Yet the Apostles taught none of this, and Christ himself does not require anything similar from us. Nor does he bid us weep for himself, who now triumphs and reigns in heaven, but for ourselves, who were the very authors of so bitter a death. Therefore go down into yourself, and consider what you deserve, you who are truly a dry, fig-tree and unfruitful wood. Apply to yourself that saying of his, so that you may set it against the suggestions of the devil and the enticements of sin, by which the flesh is easily deceived. Likewise, if some who are far better than you are afflicted, call that same thing to mind, and believe that they are afflicted as an example for you, and that harsher and heavier punishments are prepared for you unless you repent from your heart. Finally, let us be so intent upon the death of Jesus Christ that, by considering it, we may be stirred to a zeal for true repentance and be confirmed in faith, by which alone he is apprehended, so that he may become salutary to us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCVII.

units.la: Ducebantur autem etiam alij duo malefici, ut cum eo necarentur. Cùm igitur venissent in locum, qui vocatur Caluaria, illic crucifixerunt eum, & malefactos: unum ad dexteram, alterum ad sinistram. Iesus autem dicebat: Pater remitte eis: nesciunt enim quid faciant. Partientes autem vestimenta eius, iecerunt sortem. Et stabat populus spectans. Sannis autem excipiebant eum etiam principes cum eis, dicentes: Alios seruauit, seruet seipsum, si hic ille est Christus Dei electus. Illudebant autem ei etiam milites, accedentes & acetum ei offerentes, dicentesque: Si tu es Rex ille Iudæorum, serua teipsum. Erat autem etiam inscriptio scripta super eum literis Græcis, & Romanis, & Hebraicis: HIC EST REX ILLE IVDEORVM.
units.tr: Two other criminals were also led out with him to be put to death. When they came to the place called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right hand and the other on his left. Then Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." And they parted his garments and cast lots. And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also scoffed at him, saying, "He saved others; let him save himself, if he is Christ, the chosen of God." The soldiers also mocked him, coming to him and offering him vinegar, and saying, "If thou be the King of the Jews, save thyself." And a superscription was also written over him in Greek, Latin and Hebrew letters: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.

units.la: Dauid Rex & Propheta celeberrimum illud de Iesu Christo vaticinium contexens, quod in Psalmo centesimo decimo describitur, inter alia dicit: Iurauit Dominus, & non pœnitebit eum: Tu es Sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedek. Quoties autem Spiritus sanctus in Scripturis illi Sacerdotium tribuit, tum eum unicum & sufficientem redemptorem atq; seruatorem humani generis esse docet. Scimus enim Sacerdotum officia fuisse, docere, sacrificare, orare pro populo & eidem benedicere. Atqui omnia ista Christus abunde præstitit. In docendo enim assiduum fuisse, Euangelica historia indicat, adeò ut se ideo in mundum venisse, ipse alicubi fateatur. Idem per Apostolos totù terrarum orbem docuit, & adhuc hodie nobiscum per Ecclesiæ ministros loquitur, quos ab illo dari Paulus scribit. De oratione item & precibus eius multa hucusq; audiuimus, sub quibus bene dicendi quoq; munus ex parte comprehenditur. Restabat ergo sacrificiū, quod in ara crucis peregit, & ita quidem ut eius meritum atq; effectus adhuc hodie duret, & ad salutem omnibus sufficiat, qui illum fide vera apprehendunt. Illius vero historiam deinceps Lucas describet, in cuius consideratione nos ita versari conuenit, ut eum propter nos ista passum esse teneamus, ut pro nostris peccatis ultima siue oblatio fieret. Et quia hic multa concurrunt, quæ singula ad tanti mysterij explicationem faciunt, de singulis ex ordine dicemus quod in præsenti dictu opus fuerit.
units.tr: King David, who was also a prophet, wove into his famous prophecy of Jesus Christ, which is described in Psalm 110, the words: "The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." Whenever the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures ascribes the priesthood to him, he teaches that he is the only and sufficient redeemer and saviour of the human race. For we know that the duties of priests were to teach, to sacrifice, to pray for the people and to bless them. Yet Christ performed all of these abundantly. That he was constant in teaching the evangelical history shows, so much so that he himself declares somewhere that he came into the world for this purpose. Through the Apostles he taught the whole world, and even today he speaks with us through the ministers of the Church, whom Paul writes were given by him. We have heard much up to now about his prayers and intercessions, under which the office of blessing is also partly included. There remained, therefore, the sacrifice, which he offered on the altar of the cross, and in such a way that its merit and effect still endure today and suffice for salvation for all who lay hold of him by true faith. Luke will describe his history in what follows, and in considering it we ought to dwell on it in such a way that we hold that he suffered these things for us, so that he might become the final offering for our sins. And since many things come together here, each of which contributes to the explanation of so great a mystery, we shall speak in order about each one as far as the present discourse requires.

units.la: Primum à loco supplicij Euangelista orditur, & illum una cum duobus alijs maleficis (quos alij latrones fuisse scribunt) ductum fuisse ait in locum, quem caluariam vulgò vocabant: nimirum à caluarijs & ossibus mortuorum, quæ illic dispersa aut congesta uisebantur. Fuit ergo iste publicus locus, in quo facinorosi omnes solebant necari, qui sceleribus pœnam capitalem meruerant. Epiphanius contra Tatianos scribens, ex ueterum monumentis prodidit, eodem in loco Adamum parentem primum humani generis mortuum atque sepultum fuisse, & ab eius caluaria illic inuenta locum hunc nomen accepisse. Quod an uere dicatur, nolim cum aliquo contendere: & quamuis non omnino absurdum uideri posset, Christum illic suæ mortis merito uitam nobis restituere voluisse, ubi primum hominem mors abstulerat, & in eo de toto genere humano triumphare cum uisa fuerat: prior tamen sententia mihi uerisimilior, & à superstitionis periculo alienior esse uidetur. Gloriantur suo Capitolio Romani, cui ab hominis capite illic inuento nomen inditum fuisse scriptores tradunt. At Christiani homines rectius & instiu hoc caluariæ colliculo gloriari possint, in quo æternus Dei Filius in assumpta carne crucifixus peccatum totius mundi expiauit. Quod ta- men ita dictum uelim, ne quis nos illorum superstitioni fauere putet, qui illius meritum certis locis alligant. Hoc enim per omnes terrarum angulos extendi, & passim inueniri per fidem notius est, quam ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Et quamuis tunc terram illam sua uita & morte Christus no- bilitare dignatus sit, postea tamen multa in illam edita sunt iræ iudiciorum Dei exempla, quæ satis docent salutis meritum aut fiduciam illi minimè alligari debere. Nunc potius obseruemus, cur in lo- cum publicis supplicijs infamem ille ductus sit cum duobus maleficis, & ibidem inter illos medius in crucem suffixus. Narrant hoc unanimi consensu omnes Euangelistæ, & sic olim per Isaiam prædi- ctum esse docent, cuius dictum illud extat: Et cum iniquis aut facinorosis reputatus est. Ita uero fi- eri oportuit, ut nos eius merito iustificati inter Dei filios numeraremur, & ut constaret illius esse- ctum ad sceleratissimos quosque etiam extendi, denique supplicia quæ isti luunt, Christi morte iam con- secrata esse, ut illis nequaquam fraudi sint aut obstaculo quoad æternam salutem, modo peccata sua agnoscant, deque illis doleant, & illius merito partam eorum remissionem fide syncera appre- hendant.
units.tr: First the Evangelist begins with the place of execution, and he says that Jesus, together with two other criminals (whom others write were robbers), was led to the place which they commonly called The Skull, namely from the skulls and bones of the dead that were seen lying scattered or heaped there. This, then, was a public place where all the wicked were accustomed to be executed, those who had deserved capital punishment for their crimes. Epiphanius, writing against the Tatians, reported from the records of the ancients that in this very place Adam, the first parent of the human race, had died and been buried, and that the place received its name from his skull, which was found there. I would not wish to argue with anyone whether this is truly said. And although it might not seem altogether absurd that Christ wished, by the merit of his death, to restore life to us in the very place where death had first carried off man, and where he had been seen to triumph over the whole human race in him, nevertheless the former opinion seems to me more probable and further from the danger of superstition. The Romans boast of their Capitol, to which, as the writers relate, the name was given from a human head found there. But Christians can more rightly and justly glory in this little hill of the skull, on which the eternal Son of God, crucified in the flesh he had assumed, atoned for the sin of the whole world. Yet I would have this said in such a way that no one thinks we favour the superstition of those who tie his merit to certain places. For it is more widely known through faith that this extends through all the corners of the earth and is found everywhere, than that it needs to be demonstrated to many. And although Christ was pleased to ennoble that land by his life and death, yet afterwards many examples of the wrath of God's judgments were published in it, which teach sufficiently that the merit of salvation or confidence should by no means be tied to it. Let us rather observe why he was led, infamous, with two criminals to the place of public punishment, and was fixed to the cross in the middle between them. All the Evangelists relate this with one accord, and they teach that it was foretold long ago through Isaiah, whose saying stands: "And he was reckoned with the wicked or malefactors."
