And indeed it had to happen in this way, so that we, justified by his merit, might be numbered among the sons of God; and so that it might be evident that the effect of his death extends even to the most wicked of all; and finally, so that the punishments which these men suffer have been consecrated by the death of Christ, so that they are in no way a hindrance or obstacle to them as regards eternal salvation, provided they acknowledge their sins, grieve over them, and lay hold of the remission of them, won by his merit, with sincere faith.

units.la: Quod ut rectius intelligatur, & uberior quoq; istius doctrinæ usus sit, crux Christi ita nobis con sideranda erit, ut eâ illi altaris loco fuisse meminerimus, in quo semetipsum pro peccatis nostris Deo Patri obtulit. Non est ergo, quòd eius ignominia aliquem offendat, quando per hanc ille triumpha- uit de mundo & principe eius, ut eiusdem virtute omnem potestatem aduersariam vincant quotquot in illum credunt. Eusebius author est, Constantino contra Christi & Ecclesiæ hostes bellum iustum & necessarium paranti, crucis effigiem in cælo apparuisse cum inscriptione ista: τούτῳ νίκα, idest, hoc signo vince. Itaque hoc sibi signum militare fecit, & sub eo milites suos eduxit, & bellum istud feli- cissimè gessit. Vbi nemo pijssimum Imperatorem adeò stupidum & næcordem fuisse putauerit, ut in crucis forma uel picta uel sculpta spem aut fiduciam aliquam collocauerit (quod posteris temporibus homines superstitiosi fecerunt) sed quia à viris pijs & eruditis edoctus erat, hoc immortalitatis Christi symbolum, & victoriæ aduersus diabolum & mortem partæ trophæum esse, hoc ipsum non ado- rationis aut cultus causa proposuit. Sed ut publicè testaretur, se illius seruum & militem esse, qui in cruce moriens nos seruauit. Eadem fide nos quoq; non à crucibus manu factis, sed à Christi crucifixi merito pendere couenit, ut nos quoq; eius virtute victoriam in medijs periculis et tribulationibus obtineamus. Debet autem in hoc toto mysterio primùm obseruari bonitas Dei, qui (ut ipse Christus testatur) ita dilexit nos, ut Filium suum unigenitum pro nobis in mortem hanc diram & infamem dederit. Fa- cit huius consideratio ad fidei nostræ confirmationem, ne de eius erga nos voluntate posthac dubite- mus. Nec enim fieri potest, ut aliquid eorum, quæ necessaria sunt, nobis ille neget, qui Filio suo par- cere noluit. Deinde in doctam acerbo crucis Christi supplicio peccati atrocitatem consideremus, quam magnam & Deo quàm maximè abominabilem esse oportet, cùm illud non alia ratione expiari po- tuerit. Quod ut eos arguit, qui dum novas expiationes & satisfactiones fingunt Christi merito dero- gant: ita nobis uehemens est ad pœnitentiam stimulus contra blanditias peccatorum & mundi illecebras, quibus nos Satan circumuenire & sua mācipia facere satagit. Sed & ipsi nobis fere delitias facimus, dum nobisipsis persuademus, non tam grauem esse peccatorum noxam, quàm multi fingant, qui plus æquo morosiores conantur omnes sub nescio quam disciplinam cogere. At qua ratione leni- culum dici potest id, quòd Angelis defectoribus ruinæ causa fuit? propter quod Adam cum tota po- steritate è Paradiso eiectus & morte multatus est? propter quod Deus ipse à nobis alienior factus creaturis omnibus maledixit, & totam hanc mundi machinā corruptioni subiecit? propter quod de- niq; Dei Filius in cruce pependit nudus & infamis, ad quod spectaculum ipsam rerum naturam & omnes mundi partes exhorruisse suo loco audiemus? Quòd si uerò hæc omnia te parum mouent, ut quorum fides propter uetustatē iam obsoleta ac dubia sit, dic quæso quisquis es, unde fames, unde pe- stilentia, unde bella, unde regnorum periculosæ mutationes & auacunq; alia sunt huius generis, origi- nem ducat? Nonne gentes olim hæc omnia ex sceleribus enasci & horum pœnas esse agnouerunt? Qui id negare volet, nimiū aut impudes aut historiarum ignarus erit. Pudeat ergo Christianos homines de peccato tā leuiter sentire, seq; rursus ei mācipare, ex cuius seruitio non aliter quàm per indignā mortē Filij Dei liberari potuerunt. De deploratis & contumacibus loquor, qui nō contenti peccauisse (quod omnibus ex infirmitate carnis accidit) peccata quae negare non possunt, defendunt, & perinde ac si bene rē gesserint, gloriantur. Est horum magnus numerus hodie, qui ne ab iis quidem abstinent, quorum olim gentes pudnit. At hi ipsum Dei Filium sibimetipsis rursus crucifigunt (ut Apostolus loquitur) & illum nouis mundi ludibrijs exponunt, dum illius professionem sceleribus inquinant: Idem meritum eius irritū sibi reddunt, eiusq; sanguinem prophanant: ipsum deniq; spiritum gratiae, cuius templa esse debebant, contristant et contumelia atroci afficiunt. Nunquam ergo inultam ferēt tam sceleratam licentiam, sed eas aliquando poenas exoluent Deo, quas is à Filij sui proditoribus & carnificibus olim requisuit. Excusant quidem se illi, quòd mundi huius consuetudini aliquid dare oporteat, quem omnino relinquere impossibile sit: At meminisse eos oportebat, nō decere ut mūdo placere studeant ij, quos Christus è mundo selegit, ut suum sint peculium: nostri potius officij esse, ut quemadmodū ille extra portam passus est, ita nos quoq; relicto mundo opprobrium illius patienter feramus, & magnis pacibus contendamus ad coelestis patriae possessionem, quam ille nobis acquisiuit.
units.tr: So that this may be understood more correctly, and so that the use of this teaching may be richer, we must consider the cross of Christ in such a way that we remember it stood in the place of an altar, on which he offered himself to God the Father for our sins. There is therefore no reason for anyone to be offended by its disgrace, since through it he triumphed over the world and its prince, so that by his power all adversary power may be conquered by all who believe in him. Eusebius reports that when Constantine was preparing a just and necessary war against the enemies of Christ and of the Church, the image of the cross appeared in the sky with this inscription: τούτῳ νίκα [by this conquer], that is, conquer by this sign. Therefore he made this sign his military standard, and led his soldiers under it, and waged that war most fortunately. No one would think that this most pious emperor was so stupid and senseless as to place any hope or confidence in a cross, whether painted or carved (which superstitious men did in later times). But because he had been taught by pious and learned men that this was the symbol of the immortality of Christ and the trophy of victory won against the devil and death, he displayed it not for the sake of worship or cult, but so that he might publicly testify that he was the servant and soldier of him who, dying on the cross, saved us. With the same faith we too ought to depend not on crosses made by hands, but on the merit of Christ crucified, so that we too may by his power obtain victory in the midst of dangers and tribulations. In this whole mystery, moreover, the goodness of God should be observed first, who (as Christ himself testifies) so loved us that he gave his only-begotten Son for us to this dreadful and infamous death. The consideration of this serves to confirm our faith, so that we may no longer doubt his will towards us. For it cannot be that he who did not spare his own Son should deny us anything that is necessary. Next, let us consider in the bitter punishment of Christ's cross the atrocity of sin, which must be great and most abominable to God, since it could not be atoned for by any other means. Just as this refutes those who, while they invent new expiations and satisfactions, detract from the merit of Christ, so it is for us a vehement spur to repentance against the allurements of sins and the enticements of the world, by which Satan strives to ensnare us and make us his slaves. But we also make light of it for ourselves, while we persuade ourselves that the harm of sins is not as grievous as many pretend, who, being more austere than is right, try to force everything under I know not what discipline. But by what reasoning can that be called a trifle which was the cause of ruin to the rebel angels? On account of which Adam was cast out of Paradise with all his posterity and punished with death? On account of which God himself, made more alien to us, cursed all creatures and subjected this whole machinery of the world to corruption? On account of which, finally, the Son of God hung on the cross naked and infamous, at which spectacle we shall hear in its place that nature itself and all parts of the world shuddered? But if these things move you little, since your faith has become obsolete and doubtful through age, tell me, I ask, whoever you are: whence come famine, whence pestilence, whence wars, whence the dangerous changes of kingdoms, and whatever else is of this kind? Did not the nations long ago recognise that all these things arise from crimes and are the punishments of them? Whoever would deny this will be either overly shameless or ignorant of history. Let Christians therefore be ashamed to think so lightly of sin, and to surrender themselves again to it, from whose slavery they could not be freed except through the unworthy death of the Son of God. I am speaking of the desperate and obstinate, who, not content to have sinned (which happens to all through the weakness of the flesh), defend the sins they cannot deny, and boast of them as if they had done well. There is today a great number of these, who do not abstain even from those things for which the nations of old were ashamed. Yet these crucify the Son of God to themselves again (as the Apostle says) and expose him to new mockeries of the world, while they defile their profession of him with crimes. They render his merit void for themselves and profane his blood; finally, they grieve the Spirit of grace, whose temples they ought to be, and subject him to atrocious insult. Therefore God will never bear such wicked licence unavenged, but will at some time exact from them those punishments which he once demanded from the betrayers and executioners of his Son. They excuse themselves, saying that one must give something to the custom of this world, which it is impossible to leave altogether. But they ought to remember that it is not fitting for those whom Christ has chosen out of the world, to be his own possession, to strive to please the world. It is rather our duty, just as he suffered outside the gate, so also to leave the world and patiently bear his reproach, and with great exertion to press on towards the possession of the heavenly homeland, which he has acquired for us.

units.la: Videamus nunc secundam huius loci partem, qua quid Christus fecerit, narratur, interea dum eum milites cruci affixerunt. Quia enim tunc acutissimos dolores passus est, cum & membris totis distenderetur, & pedes manusq; eius perforantur, non temere miretur aliquis, quibus vocibus tunc usus sit, & num uel impiorum militum crudelitatem corripuerit, uel impatientia superatus querelas fuderit amarulētas & doloris plenas? ita enim nos solemus, qui nobis iniuriam graue putamus fieri, si quādo durius tractamur. Sed lōge aliter ille, qui cùm haec omnia ex aeterno Patris decreto propter nos pateretur, ad preces conuersus dixit: Pater remite eis, nesciunt enim quid faciant. Atqui initio diximus, inter Sacerdotis officia hoc quoq; censeri, ut pro populo oret & intercedat apud Deum. Ergo hic proprio Sacerdotis munere fungitur, & ideo preces illas facit, ut se non solum victimam pro peccatis mundi esse, verumetiam Sacerdotem esse testaretur, per quem illam offerri oporteat. Itaque magnus huius intercessionis usus est, & eorum errorem ualidissimè confutat, qui nouum sacerdotium & nouos sacerdotes finxerunt, qui uel Christum quotidie offerant, uel illius meritum nouo quodam sacrificij genere nobis applicent. Nam ille solus seipsum obtulit, neque aliquis unquam repertus est, quem hoc honore dignatus sit Deus, ut eum sui Filij sacrificum aut immolatorem faceret. Idem suum sacrificium & meritum nobis solus quoq; applicat per suam intercessionem & Euangelij praedicationem, ut alibi demonstrauimus. Procul ergo cum suo illo sacerdotio facessant Romanenses illi Camarim (ut Prophetae uerbo utar) qui illius honorem sibi uendicare audent. Est autem haec Christi oratio digna, cuius singulas partes aliquanto diligentius examinemus.
units.tr: Let us now consider the second part of this passage, which tells what Christ did while the soldiers fixed him to the cross. Since he then suffered the most acute pains, when his whole body was stretched out and his hands and feet were pierced, one might fairly wonder what words he used at that time. Did he rebuke the cruelty of the impious soldiers, or, overcome by impatience, pour out bitter complaints full of pain? That is how we are accustomed to act when we think we are wronged, if we are handled too harshly. But he was altogether different. Although he suffered all these things by the eternal decree of the Father for our sake, he turned to prayer and said: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." Indeed, at the beginning we said that interceding and praying before God for the people is also counted among the duties of a priest. Therefore here he performs the proper office of a priest, and so he makes that prayer, to testify that he is not only the victim for the sins of the world but also the priest through whom that victim must be offered. Thus this intercession has great use, and it most powerfully refutes the error of those who invented a new priesthood and new priests, who either offer Christ every day or apply his merit to us by some new kind of sacrifice. For he alone offered himself, and no one has ever been found whom God has deigned to honour so highly as to make him a sacrificer or immolator of his Son. He alone also applies his own sacrifice and merit to us, through his intercession and the preaching of the Gospel, as we have shown elsewhere. Let those Romanists, then, depart far away with their priesthood, as the prophet says, "Chemarim", who dare to claim that honour for themselves. This prayer of Christ is worthy, and we shall examine its individual parts a little more carefully.

units.la: Prima est, ut pro quibus nam oret obseruemus. Pro illis nimirum, qui eum crucifigebant: quos milites fuisse ex toto historiae contextu apparet. At quia cōstat omnes homines mortis eius reos esse, oratio haec simul ad nos quoque & alios omnes extenditur. Est hoc memorabile bonitatis & mansuetudinis exemplum, quod eò illustrius fiet, si quid hucusque cum illo gestum fuerit, expendas. Nam hi milites sunt procul dubio, quorum opera captus fuit. Hi sunt, qui eum uirgis & flagellis caeciderunt, qui militari ueste indutum & spinis coronatum conspuerunt, & omni opprobriorum genere obruerunt. Hi sunt, qui ut crucem propriam gestaret, eum coegerunt, qui paulo ante (ut Marcus scribit, uinum illi dederunt myrrhatum. Denique hi ipsi nunc illum crudeliter distendunt, clauis acutis manus & pedes transfuerberant, ut mox sublime erigere possint. Pro illis tamen orat, & cùm praesentem uideret Matrem Virginem, dolore & tristitia confectam, cùm Ioannes adesset dilectus ille discipulus, cùm praesto essent mulieres Galilaeae, quae officijs suis illum diu iuuerant, nihil tamen adhuc eum istis agit, sed eorum salutem prae omnibus alijs cordi habet, qui omnia hostiliter faciebant. Procul ergo abfuit à uindicta cupiditate, & suo exemplo doctrinam eam confirmat, qua monet, ut hostes nostros diligamus, & bene precemur illis qui nos diris devouent. Simile affectum in Mose cernimus, qui è libro Dei deleri cupiebat, ut eos seruaret, qui ipsum nō semel conuitiati fuerant. Et Paulus anathema optabat fieri pro Iudaeis, qui eius vitae dies noctesq; insidiabantur. Ifiorum exempla nos imitari conuenit, ut nos germanos Dei filios esse testemur.
units.tr: The first thing is to observe for whom he prays. Certainly for those who were crucifying him, who clearly were soldiers, as appears from the whole context of the history. But since it is agreed that all men are guilty of his death, this prayer extends at the same time to us and to all others. This is a memorable example of goodness and gentleness, and it will shine out all the more clearly if you weigh what had been done to him up to that point. For these soldiers were undoubtedly the ones by whose work he was seized. These are the ones who beat him with rods and whips, who spat upon him when he was clothed in a soldier's garment and crowned with thorns, and who overwhelmed him with every kind of insult. These are the ones who forced him to carry his own cross, and who, a little before (as Mark writes), gave him wine mixed with myrrh. Finally, these same men now cruelly stretch him out, and they pierce his hands and feet with sharp nails, so that they may soon be able to raise him aloft. Yet he prays for them. And although he saw his mother, the Virgin, present, worn out with grief and sadness, although that beloved disciple John was there, although the Galilean women were at hand, who had long helped him with their services, he still does nothing against those men, but holds the salvation of those who did all these things in hostility dearer than all others. Therefore he was far from any desire for vengeance, and by his own example he confirms the teaching that bids us love our enemies and bless those who curse us. We see a similar affection in Moses, who wished to be blotted out of the book of God, so that he might save those who had reviled him more than once. And Paul wished to be made an anathema for the Jews, who lay in wait for his life day and night. It is fitting that we imitate the examples of these men, so that we may show ourselves to be true sons of God.

units.la: Quid uero illis precatur aut petit? Ut pater ipsis hanc iniquitate remittat. Ita Stephanus cùm lapidum undiq; ruentium grandine obrueretur clamabat: Domine, ne statuas illis peccatum hoc. At qui peccatorum remissione omnem salutem contineri constat, quando propter illa sola nobis Deus iratus scitur, & à nobis alienatur. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates. Quod autem istorum nomine hic orat, id per Euangelium omnibus offert & confert, qui illud cum fide audiunt. Et quia Sacerdotium eius æternum est, æternus etiam est huius intercessionis effectus, situti mortis quoq; eius meritum perpetuò durat. Et istis profuisse preces has Christi, rei euentus docuit. Ad ipsum certè Centurionem illarum fructus redundauit, qui non multo post cuiusdam signis & prodigijs quæ fiebant illo expirante, præclarum de eo testimonium tulit. Et ad primam Petri concionem, quam die Pentecostes Hierosolymis habuit, aliquot millia eorum ad fidem conuersi sunt, qui illum ad crucis supplicium postulauerant. Debet ergo hoc Christi factu nos excitare, ut ipsum agnoscamus nostrum esse mediatorem atq; aduocatum apud Patrem, neq; nunc duriorem fingamus, quàm olim fuit, cum in terris ageret, aut apud quem nouis aut intermedijs intercessoribus opus sit. Ad se tam uenire iubet omnes qui laborant & onerati sunt: neq; eos reijcit qui ad ipsum ueniunt. Idem gloriam suam nemini communicat: & satis notum est illud Ioannis: Si quis peccauerit, habemus aduocatum apud Patrem, Iesum Christum iustum. Cui Paulus consentiens clamat: Vnus Deus, & unus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus.
units.tr: But what does he pray for them or ask for them? That the Father should forgive them this iniquity. So Stephen, when he was being overwhelmed by a hail of stones falling from every side, cried out: "Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge." Yet it is agreed that all salvation is contained in the forgiveness of sins, since God is known to be angry with us and estranged from us on account of sins alone. Therefore David said: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven." Now, what he asks on behalf of these men, he offers and bestows through the Gospel on all who hear it with faith. And because his priesthood is eternal, the effect of this intercession is also eternal, just as the merit of his death endures continually. The event itself has shown that these prayers of Christ benefited these men. Certainly the fruit of them came to the centurion himself, who, not long after, when Christ had expired, and the signs and portents that occurred were seen, bore a notable testimony concerning him. And at Peter's first sermon, which he preached at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, several thousand of those who had demanded his crucifixion were converted to the faith. This deed of Christ ought therefore to stir us to acknowledge that he is our mediator and advocate with the Father, and we should not imagine him harsher now than he was once, when he lived on earth, nor imagine that we need new or intermediate intercessors. He calls all who labour and are burdened to come to himself, and he does not reject those who come to him. Likewise he shares his glory with no one, and that saying of John is well known: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." Paul agrees with this and cries out: "There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

units.la: Porrò ratione quoq; aut argumento suâ hanc precatione confirmat, dicens: Nesciunt enim quid faciant. Sciebant quidem se hominem innocentem occidere, cum eius innocentia tam multis testimonijs probata esset, sed eundem Dei Filium esse nesciebant. Nam si cognouissent (inquit Paulus) neque quam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Et Petrus cum Hierosolymitanum populum huius sceleris ac cruciaret, consolationis causa idem illud mitigans subijcit: Sed nunc fratres, scio quod per ignorantiam fecistis, sicuti & principes uestri. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi nulla prorsus illorum culpa fuerit. Nam ut nihil aliud accedat, per se scelus atrocissimum est, hominem iustum damnare, & sanguinem innoxium fundere. Itaq; à solius peccatii in Spiritum sanctum reatu illos eximit, eò quod eorum simi les essent, qui Regis filium pannis laceris uestitu iniurijs afficiunt, nunquàm id facturi, si quis sit nouis sent. Et sunt hæc bonitatis & mansuetudinis paternæ uerba, quàm in Deo uehementissimâ esse, Scriptura docet. Et huc pertinet quod Dauid ait: Vt pater miseretur liberorum, ita Dominus miseretur timentium eum. Ipse enim nouit conditionem nostram, recordans quod simus puluis. Est quidè ignorantia quoq; supplicio digna, eo quod hominem Dei ignorantem esse minimè decet. At quæ illius est benignitas, parcit nobis, neq; imputat quæcunq; ex ignorantia et naturali infirmitate præter officium facimus. Interim nemo sibi hanc peccandi licentiam uenetur. Nam qui huic afuescunt, ij tandem in durati & iusto Dei iudicio in sensum reprobum traditi, cum Pharaone clamant: Quis est Deus, quem audire oporteat? Et hæc ignorantia illa crassa & uoluntaria est, quam ille inultam non sinit.
units.tr: Moreover, he confirms this prayer also by a reason or argument, saying: "For they do not know what they are doing." They did indeed know that they were killing an innocent man, since his innocence had been proved by so many testimonies, but they did not know that he was the Son of God. For, as Paul says, "If they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." And Peter, when he was accusing the people of Jerusalem of this crime, and wishing to soften it for their consolation, added the same point: "But now, brethren, I know that you did it in ignorance, as did also your rulers." This should not be understood as if they had no guilt at all. For, even apart from anything else, it is a most atrocious crime in itself to condemn a righteous man and to shed innocent blood. Therefore he excuses them from the guilt of the sin against the Holy Spirit alone, because they were like those who insult a king's son, dressed in ragged clothes, and would never do so if they knew who he was. These are words of fatherly goodness and gentleness, which Scripture teaches to be most abundant in God. And to this pertains what David says: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him. For he knows our frame, and remembers that we are dust." Indeed, ignorance too is worthy of punishment, because it is by no means fitting for a man of God to be ignorant. Yet such is his kindness that he spares us, and does not impute to us whatever we do contrary to duty through ignorance and natural weakness. Meanwhile, let no one seek this licence for sinning for himself. For those who grow accustomed to it, they at last become hardened, and, given over to a reprobate mind by the just judgment of God, they cry out with Pharaoh: "Who is the Lord, that I should obey him?" This ignorance is gross and wilful, and he does not allow it to go unpunished.

units.la: Sequitur tertia huius loci pars, quæ partitionem uestium Christi inter milites factam continet. Hanc paucis Lucas absoluit: Ioannes autem diligentius singulas quoque huius facti circunstantias narrat, & ne quid fortuitum aut uulgare putemus, uaticinium ex Psalmis adducit, quo docet hoc etiam ex Patris decreto factum esse. Diximus illic quæ de toto hoc negotio dicenda uidentur, sufficiat ergo nunc summa rerum capita perstrinxisse. Primò paupertatem, quæ inter peccati pœnas non postrema est, cum ignominia in se ille recepit, & nudus in cruce pependit, ut nos sua nuditate tegeret. Deinde paupertatem suo exemplo consecrauit, ne nos propter illa Deo minus gratos & acceptos esse putemus. Tertiò luxum & fastum uestium damnauit, qui quàm Deo displiceat, alibi diximus. A Christianis certè hominibus illum procul abijci debere hoc unum exemplum abundè docet. Quid enim absurdius est, quàm uestitu eos superbire, qui in Christo crucifixo & eius nuditate spem salutis collocant? Postremò patientiam nobis commendat, ne murmuremus, si quando facultatibus nostris spoliamur, & omnium egeni atq; nudi in exilium eijcimur. Ita enim nos suæ inopiæ socios facit Dominus, ut Regni sui cœlestis thesauris nos donet. Imò uolupe sit, nos etiā huius sæculi bonorum laboriosa & solicita administratione liberatos esse, ut expeditiores simus ad Regnum Dei ad quod uocamur. Biantem illum Prienæum hoc nomine ueteres commendant, quòd cùm patria ab hostibus diriperetur, ipse omnibus sarcinis relictis abiret, dicens: Omnia mea mecum porto. Ergo non sua sed fortunæ bona putabat, quæ ab hostibus diripi possunt, & sine quibus uita sustentari potest. Aliquando æquius omnium rerum
units.tr: There follows the third part of this passage, which contains the division of Christ's garments among the soldiers. Luke finishes this briefly, but John narrates more carefully each circumstance of this deed, and, lest we think anything accidental or common, he adduces a prophecy from the Psalms, by which he teaches that this too was done by the Father's decree. We have said there what seems to be worth saying about this whole matter, so it is enough now to touch briefly on the main heads. First, he took upon himself poverty, which is no small part of the punishments for sin, together with its disgrace, and he hung naked on the cross, so that by his nakedness he might cover us. Then he consecrated poverty by his own example, so that we may not think that on account of it we are less pleasing and acceptable to God. Third, he condemned luxury and pride in clothing, which we have said elsewhere is displeasing to God. That this one example abundantly teaches that such things should be far removed from Christian people is certain. For what is more absurd than for those to take pride in their clothing who place their hope of salvation in Christ crucified and in his nakedness? Last, he commends patience to us, that we should not murmur if at any time we are stripped of our possessions and cast out into exile, poor and naked of everything. For thus the Lord makes us companions of his poverty, so that he may give us the treasures of his heavenly kingdom. Indeed, it is useful that we should be freed from the laborious and anxious management of the goods of this age, so that we may be more unencumbered for the kingdom of God, to which we are called. The ancients praise that gaping Bias of Priene for this reason: when his homeland was being plundered by enemies, he himself left all his baggage behind and went away, saying: "I carry all my possessions with me." So he thought that the goods which can be plundered by enemies, and without which life can be sustained, are not his own but belong to fortune. Sometime a more just [...]

units.la: 3. Confirmatio petitionis. — 1. Cor. 2. — Act. 9. — Psal. 103. — Vestes Christi diuiduntur. amissionem Christianus feret, qui se in Christo omnes æternæ salutis thesauros possidere nouit, quos neq; fures rapere, neq; erugo aut tineæ corrumpere possunt?
units.tr: 3. Confirmation of the petition. — 1 Cor. 2. — Acts 9. — Ps. 103. — Christ's garments are divided. Will a Christian bear the loss of these things when he knows that in Christ he possesses all the treasures of eternal salvation, which neither thieves can steal nor rust or moths destroy?

units.la: Quarta huius loci parte conuitia & opprobria narrantur, quæ in cruce pendens Dominus sustituit. Et stabat (inquit Lucas) populus spectans. Marcus & Matthæus aliquos ex illis non otiosos spectatores fuisse scribunt, sed capitibus per ludibrium motis in illū opprobria iecisse, dicentes. Vah, qui dissoluis templū, & triduo ædificas: Serua teipsum, & descende de cruce. Idē nostrer etiā hic non omnino obscurè innuit, quando principes etiā eum sannis excepisse scribit, & dixisse: Alios seruauit, seruet seipsum, si hic est ille Christus Dei electus. Accedūt his milites, qui pro suo more licentia & petulantia maiori insultantes acetum quoq; sitienti propinauerunt. Vbi rursus obseruari debet, hæc illum propter nos sustinuisse, ut pro illis satisfaceret, qui Dij fieri voluerūt, non contenti ea sorte, quam illis Deus dederat. Primi quidē in eo peccarunt parentes nostri, Adamus & Eua, sed ex ipsis super bia ista in omnes posteros propagata est, sicuti exemplis infinitis poterat demonstrari. Nam ut nihil nunc de eo dicamus, quòd aduersus Dei verbū & leges homines efferuntur, & in has sibi imperium sumunt (quod vitium nimis vulgare est) quàm multi inter gentes se Deorū filios esse gloriati sunt, qui ex stupris, adulteriis & incestibus fere nati fuerunt? Quis item Semideos omnes enumerauerit? Quis Alexandrum Macedonem ignorat suspectam fecisse matris pudicitiam, ut Iouis Hammonij filius esse crederetur? Taceo Romanos Imperatores, qui in Deorum numerum à suis adulatoribus relati sunt: quibus nouissimis temporibus Pontifices successerunt, qui diuina & humana iura in sua potestate esse clamant, sibi deniq; in cœlos ius sumūt, ut suis Canonizationibus inter Diuuos cœlites collocent, quos ipsi illo honore dignos iudicarint. Hæc ideo commemoramus, ne quis temere factū existimet, quod omnis loci & ordinis homines Christo tā insolenter tamen impiè illuserunt. Quia enim affectatæ diuinitatis crimen frequentius est quā vulgo putetur, huius quoq; pœnā ipsum subire oportuit, ne quod scelus sit, quod ipsius merito non expiatum esse putetur. Deinde oportuit eum ab omnibus quasi uno ore oppugnari conuitijs atq; opprobrijs, ut nos per illum vincamus. Adhæc scandalo medetur hæc pars, ne quis offendatur, si hodie quoque quis illum unanimi omnium ordinum consensu damnari eiusq; doctrinam contumeliosissimè proscindi audiat. Extant enim de hoc Prophetarum vaticinia, inter quæ euidens cumprimis est, quod in Simeonis Cantico vidimus. Et continent opprobria ista nouū innocentiæ Christi testimonium. Quis enim putauerit improbos illos & petulantes contumeliatores dissimulaturos fuisse, si quod crimen vel in speciem probabile in illo hæsisset? Iam certè tempus erat illud diuulgandi, ut docerent illum pœnas suis delictis dignas luere. Quid verò illi exprobrant? Nihil quam quod aut per calumniam male detortum est, aut laudem quoq; merebatur. Obijciunt, quod templum se destruere & intra triduum rursus ædificare posse dixerit. Hanc verò calumniam esse impudentem alibi demonstrauimus. At si quid huius omnino dixisset, nū id tanto supplicio dignum erat? Addunt: Alios seruauit, seruet seipsum. Atqui constabat, multos per ipsum seruatos fuisse. Num verò id reprehensionem meretur? Et si seipsum seruare nō potemt, certè commiseratione potius quàm opprobrio dignus erat. Sed cur non cogitant arcano aliquo consilio fieri, quod qui tam multis salutem dederit, nunc seipsum non seruet? Vides ergo istos homines Christi innocentiam asseruisse suis opprobrijs, suam verò prodidisse improbitatem & impia audacia, qua aduersus Deum insurrexerunt. Accidit hoc ipsum omnibus, qui hodie nobis conuitiantur, & doctrinam Euangelij, fidem in unum Deum per Iesum Christum & alia huiusmodi exprobrant. Quid enim horum reprehensione dignum est? Aspergunt ista multis sannis atq; dicterijs, si quando se victoria potitos esse putant, quod non aliud est quàm acetum propinare in cruce Christi pendentibus. At non debent ista nos mouere, quibus perfecto patientiæ exemplo Christus præiuit. Alteri autē isti meminerint quæso, ut hanc Iudæorum petulantiam ultus sit Deus. Nec enim horribili solum excidio urbs illorum cum templo euersa est: quod nec ipse Titus Romanæ militiæ Imperator prohibere potuit, sed ipsi quoque ludibrium totius mundi facti sunt, & ubiq; locorum iniurijs atq; contumelijs atrocissimis exagitantur. Sentient idem procul dubio, quicunq; illos imitantur. Nam qui mercedem bonam promisit ei, qui uni ex discipulis suis poculum aquæ frigidæ dederit, is suas quoq; pœnas illis iam præparauit, qui acerbum illud acetum suis laborantibus infundunt.
units.tr: In the fourth part of this passage the insults and reproaches are related which the Lord endured while hanging on the cross. Luke writes, "And the people stood beholding." Mark and Matthew write that some of those present were not idle spectators, but shook their heads in mockery and hurled abuse at him, saying: "Ah, you who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself and come down from the cross." Our author also hints, not very obscurely, that the leaders too greeted him with scorn, writing that they said: "He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, the chosen one." Then the soldiers came up and, in their usual manner, with greater license and wantonness, mocked him and offered vinegar to him as he thirsted. Here it must be noted again that he bore these things for our sake, so that he might make satisfaction for those who wished to become gods, not content with the lot that God had given them. Our first parents, Adam and Eve, sinned first in this, but from them this pride has been passed on to all their posterity, as can be shown by countless examples. To say nothing now of how men rise up against the word and laws of God and claim authority for themselves in defiance of them (a fault that is all too common), how many among the nations have boasted that they were sons of the gods, born almost all of debauchery, adultery and incest? Who could list all the demigods? Who does not know that Alexander of Macedon cast suspicion on his mother's chastity so that he might be believed to be the son of Jupiter Ammon? I pass over the Roman emperors, who were numbered among the gods by their flatterers; and in the most recent times they have been succeeded by Pontiffs who cry out that divine and human law lie in their power, and who finally claim for themselves the right to the heavens, so that by their canonizations they may enrol among the heavenly saints those whom they themselves have judged worthy of that honour. We mention these things so that no one may think it was done without reason that men of every place and rank mocked Christ so insolently and impiously. For since the crime of claiming divinity is more common than is generally thought, it was fitting that he should undergo its punishment, lest any wickedness should seem not to have been expiated by his merit. Further, it was fitting that he should be assailed with reproaches and insults by all, as if with one voice, so that through him we might conquer. Moreover, this part serves as a remedy against scandal, so that no one may be offended if he hears today too that Christ is condemned by the unanimous consent of all orders and his doctrine most abusively torn to pieces. For there are prophecies of this in the Prophets, the clearest of which, above all, is what we saw in the Canticle of Simeon. And these reproaches constitute a new testimony to the innocence of Christ. For who would suppose that those wicked and wanton revilers would have held their peace, if any charge, even one that looked plausible, had been found against him? Surely this was the time to publish it, so that they might show that he was paying the penalty his crimes deserved. But what do they actually reproach him with? Nothing except what was either twisted by slander or even deserved praise. They object that he said he could destroy the temple and build it again within three days. We have already shown elsewhere that this calumny is shameless. But even if he had said anything of the kind, was it deserving of so great a punishment? They add: "He saved others; let him save himself." Yet it was well known that many had been saved through him. Does that deserve reproach? And if he could not save himself, he was surely deserving of pity rather than of insult. But why do they not consider that it happens by some hidden counsel that he who has given salvation to so many does not now save himself? You see, then, that these men by their reproaches asserted the innocence of Christ, while they betrayed their own wickedness and the impious audacity with which they rose up against God. The same happens to all who today revile us and reproach the doctrine of the Gospel, faith in the one God through Jesus Christ, and other things of this kind. For what among these deserves reproach? They spatter these things with many jeers and taunts whenever they think they have gained the upper hand, which is nothing other than offering vinegar to those hanging on the cross of Christ. But these things ought not to move us, for Christ has gone before us as the perfect example of patience. As for those others, I ask them to remember how God has avenged this wantonness of the Jews. For their city was overthrown together with the temple, not only by a dreadful destruction, which not even Titus himself, the commander of the Roman army, could prevent, but they themselves were made a mockery to the whole world, and everywhere they are harassed with the most atrocious injuries and insults. Undoubtedly, all who imitate them will feel the same. For he who promised a good reward to anyone who gives a cup of cold water to one of his disciples has already prepared punishments for those who pour that bitter vinegar on his sufferers.

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci pars, quæ Crucis illius saluificæ Christiq; in ea pendentis titulum siue inscriptionem cōtinet. Fuit enim mos iste tunc publicè receptus, & causæ tam diri supplicij summa tim describtæ supra suspensorū capita affigerentur. Quia autem Pilatus quod de Christo scriberet non habebat, eò quòd nullius sceleris esset conuictus, hoc unū inscriptione illa completi voluit, quod Sacerdotes in primis userant: scilicet regnū, affectare, & se dicere Regem Iudæorū. Itaq; Latinis, Græcis ac Hebraicis literis scribit: HIC EST REX ILLEIVDAEORVM. Vel ut alij annotarunt: IESVS NAZARENVS REX IVDAEORVM. Quod illum in Iudaicæ gentis contumeliā fecisse non est dubium, & id quoq; animaduerterunt Sacerdotes ac Seniores, & ideo (ut Ioannes prolixè narrat) inscriptionem hanc voluerunt mutari. Interim nihil hic sine numine aut diuinæ prouidentiæ decreto factum est. Nam Pilati manū direxit, ut quamuis nihil minus vellet facere, & longè alio affectu duceretur, Christi tamen præco fieret, & publicè tribus linguis, quæ tunc in orbe inter omnes alias eminebat, testaretur, Iesum hunc, qui medius inter latrones pendebat, esse Regem illum per Prophetas promissum, & fortissimū vindicem omnium, qui ipsum fide vera apprehendunt, confitentur & prædicant. Et cruci quidem imponitur hæc inscriptio, ut eo typo adumbraretur, Regnum eius tunc maximè florere ac triumphare, quando totum oppressum esse putatur adeoq; per illos ipsos exaltari ac propagari, qui in illo deprimendo præcipuam operam naauant. Tribus autem linguis principalibus titulum hunc describi voluit Spiritus sanctus, ut Regnū hoc per totum orbem extendi doceret, & omnibus constaret Christū esse Regem illū, cui à Patre dictum est: Postula à me, dabo gentes ut sint hæreditas tua: & terminos terræ, ut sint possessio tua: Et de quo Daniel scripserat: Dominatus est ei traditus, & honos, & regnum: ut omnes nationes, populi & linguæ seruiant ei. Poterant hæc multis tractari, sed quia de illis in Marci & Ioannis expositione diximus, sufficiat ea obiter perstrinxisse. Præstat tamen tenere, quod in tota hac actione memoratu dignissimū esse Spiritus sanctus iudicauit. Cū enim Sacerdotes & Seniores isto Christi præconio sibi totiq; genti iniuriam fieri sentirent, ideoq; ut ea Inscriptio mutaretur, postularent, Pilatus qui in re maioris momenti, nimium facilem se illis præbuerat, nunc durior factus, cum indignatione eos reijcit, dicens: Quod scripsi, scripsi. Ita uero significatum fuit, nunquam defuturos Iesu Christo aduersarios, qui clament: Nolumus hunc regnare super nos: at eosdem nunquam effecturos esse quod uolunt. Rata enim & in æternū firma erunt, quæ de illo ex Spiritus sancti suggestione scripserunt sancti Dei homines, Prophetæ & Apostoli. Regnabit ergo ille ad dexteram Patris sui, donec posuerit omnes inimicos suos scabellum pedum suorum, gens autem & regnum, quæ non seruierint ei, peribunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, which contains the title or inscription of that saving Cross and of Christ hanging on it. For this custom was then publicly accepted, and the summary of the causes of so dreadful a punishment was written out and fixed above the heads of those who were hanged. But since Pilate had nothing to write about Christ, because he had been convicted of no crime, he wished to fulfil in this inscription the one thing the priests especially charged him with, namely that he aspired to a kingdom and called himself King of the Jews. And so he wrote in Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS. Or, as others have noted: JESUS OF NAZARETH, KING OF THE JEWS. There is no doubt that he did this to insult the Jewish nation, and the chief priests and elders also noticed this, and therefore (as John relates at length) they wished this inscription to be changed. Yet nothing here was done without the divine will or the decree of divine providence. For he guided Pilate's hand so that, although he wished to do the very opposite and was moved by an entirely different disposition, he nevertheless became a herald of Christ and bore public witness in three languages, which were then pre-eminent among all others in the world, that this Jesus, who hung between the thieves, is that King promised through the Prophets, and the most mighty avenger of all who lay hold of him by true faith, confess him and proclaim him. This inscription is placed on the cross so that the type might show that his kingdom flourishes and triumphs most when it is thought to be wholly crushed, and is exalted and spread through those very men who take the chief pains to crush him. The Holy Spirit wished this title to be written in three principal languages, to teach that this kingdom is extended through the whole world, and to make it plain to all that Christ is that King to whom the Father said: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession"; and of whom Daniel wrote: "Dominion and honour and kingdom were given to him, that all nations, peoples and tongues should serve him." These matters could be treated at length, but since we have spoken of them in our exposition of Mark and John, it is enough to have touched on them briefly here. Yet it is well to keep in mind what the Holy Spirit judged most worthy of remembrance in this whole action. When the chief priests and elders perceived that this proclamation of Christ was an injury to themselves and to their whole nation, and therefore demanded that the inscription be changed, Pilate, who in a matter of greater importance had shown himself far too compliant towards them, now grew harder and, with indignation, sent them away, saying: "What I have written, I have written." By this it was signified that Jesus Christ will never lack adversaries who cry, "We will not have this man reign over us," but that these same men will never achieve what they want. For what the holy men of God, the Prophets and Apostles, wrote about him under the prompting of the Holy Spirit will stand firm and fixed for ever. He therefore shall reign at the right hand of his Father until he has put all his enemies under his feet as a footstool; but the nation and kingdom that have not served him will perish. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 208.

units.la: Vnus autē ex maleficis, qui erant suspensi, conuitiabatur ei, dicens: Si tu es Christus ille, serua teipsum, & nos. Respondens autem alter obiurgauit eum, dicens: Ne tu quidē Deum times, quod in eadem fis, damnatione? Et nos quidem iustē (nam digna factis recipimus) iste verò nihil absurdū fecit. Dixitq; Iesu: Domine, memento mei cum veneris in Regnum tuum. Tum dixit ei Iesus: Amen dico tibi, hodie mecū eris in paradiso. Erat autem quasi hora sexta, & tenebræ factæ sunt super totā terram vsq; ad horā nonam. Et obscuratus est Sol: & aulæum templi scissum est mediū. Cumq; clamasset voce magna Iesus, ait: Pater, in manus tuas depono spiritum meum. Et cum hæc dixisset, expirauit. Cūm vidisset autem Centurio quod factum fuerat, glorificauit Deum, dicens: Verè hic homo iustus erat. Et omnis turba quæ simul ad hoc spectandum accesserat, spectans quæ facta fuerant, verberans pectora sua reuertebatur.
units.tr: Then one of the malefactors who were hanged railed on him, saying: "If thou be Christ, save thyself and us." But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: "Dost not thou even fear God, seeing thou art in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward of our deeds; but this man hath done nothing amiss." And he said unto Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." And Jesus said unto him: "Verily I say unto thee, to day shalt thou be with me in paradise." And it was about the sixth hour, and there was a darkness over all the earth until the ninth hour. And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst. And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." And having said this, he gave up the ghost. When the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying: "Certainly this was a righteous man." And all the multitude that came together to that sight, beholding the things which were done, returned smiting their breasts.

units.la: QVoniam Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, ideo in mundū uenit & in assumpta carne mortuus est, ut peccatores saluos faceret, multa exempla in passionis et mortis suæ historiā incidere oportuit, quæ homines peccatores ab illo non reijci, nō pro meritis suis damnari aut puniri, sed potius beā igne recipi & seruari docerent. Ad hunc ergo scopum referri debent quae de discipulorum contentionibus in ultima Cœna obortis, deq; eorundem infirmitate, fuga & dispersione audiuimus. Huc turpis ille Petri lapsus pertinet, qui illum tertio abnegauit, & quod (ut nuper dictum est) pro illis apud Patrem intercessit, qui ipsum in crucem suffixerunt, & omni opprobriorum genere insectati sunt. At inter huius generis exempla prae aliis memorabilia sunt, quae hoc loco describuntur. Narrat enim Lucas actionem, quae illi cum latronibus intercessit, quorum alterum in ipso mortis articulo ad se conuersum in gratia recepit & saluum fecit. Deinde signa describit, quae eius mortem partim comitata partim secuta sunt, & ut his visis Centurio, qui supplicij illius executioni praerat, una cum multis aliis ex turba prompte scua rectius de illo sentire coeperint, uerae poenitentiae femine concepto, quod postea fructus haud dubie tulit non poenitendos. Quae omnia a nobis eo diligentius considerari debent, quia non obiter modo gratiam Dei nobis commendant, sed totam salutis in illo consequendae rationem una cum uirtute meriti ac mortis eius, ceu in tabula depictam proponunt.
units.tr: Since the Son of God, Jesus Christ, came into the world and died in assumed flesh in order to save sinners, many examples had necessarily to fall into the history of his passion and death, which would teach that sinful men are not rejected by him, nor condemned or punished for their own merits, but rather received by him in blessedness and kept safe. To this aim must be referred what we have heard of the contentions that arose among the disciples at the last supper, and of their weakness, flight and dispersion. To this belongs that shameful fall of Peter, who denied him three times, and also the fact that (as was said recently) he interceded with the Father for those who fastened him to the cross and assailed him with every kind of reproach. But among examples of this kind, those described in this place are especially memorable. For Luke relates the exchange that took place between him and the robbers: he received into grace and saved the one of them who turned to him at the very point of death. Then he describes the signs which accompanied his death, partly during it and partly after it, and how, when these things were seen, the centurion who presided over that execution, together with many others from the crowd, began to judge of him more rightly, having conceived the seed of true repentance, which afterwards undoubtedly bore fruit not to be repented of. All these things must be considered by us the more carefully, because they do not merely commend the grace of God to us in passing, but set before us, as if painted on a tablet, the whole manner of obtaining salvation in him, together with the power of his merit and death.

units.la: Quoad latronum historiam, Matthaeus & Marcus paucis rem expediunt, & eos quoq; illum probris affecisse scribunt. Lucas unum modo tantae impietatis reum facere uidetur, & ideo quod alteri illi narrant, plerisq; per Synecdochen exponunt. At probabilior mihi uidetur eorum sententia, qui initio quidem utrunq; id fecisse, postea autem alterum sceleris poenitentia ductu illius gratia implorauisse putant. In qua sententia Chrysostomus fuisse apparet, qui cum multa mansuetudinis Christi exempla ex ordine recitaret, huius quoq; meminit, quod latronē, qui ipsum paulo ante accusauerat, in paradisum intro duxerit. Est ergo historia haec multis nominibus digna, cuius singulas partes ex ordine uideamus, ubi tamen propter ea, quae in Marco dicta sunt, breuitati studebimus. Prima latronē illum infelicem proponit, cuius impietas quidē narratur, conuersio autem siue poenitentia tacetur: nimirū quòd ea nulla fuerit. Vnus (inquit) ex maleficis, qui erat suspensi, conuitiabatur ei, dicēs: Si tu es Christus ille, serua teipsum & nos. Est hoc animi impij & reprobi argumentū, quādo neq; eiusdē supplicij horribiles cruciatus, linguae petulantiā coercere potuerūt. Et tamen apparet, illū non omnino ignarum fuisse eorū, quae de ipse Israelis, Christo nimirū uenturo dicebantur. Dicit enim: Si tu es Christus ille: Quasi dicat, quē & patres nostri & nos tato iam tempore expectauimus. Et facit hoc ad scelus amplificandū, quòd de promisso illo Seruatore nihil magnificum sentit, sed perinde ac si latronibus impunitate conferre debeat, ab illo opē petit. At hic animo repetere oportet, quod supra audiuimus, Christū inter duos illos latrones medium fuisse suspensum. In eo enim apparet, quae totius humani generis codicio sit, quae ite causa sit, quòd multi a salute excidat, quā illis Christus sponte offert. Etenim latrones istos homines fuisse scelerates, & nunc dignas factis suis poenas exoluisse, ex alterius confessione constat. Atqui eadem est omniū hominum conditio. Nam licet nō omnes latrones, fures, sicarij, proditores & mundi iudicio malefici simus, peccatores tamē sumus, quorū cogitationes ab ineunte aetate malae sunt, & quin singulas horas prauis cupiditatibus abrepti ea facimus et dicimus, quae Deo displicet. Adhaec poenas peccatorū quotidie sentimus: quia quicquid in mundo est morborū, egestatis, seditionū bellorū & periculorū, illud omne ex peccato est. Imò si in nos suo iure Deus uti uelit, nō cruces modò, rotas, gladiū, ardentes rogos & dirissima quaeq; supplicioru tormenta meruimus, sed digni sumus, qui ad aeternos infernalis ignis cruciatus danemur: & ideo sanctissimi quiq; precatur: Ne intres Domine in iudicium cum seruo tuo. Ite: Remitte nobis debita nostra. Vt uerò inter latrones istos medius pendit Christus brachijs ad utrūq; expansis: Ita in medio humani generis ide ille constitutus, ex Zione Apostolos emisit, per quos suae mortis meritu hodie etiā omnibus offert, et quasi expansis ulnis omnes inuitas clamat: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, & ego requie uobis praestabo. Quae ergo causa est, quòd pauciores seruantur, plurimi autē pereunt? Hæc nimirū, quòd pleriq; prioris istius latronis similes, neq; se à Deo puniri & poena dignos esse agnoscūt, neq; ad ipsum conuersi de suis sceleribus poenitentia agunt: In Christo autē nihil praeter ea quae carnis sunt quaerunt, & nisi ea inueniant, mox ei conuitiantur, & mundi infelicis exemplum secuti Euangelium eius proscindunt atq; conculcant. Itaq; damnationis causa ex hominibus est, sicuti per Hoseam Dominus testatur
units.tr: As to the history of the robbers, Matthew and Mark deal with the matter briefly, and they likewise write that both of them reviled him. Luke seems to make only one guilty of such impiety, and so many expositors explain what the others relate of both by synecdoche. But the opinion of those seems more probable to me who think that at first both did so, but that afterwards one of them, moved by repentance for his crime, implored Christ's grace. Chrysostom evidently held this view: when he recited in order many examples of Christ's gentleness, he also mentioned this one, that he led into paradise the robber who had a little before accused him. This history is therefore worthy of many observations, and let us look at its individual parts in order, though here we shall aim at brevity because of what was said in Mark. The first part presents the unhappy robber, whose impiety is indeed narrated, but whose conversion or repentance is passed over, clearly because there was none. "One of the malefactors," it says, "who was hanged, railed on him, saying: If thou be that Christ, save thyself and us." This is a sign of an impious and reprobate mind, since not even the dreadful torments of the same punishment could restrain the wantonness of his tongue. And yet it is clear that he was not wholly ignorant of what was said about the Christ of Israel who was to come. For he says, "If thou be that Christ," as if to say: the one whom our fathers and we have been waiting for so long. And he does this to magnify his crime: he has no lofty thoughts of that promised Saviour, but, as if he owed the robbers impunity, he asks help from him. Here, however, we must recall what we heard above, that Christ was hanged in the middle between those two robbers. For in this it appears what the condition of the whole human race is, and what the reason is why many fall away from the salvation that Christ freely offers them. Indeed, from the confession of the one, it is established that those robbers were wicked men, and had now paid the punishments due to their deeds. Yet the condition of all men is the same. For although we are not all robbers, thieves, assassins, traitors and, in the judgement of the world, malefactors, we are nonetheless sinners, whose thoughts have been evil from our earliest age, and who, carried away by wicked desires every hour, do and say those things which displease God. Moreover, we feel the punishments of sins every day, because whatever disease, want, sedition, war and danger there is in the world, all of it comes from sin. Indeed, if God wished to use his right against us, we have deserved not only crosses, wheels, the sword, burning pyres and the most dreadful torments of every kind of punishment, but we are worthy to be condemned to the eternal torments of infernal fire; and therefore the holiest of men pray: "Enter not into judgement with thy servant, O Lord," and, "Forgive us our debts." But just as Christ hung in the middle between those robbers with his arms stretched out on either side, so he, placed in the middle of the human race, sent out the Apostles from Sion, through whom, by the merit of his death, he offers himself even today to all, and, as with arms outstretched, calls all who are weary and heavy laden to himself: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." What then is the cause that fewer are saved, while very many perish? Surely this: that most men are like that first robber, who neither acknowledge that they are punished by God and deserve punishment, nor turn to him and repent of their sins. Instead they seek nothing in Christ beyond what belongs to the flesh, and if they do not find these things, they soon revile him, and, following the example of this unhappy world, they tear apart and trample underfoot his gospel. Therefore the cause of damnation lies with men, as the Lord testifies through Hosea.

units.la: Quid ergo fieri oportet? Alterū latronē uide, quae secunda huius actionis pars est. Quid uerò ille? Obiurgauit sociū, dicēs: Ne tu quidē Deū times, quādo in eadem sis damnatione? Et nos quidem iustè (nam digna factis recipimus) iste uerò nihil absurdum aut iniquū fecit, &c. Breuis oratio, sed quæ multa continet animi uerè pœnitentis & conuersi argumenta. Primò displicet ei socij impia pe tulantia, & graviter eà corripit, ut salutis sociū habere posset, quem uitæ anteàctæ et sceleru socium habuerat. Et ut hoc facilius impetret, ad uerā pietatis & sapientiæ principiū eū remittit, Dei timorem uidelicet: ita simul innuens, hanc ipsis omnium facinorum antea causam fuisse, quòd Deum non sint reueriti. Deinde præsentis supplicij eum admonet, ut saltem in huius acerbitate Dei iram ipsos punientis agnoscat. Tertiò se illi coniungens sua quoq; peccata fatetur. Nos (inquit) iustè pu nimur, & digna nostris factis præmia recipimus. Quartò præclarum Christo reddit innocentiæ testi monium, & quàmuis illum totius Concilij authoritate damnatum esse, & in eius damnationem Pi latum consensisse sciat, alta tamen & liberauoce clamat: Hic nihil absurdū, iniquum aut indecens fecit. Quod quid aliud erat, quàm Sacerdotes & Seniores populi unà cū Præside iniquitatis & iniu stitiæ summæ accusare? Neq; in his pedem sistit, sed mox ad Christum conuersus ait: Domine, me mento mei cum ueneris in Regnū tuum. Vt Christus fui meminerit petit, nimirum ad gratiā & mi sericordiā eius respiciens, qua Deus ad se couersos respicere solet. Itaq; Deum agnoscit hoc dicendo, & paucis comprehendit, quod Dauid fuius dixit in Psalmis: Memor sis miserationū tuarum ô Do mine, & bonitatis tuæ: quoniā à seculo sunt. Peccatorū adolescentiæ meæ ac sceleum meorum ne sis memor: memor autē mei sis secundum benignitatē tuam, propter bonitatē tuam ô Domine. Eodem igitur, quo olim Dauid, nunc latro iste spiritu precatur. Estq; hoc fidei exemplum, cuius simile num uspiam extet, nescio. Nam Dominū suum agnoscit, quem eiusdem supplicij socių habebat. Regnum ei tribuit, qui iam iam moriturus omniū conuiciis petebatur. Immortalem fatetur, quando ut sui in Regno suo meminerit, orat. Deniq; cùm nihil præter manifesta & horrenda irati Dei argumenta ob oculos sibi posita uideret, de salute tamen sua optimè sperat, & per omnia obstacula in beati illius Regni cōtemplationem penetrat. Hæc ergo illa fides est, quæ ea nobis præsentia sistit, quæ nusquam extare putantur, & coràm demonstrat, quæ nullo humano sensu possunt percipi. Est hoc memorabile exemplū, quo docemur, nunquā Christo testes defuturos esse, qui ersi mundo contemptissimi uideantur, magnæ tamē authoritatis sunt apud Deum, & testimoniū eorum omnibus illis arguendis suffi cit, qui aduersus eum conspirant. Præcipuū autem huius exempli caput est, ratio salutis consequen dæ, quæ hic euidentissimo typo adumbratur, imò perfectè depingitur. Opus est ante omnia generali peccatorū agnitione, quæ quàm illa atrocia & grauia sint, nos edoceat. Quam quia nobis non fugge rit carnis sensus, quæ illis delectari solet, ex Lege petatur oportet. Vbi in primis uidendū est, ne con scientiæ dicta & terrores scurriliter eludere conemur, quibus nos illa intra animos nostros continu cit. Huic accedat necesse est priuata aut peculiaris nostrorum peccatorum agnitio, ne dum de aliis uerba facimus, nobisipsis turpiter & pernitiose blandiamur, quæ maxima est uerę pœnitentiæ re mora. Et quia hic caro tardior est & stupidior, multum proderit iudiciorum Dei exempla obseruā uisse, & ea quidem in primis, quæ nobis frequenter accidunt. Errant in eo multi, quòd fortuita pu tant esse ea, quibus illis aures uellicat Deus, & per quæ ad suorum peccatorū cognitionem atq; pœni tentiam excitari debebant. Accedat his contritio cum publica confessione scelerum et misericordiæ Dei implorationē coniuncta: quæ si ex fide emanet, proculdubio illa remittet Deus, & salutem certò cōsequemur. Hæc illa ratio est salutis, quam sacræ literæ passim docent, & quæ iam inde ab origine rerum infinitis exemplis probata atq; confirmata est. At quia de ea sæpe diximus, & noua subinde dicendi occasio datur, sufficiat nunc summa rerum capita in mentem reuocauisse.
units.tr: What, then, ought to be done? Look at the other thief, which is the second part of this episode. And what did he do? He rebuked his companion, saying: "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? We indeed justly (for we receive what our deeds deserve), but this man has done nothing absurd or wrong, etc." This is a brief speech, but it contains many marks of a truly penitent and converted mind. First, he is displeased with his companion's impious defiance and rebukes him sharply, so that he might gain as a companion to salvation the man whom he had had as a companion in his former life and crimes. And to win him over more easily, he refers him to the true beginning of piety and wisdom, namely the fear of God, thereby hinting at the same time that the cause of all their earlier crimes had been that they did not reverence God. Next, he reminds him of the punishment they now suffer, so that at least in its bitterness he may recognise the anger of God punishing them. Third, by joining himself to him, he confesses his own sins too: "We," he says, "are justly punished, and we receive rewards worthy of our deeds." Fourth, he bears a splendid testimony to the innocence of Christ, and although he knows that Christ was condemned by the authority of the whole council, and that Pilate consented to his condemnation, he cries out boldly and with a loud voice: "This man has done nothing absurd, wrong or unbecoming." What else was this than accusing the priests and elders of the people, together with the governor, of supreme iniquity and injustice? Nor does he stop at these points, but soon turning to Christ he says: "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom." That he asks Christ to remember him shows that he looks to the grace and mercy of Christ, which God is accustomed to show to those who turn to him. So by saying this he acknowledges God, and in a few words he sums up what David said in the Psalms: "Remember your tender mercies, O Lord, and your kindnesses, for they have been from of old. Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; but according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness' sake, O Lord." Therefore the thief now prays in the same spirit in which David once prayed. And this is an example of faith such as I do not know whether anywhere else exists. For he acknowledges his Lord, whom he had as a companion in the same punishment. He ascribes a kingdom to one who was just about to die and was being assailed with the reproaches of all. He confesses him to be immortal, when he prays that he may be remembered in his kingdom. Finally, although he saw nothing before his eyes but the plain and dreadful signs of an angry God, he nevertheless hopes most confidently for his own salvation, and through all obstacles he penetrates to the contemplation of that blessed kingdom. This, then, is the faith which sets before us those things that are thought nowhere to exist, and displays before our eyes what cannot be perceived by any human sense. This is a memorable example, by which we are taught that there will never be lacking witnesses to Christ, who, though they may seem most contemptible to the world, are of great authority with God, and whose testimony is sufficient to convict all those who conspire against him. But the chief point of this example is the way of obtaining salvation, which is here shadowed forth by a most evident type, indeed portrayed perfectly. Above all there is need of a general recognition of sins, which teaches us how atrocious and grave they are. Since the sense of the flesh, which is wont to delight in them, will not allow us to see this, it must be sought from the Law. Here, first of all, we must take care not to try to mock with buffoonery the warnings and terrors of conscience, by which they are driven continually within our minds. To this must necessarily be added a private or particular recognition of our own sins, lest, while we speak of others, we shamefully and destructively flatter ourselves, which is the greatest hindrance to true repentance. And because the flesh here is slower and more dull, it will be of great benefit to have observed the examples of God's judgments, and especially those which happen to us often. Many err in this, in thinking that those things by which God pricks their ears are accidental, and through which they ought to have been stirred up to recognise their sins and to repent. Let there be added to these contrition joined with public confession of wickedness and the imploring of God's mercy: which, if it flows from faith, undoubtedly God will forgive, and we shall certainly obtain salvation. This is the way of salvation which the holy Scriptures teach everywhere, and which from the very beginning of things has been proved and confirmed by countless examples. But since we have often spoken of it, and a fresh occasion for speaking is constantly given, it is enough now to have recalled to mind the chief heads of the matter.

units.la: Facit autē in præsenti ad illius confirmationē ipsius Christi calculus, qui absq; mora latroni re- spondit, dices: Amen dico tibi, hodie mecū eris in paradiso. Est hoc unū ex præcipuis eius dictis, quod eo diligentius expendi & teneri debet, quòd & in causa omniū grauissima, & iam iam moriturus il lud protulit. Et occurrit in eius consideratione primo statim loco admirabilis & plus quàm paterna illius facilitas, qui homine sceleribus multis infamem & capitale supplicii iam cū publica infamia luentem tam benignè in gratia recipit, & neq; uerbis durioribus compellat, neq; quicquā eorū expro brat, quæ prius designarat. Iam enim non corripiendi aut cū illo expostulandi, sed miserum & affli ctum consolandi tempus erat. Non est ergo quòd repulsam ipsi timeamus, modo uera fide ad eū con uersi eius misericordiā imploremus. Simul autem hoc Christi exemplum imitentur doctores, quibus cum peccatoribus res est, quos animis suis contritos, & de salute sua seriò solicitos esse uident: nē
units.tr: Moreover, in the present case the reckoning of Christ himself serves to confirm this, for he, without delay, answered the thief, saying: "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." This is one of his principal sayings, which ought to be weighed and held the more diligently because it was uttered in the gravest of causes and by one who was just about to die. And in considering it, there presents itself at once, in the first place, the wonderful and more than fatherly kindness of him who so graciously receives into grace a man infamous for many crimes and already paying the capital penalty with public disgrace; he neither addresses him with harsher words nor reproaches him with any of the things he had previously set forth. For this was no longer the time to rebuke him or to argue with him, but to console the wretched and afflicted man. There is therefore no reason for us to fear rejection, provided that, converted to him by true faith, we implore his mercy. At the same time, let teachers, who have to deal with sinners whom they see to be broken in spirit and seriously anxious about their salvation, imitate this example of Christ: not to terrify them with untimely quarrels and reproaches, when they must be strengthened by friendly consolation and the promises of grace.

units.la: Christus pardi- disum promitit ad se conuer- so. intempestiuis iurgijs & exprobrationibus eos terreant, quos amica consolatione et gratia promissionibus confortari necesse est. Christus certè hunc nō modo benignè recipit, sed salutē quoq; præsentem pollicetur, perinde ac si quis medicus ægroto iam de vita desperanti dicat: Iamiam valetudini integræ restitueris, ac viues. Ita Dominus cum graui obtestatione huic ait: HODIE mecū eris in paradiso. Ita uero sui meriti uirtute exprimit, quæ tanta est, ut nobis seruandis & tam à pœna quàm culpa liberandis sufficiat. Confirmantur ergo isto exemplo omnes illius promoissines, quibus nostræ salutis certitudo nititur, quales sunt: Amen amen dico uobis, qui audit uerba mea, & credit ei qui misit me, habet uitam æternā: & in iudicium non veniet, sed à morte transfuit in vitā. Itē: Vbi ego sum, illic erit minister meus. Volo Pater, ut ubi sum ego, illic sint quos dedisti mihi. Confutantur ergo hic ualidissimè Pontificij illi calefactores, qui Purgatorij ignis fornaces plus quàm Alchymisticos construxerunt, in quibus animas corporibus solutas à sordibus peccatorum purgari oporteat, priusquam ad Regni cœlestis possessionem & beatorum consortium admittantur. Atqui sanguis filij Dei (clamat Ioannes) nos emundat ab omni peccato. Qui cùm huic latroni purgando sufficiens fuerit, nē nimium iniqui meriti Christi æstimatores sunt, qui illius virtutem nunc inefficaciorem esse fingunt, quæ superstitiosis illis & carbonarijs adminiculis opus habeat. Nobis semper firmum ratumq; maneat hoc nostræ fidei axioma, Christi merito cœlos nobis patefactos esse, nec quicquam obstare, quin ad beatæ immortalitatis sedes eorum animæ colligantur, qui in vera fide & nominis illius invocatione decedunt. Beati mortui (inquit Angelus) qui in Domino moriuntur: Etiam dicit Spiritus: Quoniam requiescunt à laboribus suis. Apocal. 14. cap.
units.tr: Christ promises paradise to the one who turned to him. Christ certainly not only receives this man kindly, but also promises him present salvation, just as if a physician said to a patient who was now despairing of life: "Soon you will be restored to full health and will live." So the Lord, with a solemn assurance, says to him: "TODAY you will be with me in paradise." And by the virtue of his own merit he expresses this, which is so great that it is sufficient for saving us and for freeing us from punishment as well as from guilt. All his promises, on which the certainty of our salvation rests, are therefore confirmed by this example, such as: "Truly, truly I say to you, he who hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life." Again: "Where I am, there my servant will be also." And: "Father, I desire that where I am, there also they whom you have given me may be." Therefore the Papists, those heated stokers who have built the furnaces of Purgatory more elaborately than the alchemists, in which souls released from their bodies must be purged from the filth of sins before they are admitted to possession of the heavenly kingdom and to the fellowship of the blessed, are strongly refuted here. Yet the blood of the Son of God, John cries, cleanses us from all sin. If that blood was sufficient for cleansing this thief, then they are too unjust estimators of the merit of Christ who pretend that his virtue is now less effective, so that it needs those superstitious and charcoal-burner's props. Let this axiom of our faith always remain firm and settled for us: by the merit of Christ heaven has been opened to us, and nothing stands in the way of the souls of those who die in true faith and in the invocation of his name being gathered into the seats of blessed immortality. "Blessed are the dead," says the angel, "who die in the Lord." The Spirit also says: "That they may rest from their labours." Apoc. 14.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad mortis Christi narrationē, quā à signis, quæ eam comitata sunt, Lucas oriditur, quāuis nō omnia recenseat, quæ apud alios habentur. Vsus eorū fuit, q diuinitati simul ac innocentiæ eius testimoniū tulerūt, fructū quoq; et meritū mortis eius adumbrarūt, adhæc Dei iudicium et pœnas denuntiauerūt hostibus eius, de quorū petulantia hucusq; multa audiuimus. Primū inter illa fuit Eclipsis Solis, quæ sub horā sextā, id est, ipso meridie facta toti terrarū orbi tenebras intexit, quæ totis tribus horis durauerūt. Tā diu enim ille inter acutissimos dolores in cruce pendit, ut sui corporis et sanguinis sacrificio pro mūdi peccatis perlitaret. Eclipsim uero illā præter ordinarium naturæ cursum in oppositione Solis & Lunæ factā fuisse alibi ostendimus, ubi ijs quoq; respondum est qui tenebras istas ad Iudæā solam restringūt. Facit autē hoc ad demonstrandū quàm atrox & dirū fuerit scelus istud, quod tunc in Filiū Dei designatū fuit. Sol certè ad indignū hoc sui conditoris supplicū exhorruit, et ne hoc spectaret, facie & radios suos abscondit. Quales ergo putandi sunt hodie, qui adhuc passione eius conuitijs & execrationibus cōspuunt, et quod multò gravius est, illius meritū negāt, imò hostiliter oppugnant? Meminerint autē illi, hic pœnas quoq; denuntiari omnibus, qui id audent facere. Est enim ille Sol iustitiæ, in cuius alis sive radijs (ut Propheta ait) est sanitas. Ergo in tenebris perēat oportet omnes ij, qui ipsum nolūt recipere, et eius lucē fastidiūt. Nā intra conscientias suas miserē anguntur, neq; aliquā diuinæ gratiæ lucē sibi fulgere uident; adhæc post infinitas huius seculi calamitates, quibus distracti oberrāt, in tenebras quoq; exteriores eijciūtur.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the account of Christ's death, which Luke relates together with the signs that accompanied it, though he does not recount all that are found in the others. These signs served to bear witness both to his divinity and his innocence, and also to foreshadow the fruit and merit of his death. Moreover, they announced God's judgment and punishments upon his enemies, of whose wantonness we have heard much so far. The first of these was the eclipse of the sun, which occurred at the sixth hour, that is, at midday itself, and cast darkness over the whole orb of the earth. It lasted for the full three hours, for he hung on the cross for so long amid most acute pains, so that by the sacrifice of his body and blood he might make atonement for the sins of the world. We have shown elsewhere that this eclipse, produced beyond the ordinary course of nature by the opposition of the Sun and Moon, was not confined to Judea, and there we also answered those who restrict that darkness to Judea alone. This serves to demonstrate how atrocious and dire was the crime then committed against the Son of God. Certainly the sun shrank from this unworthy punishment of its own Creator, and hid its face and rays so as not to witness it. What sort of people, then, must we think today are those who even now heap insults and curses upon his passion and, what is much more serious, deny his merit, indeed attack it with hostility? Let them remember that punishments are declared here also against all who dare to do this. For he is that Sun of righteousness, in whose wings or rays (as the Prophet says) there is healing. Therefore all those who are unwilling to receive him and scorn his light must perish in darkness. For they are miserably tormented within their own consciences and see no light of divine grace shining upon them; moreover, after the countless calamities of this age, amid which they wander distracted, they are also cast into outer darkness.

units.la: Alterū signū, cuius Lucas meminit, aulæi aut ueli scissio fuit, quo Sanctū sanctorū ab exteriori parte templi distinguebatur. At priusquā illud scinderetur, Ioannes Christū dixisse scribit, Consummatū est: quo dicto testabatur iā impleta esse, quæcūq; de humani generis redemptione olim promissa & prædicta fuerunt. Erat autē interius illud Sacrariū typus Cœlorū, aut loci illius beati, quem nobis Deus præparauit. Itaq; significabat ista ueli sciccio, abrogatas iā esse Legis ceremonias, & patefactam uiā illam sanctorū, quæ ad Regni cœlestis possessionē nos deducit. At quia Iudaicā rempub. simul & cultū illum Leuiticū durare oportuit usq; ad Christum, qui umbris istis finem impositurus erat, simul testari uoluit Deus, iā tempus illud fatale aduenisse, quo templum cum urbe excindi, cultum & rempub. ista aboleri & euerti oporteat, sicuti olim à Daniele fuerat prædictū. Fiet ergo hæc quoq; grauis comminatio, nihil nimirū posthac reliquum fore, quò Iudæi defendantur et inuentur, si in Christū ingrati esse pergant. Et debet hoc ad se transferre etiā illi, inter quos Ecclesiæ suæ & Euangelio locū fecit Deus. Nam ut Iudæorū respub. salua fuit propter cultū illum typicū, quàm diu eius usus erat aliquis, eadem autē mox euersa est, quando illum in Christi contumeliā mordicus retinere noluerūt: Ita respublicas hodie etiā cōservat Deus, ut Ecclesiæ & Verbo suo hospitiū præbeat: quod fi idfacere detrectant, & Christū eiectū uolunt, eadē omni præsidio spoliatæ pereunt. Exempla huius rei multa extant in historijs, & hodie quādam uidimus, quæ utinā omnes diligentius expenderent.
units.tr: The second sign Luke mentions was the tearing of the veil, which separated the Holy of Holies from the outer part of the temple. But before the veil was torn, John writes that Christ said, "It is finished." By that word he testified that everything promised and foretold of old concerning the redemption of the human race had now been fulfilled. That inner sanctuary was a type of heaven, or of that blessed place which God has prepared for us. So the tearing of the veil signified that the ceremonies of the Law were now abrogated and that the way into the holy place was opened, which leads us to possession of the heavenly kingdom. But because the Jewish commonwealth and that Levitical worship had to endure until Christ, who was to put an end to those shadows, God also wished to testify at the same time that the fated time had come when the temple and city were to be destroyed, and that worship and commonwealth were to be abolished and overthrown, as Daniel had foretold long before. So this too is a grievous threat: nothing at all will remain thereafter to which the Jews may flee for protection and be found, if they persist in being ungrateful to Christ. And this threat ought also to be applied to those among whom God has given a place to his Church and Gospel.
