For just as the Jewish commonwealth was preserved because of that typical worship, as long as there was some use of it, but was soon overthrown when they refused to cling to it to the reproach of Christ, so God now preserves commonwealths so that they may provide a home for his Church and Word. But if they refuse to do this and wish Christ cast out, they perish, stripped of all protection. Many examples of this are found in histories, and today we have seen some, which I wish everyone would weigh more carefully.

units.la: Cæterum eodē momento, quo aulæu istud scissum fuit, Christus quoq; expirauit, & ne hoc quidem absq; miraculo. Nam præter commune more morientiū, qui uel paulatim sensibus deficiūt, uel subita morbi ui obruti nihil loqui, & uix singultire possunt, illis alta uoce exclamauit: Pater, in manus tuas depono spiritū meum. Fuit ergo uox ista uere morientis (quando morte anima & corporis dissolutionem, aut illius ab hoc discessum esse, philosophi definierunt) at eadem diuinæ uirtutis quoq; argumentum est, & illum animā suā sponte pro nostra salute deposuisse testatur, sicuti antea se factur ū prædixerat. At cū in ipso etiam mortis articulo se huius uictorem & dominum esse tam aperto indicio ostendat, minimè dubitare nos conuenit, quin uerus ac potentissimus Seruator sit, qui & nos in ipsa morte tueri possit. Adhæc de animarū nostrarū conditione nos suo exemplo admonet. Sunt hæ spiritus, si essentia earum spectes, quod Moses non obscure docuit, de Adami creatione inter alia dicens: Inflauit Dominus in nares eius spiritū uitalem, & factus est homo in animam uiuentem. Et in præsenti Christus, quem animam humanā unā cum corpore assumpsisse, alibi demonstrauimus, illam spiritū dicit. Est autē spiritus ille immortalis, qui cum corpore nequaquā extinguitur aut moritur. Absurdū enim foret, illum tū corpore mori, cuius beneficio istud uuiit. A corpore autē discedens ad suum locum colligitur: piorum quidem & credentium spiritus ad Deū, qui illos dedit: impiorum uero ad sui similes, ut cum his æternùm crucientur. Itaq; quando nobis hinc migrandum est, non Angelis, nō Diuis, multò minus autē Monachis aut Sacrificulis, sed uni Deo Patri per Iesum Christum animas nostras commendare debemus, qui ad se collectas seruabit, ut æternum uiuant & gaudeant.
units.tr: At the very moment the veil was torn, Christ also expired, and not even this without a miracle. For beyond the common manner of dying men, who either gradually lose their senses or, overwhelmed by a sudden violence of disease, can say nothing and scarcely gasp, he cried out with a loud voice: "Father, into your hands I commend my spirit." So this was truly the voice of one dying (since philosophers define death as the dissolution of soul and body, or the soul's departure from the body), yet it is also a proof of divine power, and testifies that he laid down his soul of his own accord for our salvation, as he had foretold before. And since at the very point of death he shows himself by such a clear sign to be its conqueror and lord, we ought not in the least to doubt that he is the true and most powerful Saviour, who is able to keep us safe even in death itself. Moreover, by his example he admonishes us about the condition of our souls. If you look at their essence, they are spirits, as Moses taught not obscurely when, speaking among other things of the creation of Adam, he said: "The Lord breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul." And so Christ, whom we have shown elsewhere to have assumed a human soul together with the body, here calls it spirit. That spirit is immortal and is by no means extinguished or dies together with the body. For it would be absurd that that should die with the body by whose benefit the body lives. Departing from the body, it is gathered to its own place: the spirits of the pious and believers indeed to God, who gave them; but those of the impious to their like, to be tormented with them for ever. Therefore, when we must depart hence, we ought to commend our souls not to angels, not to saints, and much less to monks or sacrificing priests, but to God the Father alone through Jesus Christ, who will keep them gathered to himself, that they may live and rejoice for ever.

units.la: Porrò expirāte Dei Filio, ingēti & horribili motu terra concussa est, adeò ut & petrę dissilierint, & monumenta multa aperta sint, in quibus multorū corpora post eius resurrectionē reuixerunt, & apparuerunt multis in urbe Hierosolyma. Arguunt hæc quoq; flagitij in illū commissi indignitatē, & simul nobis nostrā duritiem exprobrant. Non potuit terra absq; horrore indignā sui creatoris necem cernere, & sub tanti sceleris pondere concremuit. At quàm multi sunt, qui etiāsi ista audiant, et ipsi de his loquantur, nihil tamen commouentur, ut uel de sceleribus commissis pœnitentiā agant, uel in posterum se illi gratos præbeant? Taceo nunc eos, qui per Christi mortem, passionem, uulnera & crucem horribili impietate deierant: eos item qui quasi ista Dei Filius frustra passus sit, se sibi ipsis sufficere sibi persuadent, & in suorū operum meritis salutis suæ fiduciā repositā habent. Sunt hi ingratissimi homines, sub quibus terrā tremere & indignari non mirū est, quando ingratitudine nihil sceleratius, nihil à natura alienius esse constat. Simul autem isto prodigio mortis suæ fructū & admirabilem Euangelicæ prædicationis effectū Dominus declarare uoluit. In illa enim uita salus quæ nostra continetur, quod ipse cū Martha loquens testatur: Ego sum resurrectio et uita, &c. Per hanc uerò totum orbem terrarum concuti & mutari oportuit, adeoq; huic omnia cedere oportuit, quæcunq; illius cursui obstare uidebantur. Nec omnino à scopo aberrabimus opinor, si terræmotu isto pijs uaticinium illud in mentem reuocatum & confirmatū fuisse dicamus, quo Zorobabelem olim in tem pli ædificatione laborantem Deus per Haggaum consolatus est, dicens: Adhuc unum modicum hoc, & ego commouebo cœlum & terram, & commouebo omnes gentes, & uenient, desiderium omnium gentium. Et rursus: Ego concutio cœlum & terram, & euertam solium regnorum, & perdam robur regnorum gentium, &c. Impleta sunt hæc Apostolorum temporibus, quando totius orbis mutatio facta est, quæ omnes gentes concussit, & quam nè Imperij quidem Romani potentia impedire potuit. Et durat hic Euangelicæ prædicationis effectus etiam hodie, quod publici motus & periculosæ regnorum mutationes abinde testantur. Non agnoscunt autē pleriq; hanc Christi uirtutem, & cùm ipsi aduersus hunc impiè insurgant suaq; insolentia seditiones atq; turbas excitent, eō nomine Euangelij doctrinam diffamant. Sed non deerit causæ suæ Christus, qui ut quotidie suorum iudiciorum specimina edit aduersus rebelles istos: ita adhuc semel totam hanc mundi fabricam concutiet glorioso suo aduentu, quando diabolum & huius seruos æternæ damnationi addicet.
units.tr: Moreover, when the Son of God expired, the earth was shaken by a huge and horrible motion, so that even rocks split and many tombs were opened, and the bodies of many who had died rose again after his resurrection and appeared to many in the city of Jerusalem. These things also show the outrageousness of the crime committed against him, and at the same time reproach us for our hardness. The earth could not look upon the unworthy death of its Creator without horror, and it trembled beneath the weight of so great a crime. But how many are there who, although they hear these things and speak of them themselves, are nonetheless not moved either to repent of the sins they have committed or to show themselves thankful to him in future? I pass over for now those who have sworn by Christ's death, passion, wounds and cross with horrible impiety; likewise those who persuade themselves, as if the Son of God suffered in vain, that they are sufficient for themselves and place their hope of salvation in the merits of their own works. These are most ungrateful men, and it is no wonder that the earth trembles and is indignant at them, since nothing is more wicked than ingratitude and nothing more alien to nature. At the same time, by this prodigy the Lord wished to declare the fruit of his death and the admirable effect of Evangelical preaching. For in that life which he himself describes, speaking with Martha, is contained our salvation: "I am the resurrection and the life," etc. Through this the whole orb of the earth had to be shaken and changed, and everything that seemed to stand in the way of its course had to yield to it. Nor, I think, shall we wander far from the goal if we say that by this earthquake that prophecy was recalled to the minds of the godly and confirmed, by which God of old consoled Zerubbabel, labouring over the building of the temple, through Haggai, saying: "Yet once, a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, and I will shake all nations, and they shall come, the desire of all nations." And again: "I shake heaven and earth, and I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms and destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations," etc. These things were fulfilled in the times of the Apostles, when a change of the whole world took place, shaking all nations, and which the power even of the Roman Empire could not prevent. This effect of Evangelical preaching endures even today, as public upheavals and dangerous changes of kingdoms bear witness. Yet most do not acknowledge this power of Christ, and while they rise impiously against him and stir up seditions and tumults through their insolence, they defame the doctrine of the Gospel on that account. But Christ will not be wanting to his cause. As he daily gives examples of his judgments against those rebels, so once more he will shake this whole fabric of the world by his glorious coming, when he consigns the devil and his servants to eternal damnation.

units.la: Reliquū est, ut uideamus, quis signorū istorū fructus, & ut morte illius affecti fuerint pleriq; ex spectatoribus. Inter hos primus est Centurio, qui Pilati nomine toti huic negotio præfuit. Is cùm uidisset quod factū fuerat, glorificauit Deū, dicens: Verè hic homo iustus erat. Marcus plus quiddam annotauit, quòd nimirũ Filiũ Dei quoq; esse confessus fuerit. Matthæus eiusdem confessionis socios facit milites quoq;, qui ei adfuerunt. De reliqua populi multitudine Lucas addit: Et omnis turba, quæ simul ad hoc spectandum accesserat, spectans quæ facta fuerat, uerberans pectora sua reuertebatur. Ecce quàm facile sit Christo suum honorem & gloriam tueri, hostium autem calumnias confutare? Paulò ante latronis testimonio ad hoc usus est. Nunc uerò, nequis illud contemnat, Centurionem & milites, imò populum totum mouet, ut de ipso testentur. Sunt autem hæc præclara diuinæ bonitatis exempla, qui Filij sui preces ita ratas habuit, ut apertos eius hostes et adhuc illius sanguine madentes, soluerit eiusdem testes atq; præcones fieri. Extant huius generis multa alia, inter quæ memorabile admodum est, quo in Paulo habemus, quem ex immani lupo pastorem gregis sui fecit fidelissimum. Nos autem horum exemplo admoniti discamus non contemnere signa, quæ præter naturæ ordinem fiunt. Si enim bonus paterfamilias suæ domus ordinem nõ turbat aut immutat absq; graui causa, multò minus hoc de Deo nos suspicari debemus, qui omnia optimè ac sapientissimè gubernat. Viderunt hoc olim Ethnici, quos prodigijs & ostentis sæpe territos & excitatos fuisse legimus, ut de Dijs suis placandis cogitarent. Quantò magis ergo nos hodie ijs commoueri decet, quæ euentura esse nouissimis temporibus, Christus ipse nuper admonuit? Sed est deplorata plane nostri seculi durities, qua fit, ut quamuis multa quotidie fiant, quæ periculosas rerum mutationes præ foribus adesse portendunt, & ad pœnitentiam Deus totum mundum magnis sui Verbi clamoribus excitet, pauci tamen ista ad se pertinere cogitent. At hoc quoq; futurum esse Dominus prædixit. Neminem ergo ista multorum securitas offendat, quin potius expergiscantur qui dormiunt, & ad gloriosum illum diem sese præparent, quo Christus Iesus uenier, ut nos in Regnum suum cælestè transferat. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: It remains for us to see what fruit these signs bore, and how many of the spectators were affected by his death. Foremost among these is the centurion, who had charge of the whole affair on behalf of Pilate. When he had seen what had happened, he glorified God, saying: "Truly this man was righteous." Mark noted something more: that he also confessed him to be the Son of God. Matthew makes the soldiers who were present with him companions in the same confession. Of the rest of the crowd Luke adds: "And all the multitude that came together to that sight, beholding what was done, returned beating their breasts." See how easily Christ maintains his own honour and glory, and refutes the slanders of his enemies! A little before, he used the testimony of the thief for this purpose. Now, lest anyone should despise it, he moves the centurion and the soldiers, indeed the whole people, to bear witness about him. These are remarkable examples of divine goodness, which so honoured the prayers of his Son that it made his open enemies, still dripping with his blood, witnesses and heralds of the same Son. Many other examples of this kind exist, among which is that very memorable one in Paul, whom he made from a savage wolf the most faithful shepherd of his flock. As for us, admonished by these examples, let us learn not to despise the signs that happen beyond the order of nature. For if a good householder does not disturb or alter the order of his house without serious cause, we ought much less to suspect this of God, who governs all things most excellently and wisely. The heathen saw this long ago; we read that they were often terrified and stirred by portents and omens, so that they thought about appeasing their gods. How much more, then, ought we to be moved today by those things which Christ himself lately warned us are to happen in the last times? But the hardness of our age is plainly desperate, with the result that, although many things happen every day which portend dangerous changes at our very doors, and although God by the great outcries of his Word rouses the whole world to repentance, few nevertheless think that these things concern them. Yet the Lord also foretold that this would happen. Let no one, therefore, be offended by the security of the many; rather, let those who sleep wake up and prepare themselves for that glorious day on which Christ Jesus will come to transfer us into his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 209.

units.la: Stabant autẽ omnes noti eius procul, & mulieres quæ erant eũ cõ secutæ à Galilæa, uidētes ista. Tum ecce vir nomine Ioseph, Senator, vir bonus ac iustus (qui nõ suffragatus fuerat cõsilio & facto eorum) ex Arimathæa ciuitate Iudæorum, qui expectabat & ipse Regnum Dei. Hic (inquam) adiens Pilatũ, petijt corpus Iesu. Et detractum inuoluit sindone, posuitq; illud in monumento, quod erat ex lapide excisum, in quo nondū quisquam positus fuerat. Porrò dies erat Parasceues, & Sabbati dies succedebat. Subsecutæ etiā mulieres, quæ cum eo venerāt ex Galilæa, spectarūt monumentum, & quomodo positũ esset corpus eius. Reuersæ verò parauerunt aromata & vnguenta: ac Sabbato quidē quieuerunt, secundum mandatum.
units.tr: And all his acquaintances stood afar off, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things. And behold, a man named Joseph, a councillor, a good and just man (who had not consented to their counsel and deed), of Arimathea, a city of the Jews, who himself also waited for the kingdom of God. This man, going to Pilate, asked for the body of Jesus. And he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid it in a tomb hewn out of rock, in which no one had yet been laid. Now it was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin. The women also who had come with him from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments; but on the Sabbath they rested, according to the commandment.

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster, Iesus Christus, cùm iam mortis hora appropinquaret, precationi suæ, quam tunc ardentissimam habuit, hunc statum & scopũ præfixit: Pater glorifica Filiũ tuum, ut & Filius tuus glorificet te. Quia autem dilectus ille Filius est, in quo Patri complacuit, ita ab eo est exauditus, ut mox in ipso mortis articulo eius gloria magis magisque elucere coeperit, cùm adhuc in cruce infami penderet. Diuinæ enim uirtutis ac maiestatis effecta sunt, quòd latroni se inuocanti paradisum confert, quòd Soli suam lucem eripit, quòd uelum templi medium disrumpens ea omnium oculis subijcit, quæ hactenus spectare nefas fuerat, quòd terram totam concutit, petras dissecat, sepulchra recludit, & mortuos in vitam restituit: quòd deniq; Centurionis & militum linguas soluit in suas laudes, populi item animos ita confortat, ut nihil ueriti suos principes, dolorem, quem ex eius morte conceperant, publico luctu testentur. Debet ad hunc quoq; scopum eius sepultura referri, quam gloriosam & magnificam fore, olim Isaias prædixerat, & in qua non levia argumenta apparent, quæ illum in corda & voluntates hominum ius atq; imperium habere ostendunt. Nobis autem omnium istorum hic usus esse debet, ut fidem nostram aduersus crucis scandalum atq; ignominiam confirment: neue dubitemus, illum nostram quoq; memoriam tueri posse & velle, si ipsi fideles simus. Porrò sepulturæ historiam hoc ordine Lucas narrat: Primò testes tam huius quàm mortis eius producit. Deinde de eius præcipuo authore disserit, et quid is fecerit, docet. Postremò quædam adijcit de instituto mulierum, quæ ipsum diu multumq; secutæ fuerunt. Ad primū caput hæc pertinent: Stabant autē omnes noti eius procul, & mulieres quæ erat eum consecutæ à Galilæa, uidentes ista. Inter notos eius possumus cognatos numerare, qui alibi phrasi Hebraica fratres dicuntur; amicos item priuatos, quos illum aliquos habuisse scimus, inter quos Lazarus Bethanien⁠sis cum sororibus & Simon Leprosus præcipui fuerunt. De mulieribus istis cap. 8. est dictum, ubi aliquarum nomina ponuntur, deq; eis dicitur, quòd illum suis facultatibus aluerint. Hi simul omnes procul steterunt, & oculati testes omnium factî sunt, quæ tam in cruce quam in sepulcro cum illo sunt gesta. Quod ego singulari diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio factum fuisse dico. Nam necesse erat, ut illum reuera mori ac sepeliri uiderent, ut certior & firmior postea apud illos esset fides resurrectionis. Exhibent præterea isti nobis elegante & dulcissimæ consolationis plenu Ecclesiæ typu, quo quæ eius in terris conditio sit admonemur, quidq; eos deceat, qui illi semel nomen dederunt. Pendet in cruce Dominus inter latrones, & post omnis generis ludibria atq; opprobria animâ quoq; Deo reddidit, & uere mortuus est. Idem tamen gregem suum, qui totus fere ex hominibus peregrinis constabat, obscuris ite & contemptis, tunc quoq; colligere & inter medios carnifices hostesq; suos acerrimos tueri potuit. Et sane, si hoc penitius inspiciamus, non sine miraculo factu esse patebit, quòd isti inter Pharisæorum insidias, Sacerdotum proditorias artes, furentis populi clamores, militum item crudelissimorum petulantiam hucusq; seruati sunt, & nunc mortem atque sepulcrum eius tuto spectare possunt. Quid, quòd Ioannes intimus ille & dilectus discipulus, cū Virgine matre sub ipsa cruce constitit, neque ullam ab aliquo iniuriam passus est? Eo autem exemplo docere voluit Dominus, neminem per secutorum minas atq; conatibus terreri debere, neq; etiam Ecclesiarum dissipationibus offendi: quia facile ipsi sit suos sub crucis uexillo colligere, & in medio hostium suorum seruare. Nam quod hic factum est, sæpe aliàs factitatum esse constat, quando Patriarchæ in crudeli Chananæorum gente, filii Israel in Ægypto, in Assyria & Babylone inter Barbaros, Deiueraq; religionis hostes, habitauerunt. Et hodie multa fiunt passim, quæ nos in hac fiducia confirmare possunt.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, when the hour of his death was now at hand, set this goal and aim for his prayer, which he then offered most fervently: "Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you." Because that beloved Son is the one in whom the Father is well pleased, he was so heard by him that, at the very moment of his death, his glory began to shine more and more, even while he still hung on the infamous cross. For they were effects of divine power and majesty: that he granted paradise to the thief who called upon him; that he took away the light from the sun; that, tearing the veil of the temple in two, he laid open to everyone's eyes those things which until then it had been unlawful to look upon; that he shook the whole earth, split the rocks, opened the tombs, and restored the dead to life; and finally that he loosed the tongues of the centurion and the soldiers to praise him, and so strengthened the hearts of the people that they, not fearing their rulers at all, bore witness by public mourning to the grief they had conceived at his death. His burial too should be referred to this same goal, which Isaiah had long before foretold would be glorious and splendid, and in which appear no slight proofs that he has right and dominion over the hearts and wills of men. But for us the whole use of all these things should be this: that they confirm our faith against the scandal and shame of the cross, and that we should not doubt that he can and will also keep our memory, if we ourselves are faithful. Now Luke narrates the history of the burial in this order. First he produces witnesses both of this burial and of his death. Then he discusses its chief author and teaches what he did. Lastly, he adds some things about the practice of the women who had followed him long and faithfully. To the first head belong these words: "And all his acquaintances stood afar off, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things." Among his acquaintances we may count his kinsmen, who elsewhere are called brethren in Hebrew idiom; likewise his private friends, of whom we know he had several, among whom Lazarus of Bethany with his sisters and Simon the leper were the most prominent. About these women there was mention in chapter 8, where some of their names are given, and it is said of them that they supported him from their means. All these stood together at a distance, and became eyewitnesses of everything done both on the cross and at the sepulchre. I say this was done by a singular counsel of divine providence. For it was necessary that they should really see him die and be buried, so that their faith in the resurrection might afterwards be more certain and firm. Moreover, these people present us with a most elegant image of the Church, full of the sweetest consolation, by which we are reminded of what its condition is on earth, and what befits those who have once given their name to him. The Lord hangs on the cross between thieves, and after every kind of mockery and reproach he also gave up his spirit to God, and truly died. Yet the same Lord was able, even then, to gather his flock, which consisted almost entirely of foreigners, obscure and despised, and to keep it safe in the midst of his executioners and most bitter enemies. Indeed, if we look into this more closely, it will be plain that it was not without a miracle that these people have been preserved, amid the snares of the Pharisees, the treacherous arts of the priests, the raging clamours of the people, and the wanton cruelty of the most savage soldiers, and can now safely behold his death and tomb. And what of the fact that John, that intimate and beloved disciple, stood with the Virgin his mother beneath the very cross, and suffered no injury from anyone? By this example the Lord wished to teach that no one ought to be terrified by the threats and attempts of persecutors, nor be offended by the scattering of churches, because it is easy for him to gather his own under the banner of the cross and keep them safe in the midst of their enemies. For what happened here is known to have happened often at other times as well: when the patriarchs dwelt among the cruel Canaanite nation, when the sons of Israel dwelt in Egypt, in Assyria and Babylon among barbarians and enemies of the true religion. And even today many things happen everywhere which can confirm us in this confidence.

units.la: Interim obseruabis, quòd istos procul stetisse scribitur, cùm Ioannes & Maria mater Domini cum sorore sua & Maria Magdalena (ut paulò ante diximus) sub cruce steterint, quod uel fidei fortioris uel dilectionis ardentioris fuit argumentum. Ex eo enim patet non eadem mensura fidem eiusq; dona à Domino distribui, sed (quod Paulus ad Corinth. prolixè docet) discrimina donorum & minoris atq; facultatum esse. Quod diligenter tenere prodest, ne uel ex abundantia donorum superbiendi, uel ex eorundem defectu aliis inuidendi occasionem arripiamus. Nam etsi ista discrimina manifesta sint, idem tamen est Spiritus, idem Dominus, idem Deus efficiens ista omnia in quibusuis. Et plurimum insolentes sunt, qui aliquos præ se contemnunt, quos longius stare uident, si quando crucis periculum imminet. Cur enim de eo desperes, qui eminus licet, tamen in Christi respicit, & eius contemplatione delectatur? Prodest certè hunc confirmare Deus, ut in melius proficiat. Et frequenter uidemus, eos, qui aliquando uix eminus pugnabant, postea propius cum hostibus Christi congressos uictoriam & præclaram martyrij coronam reportauisse: alios item turpiter succubuisse, qui prius præ aliis feruere putabantur. Exemplo nobis sit Petrus, qui in horto cum armata militum cohorte congressi ausus, paulò post ad pontificias prunas tepefactus Christum turpiter abnegauit. E contra mulieres ista, quarum aliquæ nunc eminus spectarunt, tertio mox die ad sepulchrum exire ausæ discipulis præ metu latitantibus, primæ Dominum resurrexisse resciuerunt, & resurrectionis testes atq; præconnes factæ sunt. Nemo igitur temere de aliis iudicet, discant potius omnes perseuerantiæ Christianæ exemplum imitari, quod in istis proponitur. Amarunt Christum & coluerunt, cùm res eius florerent, & miraculis clarus esset. Eundem adhuc amant & colunt, neq; eos motus ille ingens, qui in eo capiendo factus est, neq; mortis periculum, neque crucis ignominia abterrere potuerunt, quò minus perstent. Et hoc illud est, quod à discipulis suis Christus requirit, quando eos demum beatos fore ait, qui in finem usq; perseuerauerint. Nam ut constantia opus est in omnibus, quæ cum laude debent perficere ita maximè in iis, quæ ad fidem & salutis æternæ negotium spectant: quia ut non solum uiuamus, sed rursus moriamur Deus suo iure à nobis exigit.
units.tr: Meanwhile you will observe that these are written as standing afar off, whereas John and Mary the mother of the Lord, with her sister and Mary Magdalene (as we said a little above), stood beneath the cross; and this was a proof either of stronger faith or of more ardent love. For from this it is clear that faith and its gifts are not distributed by the Lord in the same measure, but (as Paul teaches at length to the Corinthians) there are differences of gifts, of greater and lesser ability. It is useful to hold this carefully, so that we do not seize the occasion either of pride from an abundance of gifts, or of envy toward others from their lack. For although these differences are plain, it is nonetheless the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God who works all these things in each one. And those are very arrogant who despise others in comparison with themselves, when they see them standing farther off whenever the danger of the cross threatens. For why should you despair of one who, though at a distance, nevertheless looks upon Christ and delights in contemplating him? God certainly is able to strengthen such a person so that he may grow for the better. And we often see that those who once hardly fought at a distance afterwards, engaging more closely with the enemies of Christ, have carried off the victory and the glorious crown of martyrdom; and others again have shamefully given way, who were formerly thought to burn with zeal beyond the rest. Let Peter be an example to us: he, who dared to meet the armed cohort of soldiers in the garden, a little later, having been cooled by the high priest's coals, shamefully denied Christ. On the other hand, these women, some of whom now watched from a distance, ventured to go out to the sepulchre on the third day after, while the disciples were hiding for fear; they were the first to learn that the Lord had risen, and were made witnesses and heralds of the resurrection. Therefore let no one rashly judge others; rather let all learn to imitate the pattern of Christian perseverance set before us in these women. They loved and honoured Christ when his affairs were flourishing and he was famous for his miracles. They still love and honour him, and neither that great tumult which arose in seizing him, nor the danger of death, nor the shame of the cross has been able to terrify them so that they would not persist. And this is what Christ requires of his disciples, when at last he says that they will be blessed who persevere to the end. For constancy is needed in all things which ought to be carried through with praise, but most of all in those which concern faith and the business of eternal salvation: because God, by his own right, requires of us not only that we live, but that we also die again.

units.la: In tota autem hac actione hoc quoq; non ostenderet, obseruari debet, quòd etsi mulieres in re sancta & pissima occupatæ fuerint, sui tamen decori memores, procul steterunt, non autem pudore posito sese medijs uiris ingesserunt. Eo exemplo illarum leuitas atq; impudentia arguitur, quæ discurrentibus uagis gaudent, uirorum colloquia & consuetudine petulanter quærunt, & ijs etiam spectaculis non sine
units.tr: Throughout this whole action we should also observe this: although the women were occupied with a holy and pious task, they remained mindful of their modesty and stood at a distance, and did not, casting aside shame, thrust themselves in among the men. By that example the lightness and shamelessness of those women are condemned, who delight in roaming about, seek out the conversation and company of men wantonly, and push themselves without restraint into those gatherings and spectacles where their sex should have kept them back.

units.la: 1.Cor.13. cōrentione sese intrudunt, à quibus sui sexus reuerentia illas reuocare debebat: qualia sunt, in quibus uel turpia & impudica multa fiunt & dicuntur, quæ bonos mores offendunt, uel etiā cū credulitate coniuncta sunt, à qua eas natura alienas esse uoluit. Possunt deniq; cōfutari hoc facto omnes, qui sub religionis prætextu faciunt, quæ à uocatione ipsorum aliena sunt: ut qui parentibus debita officia negant, ne uotum ordini suo factum violent: qui relictis uxoribus & liberis per omnes terras discurrūt, ut apud truncos & saxa peccatorum remissionem inueniant: qui cum coniugibus diuortia faciunt, ut sacrifici aut monachi fiant: qui deniq; deposito magistratu et Reipub. cura, ad quam uocati sunt di uinitus, sacris initiantur. Quid enim horū à nobis requirit Dominus? Quid huius iste iussit? Damnantur, qui partem sui officij maliti​osè negligunt, & tu te Deo probari arbitraris, si stationem tuam omnino deseras? Nec est quod religionis prætextu te pallies, quando hæc omnem ætatem conditionem & uitæ genus decet, & pietatis summa in obedientia consistit, quam Deus per prophetam omnibus sacrificijs præstantiorem esse testatur.
units.tr: 1.Cor.13. Such gatherings are those where much that is shameful and immodest is said and done, which offends good morals, or which are bound up with credulity, from which nature wished women to be free. Finally, by this deed all can be refuted who, under the pretext of religion, do what is foreign to their calling: those who deny the duties owed to their parents, lest they break a vow made to their order; those who leave their wives and children and wander through all lands, seeking forgiveness of sins at tree trunks and stones; those who divorce their wives so that they may become priests or monks; and those who, laying down the magistracy and the care of the commonwealth to which God has called them, are initiated into sacred rites. For what of these does the Lord require of us? What did he command in this way? Those who maliciously neglect part of their duty are condemned, and do you think you please God if you abandon your station altogether? Nor is there any reason for you to cloak yourself in the pretext of religion, since these things befit every age, condition and way of life, and the sum of piety consists in obedience, which God through the prophet declares to be better than all sacrifices.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad præcipuū sepulturæ Christi authorē, qui in tota ista actione primas tenuit. Fuit is Iosephus, patria Arimathæus, homo diues (quod Matthæus annotauit) ordinis Senatorij, honestus quoad uitā & mores, iustus autē quoad munus Senatorium: quod ut multis haud dubiè exemplis sæpe aliàs declarauit, ita in Christi causa iustitiæ specimen dedit singulare, quando non consensit illorum consilio, qui innocentem & bene de omnibus meritū damnauerunt. Vbi ego eum non aliqua dissimulatione (ut ignaui solent) usum esse, aut emanissse putauerim, ne quid in causa odij & inuidiæ plena dicere aut facere cogeretur: sed procul dubiò in illo defendendo officiū fecit, et cum se nihil proficere uideret, aduersus iniquam damnationis eius sententiam publicè protestatus est, ut omnibus uulgo constaret, eum illi nequaquam consensisse. Addit his uirtutibus Ioannes quod præcipuum est, nimirum quòd discipulus Iesu fuerit, & hoc cum eo conuenit quòd in præsenti Regnum Dei expectā uisse dicitur: qua locutione supra Simeonis quoq; fidem & pietatem Lucas cōmendauit. Solent enim Prophetæ totū humanæ redemptionis ac salutis negotiū, cuius authorem faciunt Messiā, sub regni parabola describere, idq; Dei Regnū dicūt, quia in eo totū consistit, ut destructo diaboli regno Deus in nobis regnet suo Verbo & Spiritu, & nos aliquando Regni eius cœlestis & æterni hæredes efficiamur. Qui ergo illo tempore Regnum Dei expectabant, quando res Iudæorum afflictissimæ erant, & uix aliqua ueterum promissionum uestigia extabant, eorum fidem eximiam & constantem fuisse oportet. Qui uerò hac spe & expectatione suffulti Christum audiebant, & eius erant discipuli, hi eo ipso testabantur, quòd hunc promissum illū humani generis Seruatorem esse agnoscerent. Fides ergo uirtutum illarum pulcherrimarū, quas modò uidimus, causa fuit: quæ etsi aliquandiu latuisset, quando Iosephus adhuc metu impeditus occultè modò Christum conuenit (quod de Nicodemo quoque & aliis nonnullis principibus Ioannes annotauit) nunc tamen aperte se prodit, ut plus omnibus illis audeat, qui antea illum publicè professi fuerat. Nam ut Marcus scribit, animo magna fiducia pleno ad Pilatum ingressus corpus Iesu ad sepulturam honorificam postulauit. Quod quid aliud erat, quàm cum Præside omnes eos iniquitatis damnare, qui illū ad mortem damnauerant, aut eius damnationi subscripserant? Fuit igitur postulatio ista admodum periculosa, & multas alias rationes caro suggerebat, quæ tutiores uideri poterant: ut nimirum obseruato diligenter loco, quo corpus abiceretur, id noctu receptū sepulturæ mandaret, aut cum Centurione de eo sibi reddendo pacisceretur, & pecunijs illud redimeret. Sed nihil istorum tentare uoluit, cum iam cum Christi non puderet am plius, & omnibus testatam esse uellet fidem suam, qua eum colebat. Nec defuit pio conatui Deus, qui & Pilati animum flexit, ut facilè consentiret petitioni non minus piæ quàm iustæ, & simul Nicodemum excitauit, ut facinoris huius longè pulcherrimi socium sese præberet: ut Ioannes scriptum reliquit, qui & ipse istorum omnium testis fuit oculatus.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the chief author of Christ's burial, who held the first place in the whole action. This was Joseph, a native of Arimathea, a rich man (as Matthew noted), of the senatorial order, upright in his life and conduct, and just in his senatorial office. As he had often shown in many undoubted instances at other times, so in the cause of Christ he gave a singular example of justice, when he did not consent to the counsel of those who condemned an innocent man who had deserved well of all. Here I do not think he acted with any dissimulation (as cowards usually do), or hid himself, lest he be compelled to say or do anything in a cause full of hatred and envy. Rather, without doubt, he performed his duty in defending him, and when he saw that he could accomplish nothing, he publicly protested against the unjust sentence of condemnation, so that it would be generally known that he had by no means agreed to it. John adds to these virtues what is chief: that he was a disciple of Jesus; and it agrees with this that he is said to have been waiting for the kingdom of God, a phrase by which Luke also commended the faith and piety of Simeon above. For the prophets usually describe the whole business of human redemption and salvation, of which they make the Messiah the author, under the parable of a kingdom, and they call it the kingdom of God, because the whole matter consists in this: that, the kingdom of the devil being destroyed, God may reign in us by his Word and Spirit, and that we may at last become heirs of his heavenly and eternal kingdom. Therefore those who at that time waited for the kingdom of God, when the affairs of the Jews were most wretched and scarcely any traces of the ancient promises remained, must have had an outstanding and steadfast faith. Those who, sustained by this hope and expectation, listened to Christ and were his disciples, by that very fact bore witness that they recognised this promised Saviour of mankind. Faith, then, was the cause of those most beautiful virtues we have just seen. Although it had lain hidden for some time, while Joseph, still impeded by fear, met Christ only secretly (as John also noted of Nicodemus and some other leaders), now it shows itself openly, so that he dares more than all those who had before professed him publicly. For, as Mark writes, he went in to Pilate with a mind full of great confidence and asked for the body of Jesus for an honourable burial. What else was this than to condemn, before the governor, all those who had condemned him to death or had subscribed to his condemnation as unjust? That request was therefore very dangerous, and the flesh suggested many other courses that might seem safer: for example, after carefully observing the place where the body was thrown, to take it secretly by night and bury it, or to make a bargain with the centurion for its return and buy it back with money. But he would try none of these, since he was no longer ashamed of Christ and wished to show to all the faith by which he worshipped him. Nor did God fail this pious endeavour: he both bent Pilate's mind so that he readily consented to a request no less pious than just, and at the same time roused Nicodemus to offer himself as partner in this most noble deed, as John has left written, who was himself an eyewitness of all these things.

units.la: Sunt hæc multa & diligenti consideratione dignissima. Lucas equidem ista narraturus demonstrandi particulā præmittit, dicens: Tum ecce uir nomine Iosephi, &c. Quasi dicat: Videte et audite rem mirā, quæ præter omnē expectationē accidit. Cùm enim res Christi, eo in cruce mortuo, deplorabilissimæ essent, cum in cruce pendens ab omnibus negligeretur, discipulis præ metu latitantibus, amicis autem & notis eius eminus quidem cum dolore & gemitu rem indignissimam spectantibus, nemine autem quicquam pro eius gloria audente: cum denique corpus eius iam ignominiosè abiectum iri uideretur: tunc prodijt uir authoritate grauis, dives item, & antea quidem occultus, nunc autem apertus discipulus, imo gloriæ & nominis eius fortissimus vindex, qui ipsum Pilatum conuenire ausus est, & corpus ipsum ad sepulturæ honorem postulare, neq; eum terruit periculum, quod ex eo vel fortunis vel existimationi eius imminere videbatur. Hæc & alia huius generis paucis hisce verbis Lucas complexus est. Et sanè est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quàm viris & inustatis rationibus regnum Filij sui Deus inter homines instaurat & prouehat. Antea quidem ille, cum doctrina & miraculis clareret, discipulos multos, & ex his aliquos apertos, alios occultos & meticulosos nimis habuit. Nunc verò quando ipsius causa non solum periclitari, sed tota perdita esse videtur, illi quidem abscondit latent, hi verò fiducia magna armati defensione eius suscipiunt, ne sepulturæ honoribus careat, qui iniquè damnatus fuerat. Rursus ergo admonemur, non temere damnandos esse eos, qui infirmiores, quàm par sit, esse videntur. Potest enim illos confirmare Deus, qui omnium corda in suis manibus habet. Curent modo illi, ne ipsi sibi blandiatur, sed in melius proficere studeat.
units.tr: These matters are many and deserve the most diligent consideration. Luke, indeed, about to narrate these things, prefaces them with a particle of showing, saying: "Then behold, a man named Joseph, etc." As if he were saying: "See and hear a marvellous thing, which happened beyond all expectation. For when the cause of Christ seemed most hopeless, since he had died on the cross, when, hanging there, he was neglected by all, the disciples lying hidden for fear, his friends and acquaintances watching the most shameful sight from afar with grief and groaning, and no one daring to say anything for his glory, and when at last his body seemed about to be cast away in disgrace, then there came forward a man of weighty authority, rich likewise, and hitherto indeed hidden, but now openly a disciple, nay, the most courageous avenger of his glory and name, who dared to approach Pilate himself and to ask for the body for the honour of burial, and whom the danger that seemed to threaten his fortunes or reputation because of this did not terrify. Luke comprised these and other things of this kind in these few words. And truly this is a memorable example, by which we are taught how, by means of men and unexpected methods, God establishes and advances the kingdom of his Son among men. Previously, indeed, when Christ shone with teaching and miracles, he had many disciples, some open, others hidden and too timid. But now, when his cause seemed not only endangered but entirely lost, those indeed lay hidden, while these, armed with great confidence, take up his defence, so that he who had been unjustly condemned should not lack the honours of burial. Once again, then, we are admonished not to condemn rashly those who seem weaker than they ought to be. For God, who holds the hearts of all in his hands, can strengthen them. Let them only take care that they do not flatter themselves, but strive to make progress for the better.

units.la: Admonet præterea locus iste, Deum quidem paruulis & hominibus mundi iudicio contemptis de lectari (quod Christus non uno loco fatetur) eundem tamen eos non omnino abijcere, qui opibus & dignitatibus clari sunt. Sunt enim hæc quoq; eius dona, quibus non raro seruos suos donat, quorum opera & ministerio singulari uult uti: quod exemplis plurimis demonstrari poterat. Hoc aute curent diui tes, ut huius sæculi bonis bene utantur, & Deo horum largitori sese gratos præbeant. Vsus autem diuitiarum hic optimus & quæstuosissimus est, si illis Christo seruiant, & huius honorem atq; gloriam prouehant. Est enim is remunerator liberalissimus, & immortali etiam laude & gloria eorum officia compensat, qui ipsius gloriam afferunt atq; tuentur. Ægyptiorum reges olim in Pyramidibus extrusos immanes sumptus fecisse legimus, ut nominis sui memoriam gloriosam ad posteros transmitterent, & in illorum fastigijs ferè aut filiorum suorum aut proprios cineres condi uolebant. Apud Romanos autem multi ex aquæductibus alijsq; operibus publicis, quæ mira industria & magnis impensis extruebantur, gloriam & nominis immortalitatem quæsiuerunt. Alij hanc ex triumphis sperarunt. Multi hodie uestium luxu & coniuiorum splendore, insignium & stemmatum ubiq; prostantium ostentatione eandem uanantur. Sed sunt hæc omnia uanitate uaniora, et si ueteres illos omnes in unum congeras, nemo ex illis tantam suis diuitijs gloriam sibi comparauit, quantâ Iosephus hoc uno facto assecutus est, quo Christi corpus honorificè sepeliuit. Discant ergo eius exemplum imitari, qui opibus suis cum laude uti cupiunt. Prouehant ueri Dei cultum. Euangelij doctrinam iuuent, Christi membris benefaciant, nec pigeat eos sumptuum, quibus gloriam nominis Dei prouehi posse uident: perire autem arbitrentur omne id, quod neq; necessitati neq; gloriæ Dei tribuitur.
units.tr: This passage also admonishes us that God, indeed, delights in the little ones and in those despised by the judgement of the world (as Christ confesses in more than one place), yet he does not altogether cast off those who are distinguished by wealth and dignities. For these also are his gifts, with which he often endows his servants, whose work and ministry he wishes to use in a singular way; this could be shown by very many examples. Let the rich take care, however, to use the goods of this age well, and to show themselves grateful to God, the giver of these things. The best and most profitable use of riches is this: if they serve Christ with them and advance his honour and glory. For he is the most generous rewarder, and he repays with immortal praise and glory the services of those who bring about and protect his glory. We read that the kings of Egypt once spent immense sums on pyramids built for themselves, so that they might transmit the glorious memory of their name to posterity, and they wished their own ashes or those of their sons to be buried in their summits. Among the Romans, many sought glory and the immortality of their name from aqueducts and other public works, which were built with wonderful industry and great expense. Others hoped for it from triumphs. Many today vainly seek the same through luxury in clothing, splendour at feasts, and the display of coats of arms and family trees everywhere on show. But all these things are emptier than emptiness itself, and if you were to gather all those ancient men into one, none of them obtained for himself such great glory from his riches as Joseph obtained by this one deed, in which he honourably buried the body of Christ. Let those who wish to use their wealth with praise therefore learn to imitate his example. Let them advance the worship of the true God, support the doctrine of the gospel, and do good to the members of Christ, and let them not grudge the expenses by which they see the glory of God's name can be advanced; but let them consider lost everything that is not given either to necessity or to the glory of God.

units.la: Qui uerò in Repub. eminent & magistratu gerunt, ij quoq; in Iosepho exemplū sibi propositū esse meminerint, quod imitentur. Comendatur ille à morū honestate, probitate, iustitia, pietate in Deum & fide. Hæ uirtutes illæ sunt reuera heroicæ, ex quibus tā propria illorū quàm publica populi totius salus dependet. Ad honestatem totá uitæ consuetudo, uictus ratio, uestitus, mores, dictorum & factorum grauitas, comercia item cum alijs, & quæcunq; eiusmodi sunt, pertinent. In quibus omnibus tenere oportet, nō eadē omnes decere, & in priuatis hominibus multa ferri posse, quæ intolerabilia sunt in ijs, qui authoritate præditi alijs exemplo esse debebāt. Hinc illa apud Romanos ueteres Censoriæ seueritatis grauitas, quæ ne fortissimis quidem & de repub. bene meritis pepercit, si mali exempli authores essent. L. Antonius certè Senatu motus est, quòd quam uirginem in uxorem duxerat, repudiauisset, nullo amicorum in consilium adhibito. Cornelium Rufinum uerò, duobus consulatibus & dictatura speciosissimè functum Fabricius Lucinus Censor indignum iudicauit, qui in Senatorio ordine retineretur, quòd decē pondo uasa argentea coparando, luxus nimij exemplū populo dedisset. Duro nimis quoq; Senatu indignus habitus est, quòd Legem de coercendis conuiuiorum sumptibus latam ipse Tribun. pleb. abrogauerat. Poterat huius generis exempla multa cōmemorari, quorū utinā memini fient hodie, qui cùm Christi nomen profiteantur, nulla tamē publicæ, quā sustinent, functionis ratione habita, uestitu lasciuiunt, uictu luxuriosō diffluunt, cū pessimis & apertis bonarū legum hostibus colludunt, scortantur deniq; mœchantur, & omnia insolenter faciunt & dicūt, quasi authoritatem suam populo non aliter, quàm morū licentia testari possint. Iulius Cæsar, cū in Repub. præ alijs excelleret, domum suam à suspicione quoque alienam esse debere dicebat. At nostros illos non pudet apertis flagitijs suam maiestatem prostituere. Debet autem cum morum honestate iustitia quoque coniungi, quae unicuique quod suum est tribuit. Patet ea latissime, & huc pertinent, quae de boni principis officio passim traducntur: ut nimirum afflictos iudicet, calumniatores coerceat, pauperes servet, inopes iuuet, animas eorum ab usuris & ui aperta liberet, denique subditorum sanguinem pretiosum ducat. Quod si qui ista non semper nec ut uellent, praestare possunt, curent saltem, ne unquam malis aliorum consiliis consentiant, neue turpiter dissimulent quod contra ius & aequum fieri uident. In primis autem pietate opus est, quae fide in Deum & eiusdem timore constat. Haec intrepidos & animosos facit, ne hominum respectu ducantur: haec ut Dei gloriam ante omnia quarant, ipsos excitat: eadem uitae totius, actionum deniq; & consiliorum omnium ipsis regula est tutissima. Et qui his uirtutibus student, ij laborum atque periculorum socios facile inueniunt. Tanta enim uirtutis uis est, ut eos quoque in sui admirationem rapiat, qui nullo eius studio teneri putabantur: & frequenter fit, ut causa bona, quamuis odij & periculi plena sit, fautores plurimos inueniat, modo unus aliquis eius patrocinium suscipiat.
units.tr: But those who stand out in the commonwealth and bear public office should also remember that Joseph is set before them as an example to imitate. He is commended for the honesty of his morals, his uprightness, justice, piety toward God, and faithfulness. These virtues are truly heroic, and on them depends the welfare of both the individual and the whole people. Honesty concerns the whole course of life: the manner of living, diet, dress, customs, the seriousness of words and deeds, and likewise dealings with others, and whatever else is of this kind. In all these things one must keep in mind that the same rules do not suit everyone, and that many things may be tolerated in private men which are intolerable in those who, invested with authority, ought to be an example to others. Hence came that severity of the censors among the ancient Romans, which spared not even the bravest men and those who had deserved well of the commonwealth, if they were authors of bad example. Lucius Antonius was certainly removed from the Senate because he had put away the virgin whom he had taken as his wife, without calling any of his friends into counsel. Cornelius Rufinus, who had served with distinction in two consulships and a dictatorship, was judged unworthy by the censor Fabricius Luscinus to be retained in the senatorial order, because he had given the people an example of excessive luxury by buying ten pounds' weight of silver plate. He was also thought unworthy by a very harsh Senate because he, being himself a tribune of the plebs, had repealed a law passed to restrain the expenses of feasts. Many examples of this kind could be recalled, and I wish that there were not some of them today: men who, though they profess the name of Christ, yet, with no regard for the public office they hold, indulge in extravagant dress, wallow in luxurious food, collude with the worst and most open enemies of good laws, and finally whore and commit adultery, and do and say everything insolently, as if they could bear witness to their authority before the people in no other way than by the licence of their morals. Julius Caesar, though he excelled all others in the commonwealth, used to say that his house ought to be free even from suspicion. But those men of ours are not ashamed to prostitute their majesty by open disgraces. Moreover, justice must be joined with honesty of morals, which gives to each what is his own. This extends very widely, and to it pertain those things which are commonly taught about the duty of a good prince: namely, that he should judge the afflicted, restrain the slanderers, protect the poor, help the needy, deliver their souls from usury and open violence, and finally hold the blood of his subjects precious. But if some cannot always accomplish these things, or not as they would wish, let them at least take care never to agree with the evil counsels of others, nor shamefully to wink at what they see being done against right and equity. Above all, however, there is need of piety, which consists in faith toward God and the fear of him. This makes men fearless and spirited, so that they are not led by regard for men; this stirs them up to seek above all the glory of God; the same is for them the safest rule of their whole life, and of all their actions and counsels. And those who labour in these virtues easily find companions in toils and dangers. For virtue has such power that it carries away even those who were thought to be held by no zeal for it into admiration of it; and often it happens that a good cause, however full of hatred and danger, finds very many supporters, provided only that someone takes up its defence.

units.la: Reliquum esset, ut de sepultura Christi & tota humandorum corporum ratione aliquid dicere mus, sed quia de illa in Marco nostro, de hac autem supra in historia de filio uiduae Naimiticae ex mortuis resuscitato diximus Homilia 67. minimè opus fuerit hic eadem repetere. Quare cum Lucas ad mulieres redeamus, quas initio omnium istorum spectatrices fuisse, & cum notis illius procul steterit est dictum. Haec nunc funus subsecutae esse dicuntur, & diligentius spectauisse, quo loco & qua ratione illud conderetur. Quod ne quis ex curiositate factum putaret, ratio eius colilij adducitur, quòd in urbem reuersae aromata & unguenta parauerint, quibus ipsae etiam corpus illud sanctum condire, & pro more gentis Christo extremum honorem impendere voluerunt. Fuit hic pius affectus, quàm uis non leuis error fuerit, quod eorum immemores, quae toties de sua resurrectione dixerat, isto officio eum adhuc opus habere arbitrantur. Quia tamen neq; malitia neq; impia superstitione peccarunt, imò Sabbati religionem sancte coluerunt (quod animi pij euidens argumentum est) huius instituti finis fuit & euentus felicissimus, sicut in Resurrectionis historia patebit. At nunc nobis considerandum uenit diuina Christi Iesu potentia, qui etsi iam nihil praeter exanime & exangue cadauer esse uideatur, ista tamen ita disposuit, ut ad resurrectionis suae gloriam facerent, simulq; imbelles atq; peregrinas mulierculas suo Spiritu armauit, ut nullum periculum ueritatem maximam tentaret. Imò per has ille de hostibus suis triumphauit, quando earum testimonio aduersus Pontificum & militum calumnias usus est, qui mendacijs resurrectionem ipsius obscurare conati sunt. Debent exempla eiusmodi diligenter obseruari, ut ijs fidem nostram confirmemus inter certamina, quae nobis mundus hic & propria caro obijciunt. Poterit nos quoque confirmare suo spiritu Deus, idq; proculdubio faciet, modò nos Filium eius Iesum Christum uera fide complexi, eius Regnum pro uirili prouehamus, & quaecunque possumus, fideliter ei praestemus obsequia. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: It would remain to say something about the burial of Christ and the whole manner of burying bodies, but since we have spoken of the former in our Mark, and of the latter above in the history of the son of the widow of Nain raised from the dead, in Homily 67, there is hardly any need to repeat the same things here. Therefore, returning to Luke, the women, who at the beginning of all these things were spectators and had stood afar off with the acquaintances of Jesus, are said now to have followed the funeral and to have watched more carefully where and how that body was laid. Lest anyone think this was done out of curiosity, the reason for their concern is given: that on returning to the city they prepared spices and ointments, with which they wished to embalm that holy body and to pay the last honour to Christ according to the custom of their people. This was a pious feeling, although it was no slight error, since, forgetful of what he had so often said about his resurrection, they thought he still needed this service. Yet since they sinned neither from malice nor from impious superstition, but indeed observed the sabbath rest devoutly (which is clear evidence of a pious mind), the outcome of this purpose was most happy, as will appear in the history of the Resurrection. But now we must consider the divine power of Christ Jesus, who, although he now seems to be nothing but a lifeless and bloodless corpse, nevertheless so ordered these things that they served the glory of his resurrection; and at the same time he armed with his Spirit these weak and foreign little women, so that no danger could shake the greatest truth. Indeed, through them he triumphed over his enemies, when he used their testimony against the calumnies of the Pontiffs and soldiers, who tried by lies to obscure his resurrection. Examples of this kind ought to be carefully observed, so that by them we may strengthen our faith amid the conflicts which this world and our own flesh throw in our way. God too will be able to strengthen us by his Spirit, and he will surely do so, provided that we embrace his Son Jesus Christ with true faith, advance his Kingdom to the best of our power, and render him faithful service in whatever ways we can. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CCX.
units.tr: HOMILY CCX.

units.la: PRimo autem die hebdomadis, profundo diluculo venerunt ad monumentum, ferentes quae parauerant aromata: & nonnullae cum ipsis. Inuenerunt autem lapidem deuolutum à monumento: & ingressae non inuenerunt corpus Domini Iesu. Et factum est dum consternatae in ea re haesitarent, ecce duo viri superuenerunt eis induti vestibus fulgurantibus. Cùm autem pauefactae inclinarent faciem in terram, dixerunt eis: Quid inter mortuos quaeritis eum qui viuit? Non est hic, sed surrexit: memententote vt locutus sit vobis, cùm adhuc in Galilaea esset, dicens: Oportet Filium hominis tradi in manus hominum peccatorum, & crucifigi, & die tertio resurgere. Recordatae sunt igitur verborum illius: & reuersae à monumento annuntiauerunt haec omnia illis vndecim, & reliquis quis omnibus. Maria autem Magdalena, & Ioanna, & Maria Iacobi, & reliquæ cum eis erant, quæ hæc dicebant Apostolis. Sed visa sunt apud eos quasi deliramentum verba earum, neq; crediderunt eis. Petrus autem surgens cucurrit ad monumentum, & cùm introspexisset, videt linea sola iacentia, abijtq; apud semetipsum mirans hoc factum.
units.tr: Early on the first day of the week, at the very break of dawn, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared, and some women with them. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. As the women were terrified and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them: "Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen. Remember how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee, saying: The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and rise again the third day." And they remembered his words, and returned from the tomb and told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them, who told these things to the apostles. But their words seemed to the apostles like idle talk, and they did not believe them. Then Peter arose and ran to the tomb, and when he stooped down he saw the linen cloths lying alone; and he departed, wondering to himself at what had happened.

units.la: ER quàm memorabile est Pauli Apostoli dictum, quod in priori ad Timotheum pronunciat, Christus Iesus in mundum venit, ut peccatores seruaret. Vt verò id & rectius intelligatur, & plus consolationis afferat, necesse fuerit tenere quænam illa sint, quæ ut seruaremur facta necessaria fuerunt. Possunt hæc tribus omnino capitibus comprehendi. Primò enim, quia omnes natura peccatores sumus, eo opus erat, qui pro nostris peccatis vltima & satisfactio fieret, atq; illa sanguinis sui merito expiaret. Deinde quia propter peccatum nos Deus abdicauerat, necesse fuit eius testamentum nouum confirmari, quo nos regni sui & bonorum suorum hæredes denuo scripserat. Postremò, ne mors nobis dominaretur, quæ per peccatum ingressa erat, illam quoq; vinci & exarmari oportuit, ne nobis porrò esset formidabilis. Atqui omnia ista solus Christus præstitit. Hic enim cum peccatum non nouisset, pro nobis peccatum factus est, id est, nostra peccata in se recepit, proq; illis in ara crucis satisfecit. Idem cùm Deus æternus & Patri ὁμοούσιος & siue coessentialis sit, in assumpta carne moriendo, nouo illi testamento suo effectu dedit, quod nisi mors testatoris intercederet, ratum esse non poterat. Et de duobus quidem hisce in passionis ac mortis eius historia hucusq; multis dictum est. Restabat ergo tertium, quod per resurrectionem suam gloriosam præstitit, in qua mortem deuicit, et ut victor gloriosus de illa simul & portis inferorum triumphauit. Quia ergo in illa salutis nostræ complementum habetur, non temere factum putabimus, quod eam omnes Euangelistæ magno studio atque diligentia describunt. Lucas certè eius narrationem ita contexit, ut singulis circumstantijs argumenta subsint, quæ ad eius certitudinem confirmandam faciunt. Nos tamen in ijs explicandis breuitati nunc studebimus, eò quod multa quæ huc pertinent in Marci & Ioannis expositione dicta sunt.
units.tr: How memorable is the saying of the apostle Paul in his first letter to Timothy: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." To understand this more rightly, and so that it may bring us more comfort, we must grasp what things were made necessary for our salvation. These can be comprehended under three heads. First, because we are all sinners by nature, there was need for someone who would make the final satisfaction for our sins and expiate them by the merit of his blood. Second, because God had disinherited us on account of sin, his new covenant had to be ratified, by which he had once again named us heirs of his kingdom and of his goods. Last, lest death should rule over us, which had entered through sin, it was also necessary that death be conquered and disarmed, so that it would no longer be fearful to us. Yet Christ alone accomplished all these things. For he, though he had known no sin, was made sin for us, that is, he took our sins upon himself and made satisfaction for them on the altar of the cross. Likewise, since he is eternal God and homoousios [ὁμοούσιος], or coessential, with the Father, by dying in the flesh he assumed, he gave effect to his new covenant, which could not have been valid unless the death of the testator intervened. Of these two things, his passion and death, much has been said so far in the history of his suffering. There remained, then, the third, which he accomplished through his glorious resurrection, in which he overcame death, and as a glorious victor triumphed over it and at the same time over the gates of hell. Since the completion of our salvation is found in that resurrection, we shall not think it without reason that all the evangelists describe it with great care and diligence. Luke, certainly, so weaves his narrative that each circumstance has evidence that serves to confirm its certainty. Yet in explaining these we shall now aim at brevity, since many of the things that pertain here have already been said in the exposition of Mark and John.

units.la: Priusquam uero ad huius loci tractationem accedamus, non oscitanter obseruari debet, omnes quidem Apostolos & Euangelistas de resurrectione Christi luculenter testari & multa dicere, quæ circa illam acciderunt, qua ratione autem illa ipsa facta sit, nequaquam exponere. Angeli quidem descensum de cælo Matthæus narrat, qui terram concusserit; & lapidem ab ostio monumenti amulserit; ut autem Christus in vitam restitutus sit, ut idem ex sepulchro prodierit, nusquam narratur. Et cum Matthæo reliqui omnes, illum reuera resurrexisse multis argumentis atque rationibus probant, resurrectionis autem formam & modum omnes quasi confulto tacent. Quam ergo huius silentij causam esse dicemus? Non aliam certè, quàm quod resurrectio ex mortuis in eorum numero habeeri debet, quæ reuera esse certum est, etiamsi qua ratione fiant, aut aliquando facta sint, nostri intellectus acumen uidere non possit. Ideo Paulus de Christi resurrectione loquens, satis habet eius causam ad Spiritum Dei uiuificum retulisse: Spiritus eius (inquit) qui excitauit Iesum à mortuis, habitat in nobis, &c. Idem nostram resurrectionem similiter ex Christi omnipotentia, quam cum Patre & Spiritu sancto communem habet, pendere docet, quando ad Philippenses scribit: Dominus Iesus Christus transformabit corpus nostrum humile, ut conforme fiat corpori suo glorioso pro efficacitate, qua poterit etiam subijcere sibi omnia. In his ergo nos quoque acquiescere debemus, quod ut ad assurgendam mortuorum resurrectionem plurimùm facit: ita multas quæstiones abrumpit, quibus impij illusores illam in dubium uocare solent. Et huc Paulus respexit, quando quærenti, Quomodo suscitantur mortui? quali item corpore prodeunt? respondet: Stulte, quod tu seminas, non uiuificetur, nisi mortuum fuerit, &c. Et mox addit, Deus dat ei corpus, ut uoluit. Quod si cui ista non sufficiunt, agedum dicat ille nobis, quæ sit conceptionis ratio in utero materno? quo vinculo anima corpori, aut fœtui potius adhuc immaturo uniatur? quî fiat, ut hoc dormiente, illa vigilet? unde sua visui, auditui, tactui, olfactui, gustui facultas? cur oculis potius quàm aurib. uideamus? cur nares olfaciant, nō autem manus? cur gustus in sola lingua & palato sit, non in gutture aut intestinis? quod organum tam acuti olfactus in musca aut culice? unde tanta pungendi & exugendi sanguinis in pulice? Quid hic nobis respondebunt physici, quod non possit firmioribus rationibus eludi & negari, quàm ab illis affirmetur? Quòd si ergo hic illi nihil respondere possunt, nisi quòd omnia haec virtute divina fiant, nimium audax eorum stultitia fuerit, qui resurrectionis mysterium scrutari audent, & nisi ipsorum curiositati satisfiat, illam in dubium vocare & ridere no erubescunt, cùm & Dei Filium in assumpta carne resurrexisse constet, & nos resurrecturos esse infinitis promissionibus & Scripturae sacrae testimonijs doceamur.
units.tr: But before we approach the treatment of this passage, it must not be carelessly overlooked that all the apostles and evangelists bear clear witness to the resurrection of Christ and tell many things that happened around it, but they nowhere explain the manner in which it itself took place. Matthew indeed relates that an angel came down from heaven, who shook the earth and rolled the stone away from the door of the tomb; but that Christ was restored to life, and how he came forth from the sepulchre, is nowhere narrated. And with Matthew all the others prove by many arguments and reasons that he truly rose, yet all of them, as if deliberately, keep silent about the form and mode of the resurrection. What, then, shall we say is the cause of this silence? Certainly no other than that the resurrection from the dead belongs among those things which are certainly real, even though the acuteness of our understanding cannot see by what means they happen, or when they have happened. Therefore Paul, speaking of Christ's resurrection, is content to have ascribed its cause to the life-giving Spirit of God: "The Spirit of him," he says, "who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in us," etc. Likewise he teaches that our own resurrection depends in the same way on the omnipotence of Christ, which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit, when he writes to the Philippians: "The Lord Jesus Christ will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body, by the power by which he is able even to subject all things to himself." In these things, then, we too ought to rest, for while they greatly help us to believe in the rising of the dead, they also cut off many questions by which impious mockers are wont to call it into doubt. Paul had this in view when, to one asking, "How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body do they come?", he replied: "Foolish man, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies," etc. And soon he adds: "God gives it a body as he wills." But if anyone is not satisfied by these things, let him tell us: what is the manner of conception in the mother's womb? By what bond is the soul joined to the body, or rather to the foetus still immature? How is it that the soul keeps watch while the body sleeps? Whence come the powers of sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste? Why do we see with the eyes rather than the ears? Why do the nostrils smell but not the hands? Why is taste only in the tongue and palate, and not in the throat or the intestines? What organ of such keen smell is there in a fly or a gnat? Whence such power in the flea to pierce and suck blood? What will the natural philosophers answer here, which cannot be mocked and denied by stronger arguments than those by which it is affirmed? If, then, they can answer nothing here except that all these things are done by divine power, the folly of those is too bold who dare to search out the mystery of the resurrection, and unless their curiosity is satisfied, they are not ashamed to call it in question and to laugh at it, since it is established that the Son of God rose in the flesh he assumed, and we are taught by countless promises and testimonies of holy Scripture that we shall rise.

units.la: His praemissis, veniamus ad Lucae narrationem, quam (ut reliqui etiā tres Euangelistae) à tempóris notatione orditur. Nam primum hebdomadis diem hunc fuisse scribit, et diei partem indicat, diluculū adhuc profundum. Atqui in parasceue Sabbati Christum mortuum & sepultum fuisse, nuper audiuimus. Vnde colligitur, hunc tertium ab eius morte diem numerari, et proinde illum eodem, quem praedixerat, die resurrexisse. Annotatur hoc diligenter & saepe, ut illius Veritas infallibilis elucesceat, quae nullis hominum consilijs aut viribus impediri potest, quò minus fiat id, quod ipse promittit siue minatur. Verissimè enim à Solomone dictum est: Non est sapientia, non prudentia, non consilium contra Dominum. Et Isaias ait: Domino exercituum aliquid constituente, quis illud faciet irritum? Voluerunt quidem Christi resurrectionem impedire Sacerdotes, & ad hoc publica Praesidis Pilati authoritate abusi sunt, qui & lapide sepulchri obsignato, & militibus audacissimis eiusdem custodiam commendauit. Sed adeo nihil profecerunt omnes illi, ut ne unius quidem horulae spatio illum impedierint, quò minus sub tertij diei initiū statim resurgeret. Sunt huius generis exempla multa in Scripturis, & huc pertinent, quae de liberatione ex Aegypto, de reditu ex Babylone & instauratione urbis atq; templi alibi recitauimus. Quorum omnium hic nobis usus esse debet, ne de ullis Christi promissionibus dubitemus. Quia ergo hunc regnaturum esse, & omnibus huius mundi regnis superiorem fore, infinita Prophetarum oracula testantur, neminem terrere debent impiorum hostium conatus, qui hodie etiam Reges & principes contra nos armant, ut illum quasi sepultum detinere possint, ne per Euangelij praedicationem in multorum animis resurgat.
units.tr: With these things set down, let us come to Luke's narrative, which, like the other three evangelists, begins with a note of time. For he writes that this was the first day of the week, and he indicates the part of the day: the deep dawn. Now we have lately heard that on the Preparation day before the Sabbath Christ was dead and buried. From this it is gathered that this was counted as the third day from his death, and therefore that he rose on the very day he had foretold. This is noted carefully and often, so that the infallible truth of it may shine forth, a truth which no counsels or powers of men can hinder, so that what he promises or threatens is not done. For it was rightly said by Solomon: "There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord." And Isaiah says: "When the Lord of hosts has determined something, who will make it void?" The priests indeed wished to prevent Christ's resurrection, and to this end they abused the public authority of the governor Pilate, who committed the sealed stone of the sepulchre and its guard to the boldest of soldiers. But all those efforts came to nothing, so that they could not hinder him even for the space of one hour from rising at the very beginning of the third day. There are many examples of this kind in the Scriptures, and to them belong those things which we have elsewhere recounted concerning the deliverance from Egypt, the return from Babylon, and the restoration of the city and temple. Of all these, we ought to make use here, so that we do not doubt any of Christ's promises. Since the countless oracles of the prophets testify that he is to reign and to be superior to all the kingdoms of this world, the attempts of impious enemies, who today also arm kings and princes against us in order to keep him, as it were, buried, ought to terrify no one; for they cannot hold him back so that he does not rise in the minds of many through the preaching of the gospel.

units.la: Secundo loco resurrectionis huius testes producuntur, quibus primis ea innotuit. Fuerunt hae mulieres ex Galilaea oriundae & eas mortis Christi spectatrices fuisse, & sepulturae eius locum diligentius obseruasse, nuper audiuimus. Praecipua inter has fuit, & (ut in Ioanne apparet) reliquis frequentior, Maria Magdalena. Comites huic facit Lucas Ioannam (quam cap.octauo Chuzae procuratoris Herodis uxorem fuisse scribit) & Mariam Iacobi (quem Minorem dicunt) matrem, quam Cleopae uxorem & Virginis Mariae sororem fuisse ex Ioanne constat. His Marcus Salomen addit, de qua nihil praeterea in scripturis traditur. Sed & adhuc alias nonnullas cum istis fuisse Lucas ait, quarum nomina omnino tacentur. Venerunt hae profundo adhuc diluculo ad monumentū: nimirum, ut aromatibus, quae in eum usum parauerant, corpus Christi inungerent, & sic ei extremum imponerent honorem. Id uero ex peculiari diuinae prouidentiae decreto factum est, ut resurrectionis testes essent primae, quae nihil minus quàm illam cogitabant, cum ad sepulchrum exirent: ne quis hic aliquid ex composito aut dolo malo factum esse putaret. Nihil nunc dico de eo, quòd simul testari voluit Dominus, se mulieribus quoq; sexus redemptorem esse, qui singulari consolatione opus habebat, eò quòd per hunc peccatum in mundum introiuit, & ideo peculiaribus quoq; plagis à Deo multatus est: ut alibi prolixè est demonstratum.
units.tr: In the second place, the witnesses of this resurrection are brought forward, those to whom it was first made known. These women were from Galilee, and, as we heard recently, they were watching Christ's death and had carefully noted the place of his burial. The chief among them was Mary Magdalene, who, as appears from John, was the most frequent of the group. Luke adds companions to her: Joanna (whom he writes in chapter eight was the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward) and Mary the mother of James (called the Less), who, as is clear from John, was the wife of Cleopas and the sister of the Virgin Mary. To these Mark adds Salome, about whom nothing else is recorded in the Scriptures. Luke also says that some others were with them, but their names are not given at all. These women came to the tomb while it was still very early dawn, intending, of course, to anoint Christ's body with the spices they had prepared for that purpose and so pay him the last honour. By a special decree of divine providence it came about that the first witnesses of the resurrection were women who, as they went out to the sepulchre, were thinking of nothing less than that event, so that no one could suppose anything had been arranged or done by deceit. I say nothing now of the fact that the Lord also wished to show that he is the redeemer of the female sex as well. Women needed special comfort, since through a woman sin entered the world, and for that reason they were also punished with particular afflictions by God, as has been shown at length elsewhere.

units.la: Meretur tamen diligentiorem consideration fidei exemplū, quod in illis praeclarum & in primis memorabile Spiritus sanctus proponit. Illa ut Christum apprehendit & nos huic inserit, ita in eo omnes quoque homines complectitur, & per charitatem operatur. Eadem quia totum hominem Christo uendicat, non patitur ut aliquem crucis ignominia offendat: adhaec inuictos reddit, qui in fine usque cum illo perseuerant. Et haec quidem omnia in istis mulieribus esse uidere. Christo enim se iam pridem consecrauerunt, hunc per longa & molesta itinera secutae sunt, eundem una cum discipulis non sine maximis impensis aluerunt: & quamuis eum in cruce pendere & morte infami mori uiderent, non potuere tamen eius memoriam & amorem ex animo expuere. Ideo ne mortuum quidem & sepultum negligunt: & quamuis resurrectionis ignorantia errent, tanta tamen in illis fidei & dilectionis Christi uis est, ut discipulis omnibus animosiores, nondum exorto die urbem exire, ad locum supplicij pergere, & sepulchro appropinquare ausint (cui milites adhibitos esse non poterant ignorare )ut extremi honoris officio erga illum defungantur. Hoc certè tam pul-chro istarum facinore, Spiritus sanctus timiditatem suam plus quàm muliebrem discipulis expro-brat,qui cùm tam magnificè Christo de sua fide & constantia promisissent, nunc in angulo quodam abstrusi latent, neq; in publicum prodire audent. Id uero ad se transferant uiri principes, qui cùm Christum gloriosum mortis & inferni uictorem esse norint, & Euangelij doctrinam profiteantur, nimiùm tamen ignaui nihil audent, si quid pro illius gloria & Ecclesiæ eius salute est faciendum. Pudeat eos à mulieribus uinci, & ab ipsis etiam discipulis superari, quos mox resurrectionis certior cognitio animosiores fecit. In primis tamen istas imitari debent matronæ Christianæ, quæ tunc demum hoc nomine dignæ iudicabuntur, si & ipsæ se totas Christo consecrent, huic fidant, hunc ament & colant, & quæ mundo dedita in ornatum corporis fastui atq; libidini seruientem insumunt, ipsæ Christi membris egentibus impendant. Hic ornatus ille uerus est, qui ut animas earum ornat ita totius uitæ morumq; consuetudinem Deo gratam & acceptam reddit. Laudatur in prophanis historijs Hypsicratea, quæ Mithridatem uirum suum sumpto habitu uirili & capillis tonsis per media arma, & tandem à Pompeio uictum per gentes feras atque barbaras sequi uoluit, in aduersæ fortunæ comes deesset, quæ læta & ridentis consors fuerat. At quanto laudabilius est Christum, dulcissimum animarum sponsum sequi, & ei adhærere, qui & ipse pro nobis extrema pati dignatus est?
