units.tr: Nevertheless, the example of faith that the Holy Spirit sets before us in these women deserves closer consideration, since it is outstanding and especially memorable. Faith lays hold of Christ and engrafts us into him, and in him it embraces all people as well, and works through love. Because it claims the whole man for Christ, it does not allow anyone to be offended by the shame of the cross; moreover, it makes those invincible who persevere with him to the end. And all these things can be seen in these women. For they had long since consecrated themselves to Christ, followed him through long and wearisome journeys, and supported him, together with the disciples, at great expense. And although they saw him hanging on the cross and dying an infamous death, they could not wipe out of their minds his memory and their love for him. So they do not neglect even his dead and buried body. And although they were in error through ignorance of the resurrection, there was such power of faith and love for Christ in them that they dared, bolder than all the disciples, to leave the city before the day had dawned, to go to the place of execution, and to approach the sepulchre (they could not be unaware that soldiers had been posted there), in order to perform the last duty of honour toward him. Certainly, by this brave deed of these women, the Holy Spirit reproaches the disciples for their timidity, which was more than womanly. Though they had so grandly promised Christ their faith and steadfastness, they now lie hidden in some corner and dare not come out into the open. Let the leading men take this to themselves: though they know that Christ is the glorious conqueror of death and hell, and though they profess the doctrine of the gospel, they are far too lazy and do nothing when something must be done for his glory and the salvation of his Church. They should be ashamed to be surpassed by women, and to be outdone even by the disciples, who were soon made bolder by a surer knowledge of the resurrection. Yet above all, Christian matrons ought to imitate these women. They will be judged worthy of that name only if they also consecrate themselves wholly to Christ, trust in him, love and honour him, and do not spend on the adornment of their bodies, in the service of pride and lust, what they give to the world, but rather give it to Christ's members who are in need. That is the true adornment, which adorns their souls and makes the whole course and habit of their lives pleasing and acceptable to God. In profane histories Hypsicratea is praised, who, when her husband Mithridates was defeated by Pompey, dressed as a man with cropped hair, and wanted to follow him through the midst of the weapons and among wild and barbarous peoples, she who had been the joyful and laughing partner of his fortune and would not be lacking as a companion in adversity. But how much more praiseworthy it is to follow Christ, the most sweet bridegroom of souls, and to cling to him, who himself deigned to suffer the utmost for us?

units.la: Quia tamen hæc carni dura & grauia sunt, proderit uidere quid istæ mulierculæ inuenerint, & quibus præmijs earum fidem tunc remuneratus sit Deus, quando omnia periculum extremum ei minitari uidebantur. Primò lapidem ab ostio sepulchri deuolutum esse inuenerunt. At qui hunc unum illas maximè solicitas habuisse Marcus scribit. Quia enim immanis ponderis erat, ipsæ uerò infirmæ & imbecillæ, intereundum de illo confultarunt, dicentes: Quis deuoluet nobis lapidem ab-ostio monumenti? Id uero nunc absq; negotio suo confectum inueniunt. Nec tamè hoc solùm labore, uerumetiam periculo, quod tale quid tentare audentibus ex militibus metuendum erat, se liberatas esse uident, cùm hi priusquam ipsæ uenirent, in urbem aufugissent. Est exemplum hoc plenum dul-cissimæ consolationis. Docet enim, Deum nunquam deesse ijs, qui in fide constantes sunt, & pro eius gloria afferenda aliquid audent. Obstant quidem multa uocationi nostræ; & non leuia modò scan-dala nobis obijcit Satan, uerumetiam montes congerit, quibus uiam obstruat, ne quò Deus nos uo-cat pergamus. Sedustoria nostra fides est, quæ inuicto robore per omnia obstacula eluctatur, & ea quoq; nobis plana, facilia & iucunda reddit, quæ impossibilia & periculosissima putabantur. Hac armatus Moses per maris rubri fluctus populum traduxit. Eadem Dauid confirmatus Goliam de uicit. Per hanc Daniel leonum ora obturauit. Huius uirtute & ope Apostoli totum terrarum or-bem subegerunt, & ipsis etiam Imperatoribus Romanis superiores facti sunt. Hæc deniq; mundum & principem eius etiam hodie uincit, & per mille rerum discrimina tutos in portu æternæ beatitu-dinis collocat. Sunt hæc diligentius obseruanda propter eos, qui in rebus difficilioribus ad humana auxilia respiciunt, & quasi illas nostris uiribus confici oporteat, mox animum despondent, si quoad has se aduersarijs impares esse uideant.
units.tr: Yet since these things are hard and burdensome to the flesh, it will be profitable to see what these little women found, and with what rewards God then rewarded their faith, when every danger seemed to threaten them with the greatest peril. First, they found that the stone had been rolled away from the door of the sepulchre. Mark writes that this was the one thing that troubled them most. For since it was of immense weight, and they themselves were weak and feeble, they had been deliberating on the matter, saying: "Who will roll away for us the stone from the door of the tomb?" But now they find it already moved, and done without any effort of their own. Nor do they see themselves freed only from labour, but also from the danger that had to be feared from the soldiers, had any of them dared to attempt such a thing; for these had fled into the city before the women arrived. This example is full of the sweetest consolation. For it teaches that God never fails those who are steadfast in faith and dare something for the sake of his glory. Indeed, many obstacles stand in the way of our calling, and Satan not only throws in no slight scandals against us, but even piles up mountains to block the way, so that we may not go where God calls us. But our faith is victorious: with invincible strength it struggles through every obstacle, and it makes plain, easy and pleasant for us those things that were thought impossible and most dangerous. Armed with this faith, Moses led the people through the waves of the Red Sea. Strengthened by it, David overcame Goliath. Through it, Daniel stopped the mouths of the lions. By its power and help the Apostles subdued the whole circle of the earth and became superior even to the Roman emperors. Finally, it conquers the world and its prince even today, and through a thousand dangers of things it places us safe in the harbour of eternal blessedness. These things must be observed more carefully on account of those who, in more difficult matters, look to human help, and who, as if those matters ought to be accomplished by our own strength, straightway lose heart if they see themselves unequal to their adversaries.

units.la: Secundò, mulieres sepulchrum ingressæ non inuenerunt corpus Domini Iesu. Vnde uero hoc? Quia hic iam resurrexerat, & discrtè corporis uocabulo uti uoluit Lucas, ut resurrectionem de hoc proprie dici & intelligi debere ostendat. Neq; mirum alicui uideri debet, quòd istarum aduenitum illæ præuenire uoluit. Nam etiamsi earum pietas atq; fides ipsi minimè displicerent, officium tamen quod illæ ipsi præstare uolebant, admittere non potuit, cùm eo propter festinam resurrectionem non opus haberet, & in Cœna Bethaniensi unctus docuisset; huius generis officia posthac in pauperes suos conferri debere. Adhæc superstitioni occurrere uoluit, quam posteris temporibus oriturampsse sciebat: ut nimirum sui meriti uirtutem homines inepti & superstitiosi apud sepulchrum istud quæ-rerent, relictis interea pietatis uerè officijs, quæ sola ei placent. Debet ergo hinc generalis doctrina peti, quòd ut meritum Christi nulli loco aut tempori certo alligatum est: ita eius corpus posthac in terris nequaquam quæri debere, & ideo falso ad hoc restringi promissiones, quibus suam præsen-tiam ille nobis pollicetur. Quod enim corpore suo in terris perficere debuit, id in cruce præstitit, ubi illud dedit pro mundi uita, & ideo iam moriturus dixit: Consummatum est. Dixit quidem ille; Vbicunq; duo aut tres congregati fuerint in meo nomine, ego ero in medio illorum: At promissionem hanc non de corporis, sed gratiæ, meriti & virtutis eius diuinæ præsentia intelligi debere, locus hic abunde docet. Quis enim mulieres istas in eius nomine congregatas fuisse negauerit, quæ ut ipsum honorarent illuc uenerant? Quis item illum ab ipsis abfuisse dicet, cum non multò post Mariæ Magdalenæ ad sepulchrum flenti se uidendum præbuerit in hortulani habitu? Attamen uerbis diuersis atq; proprijs scribit Lucas, illas corpus in monumento non inuenisse. Dicet fortasßis aliquis, hoc ideo sic dici quòd illud non uiderint, etiamsi præsens adesset. Sed huic obiectioni confutandæ Angeli uerba sufficiunt, qui paulò post eas reprehendet hoc nomine, quòd illum isthic quærant, & ipsum non adesse testabitur. Quòd si quibus uidemur de illius maiestate minus honorificè sentire, aut etiam illius omnipotentiam negare, quòd corpus eius omnipræsens esse negamus, eos non nobis, sed Lucæ litem mouere oportebat, qui scripsit: Et ingressæ non inuenerunt CORPVS Domini Iesu. En corpus illas inuenisse negat. Quæ autem huius dicti ratio alia potest afferri, quàm quæ mox ab Angelo reddita est, dicente: Non est hic, sed surrexit?
units.tr: Secondly, the women who entered the sepulchre did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. How so? Because he had already risen; and Luke deliberately used the word "body," to show that the resurrection ought to be understood as applying properly to this body. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that he wished to forestall the arrival of these women. For even if their piety and faith did not displease him at all, he could not accept the service that they wished to render him, since he had no need of it on account of his speedy resurrection; and at the supper at Bethany, when he was anointed, he had taught that services of this kind ought afterwards to be given to his poor. Moreover, he wished to meet a superstition that he knew would arise in later times: foolish and superstitious men would seek at that sepulchre the power of their own merit, while meanwhile they neglected the true duties of piety, which alone please him. From this, therefore, a general doctrine must be drawn: just as the merit of Christ is not bound to any fixed place or time, so his body is by no means to be sought on earth hereafter, and therefore the promises by which he pledges his presence to us are wrongly restricted to this. For what he had to accomplish on earth in his body, he accomplished on the cross, where he gave that body for the life of the world, and therefore, about to die, he said: "It is finished." He indeed said: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them." But this place sufficiently teaches that this promise must be understood not of the bodily presence but of the presence of his grace, merit and divine power. For who would deny that these women were gathered in his name, since they had come there to honour him? Who again would say that he was absent from them, when not long after he showed himself to Mary Magdalene weeping at the sepulchre, in the appearance of a gardener? Yet Luke writes in different and distinct words that they did not find the body in the tomb. Perhaps someone will say that it is said in this way because they did not see it, even though it was present. But the words of the angel suffice to refute this objection; a little later he rebukes them for seeking him there, and he testifies that he is not present. But if we seem to some to think less honourably of his majesty, or even to deny his omnipotence, because we deny that his body is omnipresent, it is not with us but with Luke that they ought to pick a quarrel, since he wrote: "And entering they did not find the BODY of the Lord Jesus." Behold, he denies that they found the body. And what other explanation of this saying can be given than the one the angel gave straightway after, saying: "He is not here, but he has risen"?

units.la: Ergone (inquis) opera & impensa mulieribus istis periit? Nequaquam. Nametsi corpus Christi non inuenerint, plus tamen quiddam & præstantius inuenerunt, quàm quærerent. Cùm enim rei inexpectatæ cogitatione consternatæ hæsitarent, ecce duo uiri superuenerunt eis induti uestibus fulgurantibus, qui Christum resurrexisse & mortis uictorem factum esse eis indicant. Estq; hoc non vulgare bonitatis Dei argumentum, quòd etsi magna esset istarum mulierum infirmitas & ignorantia, noluit tamen diu dubias & suspensas tenere, sed læta resurrectionis nuntio eas consolatur. Ita solet ille cum omnibus agere, qui ipsum serio quærunt, & generalis promissio est: Omnis qui quærit inuenit. Quod ergo hodie inter odiosas de fide & religione controuersias multi rerum incerti hærent & queruntur, non aliqua Dei salutem ipsis inuidentis malignitate, sed illorum uitio & scelerata contumacia fit, qui Veritatem neq; quærunt, neq; oblatam eius lucem admittunt, eò quòd hanc illorum cupiditatibus & studijs prauis uident aduersam esse.
units.tr: "Then," you may say, "did these women lose their labour and expense for nothing?" Not at all. Although they did not find the body of Christ, they found something greater and more excellent than what they were seeking. While they stood perplexed, thrown into confusion by an unexpected event, suddenly two men appeared to them in shining garments, who told them that Christ had risen and had conquered death. This is no small proof of the goodness of God: though these women were weak and ignorant, he did not keep them long in doubt and suspense, but comforted them with the joyful news of the resurrection. This is how he usually deals with all who seek him earnestly, and his general promise is: "Everyone who seeks finds." Therefore, when many people today hang back in uncertainty and complain amid the hateful controversies about faith and religion, this is not due to any malice of God envying their salvation, but to their own fault and wicked obstinacy, since they neither seek the truth nor admit its light when it is offered, because they see that it opposes their desires and corrupt pursuits.

units.la: Quod autem Angeli cum uestibus fulgurantibus apparent, ad resurrectionis gloriam facit. Solebant olim in triumphis imperatores purpuram auro cotextam gestare, & sublimes currus splendidè ornato uehebantur, populus autem nitidis uestibus indutus spectabat, ut ita simul omnes victoriæ magnificentiam & ex ea enatam lætitiam testarentur. At quia inter homines nulli erant, qui Christum iam de morte & diabolo triumphare intelligebant, non tamen defuerunt ei ministri, qui victoriam eius omni magnificentia & splendore celebrarent: Angeli nimirum, qui cælesti fulgore radiantes se conspiciendos præbuerunt, & ita testati sunt se huius ministros esse, adhæc paratos esse, ut eius gloriam prouehant atq; iuuent. Est ergo Christus ille ipse, quem Daniel olim uidit, similem Filio hominis, qui usq; ad antiquum dierum peruenit (utpote Patri æterno coæternus & coessentialis) & cui ipsi quoq; Angeli cesserunt, ut ad illius dexteram consideret, & dominatum atq; Regnum acciperet æternum. Ut uero hoc facit ad illustrandam eius maiestatem, & irrefragabile est diuinitatis eius ueræ & æternæ testimonium: ita nos hinc consolationem petere debemus, quòdis nobis Vindex & Redemptor datus sit, cui myriades Angelorum seruiunt, & qui nobis quoq; hanc gratiam impetrauit, ut eorundem ministerio subleuemur & custodiamur, sicuti non semel luculentis Scripturarum testimonijs atque exemplis demonstrauimus.
units.tr: That the angels appear in shining garments serves to show the glory of the resurrection. In former times, generals in triumphs used to wear purple woven with gold, and were carried in lofty chariots richly adorned, while the people, dressed in bright garments, looked on, so that all together might bear witness to the splendour of the victory and the joy that came from it. But since there were no men who understood that Christ was now triumphing over death and the devil, there were nonetheless ministers who would celebrate his victory with every kind of magnificence and splendour: namely the angels, who, shining with heavenly brightness, presented themselves to be seen, and so showed that they were his servants and were ready to advance and help his glory. Christ is therefore that very one whom Daniel once saw, "like the Son of man," who came to the Ancient of days (being co-eternal and co-essential with the eternal Father), and to whom even the angels yielded, so that he might sit at the right hand of God and receive dominion and an everlasting kingdom. Now, while this serves to illustrate his majesty, and is an unanswerable witness to his true and eternal divinity, we ought also to draw consolation from this: that he has been given to us as Defender and Redeemer, whom myriads of angels serve, and who has also obtained for us this grace, that we are sustained and guarded by their ministry, as we have shown more than once by clear testimonies and examples of Scripture.

units.la: Sed præstat nunc hos de Christi resurrectione concionantes audire, ubi prius obseruauerimus prædicationis Euangelicæ certitudinem, cuius hoc argumentum est euidentissimum, quòd non hominum solum, uerumetiam Angelorum ministerio promulgata est. Nam Gabriel de toto incarnationis Filij Dei mysterio apud Mariam uirginem concionem luculentissimam habuit, qua Regni quoq; eius statum atque rationem omnem complexus est: ut iam de iis nihil dicamus, quæ idem prius cum Zacharia Ioannis Baptistæ parente egerat. Nunc resurrectionis quoq; testes sunt Angeli, sub qua mortem quoq;, & quæcunq; ille propter nos fecit atq; passus est comprehendi, satis notum est. Nemo igitur Euangelij doctrinam contempserit, ut quæ ab hominibus confitta, præcones quoq; habuerit uiles & obscuros, quorum fides alicui merito dubia atq; incerta uideri debeat. Rectè enim Paulus Apostolus priorem Galatarum fidem hoc argumento commendat, quòd non in carnis infirmitatem respexerint, sed in ea refulgens Spiritus Christi experimentum obseruarint, ideoq; ipsum ut Angelum Dei exceperint. Quod ergo idem ille de Lege dicit, eam per Angelos ordinatam siue promulgatam esse in manu Mediatoris Christi, id non minus ad Euangelij doctrinam debet referri, quae ut nobis ab ipso Dei Filio tradita est, ita Angelorum quoque testimonio comprobatur. Sed accedamus ad huius loci concionem, quae tribus partibus constat.
units.tr: But it is now good to hear these men preaching about Christ's resurrection, after we first note the certainty of the Gospel proclamation, of which this is a very clear proof: that it was published not only by the ministry of men but also of angels. For Gabriel delivered a most distinguished sermon to the virgin Mary about the whole mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, in which he also embraced the state and the whole manner of his kingdom; not to mention what he had earlier treated with Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist. Now the angels are also witnesses of the resurrection, and it is well known that under this resurrection are comprehended his death, and everything else he did and suffered for us. Let no one therefore despise the doctrine of the Gospel on the ground that, having been invented by men, it has had worthless and obscure heralds, whose faith ought therefore to seem doubtful and uncertain to anyone. For the Apostle Paul rightly commends the earlier faith of the Galatians on this ground: that they did not look to the weakness of the flesh, but observed in it the shining experience of the Spirit of Christ, and therefore received him as an angel of God. What the same Paul says of the Law, that it was ordained or published by angels in the hand of Christ the Mediator, must be referred no less to the doctrine of the Gospel, which, as it was delivered to us by the Son of God himself, so is also confirmed by the testimony of angels. But let us come to the sermon of this passage, which consists of three parts.

units.la: Prima consolantur mulieres expauefactas. Nam ut Matthaeus & Marcus annotauerunt, dicunt eis: Ne expauescatis: Vel, ne timeatis uos. In praesenti non sine reprehensionis specie dicunt: Quid inter mortuos quaeritis eum qui uiuit? Habet autem correptio ista ualidissimum consolationis argumentum, quando illum uiuere dicunt, quem illa a morte adhuc detineri arbitrabantur. Estq; hoc fere commune omnibus correptionibus, quibus suorum siue ignauiam siue infirmitatem Deus reprehendit, quod dulcissimis consolationibus condita ad fidei confirmationem faciunt: perinde ac si medicus aegrotum de uita nimis deiecto animo desperantem reprehendat, eo ipso argumento often- dens bonam adhuc spem superesse. At hoc loco prae aliis memorabile est, quod Angeli ijdem mulieres istas consolantur, qui prius militibus terrori fuerat, & eos tantum non metu examinarant. Quod si causam quaeris, non alia reddi potest, quam quae ex Angelorum uerbis apud Marcum descriptis elicitur: quod nimirum illae Iesum serio quaererent & eius honorandi studio pio tenerentur, hi uero eundem perpetuo extinctum atq; sepultum uellent. Unde colligimus Christi maiestatem solis impijs terrificam, pijs autem & credentibus iucundam & salutare esse. Equidem hodie quando per Euangelij praedicationem ille suam uirtutem exerit, pios omnes exultare uidemus, eo quod sese conscientiarum carnificina & superstitionum iugo liberari sentiunt: impijs e contra hypocritis miserè tumultuantibus, qui & quaestum suum euerti uident, eo; uehementius intra animos suos excruciantur, quo clarius Euangelicae doctrinae radijs illi feriuntur. Fit idem in nostrae resurrectionis & nouissimi diei consideratione, ut alibi prolixè ostendimus. Ut enim nihil terribilius est impijs, quam cum aduentus Christi & uniuersalis illius iudicij mentionem fieri audiunt (quomodo enim iudicem ferrent, qui Seruatorem & Redemptorem nolunt agnoscere?) Ita pij & credentes summam ex eo consolationem atq; uoluptatem capiunt; quod diem redemptionis aliquando fore sciunt, quo Christum uenire conspicient, qui abolito hoc mundo ipsos in Regni sui caelestis consortium recipiat. Imò haec illa spes est, quae mortem quoq; ipsam illis iucundam & optatam reddit; quam impij ut extremum malum timere, & ad eius mentionem toti exhorrescere consueuerunt.
units.tr: In the first part, the women who were terrified are comforted. For, as Matthew and Mark have noted, they say to them: "Do not be afraid," or, "Do not let yourselves be frightened." In the present verse they say, not without an appearance of rebuke: "Why do you seek the living among the dead?" That rebuke, however, has a very strong argument of consolation, since they say that he is alive whom the women thought was still held by death. This is almost common to all the rebukes with which God reproves the sloth or weakness of his own people: they are seasoned with the sweetest consolations, to confirm their faith, just as when a physician rebukes a patient who, with his spirit too cast down, despairs of life, and by that very argument shows that good hope still remains. But in this passage it is especially memorable that the same angels who had earlier terrified the soldiers, and had almost struck them dead with fear, now comfort these women. If you ask the reason, none can be given other than what is drawn from the words of the angels recorded by Mark: namely, that these women were seeking Jesus earnestly and were held by a devout zeal to honour him, while the soldiers wanted him utterly extinguished and buried. From this we gather that the majesty of Christ is terrifying only to the wicked, but pleasant and salutary to the godly and believing. Indeed, today, when he exerts his power through the preaching of the Gospel, we see all the godly rejoicing, because they feel themselves freed from the torture of conscience and from the yoke of superstitions; but the wicked hypocrites wretchedly rage, since they see their gain overthrown, and they are tormented within their minds all the more violently as those rays of the Gospel doctrine strike them more clearly. The same happens in the consideration of our resurrection and the last day, as we have shown at length elsewhere. For just as nothing is more terrible to the wicked than when they hear mention of the coming of Christ and his universal judgment (for how could they bear a judge who are unwilling to acknowledge a Saviour and Redeemer?), so the godly and believing take the greatest consolation and joy from it, because they know that there will one day be a day of redemption, when they will see Christ come, who, when this world has been abolished, will receive them into the heavenly fellowship of his kingdom. Indeed, this is that hope which makes even death itself pleasant and desired for them, whereas the wicked are accustomed to fear it as the greatest evil, and at the mention of it to shudder utterly.

units.la: Secunda sua concionis parte resurrectioni Christi testimonium multiplex & luculentum Angeli perhibent. Facit ad eius confirmationem correptio illa, quam modo attigimus, quamuis eadem consolationi quoq; seruiat. Docet enim rem istam adeo certam esse, ut correptione & reprehensione digni sint, quicunq; de ea uel leuiter dubitent. Ideo non contenti dixisse, illum uiuere, mox addunt, Non est, HIC. Et hoc quoque explicantes, ne quis furto sublatum cogitaret, dicunt, SVRRE- XIT, & ita illum mortis uictorem esse factum docent, ut qui huius vincula uirtute propria aboruperit. Apud Marcum oculari quoq; demonstratione utuntur, dicentes: ECCE locus, VBI posuerant eum. Fuit illa apud mulieres istas eò efficacior, quòd locum hunc diligenter obseruauissent. Quia autem stupor nimius illarum animos atq; sensus tenebat, ut tantae rei mysterium non possent concipere, ipsius Christi uerba illis in mentem reducunt: Mementote ut locutus sit uobis; cum adhuc in Galilaea esset, dicens: Oportet Filium hominis tradi in manus hominum peccatorum, & crucifigi, & die tertio resurgere. Facit huc quod supra Cap.9. illum discipulis dixisse audiuimus. Dum uero id Angeli repetunt, simul & crucis scandalum remouent, & illas ad diligentem resurrectionis considerationem excitant. His mox tertiam partem subijciunt (quam à Marco diligentissimè annotatam Lucas omisit) qua iubent, ut hoc omne discipulis annuntient, & Petro quidem in primis, ut is se in gratia receptu esse intelligeret, qui turpi Christi abnegatione exitiu meruerat. Est hoc ingens & memorabile misericordiae Dei exemplum, ex quo consolationem petere debent, qui scelerum conscientia presi de salute sua dubitant. Et simul hic suae fidei & pietatis fructum uberrimum recipiunt mulieres, quae etsi corpus Christi non inuenerint, illum tamen resurrexisse audiunt, & resurrectionis istius testes atq; praecones fiunt, imò hanc ipsis Apostolis annuntiare iubentur: ut non immeritò eas Apostolorum Apostolas factas fuisse dixeris. Ita uero simul illorum ignauiam Dominus ulcisci siue multare uoluit, ut ex mulieribus resciret, quae illae ex Angelorum relatione didicerant.
units.tr: In the second part of his sermon, the angels bear manifold and clear witness to the resurrection of Christ. That rebuke which we have just touched upon contributes to its confirmation, although it also serves for consolation. For it teaches that the matter is so certain that whoever doubts it, even slightly, deserves correction and reproof. Therefore, not content to have said that he is alive, they immediately add, "He is not here." And explaining this too, lest anyone should think he had been taken away by theft, they say, "He has risen," and so teach that he has become the conqueror of death, who by his own power has broken its bonds. In Mark they also use an ocular demonstration, saying: "See the place where they laid him." This was all the more effective for those women because they had carefully observed the place. But since excessive amazement held their minds and senses, so that they could not grasp the mystery of so great a thing, the angels bring back to their minds the very words of Christ: "Remember how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee, saying: The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again." What the angels here repeat is related to what we heard him say to the disciples above, in chapter 9. And while they repeat this, they at the same time remove the scandal of the cross and rouse the women to a careful consideration of the resurrection. Immediately after this they add a third part (which Luke omitted, though Mark recorded it most diligently), in which they order that all this be announced to the disciples, and especially to Peter, so that he may understand that he has been received back into grace, who had deserved ruin by his shameful denial of Christ. This is a great and memorable example of the mercy of God, from which those should seek consolation who doubt their salvation because of the awareness of their sins. At the same time these women receive the most abundant fruit of their faith and piety: although they did not find the body of Christ, they hear that he has risen, and they become witnesses and heralds of this resurrection; indeed they are ordered to announce it to the Apostles themselves. So you may rightly say that these women were made apostles of the apostles. In this way, however, the Lord also wished to punish or chastise their sloth, that the Apostles should learn from women what they had learned from the angels' report.

units.la: Porrò omnium, quæ ab Angelis dicuntur, hic scopus atque finis est, ut Christum illum crucifixum resurrexisse, & in corpore quidem illo resurrexisse ostendant, quod in cruce suspensum & pro mundi peccatis immolatum fuit. Itaq; ista ad articuli illius in Symbolo Apostolico explicationem faciùt, quo illum tertio die à mortuis resurrexisse fatemur. Merebatur autè hoc diligentiorem demonstrationem, eò quòd ex Christi resurrectione tota nostræ redemptionis atque salutis ratio dependet. Quia enim illa mortem deuicit, quæ per peccatum ingressa erat, hoc quoq; expiatum & sublatum esse, evidenter docet. Ideo Paulus eum propter peccata nostra in mortem traditum, propter nostram verò iustificationem resuscitatum esse dicebat. Deinde asseruitur hic animarum nostrarum immortalitas. Nam Christum cum corpore animam quoq; humanam assumpsisse alibi demonstrauimus: eam verò in morte non euanuisse aut periisse, ex eo apparet, quòd ad corpus reuersa, hoc in vitam restituit. Præterea nostrorum corporum resurrectionem & omnes, quæ de hac extant promissiones Christus suo exemplo confirmare voluit: quod Paulus in priori ad Corinthios prolixè admodum demonstrat. Habet itē historia hæc vitæ Christianæ typum, qui nos omnes officij nostri admonet. Vt enim Christus pro peccatis quidem nostris mortuus est, in morte autem non mansit, sed ad vitam cælestem resurrexit: ita nos quoq; peccato mori, & in illo aduitæ nouitatem resurgere debemus. Pertinet huc quod Paulus ad Rom. 6. Cap. copiosè tradit. Nos autè hæc omnia breuiter perstringimus, quia de illis alibi plura diximus.
units.tr: Moreover, the purpose and goal of everything the angels say here is to show that the Christ who was crucified has risen, and that he rose in that same body which hung on the cross and was sacrificed for the sins of the world. Therefore these words serve to explain the article of the Apostles' Creed in which we confess that he rose from the dead on the third day. This deserves a more careful demonstration, because the whole reasoning of our redemption and salvation depends on Christ's resurrection. For since he overcame death, which had entered through sin, it clearly teaches that sin too has been atoned for and removed. So Paul said that he was handed over to death for our sins, but raised for our justification. Next, the immortality of our souls is asserted here. We have shown elsewhere that Christ took on a human soul along with his body; that this soul did not vanish or perish in death is evident from the fact that it returned to the body and restored it to life. Furthermore, Christ wished by his own example to confirm the resurrection of our bodies and all the promises that exist concerning it, as Paul demonstrates at great length in the first letter to the Corinthians. This history also has a type of the Christian life, which reminds us all of our duty. For just as Christ indeed died for our sins, but did not remain in death, rising instead to heavenly life, so we too ought to die to sin and rise into newness of life in him. What Paul sets out at length in Rom. 6. belongs here. But we touch on all these things only briefly, since we have spoken about them more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Sed ad mulieres istas redeamus, quæ auditis Angelorum verbis mox recordantur eorum, quæ aliquando ipsis Christus dixerat. Est hoc animi pij indicium, quo admonemur, sæpius accidere, ut semen Verbi animis reconditum ita delitescat, ut nulla fructus ex eo nascituri spes reliqua esse videatur: at tunc admonitio seria in tempore & commodè adhibita illud suscitare potest, ut nouis incrementis auctum emicet. Istæ certè non in otiosa aut inani recordatione consistunt, sed mox à monumento in urbem reuersæ discipulis rem omnem annuntiant, cum quibus alij quoque nonnulli collecti fuisse indicantur. Videtur hoc cum Marci narratione pugnare, qui illas timuisse scribit, & nemini quicquam dixisse. Sed hoc ita accipi debet, quòd inter eundum nihil effutiuerint, donec ad discipulos uentum fuit, quibus ista renuntiari oportuit. Procul ergo abfuerunt à garrulitatis vitio, quo multæ laborant adeò, ut temere quæuis diuulgantes sæpe turbas dent maximas, & tam seipsas quàm alias in periculum adducant. Fidei autem argumentum est, quòd Angelorum iussis obediunt. Poterant enim eas multa terrere, ne rem hominum iudicio incredibilem primæ spargerent, neue Sacerdotum & Seniorum odia aduersus se provocarent. Sed habet fides coniunctam sibi obedientiam, quæ omnes hominis sensus atq; humanæ sapientiæ rationes Deo subijcit, neq; moras nectit in ijs, quæ ex illius mandato facere iubetur. Decet illa omnes Christianos, in primis autem Verbi Euangelici administros, ne quid eorum dissimulet, quæ prædicare iussi sunt. Quàm enim turpis ignauia fuerit, illos mulierculis istis timidiores inueniri, quæ Christi resurrectionem annuntiare ausæ sunt in ea urbe, in qua illius ferocissimi hostes regnabant? Videtur certè harum exemplum Apostolos animauisse, ut eandem posteà admirabili fortitudine prædicarent, & Christi mandatum Sacerdotum atq; Seniorum minis intrepidè opponerent, qui ipsis silentium indicebant.
units.tr: But let us return to those women, who, on hearing the angels' words, at once recall what Christ had once said to them. This is a sign of a devout mind, by which we are reminded that it often happens that the seed of the Word lies hidden in our minds in such a way that there seems to be no hope left of fruit springing from it; but then a serious admonition, applied at the right time and in a fitting way, can stir it up so that it shines forth, grown by new growth. Certainly these women did not stop at an idle or empty remembrance, but at once returned from the tomb to the city and announced the whole matter to the disciples, with whom certain others are said to have been gathered. This seems to conflict with Mark's account, who writes that they were afraid and said nothing to anyone. But this must be understood to mean that they said nothing on the way, until they came to the disciples, to whom it was fitting that these things be reported. They were therefore far from the fault of garrulity, from which many suffer, so that by rashly spreading whatever comes to them they often cause the greatest disturbances and bring both themselves and others into danger. But their obedience to the angels' commands is a proof of their faith. For many things could have terrified them, so that they would not spread at first a matter that was incredible by human judgment, nor provoke the hatred of the priests and elders against themselves. But faith has obedience joined to it, which subjects all human senses and all the reasonings of human wisdom to God, and does not delay in those things which it is commanded to do by his order. This befits all Christians, and above all the ministers of the Gospel Word, that they should conceal none of the things they have been bidden to preach. For how shameful would it be for them to be found more timid than these little women, who dared to announce Christ's resurrection in that city where his fiercest enemies held sway? Certainly the example of these women seems to have encouraged the Apostles, so that they might afterwards preach with remarkable courage and fearlessly set Christ's command against the threats of the priests and elders, who ordered them to be silent.

units.la: In præsenti tamen magna adhuc infirmitate ijdem laborauerūt. Nam etsi nihil aliud audirent nunc, quam quod ex ipsius Christi ore aliàs audiuerant, & procul dubiò, mulieres Angelorum verba diligenter exposuissent, tamen deliramentum esse putarunt quicquid dicebatur, & non crediderunt eis. Fuit hæc singularis quædam stupiditas cum ingratitudine & aliqua iniuriæ specie coiuncta. Quid enim hoc aliud fuit, quàm mendacij arguere pias illas fœminas, quarum fides tot argumentis perspecta ipsis erat, & quarum tam multa tamq; præclara in Christum & totum ipsorum ordinem beneficia extabant? Adumbratur autem horum exemplo, quomodo carnis nostræ ratio de resurrectione mortuorum iudicet. Fatentur quidem hanc vulgo omnium ferè sectarum homines, & hodie nobis cum in hoc articulo Iudæi & Turcæ consentiunt, nisi quòd hi Mahumetis impuri fabulis decepti Elysios quosdam campos & fœdas voluptates fingūt, quibus tunc suarum superstitionum sectatores Deus remuneraturus sit. Sed quà parum fidei adhibeant propriæ confessioni plerique, ex mortis ignauo metu & effreni morū licentia apparet. Paulus gentibus tribuit, quòd mortuos suos immodicè lugeant, & huius causam adducit, quòd sibi resurrectionis ignorent. Quis ergo de hac certos esse dixerit eos, qui hodie
units.tr: Yet in the present moment the same Apostles still laboured under great weakness. For although they now heard nothing other than what they had heard from Christ's own mouth at other times, and although the women, no doubt, had carefully set out the angels' words, they nevertheless thought whatever was said to be nonsense, and did not believe them. This was a singular stupidity, joined with ingratitude and some appearance of injustice. For what else was it than to accuse of lying those devout women, whose faith was well known to them by so many proofs, and whose many and splendid services to Christ and to their whole company stood out? Yet by their example is shown how our flesh judges concerning the resurrection of the dead. Most people of nearly every sect confess it in words, and today Jews and Turks agree with us on this article, except that the latter, deceived by the impure fables of Mahomet, imagine certain Elysian fields and foul pleasures with which God will then reward the followers of their superstitions. But how little faith most people put in their own confession is clear from their cowardly fear of death and their unbridled licence in morals. Paul ascribes to the Gentiles that they mourn their dead immoderately, and he gives the cause, that they do not know the resurrection. Who, then, would say that those are certain of it who today, not content to have conducted their dead with the private grief that the feeling of humanity and the longing for the departed bring forth, also hire mourning men and women and troops of monks, who increase that sorrow with mournful dirges, and foster it besides with a dress not so much mournful as monstrous?

units.la: 2. Thess. 4. qui hodie non contenti suorum funera cum luctu priuato duxisse, quem humanitatis sensus & defuncti desiderium parit, insuper praeficos & praeficas, & agmina Monachorum conducunt, qui threno-dijs flebilibus dolorem illum augeant, adhaec uestitu quoq; non tam lugubri quam portentofo eundem foueant? Verum tamen magnum hic inter pios & impios discrimen est. Hi enim resurrectione aper-tè & pertinaciter negant, imò ut extremi iudicij terroribus sese liberent, scurrilibus etiá dictis elu-dunt omnia, quae de illa dicuntur. Est horum magnus numerus hodie, & passim audiuntur uoces il-lae, quas Petrus illis illusoribus tribuit, quos nouissimis temporibus exorituros esse uaticinatur. Pij autem partim ignorantia partim fidei imbecillitate fluctuant, doctrinam uero illam adeo non ode-runt, ut ea etiam delectentur, & ueram esse cupiant, licet ei nondum plenam fidem possint adhibere. Huius generis discipulorum incredulitatem fuisse apparet in Petro, qui unà cum Ioanne excurrit ad monumentum, quod nunquam facturus fuisset, si ab omni fide prorsus fuisset alienus. Et ubi eo uenit, in illud ingressus certa corporis resuscitati indicia inuenit, lintea nimirum illic iacentia, et suda-rium seorsim inuolutum. Nam si quis corpus auferre uoluisset furtim, procul dubio illud cum sindone sustulisset, cum periculi metus moram nullam admitteret, lintea autè propter myrrham & aloen (quae picea & uiscosa naturae sunt) nō ita facile detrahi potuissent. Verūtamen etsi ista sic iacentia spe fuisset, non poterat tamen adhuc fidem certam animo concipere, neque etiam negare poterat quod nihil res retulerant. Itaq; abit cum admiratione, quae rei magis incertum reddit. Causam huius dubitationis Ioannes his uerbis indicat. Nondum enim nouerant scripturam, quòd oporteret illum à mortuis resurgere. Fuit autem ignorantia haec turpior, quàm ut eos deceret, qui Dei Filio tam diu praecepto re domestico usi erant: & proinde incredulitas quoq; ista non potest omnino excusari. Attamen magnus quoq; eius usus fuit: quia testimonio Apostolorum, de Christi resurrectione fidem maiorem facit, quae dubia uideri poterat, si nimiū credulos sese praebuissent. Ita nostris uitijs & infirmitatibus diuina prouidentia bene uti solet, ut in multis aliis exemplis uidimus. Sunt ea obseruanda in eum finem, ne mox animum despondeamus, si quid huius nobis accidit. Interim uero Petrū imitati cum nostra incredulitate luctemur, & quae Deus nobis offert, adminicula non negligamus. Fuit illi salutis principium, quòd post factam Christi abnegationem, ad Ecclesiam, quae tunc paruo illo discipulorum cœtu constabat, redijt. Illic ergo audit laetum de illius resurrectione nuntium: cui etsi non omnino credat, non tamen impie contradicit, imò rei veritatem cupit cognoscere, neq; moram aliquam interponit in negotio hoc, ex quo Christi gloria & ipsorum omnium salus dependebat. Horum memineri nt hodie quotquot suae incredulitatis, uel potius perfidiae, patrocinium in Petro quaerunt, cùm ab Ecclesia manifestam secessionem faciant, Verbum Dei audire dedignentur, occasiones item omnes rideant atq; contemnant, quibus fides eorum poterat confirmari, & ipsi in uiam reduci. Sunt hi sibi ipsis exitij authores. Nos itaq; feria mortis IesuChristi meditatione excitati hoc agamus, ut ille in nobis uiuat, donec huius uitae uinculis liberati in Regnum eius caelestè transferamur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: 2. Thess. 4. Nevertheless there is a great difference here between the pious and the impious. For the latter openly and stubbornly deny the resurrection, and indeed, in order to free themselves from the terrors of the last judgment, they mock everything that is said about it, even with scurrilous remarks. Their number today is great, and everywhere those voices are heard which Peter attributes to those mockers whom he predicted would arise in the last times. The pious, however, waver partly from ignorance and partly from weakness of faith; yet they do not so hate that doctrine that they do not delight in it, and wish it to be true, even though they cannot yet give it full faith. The unbelief of disciples of this kind appears in Peter, who ran together with John to the tomb, which he would never have done if he had been wholly estranged from faith. And when he came there, on entering he found certain clear signs of the body having been raised: namely the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been wrapped separately. For if anyone had wished to steal the body away secretly, he would undoubtedly have carried it off together with the shroud, since fear of danger would allow no delay; but the linen cloths, because of the myrrh and aloes (which are pitchy and sticky by nature), could not have been removed so easily. Nevertheless, although these things lying thus gave hope, he could not yet conceive certain faith in his mind, nor could he deny what the facts showed. So he went away in wonder, which makes the matter more uncertain. John indicates the cause of this doubt in these words: for they did not yet know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. But this ignorance was too shameful to befit men who had been so long used to the teaching of the Son of God in their own household; and therefore this unbelief also cannot be wholly excused. Yet it also had great use: for by the testimony of the Apostles it makes the faith concerning Christ's resurrection greater, which might have seemed doubtful if they had shown themselves too credulous. Thus divine providence is accustomed to make good use of our faults and infirmities, as we have seen in many other examples. These things are to be noted to this end, that we should not at once lose heart if anything of this kind happens to us. Meanwhile, imitating Peter, let us struggle with our unbelief, and not neglect the helps which God offers us. It was the beginning of his salvation for Peter that, after making his denial of Christ, he returned to the Church, which at that time consisted of that small gathering of disciples. There he hears the joyful news of his resurrection; and although he does not wholly believe it, he does not impiously contradict it, but rather desires to know the truth of the matter, and does not interpose any delay in this affair, on which the glory of Christ and the salvation of them all depended. Let those remember these things today who, as the defence of their unbelief, or rather perfidy, seek a pattern in Peter, while they make a manifest secession from the Church, disdain to hear the Word of God, and mock and despise all the opportunities by which their faith could be confirmed and they themselves brought back to the way. Such people are the authors of their own ruin. Let us therefore, roused by the meditation on the death of Jesus Christ on this day, take care that he lives in us, until, freed from the chains of this life, we are carried over into his heavenly kingdom. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXI.

units.la: Et ecce duo ex ijs ibant eo ipso die in vicum distantem stadijs sexaginta ab Hierusalem, cui vico nomen est Emmaus: & colloquebantur inter se de ijs omnibus, quae euenerant. Et factum est dum colloqueretur & secum mutuò rogitarent, ipse Iesus accessit, & vnà iter faciebat cum ipsis: oculi autem eorum tenebantur, ne eum agnoscerent. Dixit autem eis: Qui sunt hi sermones, quos conseritis inter vos ambulantes, & quid estis tetrico vultu? Respondens autem alter, cui nomen Cleopas, dixit ei: Tu solus aduena es in Hierusalem, & ignoras quae in ea facta sunt his diebus? Ipse verò dixit eis, Quae? At illi dixerunt: Quae facta sunt Iesu Nazareno, qui fuit Propheta, potens operibus & sermonibus coram Deo & toto populo: Et quomodo eum tradiderunt principes Sacerdotum & magistratus nostri vt morti damnaretur, & cru-cifixerunt eum. cifixerunt eum. Nos autem sperabamus illum esse, qui redem-pturus esset Israelem. Atqui praeter haec omnia tertium hunc diem agit hodie, ex quo haec facta sunt. Sed & mulieres quaedam ex nobis obstupefecerunt nos, quae diluculo venerunt ad monumentum: & non invento eius corpore venerunt, dicentes, se etiam visionem Angelorum vidisse, qui dicunt eum viuere. Et abierunt quidam eorum, qui erant nobiscum, ad monumentum, & ita invenerunt prout mulieres dixerant, ipsum vero non viderunt.
units.tr: And behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was sixty furlongs from Jerusalem, and they talked together of all these things which had happened. And it came to pass, while they communed together and reasoned, that Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were holden, that they should not know him. And he said unto them, What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad? And the one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering said unto him, Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast thou not known the things which are come to pass there in these days? And he said unto them, What things? And they said unto him, Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, which was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people: and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to be condemned to death, and have crucified him. But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel. And beside all this, today is the third day since these things were done. Yea, and certain women also of our company made us astonished, which were early at the sepulchre; and when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive. And certain of them which were with us went to the sepulchre, and found it even so as the women had said: but him they saw not.

units.la: Quoniam in resurrectione Domini nostri, Iesu Christi, salutis nostrae complementum est, & eadem nostrorum quoque corporum resurrectionem argumento irrefragabili probat atque confirmat: non temere factum putabimus, quod Dominus postquam a mortuis suscitatus est, non mox in caelos ascendit, sed per totos dies quadraginta cum discipulis suis conuersatus, se vero & naturali suo corpore, quod ex Maria virgine assumpserat, & in quo passus erat, vere resurrexisse, multis apparitionibus & argumentis evidentissimis demonstrauit. Multis enim confirmari oportuit eum articulum, qui & fidem nostram maxime confirmat, & praecipuum est ad vitam pie transfigendam incitamentum. Quoad vero apparitiones illas, Evangelistae selectiores modo describunt, & alij quidem alias narrant, ut narrationibus eorum in unum collatis & diligentius expensis in fide magis confirmemur. Inter omnes tamen non postremo loco collocari debet, cuius historiam Lucas in praesenti commemorare coepit. Nam praeter certissima sensuum experimenta & Scripturae veteris testimonia, quibus & ipsius resurrectionis Christi & corporis resuscitati veritas probatur, omnis generis affectus & colloquia concurrunt, quibus totum hoc negotium illustratur, ut omnium hominum institutioni simul & consolationi mirifice seruiat. Finis & usus omnium quae dicuntur, hic est, ut credamus, Iesum Christum eo ipso corpore, quo ex Virgine natus & in quo mortuus est, revera resurrexisse, & sua morte atque resurrectione omnia impleuisse, quae in Lege & Prophetis olim praedicta fuerunt, & proinde verum atque unicum esse humani generis Redemptorem.
units.tr: Since the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ is the completion of our salvation, and by an unanswerable argument also proves and confirms the resurrection of our own bodies, we shall not think it done rashly that the Lord, after he was raised from the dead, did not at once ascend into heaven, but spent whole forty days with his disciples, and by many appearances and most evident proofs showed that he had truly risen again, both in his natural body, which he had taken from the virgin Mary and in which he had suffered. For this article, which above all confirms our faith and is the chief incitement to living a godly life, had to be confirmed by many means. As for those appearances, the Evangelists describe only the more select ones, and some relate one thing, others another, so that by bringing their narratives together into one and weighing them more carefully we may be the more confirmed in faith. Yet among them all, the one whose history Luke now begins to recount should not be placed in the last rank. For besides the most certain experiences of the senses and the testimonies of the Old Scripture, by which the truth both of Christ's own resurrection and of his raised body is proved, every kind of feeling and conversation comes together here, by which this whole matter is illuminated, so that it serves wonderfully both the instruction and the comfort of all men. The aim and use of everything that is said is this: that we believe Jesus Christ truly rose again in that very body in which he was born of the Virgin and in which he died, and that by his death and resurrection he fulfilled all things which were foretold of old in the Law and the Prophets, and therefore that he is the true and only Redeemer of mankind.

units.la: Rursus autem temporis notationem expressam ponit Euangelista, & haec eodem die facta esse dicit, cuius diluculo Christum resurrexisse, & mulieres sepulchrum vacuum inuenisse dixerat. Facit hoc ad declarandam Christi fidem, qui cum discipulorum suorum infirmitatem probe nosset, noluit illos diutius suspensos tenere, sed eo ipso die certiores facere de eo, quod cognitu & creditu in primis necessarium erat. Solet enim infirmitatis nostrae rationem habere Deus, & quia nos inter metum & spem semper fluctuare, adeoque in aquis natantium similes esse novit, subinde adminicula ipse nobis offert, quibus apprehensis fidem iamiam subsidentem erigere nosque ipsos quasi novis viribus confirmare possimus. Exempla huius bonitatis multa passim occurrunt, & eandem in nobismetipsis quotidie experimur: sed quae nostri ingenij infelicitas est, non semper animaduertimus Dei manum, quam is nobis periclitantibus porrigit.
units.tr: Again, the Evangelist gives an explicit note of time, and says these things were done on the same day on whose early morning he had said that Christ rose and the women found the tomb empty. This serves to commend Christ's faithfulness: since he knew well the weakness of his disciples, he did not want to keep them in suspense for longer, but on that very day to inform them about what was first of all necessary to know and to believe. For God is wont to take account of our weakness, and since he knows that we always waver between fear and hope, and are like men swimming in waters, he from time to time offers us supports, by grasping which we can raise up faith that is already sinking and, as it were, strengthen ourselves with new powers. Many examples of this goodness occur everywhere, and we experience the same thing every day in ourselves. But by the unhappiness of our own understanding, we do not always notice the hand of God which he stretches out to us when we are in danger.

units.la: Porro diligentius describuntur personae, quibus illo die Dominus apparuit. Fuerunt duo ex discipulis, non quidem ex duodecim Apostolorum, sed ex Septuaginta illorum numero, de quibus supra Cap.10. est dictum. Alterius nomen postea exprimitur, Cleopas: unde apparet eum ipsum fuisse, a quo Maria Cleopae nomen accepit, quam Diuae Virginis sororem, Iacobi vero minoris & Iosis matrem fuisse, nuper diximus. Alterius nomen tacetur, ut non absque causa eorum audaciam admiremur, qui hunc olim vel Lucam, vel Nathanaelem dicere ausi sunt. Unde enim hoc acceperunt? aut quae coniecturae satis graues fingi possunt, quibus istud probent? Lucas certe in sui operis proemio se ex eorum numero diserte eximit, qui Christi & rerum ab eo gestarum testes oculati fuerunt. Quae autem ratio iubet, ut alterum hunc Nathanaelem potius quam Matthiam aut Barnabam, aut quemuis aliū ex Christi familiaribus fuisse dicamus? Desinant ergo ea curiosius inquirere pij, quae Spiritus sanctus consulto tacuit. Nam ut illa ad salutē non sunt necessaria cognitu, ita Christi causa & fidei nostrae certitudo non ab hominū authoritate pendet, sed aeterna Verbi Dei veritate nititur. Hoc potius in duobus istis obseruemus, tales fuisse, ut nihil minus de illis possimus suspicari, quam quòd fabulam aliquam comminisci voluerint, qua Christi resurrectionem falso aliquibus persuaderent. Vt enim in omnibus eorum dictis ingenua simplicitas & omnis fraudis expers animus apparet, ita reliſti alijs discipulis in urbe, ipsi Emmauntem proficiscuntur, oppidum, quod nullo unquam Christi faſto nobilitatum fuisse legimus: & illic pernoctaturi erant (ut suo loco audiemus) nisi Christus praeter omnem expectationem sese manifestans, ipsos consilium mutare coegisset. Inter eundum vero col-loquuntur inter se de omnibus ijs, quae evenerant circa Christi mortem, & quae de eius resurrectione ex mulieribus audiverant. Nec obiter modo colloquuntur, sed conferunt suas sententias seq; mutuo interrogant. Non ergo vulgare aut otiosum fuit colloquium illud, qualia esse solent plerunq; eorum, quae ab iter facientibus fallendi temporis & levandi taedij causa instituuntur: sed ferio salutis studio accensi, & sancto Christi amore ardentes fidem suam (quae etsi iam perplexior fluctuaret, minimè tamen extincta erat) colloquio illo & piis quaestionibus fulcire atq; fovere studuerunt: sicuti in ijs patebit, quae mox sequentur.
units.tr: Next, the persons to whom the Lord appeared on that day are described more carefully. They were two of the disciples, not indeed of the twelve Apostles, but of that number of the Seventy, concerning whom it was said above in chapter 10. The name of the other is given afterwards, Cleopas; whence it appears that he was the very man from whom Mary received the name Cleopas, whom we lately said was the sister of the blessed Virgin and the mother of James the Less and Joses. The name of the other is not told, so that we may wonder, not without cause, at the boldness of those who have dared to say that he was once either Luke or Nathanael. For where did they get this? Or what sufficiently weighty conjectures can be invented by which they prove it? Luke, at least, in the preface to his work plainly sets himself apart from those who were eyewitnesses of Christ and of the things he did. And what reason bids us say that this second man was Nathanael rather than Matthias or Barnabas, or any other of Christ's close companions? Let the godly therefore cease to inquire too curiously into those things which the Holy Spirit deliberately passed over in silence. For just as those things are not necessary to know for salvation, so the cause of Christ and the certainty of our faith do not depend on the authority of men, but rest on the eternal truth of the Word of God. Rather let us observe this in these two: they were such men that we can suspect nothing less of them than that they wished to devise some fable by which they might persuade certain people falsely of Christ's resurrection. For just as in all their words a candid simplicity and a mind free from all deceit appears, so, leaving the other disciples in the city, they themselves set out for Emmaus, a town which we read was never made famous by any deed of Christ; and there they were going to spend the night (as we shall hear in its place), had not Christ, revealing himself beyond all expectation, made them change their plan. Indeed, as they went, they talked together about all those things which had happened concerning Christ's death, and about what they had heard from the women concerning his resurrection. Nor do they merely talk in passing, but they compare their opinions and question one another. That conversation, then, was not an ordinary or idle one, such as those usually held by travellers to pass the time and relieve weariness; but, kindled with a earnest zeal for salvation and burning with holy love for Christ, they sought to prop up and foster their faith (which, though now wavering more perplexedly, was by no means extinguished) with that talk and with pious questions, as will become clear in what follows.

units.la: Est igitur exemplum hoc pietatis non vulgare, quo docemur, quae & qualia esse debeant Christianorum hominum colloquia omni tempore, maximè autem tunc, quando rebus afflictissimis tota salutis spes collapsa esse videtur. Quàm enim tristis tunc rerum facies fuerit, & quàm graviter piorum fides tentata fuerit, quando Christum in cruce mori, & corpus eius sepulturae mandari viderint, non opus est multis exponere. Veruntamen non potuit vel crudele illud spectaculum, vel tristis eiusdem recordatio istorum animos ita perterrefacere, quin pio colloquio se mutuo confirmarint, & de Christo honorificè locuti sint, etsi nulla de eius regno spes reliqua esset. Debent istos imitari, quicunq; in vera fide volunt progressus facere. Ut enim sermo animi index est, ita eiusdem in hominum animis vel commovendis vel mutandis magnae vires sunt, & frequenter impijs colloquijs quorundam fidem euer-ti videmus, rursus autem pijs sermonibus eos confirmari, qui iam labascebant, & fidem prorsus abiecisse videbantur. Nec temere Paulus Menandri versum dignum iudicauit, quem suis scriptis in-sereret: Corrumpunt mores bonos, colloquia prava. Et satis nota sunt, quae passim de oris & linguae custodia in Scripturis traduntur. Quibus idem Apostolus subscribens monet, ut sermo noster salè conditus sit, cum prius in eadem epistola dixisset: Sermo Christi inhabitet in vobis opulenté, cum omni sapientia docendo & commonendo vos mutuò, &c. Sed utinam ista tam facilè omnibus persuaderentur, quàm facilè à nobis dicuntur. At ea est nostri saeculi infelicitas, ut unum hoc sufficere possit ad arguendum impiam levitatem multorum, qui se ab omni fide & religionis sensu alienissimos esse testantur. Quando enim res secundae affluunt, sermonibus vanis, spurcis & obscaenis delectatur: & ea saepe viri & mulieres in frequenti hominum corona & in convivijs tam publicis quàm privatis proferunt, quae in lenonibus quoq; & scortis nimia videri poterant. Quid, quòd non sine impensis magnis aluntur Mimi & scurrae, qui fabulis impudicis taedium temporis fallant apud eos, qui non nisi rebus serijs & gravibus debebant occupari? Et apud principes viros in pretio sunt, qui magni esse putantur eius rei artifices: adeò ut religionem quoq; ludibrio habere, & resurrectionem mortuorum scurrilibus dictis exagitare, omnia deniq; impijs iocis in dubium vocare possint, quae de vita aeterna & novissimo Christi adventu, aut mundi huius fine dicuntur. Sunt hi illusores illi, quos novissimis temporibus exorituros esse, Petrus praedixit, & à quorum commercijs, ut praesenti aliqua peste, Chri-stiani homines abhorrere debebant. Taceo nunc libros fabulosos, quos hodie in omnium fere gen-tium linguis leuissimi & impijssimi homines conscribunt, & in lucem edunt, ut toti mundo notum fiat, quantum possint fabulando: eosque ut lectu dignissimos nobilissimis heroibus & alijs uiris praestantibus nuncupare audent. Regnat ea licentia in primis apud nos, ô viri Germani, quos vel sola nominis patrij recordatio gravitatis admonere, & ad ea quae sunt magis seria, excitare de-bebat: ut iam nihil de eo dicam, quod plane turpissimum est, ex ea terra tam infelices & puden-dos fœtus prodire, quae renascentem novissimis hisce temporibus nostris Evangelij lucem primau-dit, & ex qua salutiferi illius radij in omnes gentes longè lateque diffusi sunt. Vtinam vero vel hic pedem sisteret impietas, & non latius adhuc progressa maiori scelere nominis Christiani pro-sessionem diffamaret. Sed ijdem illi, qui dum pace & otio abundant, hac vanitate gaudent, mox si quid tristius accidit, & fidei causa periclitari videtur, in dira convitia erumpunt, quibus & uni-versam Christi doctrinam proscindunt, & eius precones horribiliter obruunt. Ita certè tunc resur-rectionis huius tam laetae tamque gloriosae obliviscuntur, ut maiori impietate aduersus Evangelij doctrinam linguas suas laxare non possent, si nihil unquam de Christo & regno eius audivissent. Sunt hi omnes Christiani nominis macula, & Ecclesiarum labes, ideoque, indignum ut in iis locis feran-tur, in quibus Evangelicae veritatis professores imperium habent. Et debebant in illis coercendis Christiani magistratus semper gravis illius sententiae meminisse, qua Christus pronuntiat, de quovis verbo otioso rationem aliquando reddendam esse. Quid ergo de illis fiet, qui impia quoq; & horren-da blasphemijs turgentia plenis buccis effundunt? Longe alia istorum mens, & alij longe sermones fuerunt, quibus inter se collocuti sunt duo isti, quorum historiam Spiritus sanctus dignam iudicavit, quae scriptis mandaretur.
units.tr: Therefore this example of piety is not a commonplace one: it teaches us what kind of conversations Christian people ought to have, and at all times, but especially when the whole hope of salvation seems to have collapsed amid the most grievous circumstances. How gloomy the situation was then, and how severely the faith of the godly was tested, when they saw Christ dying on the cross and his body committed to the tomb, there is no need to set out at length. Yet neither that cruel spectacle nor the sad memory of it could so terrify those men that they did not encourage one another with pious conversation and speak honourably of Christ, even though no hope of his kingdom remained. All who wish to make progress in true faith ought to imitate them. For just as speech is an indicator of the mind, so it has great power to stir or change men's minds. We often see the faith of some overthrown by impious conversation, and again those who were already wavering, and seemed to have cast off faith altogether, confirmed by godly talk. Paul did not rashly judge worthy of inclusion in his writings the verse of Menander: "Evil conversations corrupt good morals." And what is said throughout the Scriptures about guarding the mouth and the tongue is well known. The same Apostle, adding to this, warns that our speech should be seasoned with salt, having said earlier in the same epistle: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another," and so on. Would that these things were as easily persuaded into everyone as they are easily said by us! But such is the unhappiness of our age that this alone may suffice to expose the impious levity of many who declare themselves utterly alien to all faith and sense of religion. For when prosperity flows in, they delight in vain, filthy and obscene talk, and men and women often utter these things in the crowded company of people, at banquets both public and private, things which might seem excessive even in pimps and prostitutes. What of the fact that mimes and buffoons, who beguile the tedium of time with impure tales among those who ought to be occupied only with serious and weighty matters, are supported at no small expense? And among great men those who are thought to be masters of this art are held in high esteem, so much so that they can make religion a laughing-stock, mock the resurrection of the dead with buffoonish words, and in the end cast into doubt by impious jokes everything that is said about eternal life, the last coming of Christ, or the end of this world. These are those scoffers whom Peter foretold would arise in the last times, and from whose company Christians ought to shrink, as from some present plague. I say nothing now of the fabulous books which the most frivolous and impious men write and publish today in almost every language of the nations, so that it may become known to the whole world how much they can do by fabricating; and they dare to dedicate these, as most worthy of reading, to the noblest heroes and other outstanding men. This licence reigns especially among us, O men of Germany, whom the mere recollection of our national name ought to remind of gravity and rouse to what is more serious. I will not even say what is plainly most shameful: that such unhappy and shameful offspring should come forth from that land which, in these latter days of ours, first saw the light of the Gospel reborn, and from which the saving rays of that light have spread far and wide among all nations. Would that impiety might at least stop here, and not, having advanced further still, spread abroad a profession of the Christian name by greater wickedness! But those same people, who abound in peace and leisure and delight in this vanity, as soon as anything sadder happens and faith seems to be in danger, burst out into dreadful reproaches, by which they tear apart the whole teaching of Christ and cruelly overwhelm its heralds. Indeed, at such times they forget this resurrection so joyful and so glorious, and they could not loose their tongues in greater impiety against the doctrine of the Gospel if they had never heard anything about Christ and his kingdom. All these people are a stain on the Christian name and a blot on the Churches, and it is unworthy that they should be tolerated in those places where professors of the Gospel truth hold power. And in restraining them the Christian magistrates ought always to remember that grave saying by which Christ declares that account must one day be rendered for every idle word. What then will become of those who pour forth from full cheeks things swollen with impious and horrible blasphemies? Far different was the mind of these two men, and far different the words with which they conversed together, and the Holy Spirit judged their history worthy to be committed to writing.

units.la: Sed & fructum eximium ex sua ista pietate retulerunt. Nam dum inter se colloquuntur, seque mutuo de rebus hisce gravibus & cognitu necessarijs interrogant, ipse Iesus ad eos accedit, & una cum ipsis iter facit. Id vero alibi quoque factum fuisse constat, ut de resurrectione sua colloquen-tibus discipulis sese praesentem exhibuerit. Huc enim pertinent, quae eodem vespere Hierosolymis fa-cta sunt, & quod cum Thoma octiduo post factum esse Ioannes narrat. Fauet ergo piorum collo-quijs Christus, quibus fidem suam testantur, aut saltem fovere student. Et qui suam praesentiam illis pollicetur, qui in ipsius nomine conveniunt, ab illis abesse non potest, qui de rebus ad gloriam suam pertinentibus inter se pie differunt. Accedit ergo ad eos propius, & una cum eis iter facit, id est, gres-sus eorum & omnes vitae actiones atque studia dirigit suo Spiritu, neuel proprijs cupiditatibus, uel diaboli praestigijs decepti a via salutis exorbitent. Sequitur ex eo benedictio Dei vera, cuius ille Me-diator est, & quae totam hominis felicitatem comprehendit tam in hoc praesenti quam futuro seculo. Vides ergo non mirum esse, quod maior pars hominum hodie infelix est, quod caecis consilijs poten-tissimi Reges seducuntur, respub. in summis difficultatibus versantur, multi priuatim in Labyrin-this inextricabilibus oberrant, quod deniq; totus terrarum orbis seditionibus & bellis tam exteris quam civilibus turbatur. Quid enim aliud fiat, quando Christum Iesum pauci quaerunt, nulli ad se alliciunt, multi vero impijs sermonibus, uanissimis dicterijs & obscoenis cantibus, adhaec morum im-probitate & sceleribus procul arcent? Corrigantur ista, imo prorsus e medio auferantur, & mox il-lum nobis appropinquare videbimus.
units.tr: But they also reaped an outstanding fruit from this piety of theirs. For while they talk together, and ask one another about these weighty matters which it is necessary to know, Jesus himself comes up to them and journeys along with them. That this also happened elsewhere is clear: he showed himself present to the disciples talking about his resurrection. For to this belong the things that were done in Jerusalem on that same evening, and what John relates as having happened with Thomas eight days later. Christ therefore favours the godly conversations of those who bear witness to their faith, or at least strive to foster it. And he who promises his presence to those who gather in his name cannot be absent from those who piously discuss among themselves matters pertaining to his glory. He therefore draws near to them and journeys along with them, that is, by his Spirit he directs their steps and all the actions and pursuits of their lives, so that they do not stray from the way of salvation, deceived either by their own desires or by the delusions of the devil. From this follows the true blessing of God, of which he is the Mediator, and which embraces the whole happiness of man both in this present age and in the age to come. You see, then, that it is no wonder that the greater part of mankind is unhappy today, that the most powerful kings are led astray by blind counsels, that commonwealths are in the greatest difficulties, that many individuals wander privately in inextricable labyrinths, and that finally the whole orb of the earth is troubled by seditions and wars, both foreign and civil. For what else should happen, when few seek Christ Jesus, none draw others to him, and many, on the other hand, by impious talk, empty sayings and obscene songs, and besides by wickedness of life and crimes, keep him far away? Let these things be corrected, or rather let them be utterly removed from our midst, and soon we shall see him drawing near to us.

units.la: Non debet autem hic oscitanter praeteriri quod additur: Oculi autem eorum tenebantur, ne eum agnoscerent. Nam licet a suis nunquam absit Dominus, non tamen semper ita se offert, ut ipsius gratiam aut bonitatem sensibus suis percipere possint: sed ut olim Iosephus fratribus suis se cum minaci potentia ostendebat, & eosdem durioribus verbis compellabat, ut fratrem suum esse nequa-quam agnoscere possent: ita frequenter Christus nobis alius apparet, quam revera sit: non quod simula-torem aut hypocritam agat, sed quod ita meretur nostra ingratitudo, quam interdum minus perter-refieri, aut disciplina seueriori coerceri & in ordinem redigi oportet. Tunc ergo peregrinam iudicis personam ille induit, & intra conscientias nostras nobis terrores excitat, quibus sensus nostri ita per-celluntur, ut latentem sub iusta seueritatis specie bonitatem uidere non possint. Vt autem Iosephus tandem fratribus se manifestauit, & in dulces quoque lachrymas solutus est, dum illos tenerrimo amore complecteba-tur (quando nimirum meliores, & patris sui obseruantiores factos esse uidebat) ita nobis quoq; Christus depositio iudicis habitu se propitium & plus quam fratrem offert, quando nos suarum promissionum non omnino immemores esse, & Patris sui amore atq; studio syncero teneri cernit. Nemo igitur de eius bonitate facile desperet, sed quamuis ille a nobis alienus esse, adeoq; peregrinari uideatur, constantes tamen simus in fidei professione, & curemus ut huic vitae atq; mo-res nostri respondeant: tunc enim nobis ille propius innotescet.
units.tr: Nor should what is added here be passed over carelessly: "But their eyes were held, so that they should not recognise him." For although the Lord is never absent from his own, yet he does not always present himself in such a way that they can perceive his grace or goodness with their senses. Rather, just as Joseph once showed himself to his brothers with a threatening authority and addressed them with harsher words, so that they could by no means recognise him as their brother, so Christ often appears to us other than he really is. This is not because he plays the pretender or the hypocrite, but because our ingratitude deserves it, and we sometimes need to be struck more sharply with terror, or restrained by a stricter discipline and brought back into line. Then he puts on the strange guise of a judge and stirs up terrors within our consciences, by which our senses are so disturbed that they cannot see the goodness lying hidden beneath the appearance of just severity. But just as Joseph at last made himself known to his brothers, and was melted into sweet tears while he embraced them with the tenderest love (since he saw that they had become better and more mindful of their father), so Christ too, laying aside the appearance of a judge, offers himself to us as kind and more than a brother, when he sees that we are not entirely forgetful of his promises and are held by a sincere love and zeal for his Father. Let no one therefore easily despair of his goodness; but even though he may seem to be alien to us and as if a stranger, let us be steadfast in the profession of faith, and take care that our life and manners correspond to it. For then he will become known to us more closely.

units.la: Porrò continetur etiam hoc loco certum atq; evidens argumentum, quo illum vero suo corpore resurrexisse, & post resurrectionem naturales corporis proprietates retinuisse probatur, uel potius demonstratur ita, ut sensibus quoque percipi possit. Nam colloquentibus discipulis ad eos accessisse dicitur. Non ergo repente aut subito apparuit (ut interdum spectra solent) ut unde nam uenisset illi nescirent: sed eum uenire & ad ipsos accedere uiderunt. Deinde iter cum illis fecit, & inter eun-dum cum eis locutus est. Ista vero motum ex loco in locum ita diserte exprimunt, ut portento simile sit, olim aliquos fuisse, & hodie etiam inueniri, qui ut corporis eius veritate negant, ita hoc in primis agunt magna contentione, ut illud neq; loco certo contineri, neq; ex loco in locum moueri euincant. Fingunt Finguntilli œconomiam siue dispensationem quandam, qua hîc & alibi posteà resurrectionem usus sit. Pudet nimirum eos, si quid eum simulauisse dicant: quia simulatio fere cum mendacio coniuncta est. Atqui quam ei tribuunt dispensationem, ego à simulatione nihil abesse uideo. Aut enim uerè istafecit Dominus, & uero suo corpore uerè iter ingressus est, aut falso: Si uerè ambulauit, uero corpore ambulauerit oportet, & idem suum motum habuit. Quòd si quid simulanter hîc factum est, falsò factum est, & proinde corporis quoque resurrectio, quam hoc argumento demonstrare voluit, in dubium veniet.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage also contains a certain and evident argument by which it is proved, or rather demonstrated, that he rose again in his true body and kept the natural properties of that body after the resurrection, so that he could be perceived by the senses too. For it is said that he drew near to the disciples while they were talking. He therefore did not appear suddenly, as ghosts usually do, so that they did not know where he had come from; they saw him coming and approaching them. Then he made the journey with them and spoke with them as they went. But these words describe his movement from place to place so plainly that it seems a marvel that there have been some, and are still some today, who deny the truth of his body yet labour with great effort to prove that he could be contained in no fixed place and moved from place to place. They invent a certain "economy," or dispensation, by which he made use of the resurrection here and elsewhere afterwards. They are ashamed, surely, to say that he feigned anything, since feigning is almost always bound up with lying. Yet I see that the dispensation they ascribe to him is no different from feigning. For either the Lord truly did these things and truly walked with his real body, or he did them falsely. If he truly walked, he must have walked in a true body and had his own real movement. But if anything was done in pretence here, then it was done falsely, and therefore the resurrection of the body, which he wished to prove by this argument, will also be called into doubt.

units.la: Obijciunt illi: At non agnouerunt Christum discipuli isti duo: Ergo non is fuit, qui antea fuerat, quoad corporis formam atq; essentiam.
