Ego verò consequentiam istam nego, & non falsam modò, sed tam futilem, tam stultam, tam ineptam & ridiculam esse dico, ut pueros eius pudere debeat. Quoties enim fit, ut non agnoscamus ad nos praeter expectationem venientes amicos, qui prius nobis notissimi & familiarissimi fuerunt? Quis autè ex eo colligit, illos in alia corpora esse mutatos, aut corporis sui naturam exuisse? Sed non opus est multa responsione, quando ipse Lucas hunc nodum felicissimè soluit, & ne quis ex eo quod dictum erat, tale quid colligeret, mox addit: Oculi autem eorum tenebantur, ne eum agnoscerent. Non ergo corporis naturam Christus exuit, neq; eius mutatione vel euacuatione factum fuit, quòd eum discipuli non agnouerunt, sed quòd eorum oculi detinerentur: occulta nimirum Dei virtute, qui aciem illorum ad tempus hebetare aut restringere voluit, ne illum discernere aut cognoscere possent. Et mirum est hoc à quibusdam non obseruari, cùm huius generis exempla plura in Scripturis occurrant. Quis enim nescit, Sodomæos olim ab Angelis percussos fuisse, ut domum Lothi & eius fores non possent inuenire? Et Syros ab Elisæo simili miraculo delusos esse scimus, ut quàmuis oculorum usum haberent, tamen neq; ipsum Elisæum, hominem aliàs multis eorum notißimum, neq; Samariam agnoscerent, sed in urbem hostilem sese duci paterentur. Quin & D. Athanasium non semel simili miraculo militum manus euasisse, qui adipsum capiendum mittebantur, historia Ecclesiastica testatur. Sed ut in Christi exemplo insistamus, si ideo eum non agnouerunt discipuli, quòd corporis veritatem exuisset, quid respondebimus ad id, quod in horto ad montem oliueti factum fuit, priusquam ille corpore suo esset clarificatus? Nonne enim tunc quoq; neq; à sacerdotum seruis, neque à militibus, imò ne à Iuda quidem agnitus fuit, qui tamen omnes eo consilio venerant, ut ipsum comprehenderent? Num uerò tunc quoque corpus uerum illum habuisse negabimus? Absit: Nam si illud non habuit, ne captus quidem uerè, nec uerè mortuus fuit: & sic tota humanitatis redemptio nobis periret. Quid ergo restat, quàm ut in Christi quidem corpore mutationem nullam factam dicamus, quæ eius proprietates naturales absorbuerit, sed miraculo quodam oculos spectatorum impeditos fuisse, ut eum agnoscere non possent?
units.tr: They object: "But those two disciples did not recognise Christ; therefore it was not the same man as before, as regards the form and essence of his body." I deny this inference, and I say that it is not merely false but so trifling, so foolish, so inept and ridiculous that boys ought to be ashamed of it. For how often does it happen that we do not recognise friends who come to us unexpectedly, though they were once the best known and most familiar to us? Who, then, concludes from this that they have been changed into other bodies, or have put off the nature of their body? But no lengthy reply is needed, since Luke himself resolves this knot most happily, and lest anyone should draw from what was said some such conclusion, he adds at once: "But their eyes were held, so that they did not know him." Christ therefore did not put off the nature of his body, and it was not through any change or loss of it that the disciples failed to recognise him, but because their eyes were held: that is, by the hidden power of God, who willed to dull or restrain their sight for a time so that they could not discern or know him. And it is strange that some do not notice this, since many examples of this kind occur in Scripture. For who does not know that the Sodomites were once struck by angels so that they could not find the house of Lot or its doors? And we know that the Syrians were deceived by Elisha by a similar miracle, so that although they had the use of their eyes, they recognised neither Elisha himself, a man well known to many of them, nor Samaria, but allowed themselves to be led into the enemy's city. Indeed, ecclesiastical history testifies that St Athanasius too more than once escaped the hands of soldiers sent to seize him by a similar miracle. But to keep to Christ's own example: if the disciples did not recognise him because he had put off the truth of his body, what shall we say to what happened in the garden at the Mount of Olives, before he was glorified in his body? For then he was recognised neither by the servants of the priests nor by the soldiers, nor even by Judas, though all had come with the purpose of seizing him. Shall we deny, then, that he had a true body at that time too? Far from it. For if he did not have it, he was not truly taken, nor truly died, and so the whole redemption of our humanity would perish. What remains, then, but to say that no change was made in Christ's body which absorbed its natural properties, but that by some miracle the eyes of the onlookers were impeded so that they could not recognise him?

units.la: Continet autem præterea utilem doctrinam locus iste, qua admonemur, sensus corporis uim suam ex Deo habere, adeò ut illis efficaciter nemo possit uti, nisi ita uelit ille, qui eos dedit. Si enim (ut Paulus ait) in illo uiuimus, mouemur & sumus, nihil utique sine illo possumus. Et ut Dei dona sunt uisus, auditus, olfactus, gustus, tactus: ita Dei quoq; beneficium est, quod iisdem recte utimur. Cogentur hoc fateri, quotquot quid ipsis & aliis hominibus quotidie accidat, paulò diligentius obseruauerint. Quoties enim fit, ut manente oculorum acie, uisu tamen fallamur? quoties in uocum perceptione decipimur? quoties gustui nostro amara uidentur, quæ dulcissima sunt? Eadem est intellectus quoq; & rationis nostræ conditio. Nisi enim hanc continua sui Spiritus luce Deus illuminet, in iis etiam fallitur, quæ uel pueris nota sunt. Et hinc est, quòd incerti rerum sæpe fiunt seq; ipsos in retia inextricabilia implicant, qui hominum sapientissimi habentur. At si hoc nobis accidit in iis, quæ ad corpus spectant, & in his frequenter fallimur, quæ sensibus nostris expositæ sunt; quid obsecro fiet, si in diuinorum & cœlestium consideratione Deus nos nostro arbitrio & nostræ rationis siue prudentiæ consilijs permittat? Hic certè cumprimis necesse est, ut Dominus mentes nostras illuminet, rationem & intellectum nostrum suo Spiritu ducat. Nam nisi in fiat, non minus pernitiosè quàm turpiter errabimus. Animalis siquidem homo (ut Pauli uerbis utar) non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Et exempla multa sunt, quæ satis docent, quàm infelices sint, qui in æternæ salutis causa suæ rationi & prudentiæ aliquid tribunt, aut proprij arbitrij uiribus confidunt. Hi enim etsi nomen Christi retineat, deq; eo multa honorificè, multa uerè & piè dicant, eundem tamen non uerè agnoscunt, & longè alium sibi fingunt, quàm ipse reuera sit: quæ errorum turpissimorum præcipua causa est. Quia tamen de hac re sæpe aliàs diximus, nunc sufficiat ista breuiter perstrinxisse.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage contains useful teaching, by which we are reminded that the senses of the body have their power from God, so that no one can use them effectively unless he who gave them so wills. For if (as Paul says) in him we live, move and have our being, then certainly we can do nothing without him. And just as sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch are gifts of God, so too it is God's benefit that we use them rightly. All who observe a little more carefully what happens to themselves and to other people every day will be compelled to admit this. How often does it happen that, though the sharpness of our sight remains, we are nonetheless deceived in what we see? How often are we mistaken in perceiving sounds? How often do things that are most sweet seem bitter to our taste? The condition of our understanding and reason is the same. For unless God illumines it with the continual light of his Spirit, it is deceived even in things known to children. And hence it is that men held to be the wisest often become uncertain of things and entangle themselves in inextricable nets. But if this happens to us in matters that concern the body, and we are often deceived about those things which lie open to our senses, what, I ask you, will happen if God leaves us to our own judgement and to the counsels of our reason or prudence in the contemplation of divine and heavenly things? Here above all it is certainly necessary that the Lord illumine our minds and guide our reason and understanding by his Spirit. For unless this happens, we shall err no less destructively than shamefully. For "the natural man," to use Paul's words, "does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God." And there are many examples which sufficiently show how unhappy are those who attribute something to their own reason and prudence in the matter of eternal salvation, or trust in the powers of their own free will. For these people, although they retain the name of Christ and say many honourable things about him, many true and pious things, nevertheless do not truly acknowledge him, and they imagine for themselves a Christ quite different from what he really is; and this is the chief cause of the most shameful errors. But since we have often spoken of this matter on other occasions, let it suffice now to have touched on it briefly.

units.la: Nunc Iesum Christum audiamus, qui cùm adistos usq; accessisset, prior eos alloquitur, dicens: Qui sunt hi sermones, quos confertis inter uos ambulantes, & quid estis tetrico vultu? Quærit quasi ipse ignarus sit omnium, ut se ipsis manifestandi occasione commodiorem inueniat, explorata prius fidei ipsorum imbecillitate, cui simul mederi voluit. Ita ferè non vocatus quoq; se sponte nobis doctorem & magistrum offert, quando uel per uerbum suum nos compellat, uel animi aures Spiritu suo uellicat, ut de ijs incipiamus cogitare, quæ nobis necessaria sunt cognitu. At nunc nos etiam atque etiam uidere oportet, ne nostra contumacia aut proteruia illum reijciamus. Est præterea hoc præclarum humanitatis & affabilitatis exemplum, quòd de rebus serijs colloquentes & animi dolorem vultu non obscurè testantes prior compellat, ita nimirum suam operam quasi offerens, si consilio suo siue exilio uti velint. Est hoc uerè charitatis officium, quod ad amicitias conciliandas & seruandas in primis facit. Debent ergo Christum imitari, quotquot in aliquos incidunt, quos animo perturbatiori & rerum atq; consiliorum incertos esse uident. Meminerint tales sibi à Deo offerri, ut exercendæ charitatis materiam habeant, & ideo amicè eos compellent, & suâ mæstis atq; dolentibus officia offerant. Peccatur in hoc uehementer à duris illis Demeis & plus quàm Stoicis Zenonibus, qui surdis auribus & siccis oculis omnium gemitus & calamitates prætereunt, Leuitæ illius & Sacerdotis similes, de quibus in Samaritani parabola cap. 10. diximus.
units.tr: Now let us hear Jesus Christ, who, when he had come up to these men, speaks to them first, saying: "What are these words that you exchange with one another as you walk, and why are you downcast in countenance?" He asks as if he were ignorant of everything, so that he may find a more convenient occasion for revealing himself to them, having first tested the weakness of their faith, which he also wished to heal. So too, though we have not called him, he offers himself to us of his own accord as teacher and master, when either he addresses us through his Word or pricks the ears of our mind by his Spirit, so that we begin to think about those things which it is necessary for us to know. But now we must look again and again, lest we reject him through our stubbornness or insolence. Moreover, this is an excellent example of kindness and affability: that when people are talking of serious matters and do not hide their grief in their faces, he addresses them first, as it were offering his own help, if they are willing to use his counsel and aid. This is truly an act of charity, and one that especially serves to win and keep friendships. Therefore all who fall in with anyone they see troubled in mind and uncertain about their affairs and plans ought to imitate Christ. Let them remember that such people are placed in their way by God, so that they may have an occasion to exercise charity; and therefore let them address them kindly and offer their services to the sorrowful and grieving. This is grievously sinned against by those harsh Demeas and Zenos, more than Stoic, who pass by the groans and calamities of all with deaf ears and dry eyes, like that Levite and priest of whom we spoke in the parable of the Good Samaritan, chapter 10.

units.la: At non minus obseruari debet discipulorum quoq; istorum facilitas, qui neq; responso dedignantur hominem ignotum, neq; priuato dolori ita indulgent, ut illum abs se reijciant. Nā etiamsi Cleopas miretur, ipsum ea ignorare, quæ & recens facta erant, & omniù sermonibus terebantur, tamen quæstionem suam repenti Domino amicè & diligenter rem exponit. Alius certè importunum dixisset eum, qui causas tristitiæ eorum uellet cognoscere. Alius etiam metu impeditus noluisset de causa periculi plena sermonem cum peregrino instituere, & fortassis suspectum habuisset. Sed superat omnes istas remoras syncerus Christi amor, quo isti ardebant, & metum omnem discutit fides, cuius scintillas ipsi hucusq; tam diligenter fouerant. Est autem narratio ista Cleopæ digna, cuius singulæ partes probè considerentur, quia ueræ pietatis & fidei cum dubitatione luctantis egregium specimen exhibent.
units.tr: At the same time, the readiness of these disciples also deserves notice. They do not disdain to answer an unknown man, nor do they so indulge their private grief that they push him away. Although Cleopas is surprised that he is ignorant of things which had just happened and were on everyone's lips, he nevertheless kindly and carefully explains his question to the Lord at once. Another would certainly have called him a nuisance for wanting to learn the causes of their sadness. Another, held back by fear, would not have wished to hold a conversation with a stranger about a matter full of danger, and would perhaps have regarded him with suspicion. But the sincere love of Christ, which burned in these men, overcomes all those hindrances, and faith, whose sparks they had so carefully nurtured until now, dispels all fear. The account of Cleopas is worth attending to, and each of its parts should be carefully considered, because they present an outstanding example of true piety and faith struggling with doubt.

units.la: Primum de quo inter se colloquantur, ostendit, & eundem magnificè describit. Quæ facta sunt (inquit) Iesu Nazareno, qui fuit propheta, potens operibus & sermonibus coram Deo & toto populo. Ingenuè ergo Iesum hunc confitetur, quem plerisq; exosum esse sciebat. Et quamuis Prophetam modò dicat, satis tamen euidenter eum à uulgarium prophetarum numero eximit, quando eum non solùm sermone aut doctrina, uerumetiam operibus potentem fuisse ait: nimirum ut ostendat eius doctrinæ coniunctam fuisse uirtutem diuinam, quæ & in illius factis miraculosis, & auditorum animis sese exeruerit. Et credibile est, Cleopam ad Mosis promissione respexisse de Magno illo Propheta, quem omnes audire debeant. Nam illum in Dei quoq; conspectu potentem fuisse dicit, ne eius autho ritatem in uulgi indocti & stolidi admiratione collocet. Debet autè à nobis quoq; talis agnosci Christus, ne in sola redemptione humani generis per illum facta hæreamus. Nam etsi illa nostræ salutis summa sit, nunquam tamen eius uere participes, aut Regno ipsius digni erimus, nisi (quod Pater cœlitus nobis mandauit) ipsum in Euangelio nobis loquentem audiamus, eidem credamus, & quam ipse nobis præscribit uitæ totius formam obseruemus. Adhæc sibi proponant hanc Christi descriptionem omnes, qui in Ecclesiæ ministerio constituti sunt. Nā hos quoq; in primitiua Ecclesia Prophetas dictos fuisse, ex priori ad Corinth. epist. satis apparet. Etsi uerò ad Christi perfectionem ipsi accedere non possint, curent tamen, ut dicendi facultatem habeant, nec obiter modo aures feriat, sed altiori tuba prædicationis in ipsas hominum mentes penetrent: adeò ut Christi in ipsis loquentis experimentum omnibus appareat. Coniungant cum doctrina quæ reliqua sunt fidelis pastoris officia, ut sedulò pro omnium salute excubent, disciplinæ Christianæ iudices sint non ignaui, & in primis, ut doctrinam suam proprio exemplo confirment. Neq; illis satis sit, si hominum & populi applausu probentur, sed Deo placere studeant, cuius ministri sunt, & cui olim suæ functionis rationem reddere cogentur.
units.tr: First he shows what they were discussing among themselves, and describes Jesus magnificently: "The things that were done," he says, "concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people." He frankly confesses this Jesus, whom he knew to be hated by most people. And although he calls him only a prophet, he nevertheless clearly sets him apart from the common run of prophets, since he says that he was powerful not only in word or teaching but also in deeds. Clearly he means that a divine power was joined to his teaching, and that it showed itself both in his miraculous works and in the minds of his hearers. It is credible that Cleopas was looking back to the promise of Moses about that great Prophet whom all must hear. For he says that Jesus was mighty also in the sight of God, so that he does not place Christ's authority in the admiration of an ignorant and foolish crowd. Christ must also be acknowledged by us in this way, so that we do not cling only to the redemption of the human race accomplished through him. For although that redemption is the sum of our salvation, we will never truly partake of it, or be worthy of his Kingdom, unless we hear him speaking to us in the Gospel (which the Father commanded from heaven), believe him, and observe the whole form of life which he prescribes for us. Moreover, let all who are placed in the ministry of the Church set this description of Christ before themselves. That these also were called prophets in the primitive Church is clear enough from the first epistle to the Corinthians. And although they cannot attain to the perfection of Christ, let them nevertheless take care to have the gift of speaking, so that their voice does not merely strike the ears in passing, but penetrates the very minds of men with the loftier trumpet of preaching, so that the experience of Christ speaking in them is evident to all. Let them join to their teaching the other duties of a faithful minister: let them watch diligently for the salvation of all, be vigilant judges of Christian discipline, and, above all, confirm their doctrine by their own example. Nor should it be enough for them to be approved by the applause of men and of the people; they should strive to please God, whose ministers they are, and to whom they will one day be compelled to render an account of their office.

units.la: Deut. 18. Secunda parte, quid cum Christo actum sit, Cleopas breuiter, sed pathetice admodum exponit his uerbis. Quomodo eum tradiderunt principes Sacerdotum & magistratus nostri, ut morti damnare tur, & crucifixerunt eum. Paucis uerbis rem indignissimam & iniustissimam comprehendit. Et huius authores facit Summos Pontifices atque magistratus, qui eum praesidi Romano tradiderint. Quàm uero periculosum fuerit hoc dicere, ex illis aestimare licet, quae postea Apostolis acciderunt, cum eadem Hierosolymitanis praesulibus exprobrarent. Dicit tamen hoc Cleopas, quia pluris facit Christi gloriam, quàm mundum hunc & propriam uitam. Veruntamen in hac dicendi libertate imbecillitas fidei non obscure sese exerit: Nos autem sperabamus illum esse, qui redempturus esset Israelem. Fuit ergo nonnihil labefactata illorum fides, cum hoc sibi praeter omnem expectationem accidisse fatentur. Cur autem praeter expectationem? Quia Messiae officiu hucusq; ignorauerunt, & loco salutis aeternae regnum terrenum atque huius seculi felicitatem sibi ipsis polliciti sunt. Est haec omnium perniciosissima fidei remora, & hic ille scandali lapis est, ad quem plerique Iudaeorum grauissimè offenderunt. Elucet autem hic carnis ingenium: quae cum tota terrenis addicta sit, in Christo quoq; regnum, opes, honores, pacem & otium somniat. Quapropter si non solum sper sua fallatur, uerumetiam aduersa & pericula incidere sentiat, mox se deceptam queritur. Et tanta huius erroris uis est, ut multorum ora & linguas ad conuitia laxet, quibus totam Euangelij doctrinam impie proscindunt. Quod hodie multis accidit, qui omnium, quae aliquando audiuerunt, memoriam excutiunt.
units.tr: Deut. 18. In the second part, Cleopas briefly but very movingly sets out what was done to Christ, in these words: "How the chief priests and our rulers handed him over to be condemned to death, and crucified him." In a few words he sums up a most unworthy and most unjust deed. And he makes the chief priests and the magistrates its authors, since they handed him over to the Roman governor. How dangerous it was to say this may be judged from what later befell the apostles, when they charged the same things against the rulers of Jerusalem. Yet Cleopas says it, because he values the glory of Christ above this world and his own life. However, the weakness of their faith shows itself not obscurely in this boldness of speech: "But we hoped that it was he who would redeem Israel." Their faith was therefore somewhat shaken, since they confess that this happened to them beyond all expectation. Why beyond expectation? Because until now they had not understood the office of the Messiah, and instead of eternal salvation they had promised themselves an earthly kingdom and the happiness of this age. This is the most ruinous hindrance to faith of all, and it is the stone of stumbling at which most of the Jews took grievous offence. Here the nature of the flesh shows itself: since it is wholly given over to earthly things, it dreams of kingdom, wealth, honours, peace and leisure in Christ too. Therefore, if its hope is not only disappointed but it also perceives adversity and dangers falling upon it, it straightway complains that it has been deceived. And so great is the force of this error that it loosens the mouths and tongues of many to reproaches, with which they impiously tear apart the whole doctrine of the Gospel. This happens today to many who shake off the memory of everything they once heard.

units.la: Non tamen eo usq; progressam fuisse istorum infirmitatem, ex tertia orationis huius parte apparet. Nam colligit in ea Cleopas omnia, quae fidem resurrectionis erigere aut quacunq; ratione confirmare poterant, dicens: Atqui praeter haec omnia tertium hunc diem agit hodie, ex quo haec facta sunt. Sed & mulieres quaedam ex nobis obstupefecerunt nos, quae diluculo uenerunt ad monumentum: & non inuento eius corpore uenerunt, dicentes, se etiam uisionem Angelorum uidisse, qui dicunt eum uiuere, &c. Primò tertij diei mentionem facit, & ita nò tam animi desiderium exprimit, cui omnis mora longa est, quàm quòd uerborum Christi recordatur, quae Angeli mulieribus, & hae discipulis in mentem reuocauerant. Deinde etsi nondum firmiter credant, tamen non dissimulat quid mulieribus acciderit, & quid eadem ex Angeli iussu discipulis renuntiauerint. Addunt his nuntij istius confirmationem, quod nimirum quidam ex discipulis eo excitati ad monumentu excurrerint, & ita inuenerint rem omnem, sicuti à mulieribus narrata fuerat. Fuit ergo in discipulis istis non parua fidei infirmitas, cuius exemplo admonemur, in sanctis etiam uitia esse, quae & correctione & gratuita Dei misericordia opus habeant. Nam ut de alijs nunc nihil dicamus, quotus quisq; est, qui non dubitare interdum se sentiat, quando de huius seculi fine, de Christi nouissimo aduentu, de carnis resurrectione & uita aeterna diligentius cogitare incipit? Quid uero de securitate dicemus, quae tacito pede obrepit, & mirifico astu nos decipit, quando nihil huius nobis euenturum putamus? At ne tunc totisuccumbamus, proderit Dei promissiones frequentius in mentem reuocare, & quae passim occurrunt fidei adminicula colligere, & ut in melius proficiamus studere. Suspectum uero sit nobis quicquid infelix caro suggerit, & ne huius rationes nos fallant, assiduis precibus Dominum Iesum Christum fatigemus, ut is fidem nostram suffulciat, infirmitati nostrae medeatur, & per omnia huius mundi obstacula ad beatae immortalitatis portum deducat. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: That this weakness of theirs had not yet advanced so far appears from the third part of this speech. For in it Cleopas gathers together everything that could raise faith in the resurrection or confirm it in any way, saying: "Yet besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened. But certain women of our company astonished us, who came early to the tomb, and when they did not find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive," etc. First he mentions the third day, and in doing so he expresses not so much a longing of the mind, to which every delay is long, as a recollection of the words of Christ, which the angels had brought to the minds of the women, and the women to the minds of the disciples. Then, although they do not yet firmly believe, he does not hide what happened to the women, and what they reported to the disciples at the command of the angels. They add to this report a confirmation: certain of the disciples, roused by it, ran to the tomb and found everything just as the women had related. So there was no small weakness of faith in those disciples, and by their example we are warned that even in the saints there are faults which need both correction and the free mercy of God. For, to say nothing now of others, how few are there who do not sometimes feel doubt, when they begin to think more carefully about the end of this age, the last coming of Christ, the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life? And what shall we say of the security which creeps upon us on silent feet and deceives us with wonderful cunning, when we think that none of these things will befall us? But lest we then wholly give way, it will help to call the promises of God to mind more often, to gather the supports of faith which present themselves everywhere, and to strive to make progress for the better. Let us regard as suspect whatever the wretched flesh suggests, and lest its reasonings deceive us, let us weary the Lord Jesus Christ with constant prayers, that he may uphold our faith, heal our weakness, and lead us through all the obstacles of this world to the harbour of blessed immortality. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXII.
units.tr: Homily CCXII.

units.la: Tum dixit eis: O amentes & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus, quae locuti sunt Prophetae. Nonne haec oportuit pati Christum, & intrare in gloriam suam? Et exorsus à Mose & omnibus Prophetis, interpretabatur illis in omnibus Scripturis quae de ipso erant. Appropinquarunt autem vico, in quem proficiscebantur, & ipse fingebat se longius ire: Sed ipsi adegerunt eum dicentes: Mane nobiscum, quoniam aduesperascit, & inclinauit dies. Ingressus est igitur vt maneret cum eis: Et factum est cùm accubuisset cum eis, sumpto pane benedixit, & fractum dedit eis. Adaperti sunt autem oculi eorum, & agnouerunt eum: & ipse ablatus est ex conspectu eorum. Tum inter se dixerunt: Nonne cor nostrum ardebat in nobis dum loqueretur nobis in via, & cum aperiret nobis Scripturas? Et surgentes eo ipso momento reuerti sunt Hierosolymā,
units.tr: Then he said to them: "O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and to enter into his glory?" And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he expounded to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. They drew near to the village to which they were going, and he made as though he would go further. But they constrained him, saying, "Abide with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent." So he went in to stay with them. And when he had sat down to eat with them, he took bread, blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened and they recognised him, and he vanished out of their sight. And they said to one another, "Did not our heart burn within us while he talked with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?" And they rose up that same hour and returned to Jerusalem.

units.la: Q Via Dominus noster Iesus Christus nobis à Patre non solum redemptor, uerumetiam doctor & magister datus est, totus in hoc uersatur, ut suos in eo articulo diligenter instituat, in quo salutis nostrae complementum habetur: Resurrectione nimirum, qua seipsum ex mortuis suscitauit, ut mortem deuictam & huius aculeum, peccatum, prorsus sublatum esse doceret. Ad hunc scopum tota haec historia pertinet, in qua se non obiter modo uidendum praebuit, uerumetiam omnem salutis nostrae rationem diligenter exposuit, eamq; Scripturarum testimonijs illustrauit, ut discipulorum infirmitati mederetur, de qua in hesterno Sermone diximus. Describitur autem hoc loco prima, quam ex mortuis rediuiuus habuit, concio: quae eò diligentius audiri debet, quòd multi hodie doctores sibi ex mortuis excitari cupiunt, per quos de futuri seculi statu & omnibus cognitu necessarijs erudiantur. Est enim insatiabilis nostrae carnis curiositas, & cum de caelestibus semper dubitet, undiq; praetextus captat, quibus suam incredulitatem excusat. At uanissimum esse quicquid in eum fine adducitur, quasi incerta & dubia sit, quae de tantis mysterijs traditur doctrina, unus Christus abunde docet: qui ut prius è sinu Patris ad nos descendit, ut huius voluntatê & Regni caelestis mysteria annunciaret: ita nunc à morte etiam redire & per dies quadraginta cum discipulis de omnibus differere voluit, quae ad salutis uerae & caelestium mysteriorū cognitionem pertinent. Priusquam uero ad concionis huius expositionem accedamus, diligenter obseruari debet eius bonitas & paterna plane facilitas, qui discipulos istos partim ignorantia Regni sui, partim fidei imperfectione laborantes tam amicè tamq; fideliter instituere dignatus est. Ex eo enim communis consolatio peti debet, illum infirmos nequaquam abijcere, modò se dociles praebeant, & ex eorum numero sint, qui proficere cupiunt.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ has been given to us by the Father not only as Redeemer but also as teacher and master, he devotes himself wholly to instructing his people carefully in that article on which the completion of our salvation rests, namely the resurrection, by which he raised himself from the dead, to teach that death has been overcome and its sting, sin, utterly taken away. To this purpose the whole of this history belongs. In it he showed himself not merely in passing, but also set out carefully the whole basis of our salvation and illustrated it with the testimonies of the Scriptures, so as to heal the weakness of the disciples, of which we spoke in yesterday's sermon. This passage describes the first sermon he preached after rising from the dead, and it ought to be heard all the more attentively because many teachers today wish to be raised up from the dead for themselves, so that through them we may be instructed about the state of the future world and about everything that needs to be known. For our flesh has an insatiable curiosity, and since it always doubts heavenly things, it seizes on every pretext by which to excuse its unbelief. But Christ alone teaches abundantly that it is most vain to bring forward anything of this kind, as if the doctrine handed down about such great mysteries were uncertain and doubtful. Just as he first came down from the bosom of the Father to us, to announce the will and the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, so now he willed also to return from death and for forty days to discourse with the disciples about all those things which pertain to true salvation and to the knowledge of the heavenly mysteries. Before we come to the exposition of this sermon, we ought carefully to observe his goodness and his plainly fatherly gentleness, in that he deigned to instruct these disciples, who were labouring partly from ignorance of his kingdom and partly from imperfection of faith, so kindly and so faithfully. From this a common consolation ought to be drawn: that he by no means casts off the weak, provided they show themselves teachable and belong to the number of those who desire to make progress.

units.la: Propositio siue status totius orationis est, non debere ita turbari ipsos propter ea, quae Christo nuper acciderint. Confirmatio autem à necessario petitur: quia haec ita fieri opertuerit: id quod diligenti & prolixa demonstratione ex Scripturis docuit. Exordium graue est, & duram increpationem continet. O amentes (inquit) & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus, quae locuti sunt prophetae. Videtur autem in suam legem peccasse, quia prohibet, ne quem fatuu aut stultum dicamus. Sed peccatum hic nullum est, quia neq; odij affectu, neq; conuitiandi aut laedendi studio abreptus sic loquitur, sed hic maximè fidi doctoris officium facit. Merebantur enim duriorem increpationem, qui de eius resurrectione uel modicum dubitabant, de qua ille toties illos praemonuerat. Inexcusabiles ité erant, quia non plenam fidem habuerant mulieribus, quarū uerba cum eius promissionibus per omnia conuenie bant. Adhaec ea est ingenij humani cōtumacia, ut nisi acriori reprehensione excitentur, qui semel ad incredulitatē propendere caeperūt, subinde in peius proficiant. Ideo istos etiam acrius pungi necesse fuit: & quia hodie magnus eorum numerus est, qui his longè deteriores, cum Christo, cuius nomen profitentur, plus quàm scurriliter ludunt, & contradicendi occasiones undequaq; captant, nulla aduersus eos administrorū uerbi uehementia nimia esse potest, sed multò acutius tales feriendi & ceu praeconis uoce ad ipsius Dei tribunal citandi sunt, si forte animo perculsi de emendatione seriò cogitēt.
units.tr: The proposition, or the subject of the whole discourse, is that they ought not to be so troubled on account of what has lately happened to Christ. The confirmation is drawn from necessity: because these things had to happen in this way, which he taught by a careful and lengthy demonstration from the Scriptures. The opening is severe and contains a harsh rebuke: "O foolish men," he says, "and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken." He seems to have transgressed his own law, since he forbids us to call anyone a fool. But there is no sin here, for he does not speak thus moved by hatred, nor from a desire to insult or to hurt, but here he is performing most truly the duty of a faithful teacher. For those who doubted even a little about his resurrection, of which he had so often forewarned them, deserved a harsher rebuke. They were indeed inexcusable, because they had not placed full faith in the women, whose words agreed in every respect with his promises. Moreover, such is the obstinacy of the human mind that, unless those who have once begun to incline toward unbelief are roused by sharper reproof, they go on from bad to worse. Therefore it was necessary to sting these men even more sharply. And since today there is a great number of those who are far worse than they, who play the buffoon more than scurrilously with Christ, whose name they profess, and seize on every occasion for contradiction, no vehemence on the part of the ministers of the Word can be excessive against them. Rather, such men must be struck much more keenly, and summoned, as by the voice of a herald, before the tribunal of God himself, if perhaps, struck in mind, they may seriously think about amendment.

units.la: In primis uero diligentem obseruationem meretur, quòd non amentes modò aut stultos dicit, sed tardos etiam corde ad credendum omnibus, quae locuti sunt Prophetae. Id enim per causae reditionem addidisse uidetur, ut intelligerent cur stultos dixisset. Ita uero in genere admonemur, reuera amentes esse & fatuos, quotquot Scripturis non credunt. Etenim si stultitia non uulgaris argumentum est, si quis uiro graui & bene de se merito nō credat, plus quàm dementes & insani sunt, qui ipsi Deo in Scripturis loquenti non fidem adhibent, quem nemo unquam mendacij arguere potuit, et cui nos totos tam anima quàm corpore debemus. Unde rursus sequitur, praecipuam & unicam hominis sapientiam esse, Scripturis credere & obedire. His enim uera rerum tàm humanarum quàm diuina rum cognitio traditur, & haec solae eam rationem nobis monstrant, qua homo mortalis cum Deo immortali coniungi & conciliari potest, in quo totius nostrae felicitatis cardo consistit. Quae causa est, quòd Moses olim Israelitas solos gentem sapientem & intelligentem esse dixit: nimirum quòd illis solis
units.tr: Above all, this deserves careful attention: that he does not merely call them foolish and senseless, but also slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. It seems he added this by way of explaining the reason, so that they might understand why he had called them foolish. In general, we are thus admonished that all who do not believe the Scriptures are in truth senseless and foolish. For if it is a sign of no common folly, when someone does not believe a man of weight and well-deserving, then those are more than mad and insane who do not give faith to God himself speaking in the Scriptures, whom no one has ever been able to convict of lying, and to whom we owe ourselves wholly, both soul and body. From this it follows again that the chief and only wisdom of man is to believe and obey the Scriptures. For in them the true knowledge of things, both human and divine, is delivered, and they alone show us the way by which mortal man can be joined and reconciled to the immortal God, in which the hinge of our whole happiness rests. This is why Moses once said that the Israelites alone were a wise and understanding nation: namely, because God had entrusted his laws and statutes to them alone

units.la: Deut. 4. solis Deus suas leges & statuta sua credidisset. Et quàm uerè haec omnia dicantur, facilè patebit si cum sacris scriptoribus philosophos gentiū conferamus, qui cùm mortaliū sapientissimi haberentur, de Deo tamen & diuinis rebus tam ridicula, tam absurda, tamq; inepta tradiderunt, ut non temere Paulus dixerit, eos in sua sapientia stultos factos esse. Quid, quòd ijsdem stultitia uisa fuit praedicatio Euangelij, qua Christus traditur, in quo omnes thesauri scientiae recòditi sunt, quiq; nobis à Deo Patre sapientia factus est? In humanis quoq; umbratilem fuisse sapientiam illam, cuius studium ijdem illi professi sunt, uel uno hoc argumento constat, quòd de Repub. quidem multa disseruerunt, nullus autem unquam repertus fuit, qui quam ipse animo conceperat Reipub. formam in aliquo populo constituere potuerit. Sed quia ista non sunt huius loci, nunc tenuisse sufficiat, nos tunc demū à stultitiae & amentiae uitio liberos fore, si Scripturis credamus, & in his tradita uitae praecepta obseruemus.
units.tr: (Deut. 4.) alone. And how truly all these things are said will be easily plain if we compare with the sacred writers the philosophers of the Gentiles, who, though they were held to be the wisest of mortals, delivered about God and divine things such ridiculous, absurd and foolish opinions that Paul did not rashly say that they had become foolish in their own wisdom. What of the fact that the preaching of the gospel, in which Christ is delivered, and in whom all the treasures of knowledge are hidden, and who has been made wisdom to us by God the Father, seemed foolishness to the same men? That in human affairs also that wisdom, to the pursuit of which those same men professed themselves devoted, was mere shadow, is clear from this one argument: they discoursed at great length about the commonwealth, yet no one was ever found who could establish in any people the form of commonwealth that he had himself conceived in his mind. But since these matters do not belong to this place, let it suffice to have held this: that we shall then at last be free from the vice of folly and madness if we believe the Scriptures and observe the precepts of life delivered in them.

units.la: Nunc in Christi uerbis pergamus, qui rationem affert, cur turbari non debeant, & ait: Nonne hac oportuit pati Christum, & introire in gloriam suam? A necessario argumentatur, quae ratio animo generosos & fortes animos efficacissima est, & communi sensu nititur. Quid enim ineptius & stultius est, quàm eo offendi, quod aliter fieri non poterat? Cur item pius turbetur propter ea, quae ex Dei consilio & certa cum ratione fiunt? Vt autem fortius animos eorum penetret, per interrogationem istud enuntiat: Nonne haec oportuit pati Christum? &c. Vis argumenti praecipua in CHRI-STI uocabulo latet, quo promissum & à patribus diu expectatum humani generis Seruatorem significari saepe iam dictum est. Vult ergo dicere, haec non potuisse aliter fieri, quia & ipse non aliter potuerit suum officium exequi, & Regnum sibi destinatum obtinere. Et consultò gloriae meminit, in quam ita ipsum ingredi oportuerit: ut huius excellentia ignominiam & scandalum crucis aboleat. Ita uerò paucis uerbis totam humanae salutis rationem & Regni Dei conditionem, quae in Scripturis prolixè traduntur, comprehendit. Erant enim omnes homines peccatores, & propter peccatum mortis aeternae obnoxij. Salus ergo instaurari non poterat, nisi & peccata expiarentur, & mortis uires frangerentur. Quod cum nemo mortalium praestare posset, Deus Filium suum negotio huic tam arduo destinauit, qui in assumpta carne utrumq; praestitit. Nam mortis suae indignae merito peccatum mundi sustulit, mortem uerò resurrectione uicit, quam non multò post secuta est Ascensio, qua quasi triumphum agens de peccato, morte, inferis & ipso diabolo, in coelum subuectus est, ut quam ex nobis assumpserat, carnem coelestis gloriae participem faceret, & in se totum genus mortale seruaret. Haec nunc breuiter perstringimus, quia saepius de illis diximus, & Christus ipse haec paucis repetens discipulos ad ea remittit, quae multoties ex ipso audiuerant.
units.tr: Now let us go on to the words of Christ, who gives the reason why they ought not to be troubled, and says: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and to enter into his glory?" He argues from necessity, which is a most effective reason for making minds generous and strong, and it rests on common sense. For what is more foolish and senseless than to take offence at what could not happen otherwise? Why should a godly man likewise be troubled at those things which come about by the counsel of God and for a certain reason? In order to pierce their minds more forcefully, he states this by means of a question: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things?" and so on. The chief force of the argument lies hidden in the name of Christ, by which it has often been said already that the Saviour of mankind, promised and long expected by the fathers, is signified. He means, then, that these things could not have happened otherwise, because neither could he himself have carried out his office otherwise, nor obtained the kingdom appointed for him. And he deliberately mentions the glory into which he had to enter in this way, so that its excellence might abolish the ignominy and the scandal of the cross. Thus in a few words he comprehends the whole basis of human salvation and the condition of the kingdom of God, which are set out at length in the Scriptures. For all men were sinners and liable to eternal death on account of sin. Salvation therefore could not be restored unless sins were expiated and the power of death broken. Since no mortal could accomplish this, God destined his Son for this so arduous task, who, in the flesh he had assumed, accomplished both. For by the merit of his undeserved death he took away the sin of the world, and by his resurrection he conquered death; not long after this followed the Ascension, by which, as though celebrating a triumph over sin, death, hell and the devil himself, he was carried up into heaven, so that the flesh he had taken from us might be made a partaker of heavenly glory, and so that he might preserve the whole mortal race in himself. We touch on these things briefly now, because we have spoken of them more often, and Christ himself, in briefly repeating them, sends the disciples back to those things which they had heard from him many times.

units.la: In praesenti autem obseruemus, illum ista sic dicere de sua morte, ut simul generalem doctrinam & consolationem comprehendat, qua nostra fidem in huius seculi afflictionibus & extremo mortis certamine sustentemus. Si enim aeternum Dei Filium ista pati oportuit, neq; alia uia fuit, per quam quoad carnem assumptam in gloriam suam ingrederetur, & quae ad ipsum iure pertinebat haereditatem adiret, quid de nobis sperabimus, qui nisi ille nos pro suis agnoscat, toti perijmus? Non est seruus maior hero suo, neq; decet ut discipuli sors melior sit quàm praeceptoris sui. Si ergo Dominus & magister noster in terris paupertatem, famem, nuditatem, labores, curas, infamiam sustinuit, si morte acerba & ignominiosa sublatus est, quid mirum aut insolens fuerit, si nobis quoq; ista omnia eueniant? Quin potius iucundum nobis esse debet, tantum in cruce ferenda ducem sequi: quando certum est, nos gloriae quoq; eius participes atq; coharedes fore, si afflictionum socij simus. Et respondet planè hisce Christi uerbis, quod Paulus de omnibus credentibus dicit, oportere ipsos per multas afflictiones ingredi in Regnum Dei.
units.tr: Here, however, let us observe that Christ speaks in this way about his death so that he comprehends at the same time a general teaching and a consolation, by which we may sustain our faith amid the afflictions of this world and in the final struggle of death. For if the eternal Son of God had to suffer these things, and there was no other way by which he could enter into his glory according to the flesh he had assumed, and take up the inheritance that rightly belonged to him, what can we hope for, we who, unless he acknowledges us as his own, are utterly lost? "A servant is not greater than his master," nor is it fitting that the disciple's lot should be better than his teacher's. If then our Lord and Master endured poverty, hunger, nakedness, labours, cares and disgrace on earth, and was taken away by a bitter and shameful death, what is strange or unusual if all these things happen to us as well? Rather, it ought to be a joy to us to follow our leader in bearing the cross, since it is certain that we shall also be partakers and co-heirs of his glory, if we are companions in his afflictions. This plainly agrees with Christ's words, and with what Paul says of all believers, that they must enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions.

units.la: Porrò quod uno uerbo dixerat Dominus, mox diligenti demonstratione ex ueteris Scripturae testimonijs petita illustrauit. Nam à Mose exorsus inde omnes Prophetarum libros percurrit, & omnia interpretatus est, quaecunq; in illis de ipso habentur. Potuit hoc commodè fieri, quando & tem-pus sufficiebat ad eam rem, & cum ijs ipsi res erat, quibus satis esse poterat, si ea cum Scripturis conuenire audirent, quorum ipsi fuerant spectatores. Est autem locus iste diligenter obseruandus, quia eo admonemur, cognitionem Christi ueram atq; solidam non aliunde quàm ex Veteris testamenti libris petendam esse. Viderant quidem eius opera discipuli, eundem concionantem audiuerant, uincu-lorum item & mortis ipsius magna ex parte spectatores fuerant: non potuerunt tamen ista illis ad salutarem eius cognitionem sufficere, quia sine eorum hucusq; ignorauerant. Itaq; noua demonstra‑tione opus fuit, qua discerent, hæc ita fieri oportuisse. Eadem hodie etiam est ratio. Exponunt qui‑dem Euangelistæ Iesu Christi historiam, miracula simul & mortê describunt, resurrectionem item narrant, & quæ eius conciones fuerint, docent. Quid uerò ista proderunt, nisi intelligamus, ista o‑mnia ex æterno Dei decreto facta esse, & cum ijs omnino conuenire, quæ olim de promisso Redempto‑re & humani generis redemptione prædicta fuerùt? Vnde uerò ista cognitio peti poterit nisi ex Mo‑se, qui mundi historiam ab ipsa origine rerum & humani generis progressum solus descripsit, & ex Prophetarū libris, quibus certa & perspicua de Regno Christi in terris instaurando uaticinia continentur? In Mose certè promissio primis parentibus data habetur de semine mulieris, à quo caput serpentis conculcari oporteat. Posteà idem illud Abrahamo promittitur, ex cuius stirpe aut posteri tate sit nasciturum. Rationem uerò omnem, qua semen illud promissum peccata expiare morte uin‑cere & salutem omnè nobis reparare debuit, posteà in sacris Leuiticis Deus adumbrauit, & quasi in tabula depictam proposuit. Secuti sunt posteà legis interpretes Prophetæ, qui mysteria ista cla‑rius exposuerunt, & quæcunq; Messias facere aut pati debebat suis uaticinijs complexi sunt. Nisi ergo demonstretur ea quæ Christus fecit & quæ cum illo sunt facta, cū promissionibus illis antiquis, cum typis legalibus & prophetarū prædictionibus conuenire, nunquā credere poterimus, nos in eius morte uitam, in eius resurrectione iustitiam, in eiusdem ascensione uictoriā & Regni cœlestis hære‑ditatē habituros esse. Locos Scripturæ, quibus hæc demonstrari possunt, non opus est nunc excutere. Hi enim illas legentibus passim occurrunt, & uidetur Lucas consultò hoc solū dicere uoluisse, quòd suæ mortis & resurrectionis mysteria atq; usum Christus discipulis in Mose & Prophetis monstra‑uerit, ut nos ad horum lectionē excitaret, & illū legis finē esse doceret: quod Apostoli quoq; ubiq; in‑culcant. Sunt hæc propter phanaticos illos diligentius obseruanda, qui Veteris Testamenti libros reij‑ciunt, quasi nunc inutiles & superuacanei sint: neq; uident aut potius uidere nolunt, se eadem opera Christianæ fidei fundamenta conuellere, quæ tota in gratuitis Dei promissionibus consistit, quas illo patribus olim dedit. Simul eorum quoq; uanitas arguitur, qui religionē Christianam, & doctrinam de sola fide in Christum iustificante, ut nuperam aut nouā damnant: cùm nullum doctrinæ genus ue‑tustius sit, nullum etiā testimonijs tam certis & solidis nitatur. Quis enim scriptor Mose uetustior inuenitur? Quos item historicos dabimus, ex quibus certa temporū series & rerū ab origine mundi gestarū ordo colligi possit, si sacros libros è medio tollas? Qui uerò Poetæ, qui philosophi digni sunt, ut cum Prophetis conferantur, quorum uaticinia tam certa tamē perspicua sunt, ut in plerisq; locis non futura prædicere, sed res gestas narrare uideri possint? Agnoscamus ergo hanc nostræ fidei di‑gnitatem, & Deo grati simus, qui Scripturas inter tam uarios tamē horribiles totius orbis motus atq; Regnorum mutationes nobis seruauit in hunc usq; diem, ut ex illis salutis nostræ rationem cer‑tam discere possimus, nosq; ipsos in omnium tentationum certaminibus confirmare.
units.tr: Moreover, what the Lord had said in a single word, he then illustrated with a careful demonstration drawn from the testimonies of the Old Testament Scripture. For beginning with Moses, he then went through all the books of the prophets and explained everything that is found in them concerning himself. This could be done conveniently, since there was time enough for the purpose, and he was dealing with men who could be satisfied if they heard that these things agreed with the Scriptures, of which they themselves had been witnesses. This passage, however, must be carefully noted, because it reminds us that the true and solid knowledge of Christ is to be sought from nowhere else than from the books of the Old Testament. The disciples had indeed seen his works, had heard him preaching, and had been largely witnesses of his bonds and of his death; yet these things could not suffice for them to know him unto salvation, because until then they had not understood them. So there was need of a new demonstration, by which they might learn that these things had had to happen in this way. The reason is the same today. The Evangelists indeed set forth the history of Jesus Christ, describe his miracles and his death together, narrate his resurrection likewise, and teach what his sermons were. But what will these things profit us, unless we understand that all of them were done by the eternal decree of God, and that they wholly agree with what was foretold long ago about the promised Redeemer and the redemption of the human race? And from where can this knowledge be drawn, except from Moses, who alone described the history of the world from the very origin of things and the progress of the human race, and from the books of the prophets, which contain certain and clear prophecies about the establishing of Christ's kingdom on earth? In Moses, certainly, there is the promise given to our first parents, of the seed of the woman, by whom the head of the serpent must be crushed. Afterwards the same promise is made to Abraham, that he would be born of his stock or posterity. Then, in the sacred Levitical laws, God shadowed forth the whole plan by which that promised seed was to expiate sins, conquer death and restore all salvation to us, and he set it forth as if painted on a tablet. Afterwards came the Prophets, interpreters of the law, who expounded these mysteries more clearly, and embraced in their predictions all that the Messiah was to do or suffer. Unless, then, it is shown that the things Christ did, and the things that happened to him, agree with those ancient promises, with the legal types and with the predictions of the prophets, we can never believe that in his death we shall have life, in his resurrection righteousness, and in his ascension victory and the heritage of the heavenly kingdom. There is no need now to search out the passages of Scripture by which these things can be shown. For they meet readers everywhere, and Luke seems to have meant to say only this, that Christ showed his disciples in Moses and the Prophets the mysteries and the purpose of his death and resurrection, so as to rouse us to reading them, and to teach that he is the end of the law; this the Apostles also everywhere inculcate. These things must be observed more diligently because of those fanatics who reject the books of the Old Testament, as if they were now useless and superfluous; they do not see, or rather they are unwilling to see, that by the same act they overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith, which rest wholly on the gratuitous promises of God that he once gave to the fathers. At the same time the vanity of those is also refuted who condemn the Christian religion and the doctrine of justification by faith alone in Christ as recent or new; whereas there is no kind of teaching more ancient, and none that rests on testimonies so certain and solid. For what writer is found older than Moses? What historians shall we name from whom a certain sequence of times and an order of events from the beginning of the world could be gathered, if you removed the sacred books from the middle? And what poets or philosophers are worthy to be compared with the Prophets, whose prophecies are so certain yet so clear that in many places they seem to narrate things already done rather than to foretell things to come? Let us therefore acknowledge this dignity of our faith, and be thankful to God, who has preserved the Scriptures for us to this day amid so many varied yet dreadful movements of the whole world and changes of kingdoms, so that from them we may learn with certainty the reason of our salvation, and be strengthened in the struggles of all temptations.

units.la: Sed reuertamur ad præsentē historiam, qua narratur, ut tandem seipsum discipulis iis manife‑stauerit Christus, qui hucusq; sub peregrini persona latuerat. Appropinquauerūt enim uico Emma‑unti quò proficiscebantur, & ubi eò uentū fuit, se ulterius iturū esse ille simulauit. Vbi non opus est rationes quærere, quibus eum à mendacij crimine liberemus. Nec enim quicquā huius illum dixisse scribitur: sed qui hucusq; ut peregrinus aliquis comes itineris iis fuerat, nunc ipsis diuertere uolen‑tibus in cœpto itinere pergit, ut & fidem istorum exploret, & maiori desiderio eorum animos accen‑dat. Et si omnino se ab illis discessurum dixisset, tamē ne sic quidem mendacij accusari posset, quan‑do multa in Scripturis dicuntur certa cum conditione, etiamsi ea nō semper exprimatur. Ita Nini‑tis excidiū intra dies quadraginta Deus per Ionam denuntiat, neq; mendax fuit, quia eiusmodi cōminationes conditionem hanc coniunctam habent, quòd per pænitentiam & feriam uitæ conuer‑sionem eas effugere liceat: sicuti Hieremiæ cap.18.docemur. Sic in præsenti ab iis etiam discessis‑set Dominus, si nulla doctrinæ eius ratione habita ipsum neglexissent, aut etiam (quod impij solent) ludibrio habuissent. Quia uerò ipsum retinere cupiunt, & eo argumento fidei suæ iam multò quàm antea confirmationis ardorem testantur, cum illis mansit. Dicitur enim, quòd ipsum adegerint, ut secum maneret. Id uerò non de violenta coactione intelligi debet, sed quòd precibus amicis & ido‑neis rationibus ipsum retinere studuerint. Et ita seipsum Lucas exponit, quando eos dixisse scribit: Mane nobiscum, quoniam aduesperascit, & inclinauit dies. Est autem hoc animi pij & grati indicium. Nam illos Christus amentes siue stultos dixerat, quod hominibus ambitiosis grauissimum conuitium esse putatur. Adhæc fidei quoq; tarditatem ipsis exprobrauerat, non quidem in rebus dubijs & insolitis (de quibus merito dubitatur) sed in ijs, de quibus certa extabant Mosis & Prophetarum uaticinia, quæ omnibus in ore erat, & de quibus toties ipse eos admonuerat. Poterat ergo importunus & insolens nimis videri, qui peregrinus & ignotus talia diceret. Sed nō offendunt ista eorum animos, qui nihil perinde in uotis habebant, quàm ut suis rationibus fallerëtur, quæ ipsos in fide remorabantur. Ideo iuuat eos tā fidi & liberi monitoris consuetudo, & ea amplius frui cupiunt. Vnde apparet eos procul abfuisse ab eorum moribus, qui conuicia in se iaci & iniuria sibi fieri putant, si quando liberius accusentur, & monitoribus suis se asperos præbent, imò odia concipiunt, quibus eos pertinacissimè persequuntur. Imitemur ergo istorum pietatem, & in primis quidem tunc huius exempli meminerimus, quando à nobis quoque Dominus abitus esse uidetur, dum tentationes immittit, quæ nos cum Dauide & Prophetis clamare cogūt: Quò usque Domine? Quò usq; obliuiscēris mei? quòusque faciem tuam abscondis? Tunc (inquam) fidei constantia & pijs precibus eum retinere studeamus, & rursus cum Dauide dicamus: Respice, respon de mihi Domine Deus meus, illumina oculos meos, ne in morte obdormia: Et ego tua bonitate nitor, exultat cor meum tua salute, &c. Qui ita res suas instituunt, ij facilem omnino ad iuuandum esse mox sentiunt eum, qui iam procul ab ipsis recessisse uidebatur.
units.tr: But let us return to the present history, in which it is related that Christ at last made himself known to those disciples, who until then had lain hidden under the appearance of a stranger. For they drew near to the village of Emmaus, where they were going; and when they had arrived there, he pretended that he would go further. Here there is no need to seek reasons by which we might free him from the charge of lying. For nothing of the kind is written as having been said by him; rather, he who until then had been with them as a stranger companion on the journey now proceeds on the road he had begun, although they wished to lodge with him, so that he might both test their faith and kindle their hearts with a greater desire. And even if he had said that he would altogether depart from them, he could not even so be accused of lying, since many things in the Scriptures are stated as certain with a condition attached, even when that condition is not always expressed. Thus God announced through Jonah that Nineveh would be overthrown within forty days, and he was not lying, because such threats carry this condition joined to them, that they may be escaped by repentance and a change of life, as we are taught in Jeremiah 18. So in the present case the Lord would also have departed from them, if they had neglected his teaching and paid no regard to him, or even (as the wicked are wont to do) had mocked him. But because they desired to keep him, and by this argument they showed a fervour of faith far greater than before, he stayed with them. For it is said that they compelled him to stay with them. This must not be understood as violent constraint, but as their striving to keep him by friendly entreaties and fitting arguments. And Luke himself explains it so, when he writes that they said: "Stay with us, for it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent." This, moreover, is a sign of a godly and grateful mind. For Christ had called them foolish and slow of heart, which is thought to be the most grievous insult among ambitious men. Besides, he had rebuked them for the slowness of their faith, not indeed in matters that were doubtful and unusual (about which doubt is rightly felt), but in things about which the prophecies of Moses and the Prophets were plain, which were on everyone's lips, and about which he had often admonished them. He might therefore have seemed too forward and insolent, being a stranger and unknown, to say such things. Yet these words did not offend the minds of those who had nothing so much at heart as to be set right in those reasons which held them back in faith. Therefore they delight in the company of so faithful and free an admonisher, and they desire to enjoy it more. From this it appears that they were far removed from the manners of those who think that insults are hurled at them and injuries done to them whenever they are accused more freely; who show themselves harsh towards their admonishers, and indeed conceive hatred, by which they pursue them most obstinately. Let us therefore imitate the piety of these men, and above all let us remember this example when the Lord seems to have departed from us as well, while he sends temptations that force us to cry out with David and the Prophets: "How long, O Lord? How long wilt thou forget me? How long wilt thou hide thy face?" Then, I say, let us strive by steadfastness of faith and by godly prayers to keep him, and again say with David: "Look upon me, answer me, O Lord my God; enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep in death. And I trust in thy goodness; my heart rejoices in thy salvation," etc. Those who order their affairs in this way soon perceive that he who seemed to have withdrawn far from them is altogether easy to be moved to help them.

units.la: Facit ad huius doctrinæ confirmationem quod sequitur. Nam cum duobus istis diuertit Christus, ut cum ipsis maneat: nec solùm cū illis diuertit, uerumetiam (quod totius actionis siue historiæ istius caput est) se illis manifestat, ut ipsum reuera à mortuis resurrexisse intelligat & in fide magis confirmentur. Id quomodo factum sit, his uerbis Lucas narrat: Et factum est cum accubuisset cum eis, sumpto pane benedixit, & fractū dedit eis: Adaperti sunt autē oculi eorū, & agnouerūt eū, &c. Quod de benedictione & fractione panis dicitur, aliqui de Cœna mystica exponunt, quasi huius actionem nunc repetierit: & hanc sententiā aliqui arripiunt, qui sub una tantum specie communicandum esse contendunt. Nam hic quoque solius panis mentionem fieri clamant, & ex eo dogma illud suum colligunt, quo altera species laicis (ita enim populum Christianum uocant) eripiunt. Sed nos potius ex eo, quod hic dicitur concludimus, eos perperam sentire, qui locum illum de Cœna illa Eucharistica exponunt. Quia enim in illa panem & uinum Christus tradidit, & ut ex poculo isto omnes bibant, diserte præcepit, minimè credi debet, ipsum tam cito suum institutum mutare uoluisse. Sed oportet eiusmodi fulcris nitantur, qui ex suo capite ædificia extruunt, quæ nullis scripturarum testimonijs apertis possunt probari. Itaq; non aliud hic factū esse putabimus, quàm quod sæpe aliàs Dominus fecit. Constat enim ex alijs locis, hoc illi solenne & usitatum fuisse, ut non nisi præmissa benedictione aut gratiarum actione cibum sumeret. Et non male sentire mihi uidentur, qui illum peculiari & propria benedicendi forma usum fuisse dicunt, qua audita duo isti acrius excitati sint in eius diligentiam contemplationem. Etenim hoc Christum nō alio consilio fecisse, rei euentus declarat. Nam mox adaperti sunt oculi eorum, qui hucusq; detenti fuerant, ut eum iam agnoscerent, quem peregrinum aut hospitem esse putauerat. Rursus autē oculorū fit mentio, ne quis in Christi corpore mutationem factam putet, quæ huius substantiā siue naturam mutauerit. Obseruauit hoc olim D. Hieronymus, qui ad Pammachium contra errores Ioannis Hierosolymitani inter alia sic scribit. Quomodo (inquies) non cognoscebant eum in itinere, si ipsum habebat corpus, quod antea habuit? Audi scripturam dicentem: oculi eorum tenebantur, ne eum agnoscerēt. Et rursum: Aperti sunt oculi eorum, & cognouerūt eum. Nunquid alius fuit quando non agnoscebatur, & alius quando agnitus est? Certè unus atq; idem erat. Cognoscere ergo & non cognoscere, oculorum erat, non eius qui uidebatur: licet & ipsius fuerit. Oculos enim eorum tenebat, ne se agnoscerent. Denique ut scias errorem qui uersatur in medio, non corporis Domini, sed oculorū fuisse clausorum, Aperti sunt oculi eorū (inquit) & cognouerunt eum. Hæc Hieronymi sunt, quæ ideo adduximus, ne quis nos noui dogmatis auctores esse clamet, aut Christi maiestatē atq; omnipotentiam negare dicat, si eorum sententiæ non subscribimus, qui ex Christo nobis hodie Vertunnum aut Proteum quendam poeticum fingunt, qui corpus habeat omnipræsens, nullis tamen sensibus comprehensibile.
units.tr: What follows confirms this teaching. For Christ turns aside with those two so that he may remain with them. He does not only turn aside with them, but, which is the chief point of this whole action or history, he reveals himself to them, so that they may understand that he truly rose from the dead and be more firmly confirmed in faith. Luke tells in these words how this happened: "And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread and blessed it, and brake it, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him," etc. Some expound what is said of the blessing and breaking of bread as referring to the mystical Supper, as though he were now repeating that action. Some who contend that the Supper should be received under one kind alone seize upon this interpretation. They cry out that only bread is mentioned here as well, and from this they draw their dogma by which they take the other kind away from the laity (for so they call the Christian people). But we rather conclude from what is said here that those who expound this passage of that Eucharistic Supper are wrong. For since Christ gave bread and wine in that Supper, and expressly commanded that all should drink from that cup, we must by no means believe that he wished to change his own institution so quickly. Those who build edifices out of their own head, which cannot be proved by any clear testimonies of Scripture, must lean on such props. Therefore we will think that nothing other was done here than what the Lord often did at other times. For it is clear from other passages that it was his custom and practice never to take food without first a blessing or thanksgiving. And those seem to me not wrongly minded who say that he used a particular and distinctive form of blessing, by which these two were stirred more keenly to attend to him and to contemplate him. For the outcome of the event shows that Christ did this for no other purpose. For immediately their eyes were opened, which until now had been held shut, so that they now recognised him whom they had thought to be a stranger or a guest. Again, mention is made of the eyes, lest anyone think that a change was made in Christ's body, one that altered its substance or nature. Jerome noticed this long ago, who, writing to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem, says among other things: "How (you will say) did they not recognise him on the road, if he had the body that he had before? Hear Scripture saying: their eyes were held, so that they should not recognise him. And again: their eyes were opened, and they knew him. Was he another when he was not recognised, and another when he was known? Certainly he was one and the same. To recognise and not to recognise therefore belonged to the eyes, not to the one who was seen, although it also belonged to him. For he held their eyes, so that they should not know themselves. Finally, so that you may know that the error lies in the middle, it was not the Lord's body but their eyes that were closed: 'Their eyes were opened,' it says, 'and they knew him.'" These are Jerome's words, which I have cited so that no one may cry out that we are authors of a new doctrine, or say that we deny Christ's majesty and omnipotence, if we do not subscribe to the opinions of those who today fashion for us out of Christ some poetic Vertumnus or Proteus, who has a body present everywhere yet comprehensible by no senses.

units.la: At dicunt illi, nox subijci: Sed ipse euanuit ab oculis eorum: & ea locutione corporis conditio
units.tr: But they say that a further point must be noted: "He vanished from their eyes," and by that expression they say that the condition of the body is denoted, one quite different from ours.

units.la: Discipulorum pietas & gratitudo.
units.tr: The piety and gratitude of the disciples.

units.la: Christus se cognoscendum præbet. nem longè aliam quàm nostra sit, denotari aiunt. At ego locutionem ueteris interpretis non damno, si sano sensu accipiatur, quem in loco supra adducto, D. Hieronymus (qui uersionis illius authorem esse creditur) indicat, qui hoc omne Dei uirtute, non corporis natura in aliam essentiam mutata factum esse docet. Quod ab oculis repentè euanuit (inquit) uirtutis Dei est, non umbræ aut phantasmatis. Quòd si aduersarij nostri euanescendi uerbum proprio suo sensu urgere uelint, ego hunc cum religionis Christianæ principijs pugnare dico, quæ Christum uerum corpus & assumpsisse & post resurrectionem quoq; retinuisse docent, & proinde ad Græcam ueritatē nobis recurrendum esse, qua Lucas hoc suum opus Euangelicū conscripsit. In ea autē sic legitur: ἠ αὐτὸς ἀφανὴς & ἐγένετο ἀπ’ αὐτῶν. Quæ uerba illum non euanuisse, aut in nihilum redactū, sed inuisibilem factum fuisse docent. Idque diuina uirtute sic fieri potuit, ut corporis naturam siue essentiam mutari nequaquam fuerit opus. Nec simpliciter ἀφανὲς, id est, inuisibilem aut inconspicuum dicit, sed ἀπ’ αὐτῶν: ut à discipulis illis non amplius uisum fuisse ostendat, cùm quoad corporis naturā uisibilis esset. Quid, quòd eadem particula discessum eius siue motum in locum alium non obscurè innuit? Mirum autem est, homines alioqui non omnino stupidos, hîc nobis portenta quædam fingere, cùm huius generis exempla in alijs quoq; habeantur, de quorum corporibus nemo unquam dubitauit, quasi non uera aut naturalia corpora habuerint. De Philippo in Eunuchi Æthiopis ab ipso conuersi & baptizati historia Lucas noster scribit: Cùm autē ascendissent ex aqua, Spiritus Domini rapuit Philippum, nec amplius uidit eum Eunuchus: pergebat itaq; per uiam suam, Philippus autē inuentus est Azoti. En Eunucho Philippus repentè subductus siue ex eius conspectu ablatus est, ut ei ἀφαντ & uel inuisibilis fuerit, qui tamen corpore nequaquā mutatus, aut in aliū couersus fuit. Et huc etiam referri cōmodè potest, quod de D. Athanasio Theodoretus scripsit, eum miraculose Sebastiani cuiusdam, quem Constantius ad ipsum capiendum miserat, manus euasisse, quàmuis ille cum quinq; millibus militū templum circundedisset, & cum multis ingressus illum quàm diligetissimè quæreret. Quòd si hæc in hominibus facta sunt, num in Dei Filio simile quid non potuit fieri, nisi corporis ueri naturam exueret?
units.tr: Christus se cognoscendum præbet. I do not condemn the wording of the old translator, if it is taken in a sound sense, the sense which Jerome himself (who is believed to be the author of that version) indicates in the passage cited above, teaching that all this was done by the power of God, not by the body's nature being changed into another essence. "That he suddenly vanished from their eyes," he says, "is the work of God's power, not of a shadow or a phantasm." But if our opponents wish to press the word "vanished" in its proper sense, I say that this clashes with the principles of the Christian religion, which teach that Christ both assumed a true body and retained it even after the resurrection. Therefore we must have recourse to the Greek text, in which Luke wrote this Gospel work. In it we read: καὶ αὐτὸς ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ’ αὐτῶν ["and he became invisible to them"]. These words teach that he did not vanish or was reduced to nothing, but became invisible. And this could happen by divine power, so that there was no need for the nature or essence of the body to be changed. Nor does he say simply ἀφανές, that is, invisible or inconspicuous, but ἀπ’ αὐτῶν ["from them"], to show that he was no longer seen by those disciples, although as to the nature of his body he was still visible. And what of the fact that the same particle does not obscurely hint at his departure or movement to another place? It is strange that men who are otherwise not altogether dull should here invent for us certain monsters, when examples of this kind are found elsewhere too, concerning whose bodies no one has ever doubted, as though they had not had true and natural bodies. Our Luke writes of Philip in the history of the Ethiopian eunuch whom he converted and baptised: "And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, and the eunuch saw him no more; and he went on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found at Azotus." See, Philip was suddenly withdrawn from the eunuch, or taken away from his sight, so that he became ἄφαντος ["invisible"] to him, and yet he was not changed in body or turned into another. And to this may also fitly be referred what Theodoret wrote about Saint Athanasius, that he miraculously escaped the hands of a certain Sebastian, whom Constantius had sent to seize him, although that man had surrounded the church with five thousand soldiers and, entering with many others, sought him most diligently. But if these things happened to men, could nothing similar have happened to the Son of God, unless he put off the nature of a true body?

units.la: Quærat autem aliquis, cur tam citò à discipulis abierit, quàm primùm ab ipsis agnitus fuit? Respondeo, quia quod tunc uoluit facere confectum erat. Nam dubios & inter metum atque spem fluctuantes consolari, iisdem crucis scandalum è medio auferre, & de sua resurrectione, quam ex mulieribus paulò ante resciuerant, certos facere uoluit. Ideo tā de hac quàm de morte sua illis prolixè disseruit, ut hæc ita fieri oportuisse, non possent amplius dubitare. Restabat ergo unū hoc, ut quod iam fidei intellectu didicerant, coràm quoq; uiderent, & resurrectionis suæ testes fierent oculati. Aperit ergo illorum oculos, seq; illis uerè uidendū atq; cognoscendum præbet. Ne tamē pro carnis ingenio quod nondum prorsus exuerant, terrenum quid animo conciperent, aut perpetuam corporis sui præsentiam sibi necessariam putarent, mox sese subducit, & ita eis occasionem præbet diligentius rumi nandi ea, quæ in itinere ex ipso audiuerant. Non ergo eis fraudi fuit subitus ille Christi discessus: & desiderio, quo eos iam magis accenderat, non multò post satisfecit, quando eadem nocte denuo ab illis uisus est, & plura adhuc resurrectionis suæ argumēta proculit, ut in sequenti sermone audiemus. Debet autem nostræ etiam institutioni seuire quod hîc factum est: Ne uidelicet terrenum quid post hac in Christo quæramus, & ne seruili superstitione hæreamus in corporis eius præsentia, quod olim officio suo in ara crucis probè defunctū est. Idenim Christus postquam eius resurrectionem per dies quadraginta abundè probauit, in cœlos subuexit, eius autem loco Spiritum sanctum nobis dedit, quī & salutis nostræ arrhabo est, & efficaciter in nobis agit, quæ nobis porrò necessaria sunt. Huius ergo uirtute animati & adiuti animos nostros in cœlum attollamus, ut illic Christo frui possimus ad uitam æternam: de corporis autē præsentia litigent, quibus fabula esse uidetur, quod ille de nouissimi seculi impostoribus dixit, qui ipsum in certis locis monstraturi sint. Vide supra cap.17.
units.tr: But someone may ask why he departed from the disciples as soon as they recognised him. I answer: because what he then wished to do was finished. For he wished to console those who were doubtful and wavering between fear and hope, to remove from their midst the scandal of the cross, and to make them certain of his resurrection, which they had learned of a little before from the women. Therefore he discoursed at length about this and about his death, so that they could no longer doubt that these things had to happen thus. There remained, then, only this: that what they had already learned by understanding of faith they should also see with their own eyes, and become eyewitnesses of his resurrection. So he opens their eyes, and presents himself to them to be truly seen and recognised. Yet lest they conceive something earthly, according to the nature of the flesh which they had not yet wholly put off, or think that his bodily presence was necessary for them forever, he immediately withdraws himself, and so gives them occasion to ponder more diligently what they had heard from him on the road. Therefore that sudden departure of Christ was no hindrance to them, and not long afterwards he satisfied the desire with which he had already kindled them more, when on the same night he was seen by them again and set forth yet more proofs of his resurrection, as we shall hear in the following sermon. What happened here ought also to serve our instruction: namely, that we should not seek anything earthly in Christ from now on, and that we should not cling with slavish superstition to his bodily presence, since his body once completed its task on the altar of the cross. For Christ, after he had amply proved his resurrection over forty days, was carried up into heaven, and in his place he gave us the Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our salvation and effectively works in us what we further need. Therefore, animated and helped by his power, let us raise our minds to heaven, so that there we may enjoy Christ unto eternal life. As for the bodily presence, let those dispute about it to whom that fable seems fitting, which he spoke of the impostors of the last age, who will promise to show him in certain places. See above, chapter 17.

units.la: Reliquum est ut uideamus, quomodo tota hac actione discipuli isti affecti fuerint, & quàm magnos breui tempore progressus in Christi schola fecerint. Vbi primum occurrit, quòd non terrentur tam subita eius disparitione aut discessu, neque ignauo metu fathiscunt, sed memori mente ea recolunt quæ in itinere illis dicta fuerunt, & quis tunc eis animus fuerit, ingenuè fatentur. Nonne (inquiunt) cor nostrum ardebat in nobis dum loqueretur nobis in uia, & cùm aperiret nobis Scripturas? Ergo non aures modò eorum Christi uerba demulserūt, sed inimos cordis recessus penetrarūt, ubi uiuo sensu uim Spiritus percepere. Ardoris autem novi mentionem non temere faciunt, quem tunc senserint, qui prius prae metu & dubitatione nimium frigebant. Est enim Verbum Dei instar ignis, ut ipse apud Ieremiam testatur, & ideo mirificos habet effectus, si quando intra animos recte admissum fueris.
