Nam carnis affectus excoquit, Dei amore accendit, & totos feruidos facit in iis, quae ad eius cultum sive gloriam faciunt. At qui ignem istum in nobis excitet, solus Christus est. Docebant inter Iudaeos Scribae & Sacerdotes: sed nemo unquam auditus est, qui cor suum ardere diceret. Ad Caiaphae prunas Petrus calefieri voluit, sed per has tantum non extinctae fuerunt quae adhuc latebant in frigenti corde fidei scintillae, & ipse turpiter abnegator factus est. At nostri illi Christi audiunt, & mox corda eorum flammas concipiunt novas, quibus omnis metus, omnis dubitatio & quicquid carnis ratio hucusque dictaverat, procul expellitur. Probent ergo se ad huius exempli regulam, quotquot verbum audiunt, & eius studium profitentur. Nisi enim hoc in animos usque descendat, necquicquam auditur. At si animis percipiatur, mox igneo ardore homines accendit, qui flammas & lucem pietatis per omnia eorum studia & vitae totius actiones diffundit. Quod ergo istas hodie rariores videmus, ex eo est, quod plerique verbum non aliter audiunt quam illi de quibus apud Ezechielem dicitur, quod ipsis cantilenae instar fuerit. Taceo nunc eos, qui loco caelestis illius ignis tartareas flammas animis concipiunt, & odio verbi Dei atque administrorum eius accensi in proprium exitium ruunt. Sunt haec deplorandae impietatis indicia: quare seriis & assiduis ad Deum precibus opus est, ut in animos nostros vere illuminare & sancto fidei ardore accendere dignetur, qui nos ad vere pietatis officia animosos & intrepidos reddat, atque actiones nostras gubernet.
units.tr: It remains for us to see how those disciples were affected by the whole of this event, and how much progress they made in Christ's school in a short time. Here we first notice that they are not terrified by his sudden disappearance or departure, nor do they faint with cowardly fear. Instead they recall with a mindful heart what was said to them on the road, and they openly confess what their state of mind was at that time. "Was not our heart burning within us," they say, "while he talked with us on the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?" So Christ's words did not merely soothe their ears; they penetrated to the innermost recesses of the heart, where they felt the power of the Spirit with a living sense. Nor do they mention this new burning without reason, since they had been growing cold through fear and doubt before. For the Word of God is like fire, as he himself testifies through Jeremiah, and so it has wonderful effects whenever it is rightly received within our minds. It burns away the desires of the flesh, kindles the love of God, and makes people wholly fervent in whatever serves his worship and glory. Yet only Christ is the one who kindles this fire in us. The scribes and priests taught among the Jews, but no one was ever heard to say that his heart burned. Peter wished to warm himself at the coals of Caiaphas, but those coals only nearly extinguished the sparks of faith that still lay hidden in his cold heart, and he became a shameful denier. Our disciples, however, hear Christ, and at once their hearts catch new flames, by which all fear, all doubt, and whatever human reason had until then dictated, is driven far away. Let all who hear the Word and profess its study therefore test themselves by the rule of this example. For unless it sinks down into the mind, it is heard in vain. But if it is received in the mind, it soon inflames people with a fiery ardour, which spreads the flames and light of piety through all their pursuits and all the actions of their whole life. That we see such people rarer today is therefore because most men hear the Word no differently from those of whom Ezekiel speaks, to whom it was like a song. I say nothing now of those who, in place of that heavenly fire, take infernal flames into their minds, and, kindled with hatred of the Word of God and of its ministers, rush headlong to their own destruction. These are signs of a deplorable impiety. Therefore we need earnest and constant prayers to God, that he would deign truly to illuminate our minds and kindle them with the holy ardour of faith, making us bold and fearless in the duties of true piety, and governing our actions.

units.la: Hunc enim ignis istius effectum in illis etiam cernimus. Nam eo ipso momento surgentes reversi sunt Hierosolymam: nimirum, ut quod audierant & audierant, discipulis reliquis annuntiarent. Atqui multa eos detinere poterant, ut saltem in crastinum usque rem differrent. Nam sub vespera demum inclinante iam die diuerterant, quare non dubium est, quin iam noctis tenebrae exortae fuerint, priusquam iter denuo possent ingredi. Deinde horis aliquot ad illud conficiendum opus erat, ut ante noctem intempestam, aut certe concubiam, eo peruenire non potuerint. Et credibile est, nocturnas profectiones non admodum tutas fuisse eo tempore, quando ad diem festum ingens ex omnibus locis hominum multitudo confluebat, inter quos multi ad seditiones plus satis propensi, plerique autem aperti hostes Christi erant. Sed nihil horum istos detinere potest, quo minus omni mora abrupta itineri se committant. Pluris enim faciunt gloriam Dei & fratrum suorum salutem, quam sua commoda: quod verae fidei per charitatem agentis proprium esse, saepe iam diximus. Imitemur ergo istos, neque nobis graue sit labores & pericula subire, quando de fratrum salute & Iesu Christi gloria agitur. Sunt enim haec verae pietatis officia, quibus ille unice delectatur, & eadem dignis praemijs remunerat, ut in sequentibus audiemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: For we see the effect of this fire in them as well. At that very moment they rose up and returned to Jerusalem, plainly so that they might announce to the remaining disciples what they had heard and seen. Yet many things could have held them back, so that they might at least have put off the matter until the next day. For they had set out only in the evening, when the day was already declining, so there is no doubt that the darkness of night had come on before they could resume their journey. Moreover, several hours were needed to complete the journey, so that they could not have reached the place before the dead of night, or at least midnight. And it is credible that night journeys were not very safe at that time, when a huge crowd of people from all places was flocking together for the festival, among whom many were all too ready for sedition, and most were open enemies of Christ. Yet none of these things could detain them from committing themselves to the road without any delay. For they valued the glory of God and the salvation of their brothers more than their own convenience. This, as we have often said already, is the mark of true faith that works through love. Let us therefore imitate them, and let it not be burdensome to us to undergo labours and dangers when the salvation of our brothers and the glory of Jesus Christ are at stake. For these are the duties of true piety, in which he alone takes delight, and which he rewards with worthy prizes, as we shall hear in what follows. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 213.

units.la: Et inuenerunt congregatos undecim, & eos qui cum ipsis erant, dicentes: Surrexit Dominus vere, & conspectus est Simoni. Tum ipsi expositerunt quae gesta erant in via, & ut fuerat agnitus ab ipsis in fractione panis. Haec autem ipsis loquentibus, stetit ipse Iesus in medio eorum, & dixit eis: pax vobis. Territi vero illi & expauefacti putabant se spiritum conspicere. Tum dixit eis: Quid turbati estis: & quare disceptationes ascendunt in cordibus vestris? Videte manus meas & pedes meos: nam ego ipse sum. Contrectate me, & videte: Nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout me conspicitis habere. Et cum haec dixisset ostendit eis manus ac pedes. Adhuc autem ipsis non credentibus prae gaudio & mirantibus, dixit eis: Habetis hic esculentum aliquid? Tum ipsi dederunt ei partem piscis assi, & aliquid ex fauo apiario: Et cum accepisset, in conspectu eorum comedit.
units.tr: And they found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying: The Lord is truly risen, and has appeared to Simon. Then they related what had happened on the way, and how he had been recognised by them in the breaking of bread. While they were still speaking these things, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them and said to them: Peace be to you. But they, terrified and frightened, thought they were seeing a spirit. Then he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, for it is I myself. Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. But while they still did not believe, for joy and amazement, he said to them: Have you anything here to eat? Then they gave him a piece of broiled fish and some honeycomb. And when he had taken it, he ate in their sight.

units.la: Cap. XXIIII.
units.tr: Chapter XXIIII.

units.la: Quoniam homini nihil terribilius est morte, & huius metu multi sæpe in fidei & charitatis leges peccant, non tam utile quàm necessarium est, ut in resurrectionis meditatione diligenter uersemur, quæ ut sanctorum omnium lætissima spes fuit, ita mortis terrores sola mitigare & depellere potest. Quia autem huius fundamentum est Christi resurrectio, hanc nobis certò constare oportet. Ideo ille multa huius indicia discipulis exhibuit, inter quæ præ aliis memoratu digna est historia duorum discipulorum, quam hucusque tractauimus. In illis enim non solùm Christi bonitas atque facilitas apparet, uerumetiam fidei cum carnis dubitationibus luctantis exemplum proponitur, quo docemur, ut illa tandem Dei Spiritu adiuta omnibus obstaculis superior fiat. Qui enim prius animis perplexi & rerum incerti erant, mox ubi se illis Christus manifestauit, nouis uiribus confirmati, testes quoque eorum fieri cupiunt, de quibus paulò ante dubitauerant. Namut nuper dictum est, per noctis tenebras non sine labore & periculo in urbem festinant, ut nuntium istud lætum ferant discipulis, quos adhuc incertos inter spem & metum fluctuare arbitrabantur. Sequitur quis huius studij ipsorum fructus fuerit, & quibus præmijs illos Dominus remunerauerit.
units.tr: Since nothing is more terrible to man than death, and from fear of it many people often sin against the laws of faith and love, it is not merely useful but necessary that we dwell diligently on the meditation of the resurrection. As the most joyful hope of all the saints, it alone can soften and drive away the terrors of death. Since Christ's resurrection is the foundation of this hope, we must be certain of it. Therefore he showed the disciples many signs of it, and among them the story of the two disciples, which we have dealt with up to now, is worthy of mention above the rest. For in it appears not only Christ's goodness and kindness, but also an example of faith struggling with the doubts of the flesh is set before us, by which we are taught that faith, at last aided by the Spirit of God, becomes superior to all obstacles. Those who before were perplexed in mind and uncertain of things, as soon as Christ revealed himself to them, were strengthened with new powers and desired to become witnesses of the things about which they had doubted a little before. For, as was said recently, through the darkness of night they hurry to the city, not without toil and danger, to bring this joyful news to the disciples, whom they thought were still wavering uncertainly between hope and fear. It follows what fruit their zeal bore, and with what rewards the Lord repaid them.

units.la: Occurrit inter hæc primum, quod undecim Apostolos cum reliquis suis familiaribus simul congregatos inueniunt, qui ipsis dicunt: Surrexit Dominus uere, & conspectus est Simoni. Ergo qui ut Christi resurrectionem alijs annunciarent, uenerant, nouum huius testimonium ex illis audiunt, quo in sua fide magis confirmentur. Et sanè non uulgare, sed dulcissimæ consolationis plenum fuit, quòd Simoni Petro inter primos sese uidendum exhibuit Christus, qui propter turpem eius abnegationem dignißimum uideri poterat, qui prorsus negligeretur. Vicissim uerò duo isti alijs quoque consolationem adhibent, dum ex ordine exponunt, quid in uia cum ipsis ille egerit, quid locutus sit, & ut tandem ipsum ex fractione panis agnouerint. Est hoc piorum officium, ut mutuis consolationibus sese confirment, & ita quisque in commune deponat, si quid habet quod aliorum ædificationi possit seruire. Ita Paulus Romanos fratres uisere cupiebat, ut & illis donum aliquod spiritua le impertiretur, & uicissim ex ipsis consolationem caperet. Et qui ita affecti sunt, eorum studia Deus irrita fieri, aut inutilia siue infrugifera esse non sinit. Nam ad illos promissio pertinet: Omni qui habet dabitur. Et hæc usura illa est uerè Christiana, qua & nobisipsis & alijs adhæc ipsi Deo, fidelißimo remuneratori fæneramur.
units.tr: Among these things, first we find that they came upon the eleven Apostles gathered together with the rest of their companions, who said to them: The Lord has truly risen, and has been seen by Simon. So those who had set out to announce Christ's resurrection to others hear from them a new testimony to it, by which they are more firmly confirmed in their faith. And truly it was not an ordinary but a most sweet consolation that Christ showed himself to Simon Peter among the first, who, because of his shameful denial, might seem most unworthy to be regarded at all. In turn, these two bring consolation to the others also, while they set out in order what he did and said to them on the way, and how at last they recognised him in the breaking of bread. It is the duty of the godly to strengthen one another by mutual consolations, and so each should contribute to the common stock whatever he has that can serve the building up of others. Thus Paul desired to visit the Romans, brothers, so that he might impart to them some spiritual gift and in turn receive consolation from them. God does not allow the zeal of those so disposed to be made vain, useless or unfruitful. For the promise applies to them: To everyone who has, more will be given. This is that truly Christian usury, by which we lend at interest to ourselves and to others, and also to God himself, the most faithful rewarder.

units.la: Accedit in præsenti alter fructus, quem duo illi unà cum reliquis discipulis ex suo studio perceperunt. Cùm enim quæ ipsi uiderant exponunt, ea autem (ut in Marco est uidere) nonnullis dubia esse uidentur, en Christus in medio eorum constitit, & eos pro more salutauit, dicens: Pax uobis. Ita uerò & uerbis eorum fidem astruit, ne pro uanis & mendacibus habeantur, & seipsum non modò reddiuiuum illis sistit, sed omnem sui meriti fructum amicè ac liberaliter eis offert: Pace nimirum, sub qua Hebrei omnem incolumitatem hominis, quoad corpus & animam, comprehendunt. Latius tamen pax illa extenditur, quam Christus nobis acquisiuit. Quia enim nos cum Deo reconciliauit, in ipso pace Dei fruimur, quæ omnem intellectum superat: eadem uerò inter homines quoq; pacis uerę & stabilis causa est: quia sub illo capite ut eiusdem corporis membra uniuntur, quotquot illum pro suo Seruatore agnoscunt. Vt uerò tunc suæ resurrectionis testibus adfuit, & coram confirmauit ea, quæ ab illis dicebantur: ita nunquam deerit illis, qui ei testimoniū fidele perhibent. Ridênt multi ea, quæ de toto humanæ salutis negotio dicuntur, in primis fabulam putat infelix mundus, si quis mortuos olim resurrecturos, & Christum ad iudicium uenturum esse dicat: sed non est, ut ista dissimulemus, ne nostra existimatio in periculum ueniat. Sæpe enim impij isti illusores in hoc seculo Christi conscientias eorum compellantis testimonio cōuincuntur: & quamuis id non omnibus accidat, olim tamen inuitis illis ueniet ipse in nubibus cœli, & suis quidem optatam pacem plenamq; redemptionē afferret, impios autem diris terroribus absorptos ad tartara detrudet.
units.tr: Another fruit, which those two gained together with the rest of the disciples from their zeal, now comes in. For when they set out what they had seen, and this seemed doubtful to some (as can be seen in Mark), behold, Christ stood in the midst of them and greeted them as was his custom, saying: Peace be to you. Thus he confirms their word by his own, so that they should not be held as vain and lying, and he not only presents himself to them as alive again, but also freely and kindly offers them all the fruit of his merit: namely peace, under which the Hebrews comprehend every well-being of man, in body and soul. Yet that peace extends more widely than the peace which Christ won for us. For since he reconciled us to God, in him we enjoy the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding; and that same peace is also the true and stable cause of peace among men, because under that Head, as members of one body, all are united who acknowledge him as their Saviour. And as he was present then to the witnesses of his resurrection and confirmed in person what they said, so he will never fail those who bear faithful witness to him. Many laugh at what is said about the whole business of human salvation. The unhappy world especially thinks it a fable if anyone says that the dead will one day rise and that Christ will come to judgement. But we must not dissemble these things, lest our reputation be put in danger. For these impious scoffers are often convicted in this age by the testimony of their own consciences, which accuse them. And although this does not happen to everyone, yet at last, against their will, he will come in the clouds of heaven, and indeed he will bring the longed-for peace and full redemption to his own, but will thrust the wicked, swallowed up by dreadful terrors, down to hell.

units.la: Est autem hoc loco admodum memorabile, quod de discipulis dicitur: quòd nimirum post certa resurrectionis Christi testimonia, adhuc dubitat, & ne proprijs quidem oculis fidē habent. Nam cùm illum coram uiderent & solita uoce loquentem audirent, territi & expauefacti, putant se spiritum conspicere. Solet hoc frequenter accidere ijs, quibus aliquid præter omnem expectationem occurrit. Tanta enim est nostrorum sensuum infirmitas, ut quæ eius generis sunt, non modò admirationem rationem pariant, quæ nos rerum incertos facit, uerumetiam exanimes interdum reddant: neque id dolor solus facit, sed gaudij quoque eundem effectum esse constat. Exemplo sunt in Romana historia duæ matres, quæ cùm totam urbem infelix cladis ad Trasimenum lacum acceptæ nuntium perter refecissent, præ lætitia spiritu interclusò extinctæ sunt: una quidem in filij sospitis complexu, cui ad portam obuia facta fuerat: altera uerò, cùm quem domi sedens ut occisum lugebat, subitò in conspectum uenire uidit. Quid ergo mirum est, si in re omnium maxima Apostoli ita expauefacti sunt, ut proprijs sensibus non potuerint credere? Præstat autem eiusmodi exempla diligenter obseruare, ut minus tribuamus nostris uiribus, quarum tanta est imbecillitas, Deum autem assiduis precibus fatigemus, ut ipse animos nostros illuminare & sensus confirmare dignetur, ne in ueri cognitione aberrent.
units.tr: It is very remarkable at this point what is said of the disciples: namely that, even after the sure testimonies of Christ's resurrection, they still doubt and do not even trust their own eyes. For when they saw him before them and heard him speaking in his usual voice, they were terrified and alarmed, and thought they saw a spirit. This tends to happen often to those to whom something befalls beyond all expectation. For so great is the weakness of our senses that such things not only produce wonder, which makes us uncertain of things, but sometimes even make people lifeless. Nor does grief alone do this; it is agreed that joy has the same effect. In Roman history there are two mothers as examples. When an unhappy report of the defeat at Lake Trasimene had struck the whole city with terror, they died, their breath cut off by joy: one in the embrace of her son, who had been saved and whom she had met at the gate; the other, seeing suddenly come into view the man whom she had been sitting at home mourning as dead. What wonder, then, is it if in the greatest matter of all the Apostles were so alarmed that they could not believe their own senses? It is better, however, to observe such examples carefully, so that we may attribute less to our own powers, whose weakness is so great, and so that we may weary God with constant prayers, that he himself may deign to enlighten our minds and strengthen our senses, lest they go astray in the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Quid uerò discipulos terruit, cùm nihil perinde optarent, quàm Christum ex mortuis sibi reddi? Putabant (inquit Lucas) se spiritum conspicere. Idè ergo hic passi sunt quod apud Matthæum, quàdo illum aquis inambulantè cernentes exclamarunt, quòd phantasma aut spectrū esse putarēt. Est enim uetus admodū de spiritibus, qui uel hominibus conuersentur, uel illorum loco appareant, opinio: quam apud gentes quoq; locum habuisse apud Platonē & alios authores inuenitur. Vocarunt hi genios, & singulis duos tribuerunt, bonum uidelicet & malū. Originē duxit hæc doctrina ex sacris litteris, quæ Angelos frequenter olim uisibili quoq; specie hominibus apparuisse, & ijsdem rerum agendarū duces et tutores fuisse tradūt. Imò constat illos adhuc ministratores spiritus esse, qui ministerij causa mittūtur propter eos, qui hæredes erūt salutis, adeoq;(ut Dauid ait) castra metari circa eos, qui Dominum timent. Sed & Christus paruulis suos Angelos tribuit, qui semper uideant faciē Dei. Quæ sententia Christianos Hierosolymitanos mouit, ut cùm Petrū quem illi adhuc catenis in carcere constrictū teneri putabant, ad ostiū pulsare ancillula dixissset, Angelum eius hunc esse respondérent. Et de Angelis quidē bonis pie omnino sentiendū est: quia (ut alias monuimus) horum consideratio aduitæ innocentiam & consolationem in periculis grauioribus multū facit. Quod autē gentiū sapientes singulis malum quoq; genium siue angelū (quos κακοδαίμονας uocant) attribuerunt, id uerò à Christiana pietate & religione alienum est: quæ diabolum quidem instar leonis rugientis circuire docet, & quærere quos perdat: eundē uerò nihil cōmercij habere cum ijs, qui Christo uerè sunt insiti. Sed alius adhuc error gentes decepit pernitiosior: quo animas defunctorum oberrare & conspici crediderunt. Et credibile est multos Iudæorū in ea sententia fuisse, quando cōstat Pythagoricam illam παλιγγενεσίαν καὶ μεταψύχωσιν, id est, animarū in alia corpora transmigratione apud quosdā fidem inuenisse. Posteris certè temporibus inter Christianos homines error ille ita obtinuit, ut maximum ex eo quæstum fecerint sacrificuli, qui animas aut incertas uagari, aut diris purgatorij ignis cruciatibus torqueri docuerunt, donec Missarum sacris multoties repetitis redimantur. Quam impietatem cùm alibi confutauerimus, non opus est nunc de ea aliquid dicere. Quoad Apostolos enim, non tam crasse ignorantes illi fuerunt, ut aliquid huius ipsis in mentem uenerit, spiritum tamen esse putauerunt eum, qui subitò & prius à nemine obseruatus in medio eorum consistebat. Nobis autem illorum infirmitas incitamento esse debet, ut maiori studio Verbum Dei audiamus, quò minus erroneis opinionibus possimus seduci. Nec enim nimia esse potest aliqua institutio, quando in sanctissimis hominibus tam multa extant, quæ nostri ingenij corruptionem arguunt.
units.tr: But what terrified the disciples, when they desired nothing more than to have Christ restored to them from the dead? They thought (says Luke) that they saw a spirit. Therefore they suffered here what is found in Matthew, when, seeing him walking on the waters, they cried out, thinking he was a phantom or a ghost. For there is a very old opinion about spirits, that they either converse with men or appear in their place; and it is found that this opinion had a place among the Gentiles also, with Plato and other authors. These called them genii, and assigned two to each person, namely a good one and a bad one. This doctrine took its origin from the sacred letters, which report that angels often appeared to men in visible form in former times and were leaders and guardians of human affairs. Indeed it is established that they are still ministering spirits, sent for the sake of those who will be heirs of salvation, and so (as David says) they encamp around those who fear the Lord. But Christ also assigns angels to his little ones, who always see the face of God. This saying moved the Christians of Jerusalem, so that when a little maidservant said that Peter, whom they still thought was held bound in chains in prison, was knocking at the door, they answered that it was his angel. And indeed we must think piously of good angels, because (as we have noted elsewhere) the consideration of them greatly helps the innocence of the godly and their consolation in graver dangers. But that the wise men of the nations assigned to each person also a bad genius or angel (whom they call kakodaimones [κακοδαίμονας]), this is alien to Christian piety and religion, which teaches that the devil goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, yet that he has no fellowship with those who are truly grafted into Christ. But another, more pernicious error deceived the Gentiles, by which they believed that the souls of the dead wander and can be seen. And it is credible that many of the Jews were of this opinion, since it is established that the Pythagorean palingenesia [παλιγγενεσίαν] and metempsychosis [μεταψύχωσιν], that is, the transmigration of souls into other bodies, found belief among some. Certainly in later times this error so prevailed among Christian people that the little priests made the greatest gain from it, teaching that souls either wander uncertain or are tormented by the dreadful pains of purgatorial fire until they are redeemed by Masses often repeated. Since we have refuted this impiety elsewhere, there is no need to say anything about it now. As for the Apostles, they were not so grossly ignorant that this idea came into their minds, yet they thought it was a spirit that stood suddenly in the midst of them, having been observed by no one before. But their weakness ought to spur us on, so that we may hear the Word of God with greater zeal, and so that we may be less easily led astray by erroneous opinions. For no instruction can be excessive, when in the most holy men there are so many things that prove the corruption of our nature.

units.la: Cæterum ut ijs, qui Deum diligunt, omnia adiumento sunt in bonū: ita feliciter quoq; toti Ecclesiæ cessit hæc discipulorum infirmitas. Nam ex ea occasione arripit Dominus de sua resurrectio ne & corporis sui ueritate dicendi, quam argumentis grauissimis asserit. Oritur autē ab increpatione graui, quæ simul causas incredulitatis aut diffidetiæ perstringit. Quid (inquit) turbati estis? & quare disceptationes ascendūt in cordibus uestris? Primò metū ignauum exprobrat, qui ut animos, ita sensus quoq; turbare solet. Exēpla in re militari sæpe occurrūt, ubi qui timore semel animo conceperunt, ita interdū uisu falluntur, ut ouiū greges aut in imis uallibus surgentes nebulas hostiū exercitū esse putent: & ijdem frequenter strepitu foliorū cadentiū terrentur, ut illum armorum crepitū esse sibi persuadeant. Et in præsenti timor obstitit, ut Christū discipuli nō possent agnoscere. Deinde carnalis prudentiæ rationes in illis reprehendit, quæ causa erat, ut animis alternaret, & intra metum atq; spem dubij penderent. Etenim ubi illis locus datur, mens neque ueritatem intueri, neq; hanc sibi oblatam ampleƈtis potesƈ. Et proprie admodum in hoc argumento ascendendi verbo Spiritus sanƈtus utitur. Vt enim nebulæ ex terra ascendentes Solis lucem obscurant: ita carnis cogitationes si admittantur, rationem impediunt, ut Verbi Dei lucem percipere non possit. Prodest ergo imo necesse est, illas excutere, & primis initijs obstare, ne apud nos locum habeant. Est autem hoc (ut alibi monuimus) non contemnendum resurrectionis Christi testimonium, quòd eos reprehensione dignos ille putauit, qui de ea dubitauerunt, quàmuis eam reuera factâ esse totis animis expeterent. Quo autem supplicio digni erunt, qui dum nostrorum corporum resuscitationem scurriliter negant illam quoque in dubium uocant? Sed audiamus quibus argumentis, se uero corpore resurexisse Christus demonstret.
units.tr: Moreover, just as all things work together for good for those who love God, so this weakness of the disciples also turned out happily for the whole Church. For on this occasion the Lord takes up the matter of his resurrection and the truth of his body, which he proves with the weightiest arguments. He begins with a severe rebuke, which at the same time censures the causes of their unbelief and doubt: "Why are you troubled? And why do doubts arise in your hearts?" First he reproves their cowardly fear, which usually disturbs the senses as well as the mind. In matters of war there are often examples of men who, once fear has taken hold of their minds, are sometimes deceived in what they see, so that they take the mist rising from low valleys for the enemy's army; and the same men are often frightened by the rustling of falling leaves, and persuade themselves that it is the clashing of arms. So too in the present case fear prevented the disciples from recognising Christ. Then he rebukes in them the reasoning of carnal prudence, which was the cause of their wavering between fear and hope and of their hanging in doubt. For when such reasoning is given room, the mind can neither look upon the truth nor lay hold of the truth that is offered to it. And the Holy Spirit uses the word "rise up" in this matter very appropriately. For as mists rising from the earth obscure the light of the sun, so carnal thoughts, if they are admitted, hinder the reason, so that it cannot perceive the light of the Word of God. It is therefore useful, indeed necessary, to shake these thoughts off and to resist them at their first beginnings, so that they may gain no place among us. This testimony to the resurrection of Christ is (as we have elsewhere observed) not to be despised, since he judged worthy of rebuke those who doubted it, although they earnestly desired that it should be true. What punishment, then, will they deserve who, while they mockingly deny the resurrection of our bodies, also call that other resurrection into doubt? But let us hear by what arguments Christ shows that he rose in a true body.

units.la: Propositio totius demonstrationis esƈ: Ego ipse sum: Idesƈ, non sum spiritus siue spectrum, sed ille ipse Iesus, qui ex Maria Virgine homo natus sum, qui in cruce mortuus & sepulchro mandatus sum: Ille ipse ergo ex mortuis resuscitatus meum corpus uobis isto. Id probat primùm certa & diligenti corporis sui descriptione, quæ partium enumeratione constat. Nam ut Theodoretus annotauit inter corporis humani propria præcipuum ferè esƈ, compositum esse. Nominat ergo Christus pedes & manus, carnem & ossa, sub quibus omnia alia membra atq; partes comprehendit. Nam apud Ioannem cum Thoma loquens lateris quoq; miminit. Nisi autem illum ueras manus & ueros pedes, uerum latus, uera deniq; omnia alia corporis humani membra habuisse fateamur, ipsum falsi accusabimus, imò impostorem fingamus oportet, qui præstigijs uoluerit discipulorum sensibus imponere: deniq; euersa & conuiƈta iacebit huius totius actionis propositio, quæ se illum ipsum esse dicit, qui primum ipsis uersatus fuerat. Possumus ergo argumentum ex uerbis eius sic formare: Corpus uerum est, quod constat carne & ossibus, uenis, neruis & sanguine, quod deniq; pedes habet & manus atq; reliqua membra necessaria: Corpus Christi resuscitatum ex carne & ossibus, uenis, neruis & sanguine constat, & membra habet eadem quæ prius. Ergo corpus est uerum, neq; suam substantiam & proprietates naturales deposuit.
units.tr: The proposition of the whole demonstration is this: "I myself am he." That is, I am not a spirit or an apparition, but that very Jesus who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, who died on the cross and was laid in the sepulchre. He therefore, that very same one, raised from the dead, has my body, which you see. He proves this first by a precise and careful description of his body, which consists in an enumeration of its parts. For, as Theodoret observed, one of the chief properties of the human body is that it is composed of parts. Christ therefore names feet and hands, flesh and bones, under which he includes all the other members and parts. Indeed, when he speaks with Thomas in John, he also mentions his side. Unless we admit that he had true hands, true feet, a true side, and in short all the other members of the human body, we shall accuse him of falsehood. Indeed we must imagine him an impostor, who by trickery wished to deceive the senses of his disciples. In that case the proposition of this whole action, which declares that he is the very one who had lived with them before, will be overthrown and refuted. We can therefore frame the argument from his words as follows: That is a true body which consists of flesh and bones, veins, sinews and blood, and which in short has feet and hands and the other necessary members. The body of Christ, raised again, consists of flesh and bones, veins, sinews and blood, and has the same members as before. Therefore the body is true, and it has not laid aside its substance and natural properties.

units.la: Facit ad huius argumenti confirmationem, quod ipsos discipulorum sensus in testimonium adduxit, adeoq; seipsum illis examinandum præbet. Videte (inquit) manus meas & pedes meos. Item: Contrectate me, & uidete. Possunt quidem præstigatores ferre ut quæ faciunt spectentur, imò spectatores ipsi alliciunt, quibus imponant: at ijdem sua propius inspici non ferunt, prorsus autem intolerabile ipsis esƈ, ut quis manum admoueat, ut uel ipsos uel instrumenta eorum contrectet. Nametsi oculi fallantur interdum, tactus tamen si cum uisu coniungatur sali non potesƈ, si quidem homo ratione & communi sensu sit præditus. Procul ergo à præstigiatorum moribus & ingenio Christus abfuit, qui corpus suum à discipulis propius inspici simul & contrectari voluit. Ideo Ioannes doctrinæ de Christo certitudinem asserturus, ab Apostolis eum prædicari dicit, quem audierint, quem uiderint oculis suis, quem deniq; manibus suis contrectarint. Quod etsi ad totum illud tempus extendi possit, quo Christus cum discipulis suis in terris uersatus est, in primis tamen ad hanc actionem & ea omnia referri debent, quæ post eius resurrectionem acciderunt. Nam quod Christum priusquam moreretur Apostoli uidissent, & cum eo familiariter egissent, ne impij quidem negabant, sed quòd illum ex mortuis resurrexisse, & proinde mortis uictorem & humani generis redemptorem esse prædicabant, id uerò plerisq; incredibile, Iudæis autem (ut in Actorum libro apparet) auditu intolerabile uidebatur. Quare Petrus quoq; apud Cornelium de ijs potissimùm disserit, quæ post resurrectionem factâ sint. Itaq; corporis Christi ueritatem nemo negare poterit, nisi qui & ipsum & Apostolos eius simul omnes mendacij arguere uoluerit, & suis imaginationibus plus tribuere quàm ijs, quibus illum resuscitatum coràm spectare & tangere datum fuit.
units.tr: What confirms this argument is that he brought forward the very senses of the disciples as witnesses, and so offers himself to be examined by them. "See," he says, "my hands and my feet." Again: "Handle me and see." Tricksters may indeed allow what they do to be watched, and indeed they entice spectators on whom they may practise their deceptions; but they do not allow their own actions to be inspected more closely, and it would be utterly intolerable to them for anyone to lay a hand on them, to touch them or their instruments. Although the eyes are sometimes deceived, the sense of touch, when it is joined with sight, cannot be deceived, provided the man is endowed with reason and common sense. Christ was therefore far removed from the habits and character of conjurers, since he wished his body to be inspected more closely and also handled by his disciples. So John, wishing to assert the certainty of the doctrine concerning Christ, says that the Apostles preach him whom they heard, whom they saw with their own eyes, and whom they touched with their own hands. And although this may be extended to the whole time during which Christ lived with his disciples on earth, it must nonetheless be referred chiefly to this action and to all those things that happened after his resurrection. For the wicked did not even deny that the Apostles had seen Christ before he died and had lived familiarly with him; but that he had risen from the dead, and was therefore the conqueror of death and the redeemer of the human race, this indeed seemed incredible to most people, and to the Jews (as appears in the Book of Acts) intolerable to hear. Hence Peter also, speaking to Cornelius, discourses chiefly about the things that were done after the resurrection. So no one can deny the truth of Christ's body, unless he wishes to accuse both him and all his Apostles of lying, and to give more weight to his own imaginings than to those to whom it was granted to see and touch him raised up.

units.la: Esƈ autem præter hoc obseruandum, quòd dicit: Videte manus meas & pedes meos: nam ego ipse sum. Ex eo enim colligimus, ita illum resurrexisse, ut ex pristina corporis forma agnosci potuerit. Nam nisi id demus, nequicquam illi eum spectauissent. Ergo tam abest, ut substantiam corporis & eius propria naturalia aboleat clarificatio, quæ resurrectionem comitatur, ut ne formam quidem prorsus tollat: sed in corpore id solum aboletur quod corruptibile & mortale esƈ, ita formæ uitia tantùm corrigerentur: deniq; ea solummodo in toto homine tollit clarificatio, quæ iam nobis ex peccato inhærent. Poterunt ergo agnosci homines in resurrectione, & quia sensus atque intellectus tunc perfectissimi erunt, se mutuò omnes agnoscent, neque ullus porrò ignorantiæ locus erit. Huc pertinet, quòd Mosem & Eliam agnouerunt tres discipuli, quando clarificationis Christi in monte Thabor spectatores fuerunt, & inter hunc & illos potuerunt discernere, licet eos antea nunquam uidissent. Et nuper Cleophas eiusq; socius Christum illico agnouerunt (ex priori nimirum forma, radian te licet & illustri) quàm primum oculi eorum aperti sunt. Nec id alicui mirum uideri debet, quando simile quid in Mose adhuc mortali carne uesfito accidit. De eo enim scribitur, quòd ex Dei colloquio nouū faciei radiantis splendorem contraxerit, quem etsi Israelitæ coràm, intueri non possent, tamen illū uerè agnouerunt. Et debent hæc diligentius considerari, quia non solùm ad confirmandam Christi resurrectionem faciunt, uerumetiam quæ nostra olim in patria cœlesti conditio futura sit docent; cuius meditatio consolationem dulcissimam affert, quæ sola nobis aduersus omnes huius sæculi afflictiones potest sufficere.
units.tr: Besides this, it must be noted that he says: "See my hands and my feet, for I myself am he." For from this we gather that he rose in such a way that he could be recognised by his former bodily form. For unless we grant this, the disciples would have looked upon him in vain. Therefore the glorification which accompanies the resurrection does not so far abolish the substance of the body and its natural properties that it does not even wholly remove its form. Rather, in the body only that is abolished which was corruptible and mortal, so that only the defects of its form are corrected. In short, glorification removes in the whole man only those things that now cling to us from sin. Men will therefore be recognisable in the resurrection, and since their senses and understanding will then be most perfect, they will all recognise one another, and there will be no further place for ignorance. To this belongs the fact that the three disciples recognised Moses and Elijah, when they were witnesses of the glorification of Christ on the mount of Tabor, and could tell the one from the others, although they had never seen them before. And lately Cleophas and his companion recognised Christ at once (of course from his former form, though radiant and illustrious) as soon as their eyes were opened. Nor should this seem strange to anyone, since something similar happened to Moses while he was still in mortal flesh. For it is written that from his conversation with God he received a new splendour of radiant face, which the Israelites could not look upon, yet they truly recognised him. And these things ought to be considered more carefully, because they serve not only to confirm the resurrection of Christ but also teach what our condition will be one day in the heavenly fatherland. The meditation on this brings the sweetest consolation, and it alone can suffice for us against all the afflictions of this age.

units.la: Debet præterea hoc loco considerari, quòd Christus corporis sui resurrectionem atque realem (ut ita loquar) præsentiam non nudis uerbis aut miraculo occulto atque incomprehensibili, sed eiusmodi argumentis probat, quæ sub sensum cadunt: Videte (inquit) quia ego ipse sum. Item: Contrectate me, & uidete. Arguit hoc eorum temeritatem, qui hodie realem & corporalem illius præsentiam in Cœna mystica statuunt, ubi nullum corporis ueri & naturalis indicium apparet. Clamant Christum dixisse, Hoc est corpus meum, & ex eo colligunt, illud ipsum corpus, quod ex uirgine natum est, manibus Sacerdotum contrectari, oraliter (sic ipsi loquuntur) manducari à dignis & indignis, denique dentibus manducantium atteri. Agnoscimus nos Christi uerba, neque ea unquam denegauimus. At quod illi ex eis concludunt, id negamus, quia nullum ueri corporis argumentum Christus nobis in Cœna exhibet, & quod olim tale quid somniantes Capernaitas duriter increpuit, & ad manducationem spiritualem remisit, quæ non aliter quàm fide perficitur. Urgent illi modum præsentiæ miraculosum & infallibilem. At nos nefas esse putamus, in religione miracula fingere, quorum scriptura nusquam meminit: aut dogmata noua miraculis uelle stabilire, quæ nemo uidet aut sentit. Quòd si uerò illi mysterium hoc ineffabile esse sentiunt, cur non suæ illos audaciæ & temeritatis pudet, qua illud effari conantur? Cur Ecclesiam Christi uocibus illis non minus barbaris quàm absurdis fatigant, quibus corpus illius corporaliter, realiter, substantialiter, et oraliter manducari contendunt? cur illud qualitatiuè & quantitatiuè, non autem localiter, adesse gerriunt? Christus, ut se uero suo corpore præsentem esse doceret, ad discipulorum captum sese demisit, suumq; corpus illis uiden dum atque palpandum præbuit. Non ergo iniuriam sibi fieri poterunt dicere, si quid huius ab ipsis quoq; postulemus. Ita enim nos facere iubent Angeli, qui Christum eo modo & forma reditypum esse pollicentur, quo illum in cælos ascendere Apostoli uiderunt. Et ipse Capernaitas (de quibus supra diximus) ad Ascensionem suam remittit, ut uel ex ea colligant, in corporis sui manducatione nihil crassum aut carnale debere animo concipi. De sensu uerborum Cœnæ alibi diximus, & proinde quicquam hic addere non est opus.
units.tr: Moreover, it must be considered here that Christ proves the resurrection of his body and his real (as I may put it) presence not by bare words or by a hidden and incomprehensible miracle, but by arguments that fall under the senses: "See," he says, "that I myself am he." Again: "Handle me and see." This rebukes the rashness of those who today assert a real and bodily presence of Christ in the mystical Supper, where no sign of a true and natural body appears. They cry out that Christ said, "This is my body," and from this they conclude that the very body which was born of the Virgin is handled by the hands of priests, is eaten orally (so they themselves put it) by the worthy and the unworthy, and finally is ground by the teeth of those who eat it. We acknowledge the words of Christ, and have never denied them. But what they infer from them we deny, because Christ shows us in the Supper no argument of a true body; and when the Capernaites once dreamed of something of this kind, he sharply rebuked them and referred them to a spiritual eating, which is accomplished in no other way than by faith. They insist on a miraculous and infallible mode of presence. But we think it wrong to invent miracles in religion, of which Scripture nowhere speaks, or to wish to establish new doctrines by miracles which no one sees or feels. But if they themselves feel that this mystery is ineffable, why are they not ashamed of their audacity and rashness in attempting to express it? Why do they weary the Church of Christ with those words, no less barbarous than absurd, by which they contend that his body is eaten corporally, really, substantially and orally? Why do they strive to say that it is present qualitatively and quantitatively, but not locally? Christ, in order to teach that he was present with his true body, lowered himself to the grasp of his disciples, and offered his body to be seen and touched. They therefore cannot say that any wrong is done to them if we ask something of this kind from them as well. For the angels likewise bid us do this, promising that Christ will return in the same manner and form in which the Apostles saw him ascend into heaven. And the Capernaites themselves (of whom we spoke above) he refers to his Ascension, so that they may gather from it that nothing gross or carnal should be conceived in the mind concerning the eating of his body. We have spoken elsewhere about the sense of the words of the Supper, and therefore there is no need to add anything here.

units.la: Redeamus ergo ad præsentem historiam, quæ nouum incredulitatis argumentum in discipulis proponit. Nam etsi resurrectionem Christi nō solum multis & grauibus, uerumetiam superfluis (ut sic loquar) testimonijs hucusque demonstratam uiderent, & hic ipsis nunc sua uidendi & contrectan di copiam faceret: adhuc tamen non credunt, sed mirantur præ gaudio. Iduerò diligenter Luas annotauit, ut eos ab impijs & contumacibus resurrectionis negatoribus distinguat. Nam non possunt quidem adhuc credere plena fide, luctantur tamen cum incredulitate sua, & nihil magis cupiunt quàm ut uerum sit quod credere nondum possunt. Itaq; infirmitas fuit quæ eos impediuit, non cotumacia, multò minus impietas. Ubi rursus apparet, quàm nobis suspecti esse debeant nostri affectus. Nam etiamsi ex bono principio enascantur, & cum gloriæ Dei atq; pietatis studio coniuncti sint, fidei tamen obstant. Quia enim homo animalis nō percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, carnis autem & uitiosæ naturæ reliquiæ in fidelibus quoque locum habent, frequenter fit, ut fidei mysteria ad rationis suæ calculum reuocent, & tunc de ijs incipiant dubitare, quæ carni difficilia aut impossibilia uidentur: & quò magis gaudent eorum commemoratione, eò plura occurunt, quæ dubios & præ gaudio solicitos reddunt. Tunc ergo uidendum est, ne affectui ita indulgeamus, ut is fidei semen prorsus extinguat, quin potius hoc uiriliter foneamus, ut locum demus Christo, qui tunc maxime suam erga nos bonitatem declarat, quando nobis auxilio suo opus esse uidet.
units.tr: Let us return, then, to the present narrative, which sets before us a new instance of unbelief among the disciples. Although they had already seen the resurrection of Christ proved by many weighty witnesses, and even (if I may put it so) by superfluous ones, and although he now gave them the opportunity to see and handle him, they still do not believe, but are astonished for joy. Luke carefully noted this, so as to distinguish them from the impious and obstinate deniers of the resurrection. For they cannot yet believe with full faith, yet they struggle with their unbelief and desire nothing more than that what they cannot yet believe should be true. Their hindrance, therefore, was weakness, not obstinacy, and much less impiety. Here again it appears how suspect our own feelings ought to be to us. For even when they arise from a good beginning, and are joined with zeal for the glory of God and for piety, they still stand in the way of faith. For "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God," and since remnants of the flesh and of our corrupt nature also remain in believers, it often happens that they bring the mysteries of faith back to the reckoning of their own reason, and then begin to doubt those things that seem difficult or impossible to the flesh. And the more they rejoice in remembering them, the more objections come to mind that make them doubtful and anxious amid their joy. We must therefore take care not to indulge our feelings to the point that they utterly extinguish the seed of faith; rather, we should cherish it manfully, and give room to Christ, who shows his goodness towards us most of all precisely when he sees that we need his help.

units.la: Facit hoc etiam in praesenti. Nam ut fluctuanti discipulorum fidei succurat, dicit eis: Habetis hic esculentum aliquid? Et ipsis partem piscis assi & fauum apiarium ei offerentibus, accipit & in illorum conspectu comedit. Eodem igitur argumento suam resurrectionem probat, quo prius uere in uitam restitutos esse probauerat, quos ex mortis suscitauit. Nam huc facit quod de filia Iairi scribitur, cui cibum dare iussit, cum eam a morte in uitam reuocauisset. Et Lazarum comedisse legimus postquam resurrexerat. In praesenti autem omnem doli suspicionem tollit, quod non ipse cibum secum allatum, sed a discipulis acceptum comedit. Nec est, quod aliquis obijciat, corpora clarificata non opus habere alimento, & ideo Christum discipulis uisum fuisse comedere, cum tamen reuera cibu nullum sumpserit. Nam fatemur nos quoq; Christum cibo nequaquam indiguisse, ut neq; nostra corpora illo indigebunt, postquam resuscitata fuerint ad uitam caelestem. Non autem ex eo sequitur, neq; illum comedisse. Cum enim qui in carne corruptibili adhuc uiuunt multa faciat honeste, & cum decoro, quibus minime indigent, quid obstat quo minus corpora clarificata, quae membris & suis partibus constant, edere possint si uelint, licet ut edant ipsis non sit opus? Et notum est illud Augustini: Non potestas, sed egestas edendi & bibendi talibus corporibus aufertur. Et ut a contrario argumentemur, quis obsecro de Mose & Helia dubitat, neri ne homines fuerint, nec ne, cum uterq; absq; cibo naturali per dies quadraginta uitam sustentauerit? Si ergo in corpore mortali & corruptibili agentibus hoc datum fuit, quod proprie clarificatorum est: cur mirum uidetur Dei Filium in clarificato corpore ad ea se demisisse, quae corruptibili corpori seruiunt? Sed ne cui haec noua uideantur, audiamus quaeso Theodoretum sui saeculi haereticis respondentem, qui hoc dilemmate utebantur: Christus a resurrectione uel egens uere sumpsit cibum, uel non egens uisus est quidem comedisse, cum reuera non ederit? Quid ad haec ille? cibo quidem (inquit) non egebat corpus, quod immortale factum fuerat. De ijs enim qui resurgunt dicit dominus: Illic nec uxores ducunt, nec nubunt, sed sunt tanquam Angeli. Quod autem ipse cibu sumpserit, testes sunt Apostoli. Beatus enim Lucas in proemio Actorum dixit, quod conuersens cum Apostolis Dominus iussit ne Hierosolimis discederent. Diuus autem Petrus dixit apertius: Qui cum eo comedimus & bibimus, postquam resurrexit a mortuis. Quoniam enim eorum qui sunt in praesenti uita proprium est comedere, necessario Dominus carnis resurrectionem offendit per cibum & potum ijs, qui eam ueram esse non putabant. Hoc ipsum autem fecit & in Lazaro, & in filia Iairi. Nam cum eam suscitasset, iussit ei dare quod comederet: & una cum Lazaro conuiuium in ijs, offendens eo argumento ueram esse resurrectionem. Haec Theodoretus. Nos ergo Euangelistarum uerbis insistamus, qui christum uere comedisse tradunt, & cum erudita illa uerbi aestate teneamus illum etiam uere resurrexisse, & quae propria sunt corpori humano seruasse: ne dum hic subtilius philosophamur, nobis nostrorum quoq; corporum resurrectio in dubium ueniat, sine qua salus constare non poterit. Excusemur ergo constanti fide Iesu Christi bonitatem, qui ne quae iusta & grauis dubitandi causa nobis reliqua esset, ad ea usq; se demisit, quibus minime indigebat: & ex eo colligamus, illum ne nunc quidem in caelis agentem nostri pudere, sed illic aduocatum fidum agere pro nobis, ut tandem nos Regni sui cohaeredes & nunquam intermoriturae felicitatis participes reddat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: He does this also in the present case. For to support the wavering faith of the disciples he says to them: "Have you anything here to eat?" And when they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb, he took it and ate in their sight. He therefore proves his resurrection by the same argument by which he had already proved that those whom he raised from the dead had truly been restored to life. For to this purpose belongs what is written of the daughter of Jairus, to whom he commanded food to be given after he had called her back from death. And we read that Lazarus ate after he had risen. In the present case, moreover, he removes every suspicion of fraud, since he did not eat food he had brought with him, but ate what he received from the disciples. Nor is there any force in the objection that glorified bodies have no need of nourishment, and so Christ only seemed to the disciples to eat, when in reality he took no food. For we too admit that Christ had no need of food at all, just as our bodies will have no need of it once they have been raised to heavenly life. But it does not follow from this that he did not eat. For while those who still live in corruptible flesh do many things honourably and becomingly, though they have no need of them, what prevents glorified bodies, which consist of limbs and their parts, from eating if they wish, even though they have no need to eat? And the saying of Augustine is well known: "It is not the power of eating and drinking, but the need, that is taken away from such bodies." And to argue from the opposite side: who, I beg you, doubts about Moses and Elijah, whether they were men or not, since both sustained life for forty days without natural food? If therefore what properly belongs to glorified bodies was granted to those acting in a mortal and corruptible body, why is it thought strange that the Son of God in a glorified body humbled himself to those things that serve a corruptible body? But lest these things seem new to anyone, let us hear, I pray, Theodoret answering the heretics of his own age, who used this dilemma: "Christ after the resurrection either truly ate, being in need, or, not being in need, only seemed to eat, since in reality he did not eat." What does he say to this? "The body," he says, "had no need of food, since it had been made immortal. For the Lord says of those who rise: 'There they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels.' That he did take food, however, the Apostles are witnesses. For the blessed Luke, in the preface to the Acts, said that the Lord, while living with the Apostles, commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem. And the divine Peter said more plainly: 'We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.' For since it is proper to those who are in the present life to eat, the Lord necessarily met the doubters of the resurrection of the flesh by means of food and drink, so that they might know it to be true. He did the same also with Lazarus and with the daughter of Jairus. For when he had raised her, he commanded that she be given something to eat, and with Lazarus he shared a meal, thereby proving by that argument that the resurrection was real." Thus Theodoret. Let us, then, keep to the words of the Evangelists, who relate that Christ truly ate, and with that learned testimony of the Word let us hold that he also truly rose, and kept what is proper to the human body. Let us not, while we philosophize more subtly here, bring the resurrection of our own bodies into doubt, since without it salvation cannot stand. Let us therefore give thanks, with constant faith, for the goodness of Jesus Christ, who humbled himself even to those things he least needed, so that no just and serious cause for doubt might remain for us. And from this let us gather that he is not ashamed of us even now, while he reigns in heaven, but there acts as a faithful advocate for us, so that at last he may make us co-heirs of his kingdom and sharers in a happiness that will never end. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXIIII.

units.la: Et dixit eis: Hi sunt sermones, quos locutus sum vobis, cum adhuc essem vobiscum: Oportere impleri omnia quae scripta sunt in Lege Mosis, & Prophetis, & Psalmis de me. Tunc aperuit eorum mentem, ut intelligerent Scripturas. Et dixit eis: ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati: & resurgere a mortuis tertio die: Et praedicari in eius nomine resipiscentiam ac remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes, incipiendo ab Hierosolyma. Vos autem estis testes horum. Ecce ego mittã promissum Patris mei super vos: Vos autem manete in urbe Hierosolyma, usque quo induamini virtute ex alto.
units.tr: And he said to them: "These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the Law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms concerning me." Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures. And he said to them: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. But you are witnesses of these things. Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you. But you remain in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high."

units.la: {a}Prolixè & diligenter hucusque Lucas universam Iesu Christi historiam exposuit, in cuius merito omnem salutem humani generis consistere certò constat, cùm solus hic nobis à Patre sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus sit. At quia nulla ad nos utilitas ex illo redire potest, nisi eum propter nos omnia fecisse, & quaecunq; fecit ad nos pertinere credamus, discipulis sese nō modò ex mortuis rediviuum exhibuit, verumetiam ijsdem diligenter usum atque fructum suae mortis & resurrectionis exposuit, illos deniq; horum praecones constituit, ut quam ipse nobis meruit salutem toti mundo praedicarent. Eam actionem in praesenti Lucas describit, & est haec diversa ab ea, quam in Galilaea institutam fuisse Matthaeus narrat, quo discipuli postea ex mandato Angeli, qui mulieribus sepulchrum visuris apparuerat, profecti fuerunt. Nam etsi tunc plenius cum illis de hac re egerit Dominus, voluit tamen nunc quoque eam attingere, ut eos in fide resurrectionis magis confirmaret, & officij ipsorum commemoratione à cogitationibus carnis abstraheret, quibus impediebantur, quò minus de ipsius Regno rectè sentirent. Est autem locus iste multa consideratione dignissimus. Continet enim ipsa salutis nostrae fundamenta (ut sic loquar) & totam ministerij Ecclesiastici rationem explicat, in qua videbimus quae illa doctrina sit, quam in Ecclesia perpetuò retinere atque praedicari necesse est.
units.tr: {a}Luke has so far set out at length and with care the whole history of Jesus Christ, on whose merit it is certain that the whole salvation of mankind depends, since he alone has been made by the Father our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. But because no benefit can come to us from him unless we believe that he did all things for us and that whatever he did pertains to us, he showed himself to his disciples, not only as one alive again from the dead, but he also carefully explained to them the use and fruit of his death and resurrection, and finally appointed them as heralds of these things, so that they might proclaim to the whole world the salvation he had won for us. Luke describes this action here, and it is different from the one which Matthew relates was carried out in Galilee, where the disciples afterwards went, at the command of the angel who had appeared to the women who were coming to see the sepulchre. For although the Lord then dealt with them more fully on this matter, he nevertheless wished now also to touch upon it, both to strengthen them more in faith in the resurrection, and to draw them away from thoughts of the flesh, by reminding them of their office, which hindered them from thinking rightly about his Kingdom. Now this passage is most worthy of careful consideration. For it contains, so to speak, the very foundations of our salvation, and it sets out the whole plan of the ecclesiastical ministry, in which we shall see what that doctrine is which must always be retained and preached in the Church.

units.la: Rursus autem à Scripturis exordiritur, sicut nuper quoq; cū discipulis duobus in via Emmaun-tina fecerat. Hi sunt (inquit) sermones, quos locutus sum vobis, cùm adhuc essem vobiscum: oportere impleri omnia, quae scripta sunt in Lege Mosis, & Prophetis, & Psalmis de me. Quibus verbis duo agit. Primò obliuiosam intellectus tarditatem illis exprobrat, qui tam difficiles & stupidi sint in iis credendis, de quibus ipse toties eos admonuerit. Culpam verò amplificat, quando se non alia illis dixisse docet, quàm quae olim de ipso in Mose & Prophetis atq; Psalmis fuerunt tradita. Fuit ergo inexcusabilis haec ofcitatia, quod neq; Scripturae veteris vaticinia, neq; ipsius Christi verba in mente revocarunt, cuius domestici discipuli tam diu fuerant. Deinde quia illos totius orbis doctores facere volebat, admonet simul, ex quibus fontibus doctrinam haurire debeant, quam toti mundo praedicent. Ex Scripturis nimirum, quae tunc in populo Dei receptae, & quarum fides atq; authoritas divinis testimonijs abunde confirmata erat. Et ne quis vel ipsis vel ipsorum successoribus sub Scriptu-rae nomine aut praetextu imponeret, diserte de qua nam loquatur ostendit: de ea nimirum, quae libros Mosis, scripta Prophetarum (ad quae historici quoq; libri pertinent, quorum authores fuisse Prophetas constat) & Psalmos continet. Et quàmuis hi quoque inter prophetica scripta numerari possint, voluit tamen eos in praesenti ab illis distinguere, ut eorum meditationem discipulis diligentius commendaret. Habet enim Psalmorum liber multa, quae in nullo alio Scripturae sacrae libro simul omnia inueniuntur: utpote varias precandi formas, quibus omnia tentationum genera & omnes vitae humanae casus comprehenduntur: gratiarum item actiones, hymnos & laudes Dei, historicas beneficio-rum & operum eius expositiones, fidei & vitae praecepta, adhortationes, correptiones, comminationes, & cum his consolationes quoq; dulcissimas: adhaec veterum minarum & promissionū Dei exempla luculenta, vaticinia item de Christo, quibus eius afflictiones, gloria, victoriae & triumphi Regni, eius per totum orbem felix propagatio evidentissimè describuntur. Merito igitur Psalmorum pecu-liarem mentionem facit Dominus, quos primitiua Ecclesia in tanto pretio & honore habuit, ut nix ulli fidelium coetus fuerint, in quibus nō aliquid ex illis populo recitaretur, sicuti in D. Ambrosij, Au-gustini & aliorum patrum scriptis est videre. Posteris autem temporibus Psalmodiae quidem retenta, sed peregrinae linguae usu inutiles factae, adhaec multorum canticorum admixtione corruptae sunt, quibus multa inepta, multa superstitiosa, multa etiam impia continentur.
units.tr: Again he begins from the Scriptures, just as he had done lately also with the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. "These are," he says, "the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the Law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms concerning me." By these words he does two things. First, he reproaches them for their forgetful slowness of understanding, since they were so hard and dull to believe those things about which he had so often admonished them. But he makes the fault greater when he shows that he had told them nothing other than what had long ago been handed down about himself in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms. This dullness was therefore inexcusable, since they recalled neither the prophecies of the Old Testament nor the very words of Christ, though they had been his household disciples for so long. Then, because he wished to make them teachers of the whole world, he also admonishes them at the same time from what sources they ought to draw the doctrine which they are to proclaim to the whole world. That is, from the Scriptures, which were then received among the people of God, and whose faith and authority had been amply confirmed by divine testimonies. And lest anyone should impose upon them, or upon their successors, under the name or pretext of Scripture, he clearly shows what he is speaking of: namely of that Scripture which contains the books of Moses, the writings of the Prophets (to which the historical books also belong, since it is established that their authors were prophets) and the Psalms. And although these too may be counted among the prophetic writings, he nevertheless chose in this passage to distinguish them from the others, so that he might more diligently commend their meditation to the disciples. For the book of Psalms contains many things which are not all found together in any other book of holy Scripture: namely, various forms of prayer, which embrace every kind of temptation and every misfortune of human life; also thanksgivings, hymns and praises of God, historical accounts of his benefits and works, precepts of faith and life, exhortations, rebukes, threats, and along with these also most sweet consolations; besides these, clear examples of God's ancient threats and promises, and also prophecies about Christ, in which his afflictions, glory, victories and the triumph of his Kingdom, and its happy spread throughout the whole world, are most plainly described. Rightly, then, the Lord makes particular mention of the Psalms, which the primitive Church held in such high esteem and honour that there was scarcely any assembly of the faithful in which something from them was not read to the people, as may be seen in the writings of St Ambrose, Augustine and other Fathers. But in later times the singing of the Psalms was indeed kept, yet it became useless through the use of a foreign tongue, and moreover it was corrupted by the mixing in of many songs, in which much that is foolish, much that is superstitious and much that is even impious is contained.

units.la: Quoad verò huius loci argumentum, nunc istud observemus, doctrinam fidei & salutis, quae Ecclesiae proponatur, non aliunde quàm ex sacris literis peti debere. Quia enim homo animalis non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, nihil in tantis mysterijs ex seipso intelliget, nihil item alios docere poterit, nisi ipsi divinitus reveletur. At Deus, qui olim cum patribus per visiones loquebatur, tandem voluntatem suam scriptis mandari voluit, & in ea re ceu scribis & amanuenfibus usus est Mose atq; Prophetis. Et ut Ifaias & Malachias fui seculi homines de multis quaerentes ad Legem remittebant: ita Christus priusquam moreretur, ex ueteribus scripturis concionum suarum argumenta sumpsisse, & nunc postquam resurrexit, idem fecisse legitur. Debet ergo hoc ipsum perpetuò obseruari, neq; audiendi sunt, qui uel ex suo capite noua dogmata fingunt, vel concilijs opus esse aiunt, in quibus doctrinae genus aut forma certa constituatur. Si enim Mosis Lex Prophetis sufficere potuit, ut ad hanc omnes relegarent: si Christus ex illa & horum scriptis docuit, quaecunq; ad fidei & salutis cognitionem faciunt: non est quod hodie Scripturas imperfectiores esse putemus, cum ab illo tempore illis accesserint Apostoli, qui & Christi Iesu historiam suis scriptis complexi sunt, & ea in illo euidenter impleta esse tradiderunt, qui prius obscuriora uideri poterant. Incerti autē & dubij fluctuent oportet inter diuersissimas de fide opiniones, quicunq; non contenti scripturis ab hominum authoritate pendent.
units.tr: As for the subject of this passage, let us now observe this: that the doctrine of faith and salvation which is set before the Church must be sought from nowhere else than from the holy writings. For since "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2.), he will understand nothing of such great mysteries from himself, and likewise will be unable to teach others, unless it is revealed to him by God. But God, who formerly spoke with the fathers through visions, at last willed that his will should be committed to writing, and in this matter he used Moses and the Prophets as scribes and secretaries. And just as Isaiah and Malachi, men of their own age, when they were asked about many things, sent people back to the Law, so it is read that Christ, before he died, drew the subjects of his sermons from the ancient Scriptures, and that after he had risen he did the same. This therefore must always be observed, and those are not to be listened to who either invent new doctrines from their own head, or say that councils are needed, in which a kind or fixed form of teaching is to be established. For if the Law of Moses was able to suffice for the Prophets, so that all were to be sent back to it, and if Christ taught from it and from the writings of these men whatever pertains to the knowledge of faith and salvation, there is no reason for us to think today that the Scriptures are more imperfect, since from that time the Apostles have been added to them, who both embraced the history of Jesus Christ in their writings and handed down that those things which might previously have seemed obscure were clearly fulfilled in him. Whoever does not rest content with the Scriptures but depends on human authority must necessarily be uncertain and doubtful, tossed about among the most diverse opinions concerning the faith.

units.la: Caeterum non obiter modò Mosis & Prophetarum dicta discipulis in mentem reuocat Dominus, sed mentem quoq; illorum aperuit, ut Scripturas intelligerent. Modum & rationem Ioannes expressisse uidetur, qui illum in eos flauisse, & dixisse scribit: Accipite Spiritum sanctum. Nam eandem historiā illic & hic narrari, ex temporis circumstantia liquidò apparet. Et quamuis apud Ioannem subijciantur, quae ad effectum & dignitatem ministerij Euangelici pertinent, idtamen non obstat, quin eadem ratione mentes quoque eorum uera Scripturarum cognitione illuminauerit, ut iam ea intelligere inciperent, quae prius nunquam uiderant. Et est hoc loco probè obseruandum, quòdidum ex Scripturis concionatur Christus, simul occulta spiritus virtute mentes discipulorum illuminat, ut illas possint intelligere, & mox hoc ipsum quod prius dixerat repetens infert: ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit CHRISTVM pati, resurgere, &c. Hoc enim facto phanaticos illos confutat Dominus, qui Spiritus reuelationes nouas somniant absque Scripturis, & has ceu inutiles reijciunt, ut quae nihil praeter mortuam literam contineant. Atqui fatemur nos quoque ipsa literarum elementa, si per se considerentur, mortua esse: sed illis ipsis Dei uerbum uiuum & efficax expressum esse dicimus, quo Spiritus ceu proprio & ordinario instrumento utitur in tradenda Dei uoluntate & patefaciendis aeternae salutis mysterijs. Et ridiculum est Spiritum iactare, qui homines à Scripturis auocet, quae ipso authore à sanctis Dei hominibus olim prodierunt. Quid quod Spiritus probare iubet Ioannes Apostolus? Quàm uero certam illos probandi regulam habebimus, si Scripturae è medio tollantur?
units.tr: Moreover, the Lord does not merely recall to the disciples' minds the sayings of Moses and the Prophets in passing, but he also opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures. John seems to have expressed the manner and method, when he writes that he breathed upon them and said: "Receive the Holy Spirit." For that the same history is related here and there is clear from the circumstances of the time. And although in John there are added the things which pertain to the effect and dignity of the Gospel ministry, this does not prevent him from having likewise enlightened their minds by true knowledge of the Scriptures, so that they began now to understand things which they had never seen before. And in this place it must be carefully noted that while Christ preaches from the Scriptures, at the same time by the secret power of the Spirit he enlightens the minds of the disciples so that they can understand them; and immediately, repeating what he had said before, he adds: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, to rise, etc." For by this act the Lord refutes those fanatics who dream of new revelations of the Spirit apart from the Scriptures, and reject these as useless, as if they contained nothing but a dead letter. Yet we too grant that the very letters of the alphabet, if considered by themselves, are dead; but we say that the living and effective Word of God is expressed in them, by which the Spirit makes use, as his own and ordinary instrument, in delivering the will of God and in revealing the mysteries of eternal salvation. And it is ridiculous to boast of the Spirit in a way that draws men away from the Scriptures, which by the authority of the Author himself were long ago brought forth by the holy men of God. Indeed, does not the Apostle John command that the spirits be tested? But what sure rule of testing shall we have if the Scriptures are taken out of the way?

units.la: Admonet praeterea locus iste, Scripturas expositione opus habere, neque satis esse ut illas obiter audiamus uel legamus. Habent enim ueteris Testamenti libros Iudaei quoque, & cum illis maiorem Euangelicae historiae partem Turcae amplectuntur: Sed nullus ad utrosque inde fructus redit, eò quòd illi Christum omnino reijcientes uelum illud sibijpsis obtendunt (ut Paulus scribit) quodeos in faciem Mosis propius intueri prohibet, hi uerò Mahumeticis fabulis dementati crucem & mortem Christi negant, sine qua is nobis salutifer esse non poterit. Et quod de linguis peregrinis idem Apostolus tradit, nullum earum in Ecclesia usum esse, nisi interpres accedat, qui quod illis dictum est, vulgari sermone explicet, ut ab omnibus percipi possit: hoc ipsum ad omnes Scripturas extendi poterit. Nam etsi uerba quoad literalem sensum intelligantur, non tamen sensum qui sub illis latet, omnes semper uidere possunt, & ideo Scriptura multis arcae loco est, quae thesauros quidem ingentes continet, sed quibus nemo frui possit, nisi clauis adsit, qua illa referetur. At illius clauis est interpretatio, quae non sensum modò uerborum indicat, sed eundem rebus praesentibus accommodat: quod Christum quoque in praesenti fecisse uidemus. Ne autem sub interpretationis praetextu fallamur, tenendum est, solum Christum esse fidum illum & germanum interpretem, qui ut finis totius Legis est, ita Spiritu suo electorum mentes aperit, ut Veritatem intelligere & amplecti possint. Hunc uero non solis Pontificibus aut horum coniuratis largitur, quos illi suo charactere signauerunt, sed omnibus, qui in ipsum credunt, & eum solum audiunt. Et quamuis non omnibus datur perfecta & plena totius Scripturae cognitio, singulis tamen largitur ille, quod ipsis pro suae conditionis ratione ad salutem sufficit. Videant modo singuli, ut in precibus assidui sint, & carnis suggestiones suspectas habeant, quibus Spiritus reuelatio maximè impeditur.
units.tr: This passage also warns us that the Scriptures need explanation, and that it is not enough simply to hear or read them in passing. The Jews too have the books of the Old Testament, and the Turks embrace most of the Gospel history along with them. Yet neither gains any benefit from them. The Jews, rejecting Christ altogether, hold that veil before their own faces (as Paul writes) which keeps them from looking closely at the face of Moses. The Turks, maddened by Mahometan fables, deny the cross and death of Christ, and without these he cannot be saviour to us. What the same Apostle teaches about foreign tongues applies equally to all Scripture: they have no use in the Church unless an interpreter comes forward to explain in the common language what was said in them, so that everyone can understand it. Although the words may be understood according to their literal sense, not everyone can always see the sense hidden beneath them. So Scripture is like a chest that holds great treasures, but no one can enjoy them unless the key is at hand to open it. The key is interpretation, which does not merely point out the meaning of the words but applies that meaning to present circumstances, as we see Christ himself doing here. Lest we be deceived under the pretext of interpretation, we must hold that Christ alone is the faithful and true interpreter. As he is the end of the whole Law, so by his Spirit he opens the minds of the elect, so that they may understand and embrace the truth. He bestows this not only on the Popes or their sworn followers, whom they have marked with their own seal, but on all who believe in him and listen to him alone. And although not all are given a perfect and full knowledge of the whole of Scripture, he nevertheless gives each person what is sufficient for salvation, according to the measure of his condition. Let each one take care to be constant in prayer, and to regard with suspicion the promptings of the flesh, which chiefly hinder the revelation of the Spirit.

units.la: Quia autem quæri poterat, quid in Scripturis potissimùm viderint discipuli, & quid hodie etiã horum successores spectare debeant, paucis summam omnium Lucas comprehendit, quando Domi- num illis dixisse scribit: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere à mortuis tertio die, & prædicari in eius nomine resipiscentiam ac remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes, incipiendo ab Hierosolyma. Comprehenditur istis verbis summa omnium librorum Veteris & Noui Testamenti, quæ in duobus omnino capitibus consistit, historia nimirum Filij Dei in carne manifestati, & eiusdem usu siue fructu. Historiam omnem sub passione aut morte & resurrectione comprehendit. Quia enim tota eius vita, quam in terris vixit, afflictionum & doloris plena fuit, ad totum quoq; illius curriculum passionis historia extendi debet. Ad resurrectionē verò omnis etiã, quæ eam comitata & secuta est, gloria pertinet. Debent autem ad ista referri omnes promissiones Dei, quæ olim patribus datæ sunt, typi item legales, prophetiæ, historia denique sacra, quæ lineam generis Christi, temporum seriem, adhæc exempla fidelium & infidelium continet. Vsus verò & fructus istorum omnium est, ut in Christo Iesu habeamus pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Quia enim non solùm peccatores, sed in peccatis mortui eramus, impossibile nobis erat ex illis ad vitā resurgere, nisi ea prius è medio auferrentur. Id verò mortis suæ merito Christus fecit, qui ita illa expiauit, ut nobis amplius imputari non possint. Itaq; ut damnatio nulla illis incumbit, qui ei per fidem sunt insiti: ita ijdem in illo peccatis moriuntur, & in eodem ad vitā nouam & cælestē resurgunt. Et hæc quidem Euangelicæ doctrinæ summa est, quam suis concionibus atq; scriptis Apostoli fusius exposuerunt. In præsenti autem non opus est de singulis multa dicere, cùm & veræ pœnitentiæ & remissionis peccatorum rationem non uno loco tradiderimus. Sufficiat ergo monuisse, quòd duo hæc inter docendum semper coniungi, utrumq; verò in solo Christo monstrari debent.
