Nam si de sola peccatorum remissione gratuita dicamus, multi ex ea peccandi licentiam captabunt. At si solam pœnitentiam quis urgeat, in desperationē multi incident. Quòd si verò absq; Christo tam hæc quam illa prædicentur, mox suorum operum iustitiam hypocritæ stabilient, & aduersus Dei gratiam & Christi meritum Pharisaica superbia se extollent.
units.tr: Since it could be asked what the disciples especially looked for in the Scriptures, and what their successors today ought to look for, Luke briefly sums up the whole matter when he writes that the Lord said to them: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem" (Luke 24:46–47). These words comprehend the sum of all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which consists entirely of two heads: namely, the history of the Son of God manifested in the flesh, and the use or benefit of that history. The whole history is comprised under his passion, or death and resurrection. For since his whole life, which he lived on earth, was full of afflictions and sorrow, the history of his passion must be extended to his whole course. To his resurrection pertains all the glory that accompanied and followed it. All the promises of God, which were once given to the fathers, must be referred to these, as well as the legal types, the prophecies, and finally the sacred history, which contains the line of Christ's descent, the sequence of times, and also the examples of the faithful and the unfaithful. The use and benefit of all these things is that in Christ Jesus we may have repentance and remission of sins. For since we were not only sinners but dead in our sins, it was impossible for us to rise from them to life unless they were first taken away. Christ did this by the merit of his death, which expiated them in such a way that they can no longer be imputed to us. Thus no condemnation rests upon those who have been grafted into him by faith; in him they die to sins, and in him they rise again to a new and heavenly life. This is indeed the sum of the Gospel teaching, which the Apostles set out more fully in their sermons and writings. Here, however, there is no need to say much about each point, since we have set out the nature of true repentance and of remission of sins in more than one place. It is enough, therefore, to have pointed out that these two must always be joined in teaching, and that both must be shown in Christ alone. For if we speak of the free remission of sins alone, many will seize upon it as a licence to sin. But if someone urges repentance alone, many will fall into despair. And if these things are taught without Christ, the hypocrites will straightway establish the righteousness of their own works, and will exalt themselves in Pharisaic pride against the grace of God and the merit of Christ.

units.la: At docet simul Dominus, quibus ista prædicari debeant: Gentibus nimirum uniuersis usq; ad extremos orbis terrarum fines, ut posteaquam cælum ascensurus dixit. Initium tamen ab Hierosolyma fieri voluit propter promissiones, quæ apud Prophetas habentur. E Zion exibit lex (inquit Isaias) & verbum Domini de Hierusalem. Et Dauid in Psalmo illo celeberrimo, quo totum Messiæ ex se nasciturî negotium complexus est: Dominus emittet virgam suæ potentiæ ex Zion. Quo loco virga non aliud quàm Euangelij prædicationem significat, quam Isaias quoq; virgam oris sui dicit, qua terram percussurus sit. Debuit autem Iudæorum genti primò prædicari Euangelium, ut suam bonitatem simul & iustitiam ea in re Deus declararet. Bonitatis enim immensæ & plus quàm paternæ opus fuit, quòd genti contumaci & incurabili, imò vrbi sanguinariæ, salutem gratuitã obtulit. Iustitiæ autem specimen præclarum est, quòd ab ingratis & pertinacibus gratiã suam ad gentes traxtulit. Deniq; hac ratione inexcusabiles facti sunt Iudæi, neq; Apostolos odij aut malignitatis insimulare potuerunt, cùm hi ipsis relictis ad gentes transfirent. Et hæc causa fuit, quòd postea etiam vbiq; gentium in Iudæorū synagogis prædicandi initium fecerunt: sicuti ex Pauli actione apud Corinthios apparet. Nam cùm illic etiam Iudæis primis prædicauisset, hi autem ei non sine diris blasphemijs contradicerent, ille excussis vestibus ad eos dixit: Sanguis vester super caput vestrum: purus ego ab hoc tempore ad gentes proficiscar. Et debent hoc iustitiæ diuinæ exemplum, quod in Iudæos æditum est, diligenter observare ciuitates illæ & gentes, quas nostro sæculo hac gratia Deus dignatus est, ut renascentis Euangelij lux ipsis primis innotuerit. Nam nisi se illi gratas & obedientes præbeant, idem eis quod infelici Iudæorum populo accidet, & in illis locum habebit, quod alibi ait Dominus: Erunt primi nouissimi, & nouissimi erunt primi.
units.tr: But the Lord also teaches to whom these things are to be preached: to all nations, namely, even to the farthest ends of the earth, as he said when he was about to ascend into heaven. Yet he wished the beginning to be made at Jerusalem, on account of the promises found in the Prophets. "The law shall go out of Zion," says Isaiah, "and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (Isa. 2:3). And David, in that most famous Psalm in which he embraced the whole work of the Messiah who was to be born from his line, says: "The Lord shall send forth the rod of his power out of Zion" (Ps. 110:2). In this place the rod signifies nothing other than the preaching of the Gospel, which Isaiah also calls "the rod of his mouth," with which he will strike the earth (Isa. 11:4). The Gospel had to be preached first to the Jewish nation, so that God might at the same time declare his goodness and his justice in this matter. It was an act of immense goodness, and more than fatherly, that he offered free salvation to a stubborn and incurable nation, indeed to a bloodthirsty city. And it is a splendid instance of justice that he transferred his grace from the ungrateful and obstinate to the nations. Finally, by this means the Jews were made inexcusable, and they could not accuse the Apostles of hatred or malice, since the Apostles left them and turned to the nations. This was also the reason that afterwards, wherever they went among the nations, they began preaching in the synagogues of the Jews, as is clear from Paul's conduct among the Corinthians. For when he had preached there first to the Jews, and they opposed him with dreadful blasphemies, he shook out his garments and said to them: "Your blood be upon your own heads; from now on I will go pure to the nations" (Acts 18:6). Those cities and nations, to which God in our age has deigned to grant this grace, that the light of the renewed Gospel should first shine upon them, ought carefully to observe this example of divine justice shown against the Jews. For unless they show themselves grateful and obedient, the same thing will happen to them as to the unhappy people of the Jews, and in their case what the Lord says elsewhere will hold true: "The first shall be last, and the last shall be first" (Matt. 20:16).

units.la: Necminus consideratione dignum est, quod eandem doctrinã ad omnes gentes extendit. Nam in eo quoq; apparet Dei bonitas, qui absq; personarum respectu salutem Filij sui merito quæsitam omnibus offert: imò missis hinc inde legatis omnes ad huius societatē inuitat. Ideo Paulus scribit, Dei gratiam omnibus hominibus salutiferam apparuisse. Quotquot ergo pereunt, non illius morositate aut invidia, sed propria culpa pereunt, dum sibi oblatam salutem impiè aspernantur. Deinde præclararum est hoc potentiæ Christi & Regni eius per totum orbem propagandi argumentum. Cùm ille Bethlehemi ex virgine homo nasceretur, Augustus Cæsar misit hinc inde edictis totius orbis censum instituit, ut se huius dominum esse testaretur. At nunc Christus, qui ante pauculos dies in cruce penderat, excusso mortis iugo vitæ restitutus, suos seruos ad omnes gentes destinat, non ut ex aliorum fortunis suæ ambitioni satisfaciat, sed ut se omnium hominum Seruatorem esse ostendat, et æternos Regni sui cœlestis thesauros plus quàm regia liberalitate in omnes distribuat. Postremò docemur hoc loco, eam salutis rationem quæ per Euangelium traditur, unicam & omnibus Dei electis communem esse, adeò ut extra hanc nullum sit aliud nomen sub cælo hominibus datum, cuius merito aut respectu quisquam seruari possit. Nam si quid huius inueniri posset, minimè opus erat Christum in mundum venire, aut huius dilectissimos seruos fructraneo labore fatigare, & periculis tantis obijcere. Confutantur igitur hic validissimè, qui vnumquemque in sua religione aut patria superstitione seruari contendunt, modò animi intentio bona sit. Quis enim de gentium intentione dubitet? Nulla certè vnquam tam barbara, tam immanis fuit, quæ Deum sciens volens cultu impio irritarit: sed omnium hic scopus fuit, quòd numen illud supremum colere, Deos suis ritibus placare & sibi propitios reddere studuerunt. Sed nihilominus illos Paulus sub tenebrarum potestate fuisse scribit, & ut per Euangelij prædicationem ad Christum adducerētur, opus fuit. Nullum ergo ex sua intentione bona fructum habuerunt. Debent hoc diligenter & sæpe meditari nostri temporis Epicurei, qui nimium familiariter cum Deo ludunt, dum religionis causam indifferentem faciunt, ne aliquem hominum offendant. Qui dum hominibus parcunt, Deo Patri et Filio Dei atrocem iniuriam faciunt, ut alibi copiose satis ostendimus.
units.tr: Nor is it less worthy of consideration that he extends the same teaching to all nations. For in this too the goodness of God appears, since without respect of persons he offers to all the salvation sought by the merit of his Son, and indeed sends ambassadors here and there to invite all into this fellowship. Therefore Paul writes that the grace of God, bringing salvation, has appeared to all men (Titus 2:11). Whoever therefore perish do not perish through his peevishness or envy, but through their own fault, since they impiously despise the salvation offered to them. Moreover, this is a notable proof of the power of Christ and of the spreading of his kingdom throughout the whole world. When he was born a man of the virgin at Bethlehem, Augustus Caesar sent edicts here and there and ordered a census of the whole world, so as to proclaim himself its lord. But now Christ, who had hung on the cross only a few days before, having shaken off the yoke of death and been restored to life, sends his servants to all nations. He does this not to satisfy his own ambition with the fortunes of others, but to show that he is the Saviour of all men, and to distribute the eternal treasures of his heavenly kingdom to all, with more than royal generosity. Lastly, we are taught in this place that the way of salvation which is delivered through the Gospel is the one and only way, common to all the elect of God, so that outside it there is no other name under heaven given to men by which anyone can be saved, whether by its merit or by regard for it. For if anything of this kind could be found, there would have been no need for Christ to come into the world, nor for his most beloved servants to wear themselves out with fruitless labour and expose them to such great dangers. Therefore those are most powerfully refuted here who contend that each man may be saved in his own religion or the superstition of his country, provided only that his intention is good. For who could doubt the intention of the nations? Certainly no nation was ever so barbarous or so savage that, knowing God, it deliberately provoked him with impious worship; rather, the aim of all of them was to worship that supreme deity, to appease the gods with their rites and to make them favourable to themselves. Nevertheless, Paul writes that they were under the power of darkness, and that it was necessary for them to be brought to Christ through the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore they gained no fruit from their good intention. Our present-day Epicureans ought to consider this carefully and often, for they play too familiarly with God when they make the cause of religion a matter of indifference, so as not to offend any man. While they spare men, they do a grievous wrong to God the Father and to the Son of God, as we have shown at sufficient length elsewhere.

units.la: Sed accedamus ad postremum huius loci actum, quo ad discipulos conuersus suum illis officium siue munus commendat, dicens: Vos autem estis testes horum: Et ecce ego mitto promissum Patris mei super vos: Vos autem manete in vrbe Hierosolyma, vsq; quò induamini virtute ex alto. Quibus verbis tria agit memoratu dignissima, de quibus ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: But let us come to the last part of this passage, in which, turning to the disciples, he commends to them their office or duty, saying: "You are witnesses of these things. And behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you. But you, remain in the city of Jerusalem, until you are clothed with power from on high." In these words he deals with three matters most worthy of mention, which we will discuss in order.

units.la: Primò munus eorum definit longè aliud quàm ipsi imaginabantur. Ipsi enim (ut sæpe diximus) regni terreni spem conceperant, in quo sibi triumphos & dignitates promittebant. Quid verò Christus? Vos (inquit) estis testes meæ mortis & resurrectionis, & ea omnia in me suum complementum habuisse toti mundo testabimini, quæ olim à Mose & Prophetis prædicta sunt. Idem iam aditurus moreem dicit, & postea in cælum abiturus hoc ipsum repetit. Vno autem verbo eos de suo officio ad monere, & simul ut ad illud se præparent extimulare voluit. Testes enim in causis controuersis sistuntur, ut per hos veritas rei cognoscatur. Illorum ergo est, ut non aliud dicant, quàm quod ipsis probè compertum est, & in eo edicendo fortes & cordati sint, & nihil affectui tribuant: sed meminerint, testem falsum Deo exosum esse, qui ut tales Talionis poena multentur præcepit. Quanto autem gravius scelus fuerit in causa Dei testem falsum agere, & quidem cum multarum animarum iactura, quæ mendaci doctrina seducuntur? Fuit ergo hic non leuis stimulus, quem licet in præsenti non admodum senserint discipuli, satis tamen constat illos huius postea probè memores fuisse, quando neq; Sacerdotum & Seniorum minis, neq; Imperatorum edictis, neq; diris inauditorum supplicio rum tormentis adduci potuerunt, ut ea silentio sepelirent, quæ Christus prædicare iusserat. Et huius similiter meminisse debet, qui hodie in Ecclesia ministerio versantur. Reliqui verò cogitent: Euangelij doctrinam nō inanem aut vulgarem prædicationem, sed testimonium esse de Iesu Christo, quod sanctissimi homines non ex suo capite, sed ex Filij Dei mandato depositerunt, & sanguine proprio confirmarunt. Non potest ergo non immanissimum scelus esse, si quis illud negare, aut ei contradicere audeat. Is enim, ut alibi Ioannis apostoli verbis docuimus, Deum ipsum mendacij arguit, quod inultum non feret.
units.tr: First, he defines their duty in a way quite different from what they themselves imagined. For they (as we have often said) had conceived hopes of an earthly kingdom, in which they promised themselves triumphs and dignities. But what does Christ say? "You," he says, "are witnesses of my death and resurrection, and you will testify to the whole world that all those things which were foretold long ago by Moses and the Prophets have found their fulfilment in me." He says this now, as he is about to depart, and afterwards, when he is about to go up into heaven, he repeats the same thing. In a single word, he wished both to remind them of their office and to rouse them to prepare themselves for it. For witnesses are summoned in disputed causes, so that through them the truth of the matter may be known. It is therefore their part to say nothing other than what they have truly learned, and to be brave and steadfast in proclaiming it, and to yield nothing to their feelings; but they must remember that a false witness is hateful to God, who commanded that such persons be punished with the penalty of retaliation. How much graver, then, will the crime be when someone bears false witness in the cause of God, and that too at the cost of many souls who are led astray by lying teaching? So this was no slight spur, which, although the disciples did not feel it very much at the time, it is nevertheless clear that they afterwards remembered well, when neither the threats of the priests and elders, nor the edicts of emperors, nor the torments of unheard-of punishments could move them to bury in silence what Christ had commanded them to preach. Likewise, those who today serve the ministry in the Church ought to remember this. As for the rest, let them consider that the doctrine of the Gospel is not an empty or common preaching, but a testimony concerning Jesus Christ, which the most holy men set forth not on their own authority but on the command of the Son of God, and confirmed with their own blood. Therefore it cannot but be the most monstrous crime if anyone dares to deny it or to contradict it. For such a one, as we have shown elsewhere from the words of the apostle John, makes God himself a liar, and this will not go unpunished.

units.la: Deinde quia munus hoc non laboris modò, sed periculi quoque plenum fore sciebat, ne in primo statim conatu succumberent, promissionem consolationis plenam adhibet, qua simul docet, quibus armis quibusue auxilijs rem hanc omnem confici oporteat. Dicit enim: Et ecce ego mittam promissum Patris mei super vos. Id verò de Spiritu sancto dicit, quem aliàs quoque illis promiserat aduocatum & consolatorem. Eum autem Patris promissum vocat, quia illum Deus olim per Prophetas pollicitus fuit. Etenim ut alia testimonia prætereamus, sufficere hic potest, quod Petrus post{ acceptum Spiritum ex Ioele postea citauit, vt eorum calumniam dilueret, qui Apostolos mu-sto ebrios esse dicebat. Est{ autem diuinitatis verae argumentum, quòd sibi potestatem mittendi Spi-ritus sancti Christus tribuit: Satis enim constat, hunc in nullius alterius quàm Dei potestate esse. Adhæc, dum illum discipulis pollicetur, euidenter suæ illos imbecillitatis admonet, vt intelligant, se ad munus hoc tam arduum nunquam idoneos fore, nec quicquam in illo cum laude effecturos, nisi cœlitus adiuuentur. Quid enim in aliis erudiendis proficiat, qui ex semetipso (vt Paulus ait) ne ad co-gitandum quidem idoneus est{? Non autem ideo discipulos perterrefacere, sed potius modestiæ admonere & simul consolari voluit. Ostendit enim totam hanc causam Dei esse, qui suo Spiritu ipsis adfuturus sit, vt quod in mandatis dedit, feliciter exequantur. Et debet hinc generalis doctrina pe-ti, Regnum Christi non carnalibus, sed spiritualibus armis propagari, inter quæ primas tenet Euan-gelij prædicatio, quam Spiritus sanctus moderatur, & in auditorum animis efficacem reddit. Facit ad huius loci expositionem quod Apostolus in posteriori ad Corinth. 10. Cap. de Apostolicæ mili-tiæ armis eleganter & graviter tradit. Nobis autem istius considerationis hic visus esse debet, ne aut nostræ prudentiæ rationibus, aut seditiosorū consilijs atq; armis confisi temere tumultuemur, & sub religionis prætextu bella moueamus non necessaria. Nam vt constat Ecclesiam sæpe legitimis Re-gum armis feliciter defensam esse: ita extraordinariæ illæ defensiones, quas absq; certa & manifesta Dei vocatione, interdum zelo præcipiti homines etiam non mali suscipiunt, fere eum finem forti-untur, quem pugna Petri ad montem oliueti habuit: & vtinam nostro seculo non tristiora & infeli-ciora exempla vidissemus.
units.tr: Next, because this duty would be full not only of labour but also of danger, lest they give way at the very first attempt, he offers a promise full of consolation, by which he also teaches with what arms and what aids this whole task must be carried out. For he says: "And behold, I will send the promise of my Father upon you." He speaks here of the Holy Spirit, whom he had also promised them on other occasions as advocate and comforter. He calls him the promise of the Father because God had promised him long before through the Prophets. For, to pass over other testimonies, it is enough here that Peter afterwards quoted from Joel, after receiving the Spirit, in order to refute the calumny of those who said that the apostles were drunk with new wine. Moreover, it is a proof of true divinity that Christ ascribes to himself the power of sending the Holy Spirit; for it is clear enough that this lies in the power of none other than God. Besides, in promising the Spirit to the disciples, he plainly reminds them of their own weakness, so that they may understand that they will never be fit for this so arduous a task, nor accomplish anything in it with praise, unless they are helped from heaven. For what good would it do someone to instruct others, if he is not even fit, of himself (as Paul says), to think anything? Yet he wished to humble the disciples not in order to terrify them, but rather to admonish them to modesty and at the same time to comfort them. For he shows that this whole cause is God's, who will be present to them by his Spirit, so that they may happily carry out what he has commanded them. And from this a general doctrine ought to be drawn: that the kingdom of Christ is propagated not by carnal but by spiritual arms, among which the first place is held by the preaching of the Gospel, which the Holy Spirit governs and makes effective in the minds of the hearers. What the apostle delivers elegantly and weightily in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 10, concerning the arms of apostolic warfare, bears on the interpretation of this passage. For us, moreover, this consideration ought to be before our eyes, so that we do not rashly stir up tumults, trusting either in our own prudence or in the counsels and arms of seditious men, and under the pretext of religion wage wars that are not necessary. For, as is well known, the Church has often been happily defended by the lawful arms of kings; but those extraordinary defences, which men, even well-meaning ones, sometimes undertake out of rash zeal and without a certain and manifest calling from God, generally achieve the same end as Peter's fight at the Mount of Olives. And would that in our age we had not seen sadder and more unhappy examples of this.

units.la: HOMILIA CCXV.
units.tr: HOMILY CCXV.

units.la: Eduxít autem eos foras Bethaniam vsq; : & sublatis manibus suis be-nedixit eis: Et factum est dum ipse benediceret eis, disiunctus est ab eis, & sursum ferebatur in cœlum. Ipsi autem adorato eo reuersi sunt Hie-rosolymam cum gaudio magno. Erantq; semper in templo laudantes & benedicentes Deum. Amen
units.tr: And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he was parted from them and carried up into heaven. And they worshipped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy. And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

units.la: Quamuis Dei Filius, Iesus Christus, mortis suæ merito peccatum totius mundi expiauerit, resurrectione autem sua mortem quoq; vicerit, nondum tamen perfecta fuit & omnibus numeris absoluta humani generis redemptio atq; salus, sed vt cœli quoq; aperirentur necesse erat, quos primi parentis lapsus nobis clauserat, & nostræ etiam carni in illis locus pararetur: deniq; illic nobis opus erat aduocato, qui causam nostram apud Patrem ageret. Oportuit ergo morti & resurrectioni illius Ascensionem accedere, qua quod reliquum erat abunde præstitit. Et hæc causa est, quòd Euangelistæ non modò priora illa, verumetiam Ascensionem eius diligenter describunt: Paulus item præcipua fidei nostræ & humanæ salutis capita in piorum consolationem paucis compleƈti volens dicit: Christus est, qui mortuus est: imò vero qui etiam excitatus est: qui etiam est ad dextram Dei: qui item postulat aut intercedit pro nobis. Debet ergo Ascensionis historia non minori studio quàm priora illa considerari, quod vt maiori cum fructu fiat, primò ipsam Ascensionem cum suis circunstantijs: deinde eiusdem fructum atq; vsum inspiciemus: postremò quid hac visa fecerint discipuli.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, Jesus Christ, by the merit of his death made atonement for the sin of the whole world, and by his resurrection also overcame death, nevertheless the redemption and salvation of the human race was not yet complete and perfect in every respect. The heavens, which the fall of our first parent had closed against us, had also to be opened, and a place had to be prepared for our flesh in them. Finally, we needed an advocate there who would plead our cause before the Father. It was therefore fitting that his Ascension should follow his death and resurrection, and it completed what remained, abundantly. This is why the Evangelists describe his Ascension carefully, and not only the earlier events. Paul likewise, wishing to comfort the godly by briefly summing up the chief points of our faith and of human salvation, says: "Christ is he who died, yes rather, who was also raised; who is also at the right hand of God; who also makes intercession for us." The history of the Ascension must therefore be considered with no less zeal than those earlier events. So that we may do this with greater profit, we shall look first at the Ascension itself with its circumstances, then at its fruit and use, and lastly at what the disciples did after seeing it.

units.la: Quoad primum, illud tenendum est, huius loci historiam non ita cum ijs, quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, conƈti, quasi nihil intercesserit. Nam quæcunq; audiuimus, ipso resurrectionis die sunt facta. Ab eo autem tempore discipuli ex Christi mandato in Galilæam profeƈti sunt, vbi per totos ferè dies quadraginta cum illis ipse versatus est, & (vt in principio Actorum Lucas testatur) de Regno Dei apud eos multis disseruit, & suam resurrectionem nouis indies argumentis confirmauit, quorum alia apud Ioan. vlt. Cap. describuntur. Illuc etiam referri debet celebris illa actio, cuius Matthæus sub finem operis sui Euangelici meminit. Tandem cùm iam tempus illud præsinitum instaret, discipulos simul omnes Hierosolymam conuocauit, & postquam illic quoq; omnia ea diligenter tradidit, quæ ad Regni sui administrationem & munus ipsorum eis cognitu necessaria erant, eosdem Bethaniam vsq; eduxit, & ipsis videntibus ex monte Oliuarum in cœlum subuectus est.
units.tr: As to the first point, we must hold that this passage is not so joined to what has been said so far, as if nothing had come between. For all that we have heard took place on the very day of the resurrection. But from that time, at Christ's command, the disciples set out for Galilee, where he stayed with them for almost forty days. As Luke testifies at the beginning of the Acts, he spoke with them about the kingdom of God at length, and confirmed his resurrection day by day with new proofs, some of which are described in John, last chapter. To this period also should be referred that well-known action which Matthew mentions near the end of his Gospel. At last, when the appointed time was at hand, he gathered all the disciples together in Jerusalem, and after he had also there carefully taught them everything that was necessary for them to know about the administration of his kingdom and their own office, he led them out as far as Bethany, and, while they watched, he was carried up into heaven from the Mount of Olives.

units.la: Quod ergo in huius historiæ consideratione primum occurrit, est locus, ex quo Dominus ascen-dit. Fuit is Bethania, quam vrbi vicinam & ad Oliuarum montem sitam fuisse satis notum est. Quoad hunc verò, hoc in primis obseruari debet, quod Cap.19. audiuimus, illum ex eo loco Hieroso-lymam contendisse, quando in ara Crucis pro mundi peccatis mori debebat. Vnus ergo idemq; locus est, ex quo infamem & diram mortem adire, & postea in cœlestem gloriam & Regni sui hæreditatem ascendere voluit. Non est hoc temere factum ab eo, qui æterna est Patris sapientia. Suaenim exemplo nos admonere voluit, nobis quoq; aditum in cœlos per Crucem patere, secundum illud Pauli: Per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi in Regnum Dei. Et huc ipsum quoque nomen Bethaniæ pertinet, quo domum afflictionis denotari alibi diximus. Docet autem nos huius loci consideratio, ne in Christo huius seculi opes, honores, victorias, multò minus autem voluptates quæramus. Nihil enim huius ille promisit, qui ex pauperculâ Virgine in stabulo natus, in obscuro & infami Galilææ oppidulo educatus, postea per omne vitæ tempus egestatem & omnis generis aduersa pertulit. Consolationè verò ex eo petere debemus, quòd ex eodem loco & Cruci obuiam prodire, & in cœlum subuehi debuit. Quæ enim nobis quoq; in hisce terris agentibus Bethania est, eadem æternæ salutis adiumentum erit, si in fide constantes fuerimus. Quoties ergo vel letto affixus decumbis, vel exul incertis sedibus oberras, vel infamia notatus ab omnibus contemneris, aut quocunq; aduerso-su excruciaris, hanc tuam Bethaniam esse memento, cui vicinus sit verus ille mons Oliuarum, Iesus Christus, in quo pacem habemus cum Deo & qui nobis cælos ea conditione aperuit, vt per huius secu-li aduersa & labores ad illorum possessionem penetremus.
units.tr: What first meets us in considering this history is the place from which the Lord ascended. It was Bethany, which is well known to have lain near the city and close to the Mount of Olives. As for the place itself, this above all must be noted: as we heard in chapter 19, he set out from that place for Jerusalem, when he was to die on the altar of the cross for the sins of the world. So it was one and the same place from which he chose first to undergo an infamous and cruel death, and afterwards to ascend to heavenly glory and to his inheritance as King. This was not done by chance by him who is the eternal wisdom of the Father. For by his example he wished to remind us that the way into heaven is also open to us through the cross, according to Paul's words: "We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations." The very name Bethany also points to this, for elsewhere we have said that it signifies the house of affliction. Moreover, the consideration of this place teaches us not to seek in Christ the riches, honours and victories of this world, much less its pleasures. For he promised none of these things, he who was born in a stable of a poor virgin, was brought up in the obscure and disreputable little town of Galilee, and afterwards throughout his life endured poverty and every kind of adversity. But we ought to draw comfort from this: that from the same place he was to go out to meet the cross and be carried up into heaven. For that Bethany which we have here while we live on earth will also be a help to eternal salvation, if we remain steadfast in faith. Whenever, therefore, you lie fixed to a bed of sickness, or wander an exile without a settled home, or are held in disgrace and despised by all, or are tormented by any other adversity, remember that this is your Bethany, next to which lies that true Mount of Olives, Jesus Christ, in whom we have peace with God, and who has opened the heavens to us on this condition: that we should reach their possession through the adversities and labours of this world.

units.la: Proximum est, vt quid postremum in terris Christus fecerit videamus, postquam in eum locum peruenit, vnde in coelos abiturus erat. Et huc pertinet quod in Actis habetur, illum adinep-tam discipulorum de regni Israelitici restitutione quaestionem admodum grauiter respondisse, & sui eos admonuisse officij, quod in suo Regno ipsi obire debebant. Post haec sublatis manibus bene dixit eis. Est autem benedicendi mos vetus, & iam olim apud patres in vsu fuit, vt vel senio confecti, vel morti vicini filijs suis solenni aliqua benedictione fausta precarentur, & prophetico spiritu eosdem de futuris, quae ipsos scire intererat, admonerent. Sic Isaacus iam senex & sensuum vigore destitutus Esauo, quem primogeniti loco habebat, benedicere voluit priusquam moreretur: quando Rebecca pio & sancto dolo benedictionem in Iacobum natu minorem transfulit, cui illam ex Dei decreto deberi sciebat: & hic patris exemplum imitatus, cum mortis horam appropinquare sentiret, filijs suis omnibus singulari cum gravitate benedixit, singulis ex ordine sua quasi fata commemorans. Postea autem benedicendi munus in Lege Deus Sacerdotibus commendauit, & formam certam verborum praescripsit, quae in dimittendis coetibus sacris vterentur, quae apud Mosem talis habetur: Benedicat tibi Dominus & custodiat te, illustret Dominus faciem suam super te, & misereatur tui. Attolat Dominus faciem suam super te, & det tibi pacem. Ne quis tamen benedicendi potestatem penes Sacerdotes ita esse putaret, quasi ex illis penderet populi totius incolumitas (quod hodie de Pontificibus superstitiose creditur) addit ibidem Dominus: Ponent nomen meum super filios Israel, & ego benedicam eis. Benedictionis ergo author verus Deus est, Sacerdotibus vero ministerium solum commissum erat, & hi benedicebant populo, quia Christi personam sustinebant, qui reuera semen illud promissum est, in quo omnes gentes benedicuntur, sicuti Abrahamo & reliquis patribus olim Deus pollicitus fuit. Itaque quod Sacerdotes nudis verbis precabantur, id Christus re-ipsa confert. Nam abolita per suae mortis meritum maledictione, quae miseros mortales premebat, peccata simul sustulit, Legis syngraphã deleuit, nobis vero iustitiam sempiternam (vt Daniel praedixerat) reduxit & cum Patre reconciliatos salutis atq; beatitudinis aeternae haeredes fecit: idê Spiritum adoptionis cordibus nostris inserit, in quo clamamus, Abba pater: deniq; tam nobis quàm ijs quae hic agentibus accidunt, ita benedixit, vt ipsi per fidem infitis, & Deu vere diligentibus omnia adiumento sint in bonum. Quae omnia Paulus vno verbo complectens, Deum nobis in Christo benedixisse scribit omni benedictione spirituali. At hic in primis obseruatu dignum est, quod solennem hunc benedicendi actum in postremum vsq; discessum distulit: & quemadmodum boni hospites amicis hospitibus valedicentes, ijsdem ξενια, id est, dona hospitalitatis largiuntur, vt his suam apud illos memoriam sanciant, & perpetua amicitiae symbola post se relinquant: ita Christus ex mundo hoc discessurus, suis benedictione reliquit, vt testaretur salutem plenam nobis partam esse, nos item ab omni maledictione liberatos & Patri reconciliatos esse, se deniq; certa gratiae Dei nunquâ inter moriturae symbola apud nos deponere, ne de illius erga nos voluntate porro dubitemus. Cotinet ergo hic proströmus eius actus multiplicem consolationem, qua nos in omni tentationis genere confirmemus. Maledictionis in Lege pronunciatae sententiâ obijcit Satan, vt salutis incertos reddat: sed tunc in mentem veniat, nos Christum habere, qui illam aboleuit, & in quo omnes gentes benedicuntur. Stringit in nos excommunicationis fulmen Antichristus, & vt vita hac indignis aqua & igni interdicit. Rursus ergo meminerimus, Christum esse qui in se credentibus benedixit, & eius benedictionem perpetuò ratâ fore, cùm ipsi omnis potestas data sit in coelo & in terra. Ideo Dauid olim dicebat: Domini est salus, super populum tuû benedictio tua. Item: Ipsi quidem maledicent, tu autem benedices. Nouerat enim Daud Abrahamo olim dictum fuisse: Benedicam illis, qui tibi benedicunt: maledicentibus vero tibi maledicâ & ego. Quò referri debet Balaami exemplum, in cuius ore maledictionem Deus in benedictionem commutauit, cùm Israelitas ille diris deuouere instituisset. Similiter quando periculis vndiq; circundati & omni humano praesidio destituti sumus, tunc cogitemus, Dei Filium sublatis in altum manibus benedixisse suis, cùm hinc discederet. Sumus ergo sub Dei Patris tutela, quae sola aduersus totius mundi furores potest sufficere. Nam si Deus nobiscum (dicebat olim Apostolus) quis contra nos?
units.tr: Next, let us see what Christ did last on earth, after he came to the place from which he was about to depart into the heavens. To this belongs what is recorded in the Acts: that he answered very gravely the disciples' untimely question about the restoration of the kingdom of Israel, and reminded them of the office they were to discharge in his kingdom. After these things, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. Now the custom of blessing is old, and it was already in use among the Fathers long ago, that those worn out with age, or near death, would pray a solemn and favourable blessing over their sons, and by the spirit of prophecy would tell them of the future things it was their concern to know. So Isaac, already old and deprived of the vigour of his senses, wished to bless Esau, whom he regarded as his firstborn, before he died; but Rebecca, by a pious and holy deceit, transferred the blessing to Jacob, the younger, to whom she knew it was owed by God's decree. And Jacob, imitating his father's example, when he felt that the hour of death was drawing near, blessed all his sons with singular solemnity, recalling for each in turn, as it were, his destiny. Afterwards, however, God committed the office of blessing to the priests in the Law, and prescribed a fixed form of words to be used in dismissing the sacred assemblies. It appears in Moses thus: The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you, and be gracious to you. The Lord lift up his face upon you, and give you peace. Lest anyone think, however, that the power of blessing lay with the priests, as though the welfare of the whole people depended on them (which is superstitiously believed today of the Pontiffs), the Lord adds in the same place: "They shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them." The author of the blessing is therefore the true God. The priests had only the ministry committed to them, and they blessed the people because they bore the person of Christ, who is truly that promised Seed in whom all nations are blessed, as God long ago promised to Abraham and the other fathers. Therefore what the priests prayed for in bare words, Christ bestows in reality. For, by the merit of his death, he abolished the curse which weighed upon wretched mortals, and at the same time took away sins, blotted out the handwriting of the Law, and restored to us everlasting righteousness (as Daniel had foretold), and, reconciling us to the Father, made us heirs of salvation and eternal blessedness. Moreover, he places the Spirit of adoption in our hearts, by whom we cry, "Abba, Father." Finally, he so blessed us, and also the things that happen to us while we are here, that to those who are engrafted in him by faith and truly love God, all things work together for good. Paul sums up all these things in one word when he writes that God has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing. But here it is first of all worth noting that he deferred this solemn act of blessing until his final departure. And just as good hosts, bidding farewell to friendly guests, give them gifts of hospitality [ξενια], that they may thereby confirm their memory of them and leave behind lasting tokens of friendship, so Christ, about to depart from this world, left his blessing to his own, to testify that full salvation has been won for us, that we too have been freed from every curse and reconciled to the Father, and finally that he never lays down among us, as a pledge of the one who is departing, the sure grace of God, so that we should doubt no longer about his will toward us. Therefore this last act of his contains manifold comfort, by which we may be strengthened against every kind of temptation. Satan throws in our face the sentence of the curse pronounced in the Law, so as to make us uncertain of our salvation; but then let it come to mind that we have Christ, who abolished it, and in whom all nations are blessed. Antichrist hurls the thunderbolt of excommunication against us, and, as if we were unworthy of this life, forbids us water and fire. Let us therefore remember again that it is Christ who blessed those who believe in him, and that his blessing will remain firm forever, since all power has been given to him in heaven and on earth. So David once said: "Your salvation is of the Lord; your blessing is upon your people." Also: "They indeed will curse, but you will bless." For David knew that it had once been said to Abraham: "I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you." To this belongs the example of Balaam, in whose mouth God turned a curse into a blessing, when he had set out to devote the Israelites to destruction. Likewise, when we are surrounded by dangers on every side and deprived of all human help, let us then think that the Son of God, lifting up his hands on high, blessed his own as he went away from here. We are therefore under the protection of God the Father, which alone is able to suffice against the fury of the whole world. For "if God is with us," said the Apostle once, "who can be against us?"

units.la: Sequitur ipsa Ascensio, quam his verbis Lucas describit. Et factum est dum ipse benediceret eis, disiunctus est ab eis, & sursum ferebatur in coelum. Plura postea in Actorum libro dicuntur, vbi nubis quoq; meminit, quæ ipsum vehiculi instar in cælum subduxerit: Ibidem Angelos producit, qui discipulos rei nouitate attonitos & in altum suspicientes allocuti sunt, & præclarum tam de illius Ascensione quàm reditu, qui sub finem seculorum futurus esset, testimonium tulerunt. Quæ omnia si in vnum conferantur, euidentissime docent, illum ipsum Iesum, qui ex Maria Virgine homo natus est, qui in cruce mortuus tertio à morte die resurrexit, & de quo hucusque sermo fuit, ex hisce terris in cœlestes sedes commigrauisse, quòs se iturum esse, non semel antea prædixerat. Scio nonnullos nescio quam œconomiam & dispensationem fingere secundum quam ista dicantur, & idem nos de Christo nimis humiliter sentire clamant, quando eum à resurrectione verum corpus & eiusdem propria reti nuisse dicimus, adhæc Ascensionem eiusmodi ei tribuimus, quæ motu ex loco in locum facta sit, et quæ corporis ipsius omnipræsentiam tollat. At videant illi, ne dum ipsi noua gloria eum ornare student, Christum nobis fingant, qualem neq; Scriptura vsquam tradit, nec quisquam sanctorum agnouit. Nec periculum est, ne humilius quàm par sit de illo loquamur, si verbis ex ipsius ore petitis cum Apostolis & Angelis dicamus, illum non amplius esse in mundo, ex mundo hoc abijsse, à discipulis disiunctum & sublatum esse, nunc in cælis considere, & quidem eo in loco, quò nos quoq; venturos esse speramus: adhæc ne in cœlis quidem corpus semel assumptum depositisse, sed salua eius substantia illud gloriæ cœlestis capax fecisse. Quid enim horum à nobis excogitatum dici potest? Nonne ipse dicit: Relin quo mundum, eo ad Patrem, expedit vobis vt abeam? Annon Lucas scribit, quòd à discipulis disiu ctus abierit, & quòd à nube subuectus sit? Annon Marcus eum sursum assumptu esse ait in cælum? Annon Paulus illi in cœlis agenti corpus tribuit, cui nostra corpora conformia fieri oporteat? Imò annon in nubibus cœli venturum, & nos in eius occursum per aerem rapiendos fore docet? Atqui omnia ista motum ex loco in locu exprimunt: quæ si altiuolantibus illis Christo philosophis eius maie state indigna videntur, non nobis, sed ipsi & Spiritui sancto litem moueant. Nos enim aliter loqui nefas est, quàm in eius schola edocti sumus. At possent nos ita loquentes illi fortassis ferre, nisi per Ascensionis articulum præsentiam corporis Christi in Cœna à nobis oppugnari, & hunc arietem vehementiorem esse sentirent, quàm qui ab ipsis eludi aut auerti possit. Sed vt id faciamus illius exemplo iubemur, qui apud Ioan. Capernaitas corporalem suæ carnis manducatione somniantes ad Ascensionem remisit, vt offenderet tunc perspicue satis intelleeturos esse, quàm absurdum hoc ipsorum commentum sit, quando ipsum videant carnem illam in cælum euehere, cuius esum corporalem ipsi nunc imaginantur. Confugiunt illi ad nescio quam carnem Christi, quæ propter personalem vnionem diuinitatis propria receperit. At nos sacrarum literarum testimonijs edocti cum Theodoreto dicimus: Vnio non confundit naturas. Et eiusdem patris verbis illos interrogamus: Si caro mutata est in naturam diuinitatis, cur ijs communicant, quæ corpus repræsentant? Est enim figura superuacanea, si ablata sit veritas, &c. Quod de Cœnae sacrae symbolis ab eo dici, ex alijs locis abunde constat. Nec est quod nouos cœlos Dædali illi nobis fabricent, quos cum neq; locum certum esse, neque in se locum aliquem continere clament, verius Vtopiam quàm Cœlum dixeris. Ignorat enim cœlos illos Scriptura, sufficit autem Christianis hominibus cœlum illud, in quo sibi à Christo locos siue mansiones certas iam paratas esse sciunt, & ex quo idem ille nouissimo die veniet ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Ista sic in Scripturis traduntur, ijsdem fidei Christianæ articuli consentiunt, et ita omnis vetustas credidit. Posteris demum temporibus nouus ille Deus Mayzim, quem Antichristo tribuit Daniel, nouo cœlo opus habuit, quòd ijdem illi primum fabricare conati sunt, qui illum infelici mun do peperenerunt. Poterant hæc prolixè tractari, sed quia de tota hac causa in Actorum Apostolicorum & Marci explicatione dictum est, satis sit nunc ista paucis perstrinxisse.
units.tr: The Ascension itself follows, which Luke describes in these words: "And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and was carried up into heaven." More is said afterwards in the book of Acts, where he also mentions a cloud, which took him up into heaven as if it were a chariot. There he introduces angels, who addressed the disciples, astonished at the novelty of the event and gazing upward, and who gave a notable testimony both to his Ascension and to his return, which is to take place at the end of the age. If all these things are brought together, they most clearly teach that this same Jesus, who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, who died on the cross and rose on the third day after death, and of whom we have spoken until now, departed from these earthly regions into the heavenly seats, to which he had foretold more than once that he would go. I know that some invent I know not what "economy" and dispensation by which these things are said, and they cry out that we think too lowly of Christ when we say that after the resurrection he kept a true body of the same nature, and when we ascribe to him an Ascension of such a kind as is made by motion from place to place, and which would take away the omnipresence of his body. But let them see to it that, while they strive to adorn him with a new glory, they do not fashion for us a Christ such as Scripture nowhere hands down and no saint has known. Nor is there any danger that we speak of him too humbly if, in words taken from his own mouth, we say with the Apostles and Angels that he is no longer in the world, that he has departed from this world, has been separated and taken up from the disciples, now sits in the heavens, and indeed in that place to which we too hope to come; and that even in heaven he has not laid aside the body once assumed, but, its substance preserved, has made it capable of heavenly glory. For what of these things can be devised by us and spoken? Does he not himself say: "I leave the world and go to the Father; is it not expedient for you that I go away?" Does not Luke write that he departed, separated from the disciples, and that he was carried up by a cloud? Does not Mark say that he was taken up into heaven? Does not Paul ascribe a body to him, who is at work in the heavens, to which our bodies must be made conformable? Indeed, does he not teach that he will come in the clouds of heaven, and that we shall be caught up through the air to meet him? Yet all these express motion from place to place. If these seem unworthy of his majesty to those philosophers who soar so high, let them direct their quarrel not against us but against him and the Holy Spirit. For it is not right for us to speak otherwise than we have been taught in his school. But perhaps they could bear us speaking thus, were it not that they sense that the presence of Christ's body in the Supper is being assailed by us through the article of the Ascension, and that this is a battering-ram too strong to be mocked or turned aside by them. But in doing so we are commanded by his example, who, when the Capernaites dreamed of a corporal eating of his flesh, referred them to the Ascension, so that they would then clearly enough understand how absurd their invention is, when they see that flesh carried up into heaven whose corporal eating they now imagine. They take refuge in I know not what flesh of Christ which, on account of the personal union with the divinity, has received the properties of the divinity. But we, taught by the testimonies of the Sacred Letters, say with Theodoret: "The union does not confound the natures." And in that father's words we ask them: "If the flesh has been changed into the nature of the divinity, why do they share in those things which represent the body? For a figure is superfluous if the truth has been taken away," and so on. That he says this of the symbols of the Holy Supper is abundantly clear from other passages. Nor is there any need for them to fabricate for us those new heavens of Daedalus, which, since they claim there is no fixed place and that they contain no place within themselves, you would more truly call Utopia than heaven. For Scripture does not know those heavens; but that heaven suffices for Christian people, in which they know that places or mansions have already been prepared for them by Christ, and from which the same one will come on the last day to judge the living and the dead. These things are so handed down in the Scriptures, the articles of the Christian faith agree with them, and so all antiquity has believed. In later times that new god Mayzim, whom Daniel assigns to Antichrist, needed a new heaven, because the very men who brought him into this unhappy world first tried to fabricate it. These matters could be treated at length, but since this whole question has been discussed in the exposition of the Acts of the Apostles and of Mark, it is enough now to have touched on them briefly.

units.la: Debent autem Christiani homines, relictis curiosis & spinosis disputationibus, fructum & vsum Ascensionis dominicae potius considerare, qui nobis multiplex occurrit. Primò redemptionis & salutis nostræ certitudinem confirmat, & Christum reuera peccati, mortis, inferorum & ipsius diaboli victorem esse docet. Potest enim triumphus dici, quem de hostibus suis in discipulorum conspectu egit, ne quam in eorum animis trepidationem relinqueret. Solent enim huius seculi Reges de victis hostibus magnis & potentibus, qui toti regno formidabiles fuerunt, triumphantes in vrbem ingredi. Præferuntur signa militaria hostibus erepta cum alijs spolijs, ipsi curru magnifico sublimes vehuntur, at hostium duces mæsti ducuntur suam fortunam habitu & lachrymis testantes quæ omnia vt victoribus gloriosa sunt, ita populi totius læticiam augent, qui hostes omnino deuictos stos & captos cernens metu omni liberatur, & principum liberalitate fruitur, qui fere pecuniam in vulgus spargere consueuerunt. Tale quid in ascensionis historia Paulus cogitare docet, qui de Christo victore & Ecclesiae suae perpetuo gubernatore scribens, illud Psalmi adducit: Cum ascendisset in altum, captiuam duxit captiuitatem, & dedit dona hominibus. Et eodem referri potest, quod apud Matthaeum discipulis dixit: Data est mihi potestas omnis in coelo & in terra. Ut vero ista ad gloriam Christi illustrandam faciunt: ita in tentationibus, quibus suam contra nos saeuitiam diabolus ostentat, adhaec aduersus mortis & inferorum terrores fidem nostram plurimum confirmant. Cur enim vel diabolum timeamus, vel mortem formidemus, aut ad inferorum mentionem contremiscamus, quando illum deuictum esse, & tam de illo quam omni eius potentia Christum triumphauisse scimus? Quin tunc ad nos pertinere cogitemus, quod Stephano se tunc ille videndum exhibuit ad dextram Dei stans, quando is ab iniquis iudicibus iamiam ad diram necem rapi debebat. Quam enim ille tunc sensit consolationem, eam omnes sentiunt, qui ipsum fide vera & constanti amplectuntur.
units.tr: Christian people, however, setting aside curious and thorny disputations, ought rather to consider the fruit and use of the Lord's Ascension, which presents itself to us in many ways. First, it confirms the certainty of our redemption and salvation, and teaches that Christ is truly the conqueror of sin, of death, of the grave and of the devil himself. For it may be called a triumph which he celebrated over his enemies in the sight of the disciples, so that he would leave no trembling in their minds. For the kings of this age are accustomed to enter the city in triumph over great and powerful enemies, who were formidable to the whole kingdom. Military standards taken from the enemy are carried before them along with other spoils; they themselves are borne aloft in a magnificent chariot, while the leaders of the enemy are led along in sorrow, attesting their fortune by their dress and tears. All these things are as glorious to the victors as they increase the joy of the whole people, who, seeing the enemy utterly overcome, bound and captured, are freed from all fear and enjoy the generosity of the princes, who are wont to scatter money among the common folk. Paul teaches us to think something of this kind in the history of the Ascension, who, writing of Christ as victor and perpetual governor of his Church, adduces that verse of the Psalm: "When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." To the same purpose may be referred what he said to the disciples in Matthew: "All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth." And just as these things serve to illustrate the glory of Christ, so they greatly strengthen our faith against the temptations in which the devil displays his cruelty against us, and likewise against the terrors of death and the grave. For why should we fear the devil, or dread death, or tremble at the mention of the grave, since we know that he has been overcome, and that Christ has triumphed over him and over all his power? Indeed, let us think that this applies to us, that he appeared to Stephen then, standing at the right hand of God, when Stephen was about to be dragged by unjust judges to a dreadful death. For whatever consolation he then felt, all feel who embrace him with true and steadfast faith.

units.la: Secundò ad salutis nostrae complementum facit Ascensio ista. Nam vt initio monuimus, deuicta iam morte & expiato peccato, vnum hoc reliquum erat, vt coelorum fores denuo nobis patefierent. Scimus enim paradisi ostium, cum exillo Adamū Deus eiecisset, Cherubim adhibitis & gladio igneo atq; versatili obstructum fuisse, ne ad carpendū fructum arboris vitae illuc se homo inferret. Quo typo significabatur Dei ira aduersus peccatum fulminans, cuius tanta vis fuit, vt nemo hominum suis viribus illam vincere & amissam vitae coelestis possessionē denuo acquirere posset. Ea denique hominis miseria est, vt (quod Paulus testatur) caro & sanguis Regnum Dei possidere nequeant. Quod ipsum Christus docet, Nicodemo dicens: Nemo ascendit in coelum, nisi qui descendit e coelo, Filius hominis, qui est in coelo. Vt ergo nobis quoq; coeli reserarentur opus erat: Et hoc Christus praestitit, quando quam ex nobis assumpserat carnem propria virtute in coelos intulit, & ad dexteram Dei Patris collocauit. Cur enim posthac de Regni caelestis haereditate dubitemus, qui Christum dixisse scimus: Vado vobis paraturus locum; & cum abiero & parauero vobis locum, rursus veniam & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi sum ego & vos sitis? Facit certe ad huius promissionis confirmationem, quod qui a nobis acceptā carnem in coelos subuexit, nobis vicissim Spiritum e coelis demisit, qui salutis nostrae arrhabo sit, & simul nos sua virtute ex verbi semine in filios Dei regeneret. Quod veteres quoq; observauisse, ex Tertulliani verbis apparet, qui in libro de Resurrect. carnis sic scribit: Quemadmodum nobis arrhabonem Spiritus reliquit, ita & a nobis arrhabonē carnis accepit & vexit in coelum, pignus totius summae illuc quandoq; redigenda. Huius autem meminisse debent, qui corpore suo diutinos morborum cruciatus sustinent, aut quibus mors hoc potissimum nomine terribilis videtur, quod corpus in sepulchro vermium escam futurum & a putredine cōsumendum, vel etiam ignominiose ab hostibus tractandum fore cogitat. Quid enim refert, quid de corpore fiat iam omnibus sensibus orbato? Nam vt veteris Poetae verbis vtar, tabes ne cadauera soluat An rogus, haud refert: placido natura receptat Cuncta sinu, finemq; sui sibi corpora debent.
units.tr: Secondly, this Ascension contributes to the completion of our salvation. For, as we noted at the beginning, death having now been conquered and sin atoned for, there remained this one thing: that the gates of heaven should be opened again to us. For we know that when God drove Adam out of paradise, the door of paradise was blocked by the Cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way, so that man could not enter there to pluck the fruit of the tree of life. By this type was signified God's wrath fulminating against sin, whose force was so great that no man could by his own strength overcome it and recover the lost possession of heavenly life. Such is at last the misery of man that, as Paul testifies, flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God. Christ himself teaches this, saying to Nicodemus: "No man has ascended into heaven, but he that came down from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven." Therefore it was necessary that the heavens be unlocked for us also; and Christ accomplished this, when by his own power he carried into the heavens the flesh which he had taken from us, and placed it at the right hand of God the Father. For why should we henceforth doubt concerning the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, since we know Christ said: "I go to prepare a place for you; and when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and receive you unto myself, that where I am, there you may be also"? This certainly serves to confirm this promise: that he who carried the flesh received from us into the heavens has in turn sent down the Spirit from heaven, who is the pledge of our salvation, and at the same time regenerates us by his power from the seed of the Word into sons of God. That the ancients also observed this appears from the words of Tertullian, who in his book on the resurrection of the flesh writes thus: "As he left us the pledge of the Spirit, so he took from us the pledge of the flesh and carried it into heaven, a guarantee that the whole sum will one day be brought there." Those who endure long torments of disease in their body ought to remember this, or those to whom death seems terrible chiefly for this reason: that they think the body will be a meal for worms in the sepulchre and consumed by putrefaction, or even treated shamefully by enemies. For what does it matter what becomes of the body, now deprived of all sensation? For, to use the words of an old poet: "Whether decay dissolves the corpses or the pyre, it makes no difference; nature receives all things into her gentle bosom, and bodies owe their end to themselves."

units.la: Christianos autem homines consoletur, quod illud ipsum corpus, quod vel terrae mandatur, vel cum contumelia abijcitur, suo tempore non ex terra modo resurrecturum, sed in coelos quoq; ascensurum esse sciant, vbi immortalitate beata coronabitur. Quin ergo cum eodem Tertulliano dicimus: Securiestore caro & sanguis, vsurpastis & caelū & Regnum Dei in Christo.
units.tr: Christians, however, may be comforted by the knowledge that this same body, which is either committed to the earth or cast out with contempt, will rise again at its appointed time, not only out of the earth but also ascend into heaven, where it will be crowned with blessed immortality. So let us say with Tertullian: "Be secure, flesh and blood; you have seized both heaven and the kingdom of God in Christ."

units.la: Tertiò ad Sacerdotium quoq; illius Ascensio pertinebat, & ideo illum ascendere oportuit, vt nos in coelis aduocatum & intercessorem habere constaret. Olim quidem in Sanctum sanctorum semel duntaxat in anno summus Sacerdos ingrediebatur, nō sine sanguine, quem pro semetipso & populi ignorantijs offerebat. Qua ceremonia (vt Apostolus docet) significabat Spiritus sanctus, non dum patefactam esse viam sanctorum, priore tabernaculo adhuc consistente. Quod ergo illic figurabatur, id Christus reipsa praestitit, quando non cum pecuino, sed cum proprio sanguine, non in manu factum Sacrarium ingressus est, sed in ipsum coelum, vt appareat nūc in conspectu Dei pro nobis. Quō Ioannes respiciens, scribebat: Si quis peccauerit, aduocatū apud Patrem habemus, Iesum Christum iustum. Et Paulus (vt initio monuimus) cum sessionis Christi ad dextram Patris meminissety, mox subiecit: Qui & postulat siue intercedit pro nobis. Vides ergo illum Ascensione sua perfecisse, quae in Regis & Sacerdotis munere adhuc restabant, & proinde nimium imprudentes esse eos, qui illius historiam nouis figmentis obscurant.
units.tr: Thirdly, his ascension also pertained to his priesthood, and therefore he had to ascend, so that we might be assured that we have an advocate and intercessor in heaven. Formerly the high priest entered the Holy of Holies only once a year, and not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the ignorance of the people. By this ceremony (as the Apostle teaches) the Holy Spirit signified that the way of the saints was not yet opened while the earlier tabernacle still stood. What was foreshadowed there, Christ actually accomplished, when he entered not a sanctuary made with hands, nor one with the blood of animals, but with his own blood, entering heaven itself, so that he now appears before the face of God for us. Looking to this, John wrote: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." And Paul, after recalling (as we noted at the beginning) Christ's sitting at the right hand of the Father, immediately added: "who also makes intercession for us." You see, then, that by his ascension he completed what remained of his kingly and priestly office. Therefore those who obscure his history with new fictions are very foolish indeed.

units.la: Postremo magnus insuper Ascensionis vsus est ad vitam pie & Christianè transfigendam. Quia enim in caelis iam viuit & regnat Christus, qui caput nostrum est, illic nostra quoque ciuitas & patria sit oportet. Itaque nostrum fuerit, vt relictis huius seculi studijs, ad caelestia aspiremus, & vitam viuamus nouam, quae illius sanguine redemptos & ex eius verbo renatos deceat. Et cur adhuc terrenis immersi haereant, qui iam illius Spiritu animantur, cui cum mundo & carne nihil commune est? Aut cur huic seculo seruiant, qui in eum finem vocati sunt, vt olim in caelis aeterna gloria cum Christo Iesu fruantur? Ita nos argumentari docet Paulus, cuius haec verba ad Colossen. tertio cap. leguntur: Itaque si resurrexistis cum Christo, superna quaerite, vbi Christus est ad dextram Dei sedens. Superna curate, non terrestria. Nam mortui estis, & vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Quando Christus vita illa nostra, patefactus fuerit, tum & vos cum eo patefietis gloriosi.
units.tr: Finally, the ascension has a great further use in shaping a godly and Christian life. For since Christ, who is our head, now lives and reigns in heaven, our citizenship and our homeland must also be there. Therefore it is fitting for us to leave behind the pursuits of this age, aspire to heavenly things, and live a new life, such as befits those redeemed by his blood and born again by his word. And why should those who are already quickened by his Spirit, to whom nothing is in common with the world and the flesh, still cling to earthly things? Or why should those serve this age who have been called to that end, that one day in heaven they may enjoy eternal glory with Christ Jesus? Paul teaches us to reason in this way, and his words are read in Colossians chapter three: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things on the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory."

units.la: Caeterum ad huius doctrinae explicationem pertinet postrema huius loci pars, qua quid discipuli Christo in caelos subuecto fecerint, narratur. Proponitur enim in illis exemplum vitae Christianae, quod qui imitantur, ij non solum Ascensionem Christi, sed mortem quoq; & resurrectionem eius verè exprimunt, & pro germanis illius discipulis censeri debent. Sic autem scribit Lucas: Ipsi autem adorato eo reuersi sunt Hierosolymam cum gaudio magno. Erant semper in templo laudantes & benedicentes Deum. Quibus verbis quatuor dicuntur, quae nobis ex ordine consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the last part of this passage, which tells what the disciples did after Christ was carried up into heaven, belongs to the explanation of this doctrine. For in it an example of the Christian life is set before us; those who imitate it truly express not only Christ's ascension but also his death and resurrection, and ought to be counted as true disciples of his. Luke writes thus: "And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy. And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God." In these words four things are stated, which we must consider in order.

units.la: Primò adorauerunt Christum, vt quem pro Deo & Domino suo iam verè agnoscebant, cum eius diuinitatem post tot opera miraculosa nunc per resurrectionem ex mortuis & gloriosam ascensionem in caelos abunde demonstratam & confirmatam esse viderent. Thomas certè qui reliquis in fide infirmior fuit, cum illum reuera ex mortuis resurrexisse cerneret, clamabat: Dominus meus, & Deus meus. Quantum ergo ad eorum fidem momenti accessisse putas ex quadraginta dierum diligenti institutione, ex praesenti Ascensionis spectaculo, & Angelorum testimonio, qui eius reditum quoque ad iudicium pollicebantur? Est hoc primum fidei Christianae caput, adeoq; omnium, quae de ea dicuntur, fundamentum: vt Iesum hunc, qui ex Maria Virgine homo natus est, aeternum Dei Filium, Patri coessentialem & Deum verum esse credamus. Talem omnes Scripturae praedicant, quarum testimonia cum alibi non semel citauerimus, & illas legentibus nunquam non occurrant, non opus est modo repetere. Et vt ita credamus necesse est, quando quam in illo collocatam habemus, salutis fiduciam nobis constare non poterit, nisi pro Deo agnoscatur omnipotenti & aeterno, qui sibi ipsi sufficiat. Exorti sunt nostro seculo impij quidam haeresum veterum instauratores, qui illum quoad humanam modo naturam Mediatorem inter Deum & nos esse docuerunt: quia nimirum illis absurdum nimis videbatur Deum ad Mediatoris officium detrahere. At ijdem non viderunt, omnibus ijs quae Christus propter nos fecit & passus est, ex eo dignitatem & virtutem omnem accedere, quod qui illa fecit, non homo nudus, sed aeternus quoq; & dilectus ille Dei Filius est. Ideo Theodoretus ipso Intercessoris aut Mediatoris nomine diuinitatem simul & humanitatem comprehendi scribit. Nam quoniam (inquit) Patri vt Deus coniunctus est, vt qui eandem habeat substantiam: vt homo autem nobis (a nobis enim seruiformam accepit) merito intercessor dictus est, vnitate naturarum diuinitatis nimirum & humanitatis, ea quae sunt distantia & disiuncta coiungens, &c. Insistamus ergo nos quoq; Scripturae & venerandae veritatis vestigijs, & ita Iesum Christum in carne manifestatum & pro nobis occisum atq; resuscitatum esse credamus, vt de eiusdem diuinitate aeterna nihil dubitemus. Simul autem obseruemus hic diligenter, vt illum discipuli adorauerint. Num aram illic loci consecrant? num sacellum extruunt? num imaginibus pictis aut sculptis historiam Ascensionis representant? num postea illuc currunt religionis ergo vt ex loci sanctitate pondus aliquod precibus illorum accedat? Nihil huius vel hic vel alibi scribitur. Sed vt tunc res ferebat, simpliciter illum adorant, vt quem pro diuinitatis natura omnipraesentem esse credunt, qui iam illic quam alibi preces ipsorum exaudire posset. Et illud Christi sciebant, qui iam tempus illud venisse dixerat,
units.tr: First, they worshipped Christ, since they now truly acknowledged him as their God and Lord, when they saw that his divinity had been abundantly demonstrated and confirmed, after so many miraculous works, by his resurrection from the dead and his glorious ascent into heaven. Thomas, certainly, who was weaker in faith than the others, when he saw that he had truly risen from the dead, cried out: "My Lord and my God." How much, then, do you think was added to their faith by the careful instruction of forty days, by the present spectacle of the ascension, and by the testimony of the angels, who also promised his return for judgment? This is the first head of the Christian faith, and the foundation of all that is said about it: that we believe this Jesus, who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, to be the eternal Son of God, coessential with the Father, and true God. All the Scriptures proclaim him thus. Since we have already cited their testimonies more than once elsewhere, and since they never fail to meet those who read them, there is no need to repeat them now. And we must believe this, for the hope of salvation that we place in him cannot stand unless he is acknowledged as God, almighty and eternal, who is sufficient in himself. In our own age there have arisen some impious renewers of old heresies, who have taught that he is Mediator between God and us only according to his human nature, because it seemed to them too absurd to ascribe to God a part of the office of Mediator. But they did not see that all that Christ did and suffered for us receives its dignity and all its power from this: that the one who did these things is not a mere man, but the eternal and beloved Son of God. Therefore Theodoret writes that by the very name of Intercessor or Mediator both divinity and humanity are comprehended. "For," he says, "he is joined to the Father as God, since he has the same substance; but as man he is joined to us (for he took the form of a servant from us), and he is rightly called intercessor, by the unity of the natures, that is, of divinity and humanity, joining together things that are distant and separated," and so on. Let us therefore also follow the footsteps of Scripture and of venerable truth, and believe that Jesus Christ was manifested in the flesh, was slain for us and raised again, so that we may have no doubt about his eternal divinity. At the same time let us observe carefully here that the disciples worshipped him. Did they consecrate an altar in that place? Did they build a shrine? Did they represent the history of the ascension with painted or carved images? Did they afterwards run there out of religious devotion, so that some weight might be added to their prayers from the holiness of the place? Nothing of this is written either here or elsewhere. But as the situation then required, they simply worshipped him, believing him to be present everywhere by the nature of his divinity, and able to hear their prayers there as well as elsewhere. And they knew the saying of Christ, that the time had come in which God is to be worshipped everywhere, in spirit and in truth, without distinction of places.

units.la: Diul. 2. qui inscribitur Incon-fusus. dixerat, quo absq; locorū discrimine Deus passim in Spiritu & veritate adorari velit. Quod exemplum si posteri imitati fuissent, qui zelo quidem sancto, non autē secundum scientiam, loca vel Christi vel Martyrum exemplis celebria consecrarunt, minus superstitionum irrepsisset in Ecclesiam. Nihil certè huius vel ab Apostolis vel viris Apostolicis vnquam factum esse legimus. Confutantur igitur horū exemplo, qui religionem & preces certis locis astringunt, qui imagines in Christi & beneficiorum eius memoriam consecrant, qui ipsum & eius meritum hinc inde monstrant, & exijs rebus superstitionis materiam atq; occasiones vænantur, quibus in syncera fide debebat confirmari.
units.tr: (Theodoret, Dialogue 2, entitled Inconfusus.) This was the saying in which God wills to be worshipped in spirit and in truth everywhere, without distinction of places. If later generations had followed this example, those who with a holy zeal, but not according to knowledge, consecrated places celebrated for the deeds of Christ or of the martyrs, far less superstition would have crept into the Church. Certainly we read that nothing of this kind was ever done either by the Apostles or by men of apostolic times. Therefore by their example are refuted those who tie religion and prayers to certain places, who consecrate images in memory of Christ and his benefits, who display him and his merit here and there, and who from these things hunt out the material and occasions of superstition, when in pure faith these should rather have been confirmed.

units.la: Secundum est, quod Hierosolymam reuertuntur, sicuti ille mandauerat, & quidem cum gaudio. Cur enim non gauderent illius militiae adscripti tyrones, qui iam nunc tam praeclarum sui imperatoris triumphum viderant? Veruntamen multa illos mouere poterant, ne in vrbem redirent. Quis enim dubitet, incommodum valde fuisse hominibus peregrinis & pauperculis diutius moram trahere in vrbe populosa? Et vt tedium istud ferre potuerint, periculosum tamen erat inter eos versari, qui cum Christi & doctrinae eius odio flagrarent, ex eius morte animos maiores conceperant ad versus omnes eos, qui eius nomen profitebantur. Et vt ingeniosa est in metu dissimulando, & suis commodis quaerendis caro, religionem praetexere poterant, & eo praetextu in Galilaeam ad sua redire, ne Spiritum sanctum, qui vbi vult spirat, loco certo alligare viderentur. At nihil horum istos moNet, quo minus animo alacri & laeto Domini mandatis obtemperent. Est hoc proprium illis, qui Iesum Christum agnoscunt Deum esse, qui coli & adorari debeat. Vt enim seruus fidelis & bonus obedientia testatur, quanti herum suum faciat: ita pij non nudis verbis & ore solo Deum iactant, sed eundem omnibus vitae officijs colunt, ne ipsis dicatur, quod hypocritis olim dictum fuit. Si ego pater sum, vbi honor est meus? si vero dominus sum vester, vbi mei timor? Hic autem in primis opus est videre, ne carnem in consilium admittamus, quae Spiritui semper reluctatur, & dum suis desiderijs fertur, Deo inobedientes facit. Ideo Euangelicae praedicationis hunc finem esse Paulus docet, vt omnis intellectus atque sensus hominis per fidei obedientiam verbo Dei subijciatur: quod Abrahamum olim fecisse constat tunc quoque, quando ea iubebat Dominus, quae non dura modo, verumetiam iniqua & inhumana videri poterant. Parum ergo adhuc in fide Christi profecerunt, qui ne in ijs quidem ei obediunt, quae absque omni periculo fieri possunt, & ex quibus commodum multiplex ad nos redundat.
units.tr: Second, they returned to Jerusalem, as he had commanded, and indeed with joy. For why should those young soldiers, enrolled in his service, not rejoice, when they had already seen so glorious a triumph of their commander? Nevertheless, many things could have moved them not to return to the city. For who would doubt that it was very inconvenient for humble pilgrims to delay for long in a crowded city? And even if they could bear that tedium, it was nonetheless dangerous to mix with those who burned with hatred against Christ and his doctrine, and who after his death had conceived greater anger against all who professed his name. And since the flesh is clever at pretending fear and at seeking its own advantage, they could have used religion as a pretext, and under that pretext gone back to their homes in Galilee, so as not to seem to bind the Holy Spirit, who blows where he wills, to a fixed place. But none of these things restrained them from obeying the Lord's commands with a willing and joyful mind. This is characteristic of those who acknowledge Jesus Christ to be God, who ought to be worshipped and adored. For as a faithful and good servant shows by his obedience how highly he esteems his master, so the godly do not merely boast of God with bare words and with the mouth alone, but honour him in all the duties of life, lest it be said to them what was once said to the hypocrites: "If I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am your lord, where is my fear?" Here, above all, we must take care not to admit the flesh into our counsel, for it always resists the Spirit, and while it is carried along by its own desires, it makes us disobedient to God. Therefore Paul teaches that this is the aim of evangelical preaching: that every understanding and every sense of man should be made subject to the word of God through the obedience of faith. Abraham is known to have done this long ago, when the Lord commanded things that seemed not only hard but also unjust and inhuman. Those therefore have made little progress in the faith of Christ who do not obey him even in those things that can be done without any danger, and from which many advantages flow back to us.

units.la: Tertiò gaudent discipuli nunc, qui prius maerore & tristitia affecti fuerunt, quoties sui discessus mentionem Christus faciebat. Mirifica ergo haec fuit animorum conuersio, quae non aliunde enasci potuit quam ex Christi cognitione quae nunc illis plenior & solidior affulgere coepit, vt antea quodiximus. Etenim sola haec gaudium verum parit, & omnia ea amolitur, quae nos contristare solent: qualia sunt peccatorum conscientia, irae Dei sensus, mortis terrores & quaecunq; aliae calamitates nobis accidunt. Nam qui Christum vere agnoscunt, ij huius merito & virtute peccatum mundi omne expiatū, Patrem nobis placatum, mortem ex peccati poena infelicem ex huius seculi palaestra in vitam transitum commutatā, aduersa deniq; omnia per illius crucem consecrata esse intelligunt, vt laeta & salubria sint patientiae Christianae exercitia, quibus renumeratio amplissima in caelis ia praeparata sit. Hinc ergo gaudiū illud nascitur, quod in medijs etiam afflictionibus mentes piorum exhilarat, & quod Paulus inter Christianos perpetuum esse vult, quia vt ex causis pijs nascitur, ita finem quoq; habet beatissimum, neq; in luctum definit, quod fere impijs ob res huius seculi fluxas & inhonestas gaudentibus solet accidere.
units.tr: Thirdly, the disciples now rejoice, though before they were filled with grief and sadness whenever Christ spoke of his departure. This remarkable change of heart could have come from nothing else than the knowledge of Christ, which now began to shine on them more fully and more solidly, as we said before. Only this knowledge brings true joy and drives away everything that usually distresses us: the awareness of sin, the sense of God's wrath, the terrors of death, and whatever other calamities befall us. For those who truly recognize Christ understand that by his merit and power the sin of the world has been wholly expiated, the Father has been reconciled to us, death, the unhappy penalty of sin, has been changed into a passage from the arena of this age into life, and finally all adversities have been consecrated through his cross, so that the exercises of Christian patience are joyful and wholesome, and a most ample reward is prepared for them in heaven.
